Part C — Technology routes and physics

Part C moves from market analysis to physics. Parts A and B asked who sells which sensors, in which markets and in what volumes. Part C asks why the technology routes behind those sales succeeded or stalled, and where their physical limits lie. It begins with a physics primer (§C0) that collects the basic relations used throughout. It then covers the taxonomy and market share of lidar technologies and the companies behind them (§C1–§C3c), why 905/940 nm silicon receivers with one mechanical scan axis won (§C4–§C6), FMCW coherent lidar (§C7–§C7b), and chip-size limits, interference and optical phased arrays (§C8–§C10). The physics needs nothing from Parts A and B, while §C2–§C3c draw on the company and unit data of Part B; the conclusions feed the supply-chain, camera-only and projection Parts that follow (D, E and F).

How to read it: each section opens with a plain-language short answer, and display equations are numbered. Every symbol is defined where it is used, even when an earlier section has already defined it. The “How the numbers are derived” blocks can be skipped; the conclusions stand on their own.

C0. Physics primer: the basic relations used in this report

This primer collects the textbook relations behind the numbers in Part C, from time-of-flight (ToF) ranging and the beat frequencies of frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) lidar to detector noise, detection statistics, weather loss and the full link budget. Later sections apply them, some restating them in their own notation and numbering. The “Used in” column of the tables in subsections 1–3, and the § pointers in the text of subsections 4–9, show where. Each subsection gives the relation, typical automotive numbers and a worked substitution, then says what it means for the sensor. Numbers are illustrative engineering estimates [E] unless tagged otherwise. Throughout, c=3.0×108c=3.0\times10^8 m/s is the speed of light.

1. Pulsed direct time of flight (dToF)

A pulsed direct time-of-flight (dToF) lidar fires a short laser pulse and times its echo; range is half the round-trip delay times the speed of light. This subsection gives the timing relations (resolution, precision, ambiguity, point rate) and then the photon budget: how many signal photons a pulse returns from a distant target, and how range scales with pulse energy and lens size. Almost every range figure for a ToF lidar in this report rests on these two sets of relations.

Symbols in the table.

  • RR is the range to the target (m), and τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c the measured round-trip delay (s).
  • τp\tau_p is the laser pulse length (s), and Δtbin\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}} the width of one time bin of the receiver’s histogram (s).
  • σt\sigma_t is the rms timing spread of a single detected photon (s). It combines the pulse shape, the detector’s timing jitter and the step of the time-to-digital converter (TDC, the on-chip stopwatch that time-stamps each detection).
  • NsN_s is the number of detected signal photons averaged into one range estimate (one point), summed over all the pulses fired at that point.
  • ΔR\Delta R is the two-target range resolution (m), σR\sigma_R the rms error of one range estimate (m), and RambR_{\mathrm{amb}} the unambiguous range (m), with the same meaning in subsection 9. Elsewhere in the report RmaxR_{\max} means the maximum detection range.
  • PRF is the pulse repetition frequency (pulses per second); PRFch\text{PRF}_{\mathrm{ch}} is that of one channel.
  • NchN_{\mathrm{ch}} is the number of channels (laser–detector pairs) firing in parallel, and Ṅ\dot N the resulting point rate (points per second).
Quantity Relation Typical numbers Used in
Range from delay R=cτ/2R=c\,\tau/2 6.67 ns of round trip per metre; 1.33 µs to 200 m throughout
Two-target range resolution ΔR≈cτp/2\Delta R\approx c\,\tau_p/2 for pulse length τp\tau_p 5 ns → 0.75 m; 1 ns → 15 cm §C3b
Histogram quantization cΔtbin/2c\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}/2 297 ps bins (Adaps ADS6311 [P]) → 4.5 cm; 3 GHz equivalent-time sampling (Sony IMX479 [P]), i.e. 333 ps bins → 5.0 cm §C5a; the 297 ps example is from §C5
Single-target precision σR≈(c/2)σt/Ns\sigma_R\approx(c/2)\,\sigma_t/\sqrt{N_s}: timing spread σt\sigma_t (pulse, detector jitter, TDC) averaged over NsN_s detected signal photons σt=100\sigma_t=100 ps and Ns=20N_s=20 → ≈0.3 cm (ideal; amplitude walk and background add) subsection 9; measured precisions in §C5a
Unambiguous range per channel Ramb=c/(2PRFch)R_{\mathrm{amb}}=c/(2\,\text{PRF}_{\mathrm{ch}}) 750 kHz ↔︎ 200 m; 300 kHz ↔︎ 500 m §C4d
Point rate Ṅ=Nch×PRFch\dot N=N_{\mathrm{ch}}\times\text{PRF}_{\mathrm{ch}} (per return) 128 channels × 12 kHz ≈ 1.5 Mpts/s (Hesai AT128) §C4d

The precision row divides by Ns\sqrt{N_s} because averaging NsN_s independent photon arrival times reduces their scatter by that factor. The gain assumes that every detected photon is time-stamped independently. A macro-pixel of 3×3 single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs, subsection 6), read out as one pixel, registers at most nine photons per shot, and only ≈8 of 20 (§C4b, Eq. (72)), so Ns=20N_s=20 must be accumulated over several shots. “Amplitude walk” is the shift of the apparent arrival time with echo strength. The unambiguous range is the distance light can go out and back before the next pulse leaves: an echo arriving later is mistaken for an echo of that next pulse.

How the numbers are derived [E], with c=3.0×108c=3.0\times10^8 m/s:

  • Range from delay: inverting R=cτ/2R=c\,\tau/2 gives τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c. One metre takes 2×1/(3.0×108)s=6.672\times1/(3.0\times10^8)\ {\mathrm{s}}=6.67 ns, and 200 m takes 2×200/(3.0×108)s=1.332\times200/(3.0\times10^8)\ {\mathrm{s}}=1.33 µs.
  • Two-target resolution: ΔR=cτp/2=3.0×108×5×10−9/2=0.75\Delta R=c\,\tau_p/2=3.0\times10^8\times5\times10^{-9}/2=0.75 m for a 5 ns pulse, and 3.0×108×1×10−9/2=0.153.0\times10^8\times1\times10^{-9}/2=0.15 m for 1 ns.
  • Histogram quantization: one 297 ps bin spans 3.0×108×297×10−12/2=0.04463.0\times10^8\times297\times10^{-12}/2=0.0446 m of range, shown as 4.5 cm. Equivalent-time sampling at 3 GHz gives bins of 1/(3×109s−1)=3331/(3\times10^9\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}})=333 ps, which span 3.0×108×333×10−12/2=0.0503.0\times10^8\times333\times10^{-12}/2=0.050 m.
  • Single-target precision: σR=(c/2)σt/Ns=1.5×108×100×10−12/20m=1.5cm/4.47≈0.34\sigma_R=(c/2)\,\sigma_t/\sqrt{N_s}=1.5\times10^8\times100\times10^{-12}/\sqrt{20}\ {\mathrm{m}}=1.5\ {\mathrm{cm}}/4.47\approx0.34 cm, shown as ≈0.3 cm.
  • Unambiguous range: Ramb=c/(2PRFch)=3.0×108/(2×750×103)=200R_{\mathrm{amb}}=c/(2\,\text{PRF}_{\mathrm{ch}})=3.0\times10^8/(2\times750\times10^3)=200 m at 750 kHz, and 3.0×108/(2×300×103)=5003.0\times10^8/(2\times300\times10^3)=500 m at 300 kHz.
  • Point rate: Ṅ=128×12×103s−1=1.536×106\dot N=128\times12\times10^3\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=1.536\times10^6 pts/s, shown as ≈1.5 Mpts/s.

Photon budget for an extended Lambertian target (one that fills the beam, such as a road surface or a car body). A Lambertian surface is perfectly diffuse: it scatters the light it intercepts so that its radiance is the same in every direction, and a fraction ρ/π\rho/\pi of the intercepted power leaves per steradian along its normal. The receiver, a lens of area ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} at range RR, subtends a solid angle Arx/R2A_{\mathrm{rx}}/R^2. It therefore collects a fraction ρArx/(πR2)\rho A_{\mathrm{rx}}/(\pi R^2) of the pulse. Counting photons, the detected signal photons per pulse are

Ns,1=EpEphρArxπR2ηoptPDETatm2N_{s,1}=\frac{E_{\mathrm{p}}}{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}\,\rho\,\frac{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}{\pi R^2}\,\eta_{\mathrm{opt}}\,\text{PDE}\,T_{\mathrm{atm}}^2(31)

where:

  • Ns,1N_{s,1} is the mean number of signal photons detected per pulse (dimensionless). Summed over the NpulseN_{\mathrm{pulse}} pulses fired at one point, it gives the Ns=NpulseNs,1N_s=N_{\mathrm{pulse}}N_{s,1} of the precision row; equivalently, Eq. (31) with the energy per point Ept=NpulseEpE_{\mathrm{pt}}=N_{\mathrm{pulse}}E_{\mathrm{p}} in place of EpE_{\mathrm{p}} gives NsN_s directly (§C6, Eq. (88));
  • EpE_{\mathrm{p}} is the optical energy of one transmitted pulse (J);
  • Eph=hν=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=h\nu=hc/\lambda is the energy of one photon (J), with h=6.63×10−34h=6.63\times10^{-34} J s Planck’s constant, ν\nu the optical frequency and λ\lambda the wavelength, so Ep/EphE_{\mathrm{p}}/E_{\mathrm{ph}} is the number of photons in the pulse;
  • ρ\rho is the target’s diffuse (Lambertian) reflectance, e.g. 0.1 for the “10% target” of range specifications;
  • ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} is the area of the receive aperture (m²), πD2/4\pi D^2/4 for a lens of diameter DD;
  • RR is the range to the target (m);
  • ηopt\eta_{\mathrm{opt}} is the transmission of the receive optics, including the filter;
  • PDE is the detector’s photon detection efficiency, the probability that a photon reaching it is counted;
  • TatmT_{\mathrm{atm}} is the one-way atmospheric transmission, squared because the light crosses the air twice.

Eq. (31) assumes a Lambertian target at normal incidence that fills the beam, and a receiver whose field of view covers the whole lit spot. It is Part A’s Eq. (5) with the constants written out and the energy counted in photons. Glossy paint or a retroreflector is not Lambertian and can return far more or far less toward the sensor, depending on angle.

  • Example: Ep=100E_{\mathrm{p}}=100 nJ at 905 nm (4.6×10114.6\times10^{11} photons; between the 905 nm Class 1 limits of 198 nJ for an isolated pulse and 79 nJ per pulse in long trains, subsection 5 and §C4c), ρ=0.1\rho=0.1, a 25 mm aperture (Arx=4.9A_{\mathrm{rx}}=4.9 cm²), R=200R=200 m, ηopt=0.5\eta_{\mathrm{opt}}=0.5 and PDE 0.25 give Ns,1≈22N_{s,1}\approx22 photons per pulse before atmospheric loss. Several pulses are usually accumulated per point.
    • Substitution. One 905 nm photon carries Eph=hν=hc/λ=6.63×10−34×3.0×108/(905×10−9)=2.20×10−19E_{\mathrm{ph}}=h\nu=hc/\lambda=6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.0\times10^8/(905\times10^{-9})=2.20\times10^{-19} J, so 100 nJ is 10−7/(2.20×10−19)=4.6×101110^{-7}/(2.20\times10^{-19})=4.6\times10^{11} photons. A 25 mm aperture has Arx=π×(1.25cm)2=4.9A_{\mathrm{rx}}=\pi\times(1.25\ {\mathrm{cm}})^2=4.9 cm², so the collected fraction of the Lambertian return is Arx/(πR2)=4.9×10−4/(π×2002)=3.9×10−9A_{\mathrm{rx}}/(\pi R^2)=4.9\times10^{-4}/(\pi\times200^2)=3.9\times10^{-9}. Then Ns,1=4.6×1011×0.1×3.9×10−9×0.5×0.25≈22N_{s,1}=4.6\times10^{11}\times0.1\times3.9\times10^{-9}\times0.5\times0.25\approx22 photons.
  • Photon-counting SNR in the return’s histogram bins is SNR≈Ns/Ns+Nb\text{SNR}\approx N_s/\sqrt{N_s+N_b}, with NsN_s the signal counts and NbN_b the background counts in the same bins, both summed over the pulses of one point. Both are Poisson-distributed, so the noise is the square root of the total count. Sunlight sets NbN_b (§C4c, §C6). Dead time (the interval after each detection during which a photon-counting pixel is blind) and pile-up (the resulting bias toward early photons) distort the histogram at high count rates (§C4b, §C6).
  • Scaling. Signal-limited range goes as R∝EpArxρR\propto\sqrt{E_{\mathrm{p}}A_{\mathrm{rx}}\rho}, because holding Ns∝EpArxρ/R2N_s\propto E_{\mathrm{p}}A_{\mathrm{rx}}\rho/R^2 fixed (at a fixed number of pulses per point) makes R2R^2 proportional to EpArxρE_{\mathrm{p}}A_{\mathrm{rx}}\rho. When background noise dominates (Nb≫NsN_b\gg N_s) and also grows with ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} (Nb∝ArxN_b\propto A_{\mathrm{rx}}), the SNR above becomes Ns/Nb∝(Arx/R2)/Arx=Arx/R2N_s/\sqrt{N_b}\propto(A_{\mathrm{rx}}/R^2)/\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}=\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}/R^2. Holding the SNR fixed then gives R2∝ArxR^2\propto\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}, i.e. R∝Arx1/4R\propto A_{\mathrm{rx}}^{1/4} (§C4d, and §C10.3a, which contrasts one spatial mode with an integrating pixel). In daylight, doubling the lens diameter (4× the area) therefore buys a factor 41/4=1.414^{1/4}=1.41 in range instead of 2 at night. When the sunlit target itself supplies the background, Nb∝ρN_b\propto\rho too, and range scales as ρ1/4\rho^{1/4} rather than ρ1/2\rho^{1/2} (§C0 subsection 10.8).
  • Small targets. A target smaller than the beam (debris, a tyre) intercepts a fraction of it that falls as 1/R21/R^2, so its return falls as 1/R41/R^4 (§E11.3, Eq. (170)).

2. FMCW coherent ranging

A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) lidar does not time a pulse. It sweeps the laser’s optical frequency and measures the frequency difference between the echo and the light being sent at that moment. That difference gives range, and its Doppler part gives each point’s radial velocity directly. This subsection lists the relations that set FMCW’s resolution, precision, receiver bandwidth and point rate. The practical point is that each coherent channel must dwell microseconds per point and digitize hundreds of MHz, and this per-channel throughput is one of the hard limits on FMCW point rates (§C7, §C7a).

Principle and symbols. The laser’s optical frequency is swept linearly over a bandwidth BB (Hz) in one ramp of duration TT (s); a triangular chirp is a rising (up) ramp followed by a falling (down) ramp. The sweep speed is the chirp rate κ=B/T\kappa=B/T, in Hz/s. The return, delayed by τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c, is mixed with a local-oscillator (LO) copy of the outgoing light, i.e. a sample of the transmitted laser kept inside the sensor. Because the laser frequency has moved on by κτ\kappa\tau during the delay, the mixed signal oscillates at that difference, the beat frequency, and the beat frequency encodes range. The table uses:

  • fbf_b: the beat frequency (Hz) produced by range alone;
  • fDf_D: the Doppler shift (Hz) of the return, and vrv_r the target’s radial velocity (m/s), the component along the line of sight, positive for an approaching target;
  • fupf_{\mathrm{up}}, fdownf_{\mathrm{down}}: the measured beat frequencies during the up- and down-ramps, each of duration TT;
  • ΔR\Delta R: range resolution (the smallest separation at which two targets appear as two peaks); σR\sigma_R: range precision (rms error for one target); Δv\Delta v: velocity resolution;
  • SNR: the signal-to-noise ratio of the beat tone after the Fourier transform (FFT, fast Fourier transform) over one ramp;
  • Δν\Delta\nu: the laser’s linewidth (Hz), the full width at half maximum of its optical spectrum, taken as Lorentzian; LcL_c: the resulting coherence length (m), the path difference over which the LO and the echo stay phase-correlated;
  • ε\varepsilon: the fractional error in the chirp rate;
  • TdwellT_{\mathrm{dwell}}: the time spent per point (s), and NchN_{\mathrm{ch}} the number of parallel coherent channels. Only the last Tu=T−τT_u=T-\tau of each ramp, its useful part, yields a clean beat, because the echo arrives τ\tau after the ramp starts. A point therefore integrates for Tint=2TuT_{\mathrm{int}}=2T_u over its up- and down-ramp, and its dwell is Tdwell=Tint+2τ=2TT_{\mathrm{dwell}}=T_{\mathrm{int}}+2\tau=2T. This is the dwell of §C7b subsection 2(b), Eq. (111), written there as Ept/Pch+2τE_{\mathrm{pt}}/P_{\mathrm{ch}}+2\tau, with EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} the optical energy a point needs and PchP_{\mathrm{ch}} the channel’s constant optical power; the report uses it throughout. The §C7a model integrates Tint=2×5T_{\mathrm{int}}=2\times5 µs, so at its 200 m design range (τ=1.33\tau=1.33 µs) its dwell is Tdwell=10+2×1.33=12.67T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=10+2\times1.33=12.67 µs;
  • NmodeN_{\mathrm{mode}}: the number of signal photons that arrive in the LO’s spatial mode and polarization during one ramp, and η\eta the overall detection efficiency, the fraction of those photons converted into signal photoelectrons. Then n‾=ηNmode\bar n=\eta N_{\mathrm{mode}} is the number of signal photoelectrons; subsection 10 uses n‾\bar n for the total over both ramps of a point.

  • What the LO does, and does not do. It lifts a weak signal above electronic noise and rejects broadband light (sunlight, other lidars) outside the IF band, the intermediate-frequency band of beat frequencies the receiver digitizes. It cannot recover photons that fall outside its single spatial mode (the antenna theorem, §C7) or that speckle fading removes (§C10.3a).
  • Mechanical scanning adds two coherent-specific errors (§C7, §C10.3a, §C4d). Here θ̇\dot\theta is the optical scan rate, the angular speed of the beam (rad/s), and DD the beam diameter on the scanner.
    • Walk-off, Δθ=2Rθ̇/c\Delta\theta=2R\dot\theta/c: during the round trip τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c the beam direction moves on, so the echo comes back at an angle Δθ\Delta\theta away from the LO’s direction. For example [E], a polygon sweeping 45,600°/s (796 rad/s) gives Δθ=2×200×796/(3.0×108)=1.06×10−3\Delta\theta=2\times200\times796/(3.0\times10^8)=1.06\times10^{-3} rad (0.061°) at 200 m (§C4d, Eq. (79)), about 3.4 times the divergence λ/D=0.31\lambda/D=0.31 mrad of a 5 mm beam at 1,550 nm.
    • Scanner-induced Doppler, Δfscan≈θ̇D/λ\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}\approx\dot\theta D/\lambda (Eq. (94) of §C7): the moving mirror spreads the return’s optical frequency by about Δfscan\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}. The same polygon with a 5 mm beam gives 796×5×10−3/(1.55×10−6)=2.6796\times5\times10^{-3}/(1.55\times10^{-6})=2.6 MHz, about 26 FFT bins of a 10 µs ramp (§C7).

In short, FMCW trades the timing electronics of ToF for a narrow-linewidth laser, a linear chirp and a fast digitizer per channel. In return it gets per-point velocity and near-immunity to sunlight.

3. Beams, pixels and sampling

How finely a lidar samples the scene is set by the beam’s divergence, the angle each receiver pixel sees, and how many points per second it can afford. This subsection gives those geometric relations, the sweep rate a mechanical scanner needs, and the étendue rule that ties aperture to field of view. Together they explain why resolution, range and scan speed cannot all be improved at once.

Symbols.

  • θb\theta_b is the full divergence angle of the transmitted beam (rad), λ\lambda the wavelength and DD the beam or aperture diameter.
  • θpix\theta_{\mathrm{pix}} is the angle one receiver pixel sees, its instantaneous field of view (IFOV). pp is the pixel pitch, ff the lens focal length, and F#=f/DF_\#=f/D the f-number, so the aperture diameter is D=f/F#D=f/F_\#.
  • RθR\,\theta is the width of the footprint, the patch a beam or pixel of angular width θ\theta covers at range RR; likewise RδθR\,\delta\theta is the spacing at range RR of points an angular step δθ\delta\theta apart.
  • ΘH\Theta_H, ΘV\Theta_V are the horizontal and vertical fields of view, and δθH\delta\theta_H, δθV\delta\theta_V the angular spacing of points along each (degrees), as in §C3b Eq. (69).
  • SS is the mechanical sweep rate: the number of times per second the scanner must sweep the beam across the field.
  • NlinesN_{\mathrm{lines}} is the number of scan lines per frame, fframef_{\mathrm{frame}} the frame rate (frames per second), and NparN_{\mathrm{par}} the number of lines read in parallel (parallel channels; Npar=NchN_{\mathrm{par}}=N_{\mathrm{ch}} of subsection 1 when each channel draws its own line).
  • fmirrorf_{\mathrm{mirror}} is the oscillation frequency of a resonant mirror.
  • Étendue is AΩA\,\Omega: the area AA through which light passes times the solid angle Ω\Omega it fills (m² sr).

The factor ≈1.3 in the divergence row is 4/π≈1.274/\pi\approx1.27: a Gaussian beam of 1/e² diameter DD spreads with a full far-field angle of 4λ/(πD)4\lambda/(\pi D). How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Divergence: θb≈λ/D=905×10−9/10−3=0.9\theta_b\approx\lambda/D=905\times10^{-9}/10^{-3}=0.9 mrad, which is 0.905×10−3×180∘/π=0.052∘0.905\times10^{-3}\times180^\circ/\pi=0.052^\circ; and 1.55×10−6/0.020=0.0781.55\times10^{-6}/0.020=0.078 mrad, or 0.0044∘0.0044^\circ.

  • Points per frame: for the Hesai AT128 grid, δθV=25.4∘/128=0.198∘\delta\theta_V=25.4^\circ/128=0.198^\circ, so (ΘH/δθH)(ΘV/δθV)=(120∘/0.1∘)×(25.4∘/0.198∘)=1,200×128=153,600(\Theta_H/\delta\theta_H)(\Theta_V/\delta\theta_V)=(120^\circ/0.1^\circ)\times(25.4^\circ/0.198^\circ)=1{,}200\times128=153{,}600; at 10 frames/s that is 1.536×1061.536\times10^6 pts/s.
  • Sweep rate: S=Nlinesfframe/Npar=128×10s−1/128=10S=N_{\mathrm{lines}}f_{\mathrm{frame}}/N_{\mathrm{par}}=128\times10\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}/128=10 sweeps/s with 128 parallel channels, and 128×10/1=1,280128\times10/1=1{,}280 with one. With 128 channels, 10 sweeps/s is one facet per frame of the Hesai AT128’s three-facet mirror turning at 200 rpm (§C4d); with one channel, a bidirectional resonant mirror would run at fmirror=S/2=1,280/2=640f_{\mathrm{mirror}}=S/2=1{,}280/2=640 Hz.

The practical consequence is that parallel channels relieve the scanner: with 128 channels a slow, robust mirror suffices, while a single beam needs a mirror more than a hundred times faster (§C4d). Taken together, the relations of this subsection set the trade-off named at its start. Halving the point spacing on both axes quadruples the points per frame, so it either quarters the frame rate at a fixed point rate or, at a fixed frame rate, needs four times the point rate, for example four times the channels. At a fixed average laser power it also leaves a quarter of the energy per point, which halves the signal-limited range, since that range scales as the square root of the energy per point (subsection 1). At a fixed pitch and f-number, a finer pixel angle also needs a longer focal length and so a larger aperture, which means larger optics and, for the same field, a larger sensor (§C6).

4. Velocity: measured or differenced

Knowing how fast an object moves matters as much as knowing where it is. An FMCW lidar measures velocity in a single look, while a ToF lidar must infer it by comparing positions in successive frames, which is noisier and slower.

  • FMCW measures each point’s radial velocity from its Doppler shift in one look. Its resolution is Δv=λ/(2T)=7.8\Delta v=\lambda/(2T)=7.8 cm/s for a 10 µs ramp (subsection 2), and its precision is finer, of order Δv/SNR=7.8/10≈0.8\Delta v/\sqrt{\mathrm{SNR}}=7.8/10\approx0.8 cm/s at 20 dB SNR [E].
  • ToF infers velocity by tracking across frames: σv≈2σR/Δtframe\sigma_v\approx\sqrt2\,\sigma_R/\Delta t_{\mathrm{frame}}. Here σv\sigma_v is the rms velocity error, σR\sigma_R the range precision of one measurement and Δtframe=1/fframe\Delta t_{\mathrm{frame}}=1/f_{\mathrm{frame}} the time between frames. The factor 2\sqrt2 appears because the velocity is the difference of two independent range measurements, each with error σR\sigma_R. Take an assumed range precision of 3 cm [E], ten times the ideal 0.3 cm of subsection 1 to allow for amplitude walk and background, and comparable with the 2–4 cm the Sony AS-DT1 measures outdoors at 10 m (§C5a). At 10 Hz (Δtframe=0.1\Delta t_{\mathrm{frame}}=0.1 s) that gives 2×0.03m/0.1s≈0.42\sqrt2\times0.03\ {\mathrm{m}}/0.1\ {\mathrm{s}}\approx0.42 m/s, i.e. ≈0.4 m/s from two frames, about fifty times FMCW’s single-look precision. It also needs points to be associated between frames. Tracking over more frames lowers the noise but adds latency.
  • Neither measures the tangential component directly. FMCW gives the radial part at once; the full vector needs several points or tracking.

5. Eye safety and sunlight (summary; details in §C4c)

Two things cap what a lidar can do with light: how much it may emit without harming an eye, and how much sunlight its receiver must reject. Both depend on wavelength, which is why the choice between 905/940 nm and 1,550 nm runs through the whole report.

  • Class 1 (IEC 60825-1:2014). IEC 60825-1 is the laser-safety standard of the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), and Class 1 is its least hazardous class, defined by limits on the emission accessible under the standard’s measurement conditions; automotive lidars are designed to it. At 905/940 nm the limits are ≈198/233 nJ per isolated small-source pulse and ≈79/93 nJ per pulse in long trains [P, IEC 60825-1:2014; §C4c]. At 1,550 nm the long-exposure limit is ≈10 mW, against ≈1 mW at 905 nm [P/E, IEC 60825-1:2014; §C4], because the front of the eye absorbs 1,550 nm light before it can be focused onto the retina. The classification must hold under reasonably foreseeable single faults, including a stalled scanner (§C4d).

  • Solar background per pixel (§C6):

    rbg=E⊙(λ)ΔλEphρsceneπΩpixArxηoptPDEr_{\mathrm{bg}}=\frac{E_\odot(\lambda)\,\Delta\lambda}{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}\,\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{scene}}}{\pi}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{pix}}\,A_{\mathrm{rx}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{opt}}\,\text{PDE}(32)

    where:

    • rbgr_{\mathrm{bg}} is the rate of background counts in one pixel (counts/s);
    • E⊙(λ)E_\odot(\lambda) is the solar spectral irradiance on the scene at wavelength λ\lambda (W m⁻² nm⁻¹);
    • Δλ\Delta\lambda is the pass band of the receiver’s optical filter (nm);
    • Eph=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda is the photon energy (J), which converts the in-band solar power into a photon rate;
    • ρscene/π\rho_{\mathrm{scene}}/\pi turns the solar irradiance into the radiance of a Lambertian scene (per steradian), where ρscene\rho_{\mathrm{scene}} is the reflectance of the sunlit scene in the pixel’s view, not the target reflectance ρ\rho of Eq. (31);
    • Ωpix\Omega_{\mathrm{pix}} is the solid angle one pixel sees (sr);
    • ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} is the receive-aperture area, ηopt\eta_{\mathrm{opt}} the optics transmission and PDE the photon detection efficiency.

    Eq. (32) is the relation §C6 uses as Eq. (89). Example [E, inputs of §C6(d)]: at 905 nm, E⊙≈0.75E_\odot\approx0.75 W m⁻² nm⁻¹ and Eph=2.20×10−19E_{\mathrm{ph}}=2.20\times10^{-19} J, so E⊙/Eph=3.4×1018E_\odot/E_{\mathrm{ph}}=3.4\times10^{18} photons s⁻¹ m⁻² nm⁻¹. With a 20 nm filter, ρscene=0.9\rho_{\mathrm{scene}}=0.9, a 0.05° × 0.05° macro-pixel (0.05∘=8.73×10−40.05^\circ=8.73\times10^{-4} rad, so Ωpix=(8.73×10−4)2=7.62×10−7\Omega_{\mathrm{pix}}=(8.73\times10^{-4})^2=7.62\times10^{-7} sr; the 2,400 × 520 grid of Sony’s IMX479 over 120° × 26°, §C5a), a 25 mm aperture (Arx=4.91×10−4A_{\mathrm{rx}}=4.91\times10^{-4} m²), ηopt=0.5\eta_{\mathrm{opt}}=0.5 and PDE 0.3, rbg=3.4×1018×20×(0.9/π)×7.62×10−7×4.91×10−4×0.5×0.3≈1.1×109r_{\mathrm{bg}}=3.4\times10^{18}\times20\times(0.9/\pi)\times7.62\times10^{-7}\times4.91\times10^{-4}\times0.5\times0.3\approx1.1\times10^9 counts/s. The background is lowest near 940 nm, where water vapour in the atmosphere absorbs part of the solar spectrum (§C4c). Narrower filters and smaller pixel angles reduce it; a larger aperture raises signal and background together.

6. Detector gain and excess noise

A single returning photon produces one electron, far too little charge for an amplifier to see. Lidar detectors therefore multiply it, either by a controlled avalanche (a linear avalanche photodiode, APD) or by a runaway one (a single-photon avalanche diode, SPAD, in Geiger mode). This subsection explains why linear gain helps only up to a point, set by the detector material, and what Geiger-mode counting and coherent detection do instead. It underlies the choice of silicon at 905/940 nm and the difficulty of InGaAs at 1,550 nm.

  • Linear APD. An APD is a photodiode biased just below breakdown. Each photoelectron is accelerated until it knocks loose further carriers by impact ionization, so the avalanche multiplies it by a random gain of mean MM (dimensionless). The randomness adds noise, expressed by McIntyre’s excess noise factor

    F(M)=kM+(1−k)(2−1M)F(M)=kM+(1-k)\left(2-\frac{1}{M}\right)(33)

    for multiplication started by the more strongly ionizing carrier. Here F(M)F(M) is the excess-noise factor, the factor by which the gain’s randomness raises the shot-noise power above that of a noiseless amplifier with the same mean gain (F=1F=1 would be noiseless). kk is the ionization coefficient (ionizations per unit length) of the weaker-ionizing carrier divided by that of the stronger one: holes over electrons in silicon, where electrons start the avalanche, and electrons over holes in the InP multiplication layer of an InGaAs/InP APD, where holes start it. A small kk means an avalanche driven by one carrier type, which is quieter. The multiplied shot noise is

    ⟨in2⟩=2qIphM2F(M)Δf\langle i_n^2\rangle=2qI_{\mathrm{ph}}M^2F(M)\,\Delta f(34)

    where ⟨in2⟩\langle i_n^2\rangle is the mean-square noise current (A²), q=1.60×10−19q=1.60\times10^{-19} C the elementary charge, IphI_{\mathrm{ph}} the primary photocurrent (the unmultiplied current, before gain; A) and Δf\Delta f the electrical bandwidth of the receiver (Hz). The signal current MIphMI_{\mathrm{ph}} grows only as MM, so its power grows as M2M^2, while the noise power in Eq. (34) grows as M2F(M)M^2F(M).

  • Consequence. Gain helps only until the multiplied shot noise 2qIphM2F(M)Δf2qI_{\mathrm{ph}}M^2F(M)\,\Delta f of Eq. (34) grows to match the noise of the amplifier that follows the detector (a transimpedance amplifier, TIA, which converts current into voltage). That is roughly the best gain; beyond it, more gain lowers the SNR. Because FF rises with slope kk (F≈kM+2(1−k)F\approx kM+2(1-k) for M≫1M\gg1), a material with a large kk reaches that point at a much lower MM. Substituting the kk of each material into Eq. (33) gives:

Detector kk FF at typical gain Practical gain
Silicon APD (905/940 nm) ≈0.02 [P, Excelitas C30902EH datasheet; I: 0.01–0.06 for the best commercial Si APDs, Martyniuk et al. 2023] 2.9 at M=50M=50; 4.0 at M=100M=100 ≈50–200 [P: 150 recommended for the C30902EH; I: 20–400 across Si APDs, Martyniuk et al. 2023, Table 3]
InGaAs/InP APD (1,550 nm) ≈0.4–0.5 [I, Campbell et al. 2004; Martyniuk et al. 2023] (§C4) 5.5 at M=10M=10; 10 at M=20M=20 ≈10–20 [P: maximum usable gain 10 minimum and 20 typical, Excelitas C30645/C30662 datasheet; I: 10–40, Martyniuk et al. 2023] (§C4)
  • How the numbers are derived [E], by substituting into Eq. (33), F(M)=kM+(1−k)(2−1/M)F(M)=kM+(1-k)(2-1/M):
    • Silicon APD, k=0.02k=0.02: F(50)=0.02×50+0.98×(2−0.02)=1.00+1.94=2.94F(50)=0.02\times50+0.98\times(2-0.02)=1.00+1.94=2.94, and F(100)=2.00+0.98×1.99=3.95F(100)=2.00+0.98\times1.99=3.95.
    • InGaAs/InP APD, at the mid-range k=0.45k=0.45: F(10)=4.5+0.55×1.9=5.5F(10)=4.5+0.55\times1.9=5.5, and F(20)=9.0+0.55×1.95=10.1F(20)=9.0+0.55\times1.95=10.1. The ends of the range, k=0.4k=0.4 and 0.5, give 5.1 and 6.0 at M=10M=10, and 9.2 and 11.0 at M=20M=20.
  • What the table means. Silicon’s small kk keeps FF near 3–4 even at a gain of 100, whereas InGaAs/InP with k=0.45k=0.45 already reaches F=4F=4 at M≈6.6M\approx6.6 and F=5.5F=5.5 at M=10M=10 [E: setting F=4F=4 in Eq. (33) gives 0.45M+0.55(2−1/M)=40.45M+0.55(2-1/M)=4, i.e. 0.45M2−2.9M−0.55=00.45M^2-2.9M-0.55=0, so M=(2.9+2.92+4×0.45×0.55)/(2×0.45)=6.6M=(2.9+\sqrt{2.9^2+4\times0.45\times0.55})/(2\times0.45)=6.6]. A 1,550 nm linear APD receiver therefore gets far less useful gain, and needs more signal photons per point.
  • Geiger mode (SPAD, SiPM). A SPAD is biased above breakdown; a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) is an array of SPAD cells whose outputs are summed. Each detected photon produces a saturated, digital avalanche with a gain of order 10510^5–10610^6, so the count carries no analog excess noise. The costs move elsewhere: the photon detection efficiency (PDE), dead time and pile-up, afterpulsing (false counts from charge trapped in an earlier avalanche) and, in SiPMs, optical crosstalk between cells (§C4b, §C5a, §C6).
  • Coherent receivers need no avalanche gain. The LO supplies it: the beat signal scales with the square root of the LO power. A balanced pair of PIN photodiodes (ordinary p–i–n diodes with unity gain, whose outputs are subtracted to cancel the LO’s own intensity noise) becomes shot-noise-limited once the LO’s shot noise exceeds the TIA’s input noise. With a TIA of input noise ith=3pAHz−1/2i_{\mathrm{th}}=3\ {\mathrm{pA\,Hz^{-1/2}}}, parity (2qILO=ith22qI_{\mathrm{LO}}=i_{\mathrm{th}}^2) needs an LO photocurrent ILO=ith2/(2q)=(3×10−12)2/(2×1.60×10−19)=28μAI_{\mathrm{LO}}=i_{\mathrm{th}}^2/(2q)=(3\times10^{-12})^2/(2\times1.60\times10^{-19})=28\ \mu{\mathrm{A}}, about 30 µW of LO light. A balanced Ge pair with 0.3–1 mW of LO stays at 82–94% of the shot-noise limit even at 125 °C, and Rogers et al. (2021) reached parity at 5 µW of LO per pixel with a TIA integrated on the same chip (§C4c).

7. Detection and false alarms

A return counts as detected when it crosses a threshold set above the noise. The threshold trades detection probability PDP_D (the chance that a real echo crosses it) against the false-alarm probability pp of each range cell (the chance that noise alone crosses it there). Noise can cross in any of the cells searched, so the chance of a false point, PFA,ptP_{FA,{\mathrm{pt}}}, grows with their number, and so does the threshold needed for a given false-point rate. That is why a stated range means little without its PDP_D and false-alarm definition (§C3b). This subsection shows how many signal photons a detection needs, first for photon counting and then for coherent detection of a speckled target.

  • Photon counting (SPAD histograms). A SPAD receiver builds a histogram of photon arrival times over many pulses, one bin per range cell. Background counts per bin are Poisson-distributed with mean bb. Write P(N≥n∣μ)P(N\ge n\mid\mu) for the probability that a Poisson count NN of mean μ\mu is at least nn. For a threshold of nthn_{\mathrm{th}} counts, the per-bin false-alarm probability is then p=P(N≥nth∣b)p=P(N\ge n_{\mathrm{th}}\mid b), and across NbinsN_{\mathrm{bins}} bins in the range window the chance of a false point is PFA,pt≈NbinspP_{FA,{\mathrm{pt}}}\approx N_{\mathrm{bins}}\,p. With a mean signal of ss counts in the echo’s bin (the NsN_s of subsection 1 and the n‾\bar n of subsection 10), PD=P(N≥nth∣s+b)P_D=P(N\ge n_{\mathrm{th}}\mid s+b). Worked cases for Nbins=1,000N_{\mathrm{bins}}=1{,}000 bins (2 ns each, over 0–300 m) and at most PFA,pt=10−3P_{FA,{\mathrm{pt}}}=10^{-3} false points per point, i.e. p=10−6p=10^{-6} per bin [E]. The daylight background b=1b=1 is illustrative; §C0 subsection 10.3 uses 2,000 bins of 1 ns and the bright-sun b=1.62b=1.62 of the §C7a model, which raises the daylight requirement from ≈13 to ≈15 counts:

    • daylight, b=1b=1 count per bin: the threshold is 10 counts, and PD=0.9P_D=0.9 needs ≈13 signal counts. The Poisson tail gives P(N≥9∣1)=1.1×10−6P(N\ge9\mid1)=1.1\times10^{-6}, just over the 10−610^{-6} budget, and P(N≥10∣1)=1.1×10−7P(N\ge10\mid1)=1.1\times10^{-7}, within it. Detection then needs the total mean s+bs+b to satisfy P(N≥10∣s+b)=0.9P(N\ge10\mid s+b)=0.9, which holds at s+b≈14.2s+b\approx14.2, so s≈13s\approx13;
    • night, b=0.01b=0.01: the threshold is 3 counts, and ≈5 signal counts suffice. Here P(N≥2∣0.01)=5.0×10−5P(N\ge2\mid0.01)=5.0\times10^{-5} exceeds the budget and P(N≥3∣0.01)=1.7×10−7P(N\ge3\mid0.01)=1.7\times10^{-7} meets it, and P(N≥3∣s+b)=0.9P(N\ge3\mid s+b)=0.9 at s+b≈5.3s+b\approx5.3;
    • daylight at PFA,pt=10−6P_{FA,{\mathrm{pt}}}=10^{-6} false points per point: the threshold rises to 12 counts and the signal needed to ≈16. The per-bin budget becomes p=10−6/1,000=10−9p=10^{-6}/1{,}000=10^{-9}; P(N≥11∣1)=1.0×10−8P(N\ge11\mid1)=1.0\times10^{-8} exceeds it and P(N≥12∣1)=8.3×10−10P(N\ge12\mid1)=8.3\times10^{-10} meets it, and P(N≥12∣s+b)=0.9P(N\ge12\mid s+b)=0.9 at s+b≈16.6s+b\approx16.6, so s≈16s\approx16.

  • Why automotive thresholds are strict. At 1.5 Mpts/s and 1,000 bins, a per-bin pp of 10−610^{-6} still gives ≈1,500 false points a second, 150 per 10 Hz frame [E: 1.5×106s−1×1,000×10−6=1,500s−11.5\times10^6\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times1{,}000\times10^{-6}=1{,}500\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}, and 1,500/10=1501{,}500/10=150]. Products therefore add multi-pulse or neighbour-consistency checks before a point is output.

  • Vendors define the terms differently. InnovizOne’s range table uses 90% true positives and a 5% false-alarm rate per pixel at 20 klx [P], and InnovizTwo’s datasheet 90% true and 1% false positives per pixel at 100 klx (§C3b); Seyond’s Falcon K1 uses >90% detection probability at 100 klx [P]. (klx is thousands of lux of ambient illuminance; 100 klx corresponds to bright direct sunlight.)

  • Coherent detection with speckle. A rough target scatters the coherent light from many randomly phased patches, and their sum at the receiver is a random speckle pattern. In a single speckle the return’s amplitude is Rayleigh-distributed, so its intensity is exponentially distributed: deep fades are common. For a single look with square-law detection (the receiver compares the beat power, not its amplitude, with the threshold),

    PD=p1/(1+SNR¯)P_D=p^{1/(1+\overline{\mathrm{SNR}})}(35)

    where pp is the false-alarm probability of the bin tested and SNR¯\overline{\mathrm{SNR}} the mean signal-to-noise ratio, averaged over the speckle fading. This is the Swerling I case of radar theory. It assumes exponentially distributed intensity (Rayleigh amplitude fading) that stays constant during the look and changes independently from one look to the next.

    • PD=0.9P_D=0.9 at p=10−6p=10^{-6} then needs a mean SNR of ≈130 (21 dB). A steady, non-fading target needs ≈20 (13 dB, Albersheim’s approximation) [E].
      • Swerling I: taking logarithms of Eq. (35), 1+SNR¯=ln⁡p/ln⁡PD=ln⁡(10−6)/ln⁡(0.9)=(−13.82)/(−0.1054)=1311+\overline{\mathrm{SNR}}=\ln p/\ln P_D=\ln(10^{-6})/\ln(0.9)=(-13.82)/(-0.1054)=131, so SNR¯≈130\overline{\mathrm{SNR}}\approx130, and 10log⁡10130=21.110\log_{10}130=21.1 dB.
      • Steady target: Albersheim’s empirical approximation for a non-fading target is SNRdB=(6.2+4.54/1.44)log⁡10(𝒜+0.12𝒜ℬ+1.7ℬ){\mathrm{SNR_{dB}}}=(6.2+4.54/\sqrt{1.44})\log_{10}(\mathcal{A}+0.12\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B}+1.7\mathcal{B}), with 𝒜=ln⁡(0.62/p)=13.34\mathcal{A}=\ln(0.62/p)=13.34 and ℬ=ln⁡[PD/(1−PD)]=ln⁡9=2.20\mathcal{B}=\ln[P_D/(1-P_D)]=\ln9=2.20. The constants 6.2, 4.54, 0.12, 1.7 and 0.62 are Albersheim’s fitted coefficients. The general form, for NpN_p pulses integrated incoherently, contains Np+0.44\sqrt{N_p+0.44}, which is 1.44\sqrt{1.44} for the single pulse here. (𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} are auxiliary numbers, not an area or a bandwidth.) That gives 9.98×log⁡10(20.6)=13.19.98\times\log_{10}(20.6)=13.1 dB, an SNR of ≈20.
    • In a shot-noise-limited coherent receiver SNR ≈ detected photons, so a single look needs ≈130 photoelectrons at 10−610^{-6} per bin. A full FMCW point is held to the stricter per-point rule of §C0 subsection 10.3 (at most 10−310^{-3} false points over a 0–300 m search, with the echo’s peak found in both chirp ramps). With one look it then needs ≈259 photoelectrons, twice the single-bin ≈130; four independent looks bring the total, summed over both ramps and all looks, down to ≈88. Polarization, wavelength or spatial diversity recovers much of the fading penalty. §C0 subsection 10.3 plots these cases against photon counting (Figure C0.10b).
    • The practical consequence is that speckle fading, more than receiver noise, sets the photon budget of a coherent lidar: a single speckle needs more than six times the signal of a steady target (130 against 20) for the same 90% detection.

8. Weather: fog, rain, snow and spray

Weather removes light on the way to the target and back, and adds false echoes near the sensor. This subsection shows how fog, rain and snow shorten a lidar’s reach, and why dense fog costs 905 nm and 1,550 nm about the same. The main results are that in fog a lidar reaches only a fraction of the visibility distance, a fraction that grows as the fog thickens, and that rain matters less through the air than through water on the window and spray.

  • Beer–Lambert, both ways. Light travelling a distance xx through a scattering medium keeps a fraction e−αxe^{-\alpha x} of its power, where α\alpha is the extinction coefficient (per unit length; absorption plus scattering). The light crosses the range RR twice, so the return is multiplied by e−2αRe^{-2\alpha R}. Visibility VV is conventionally the distance at which contrast falls to 2%, so e−αV=0.02e^{-\alpha V}=0.02 and α=ln⁡(1/0.02)/V≈3.912/V\alpha=\ln(1/0.02)/V\approx3.912/V in fog (some standards use 5%, giving α=ln⁡(1/0.05)/V≈3.0/V\alpha=\ln(1/0.05)/V\approx3.0/V). Visibility is defined for visible light, near 550 nm.
  • Fog. Kim’s model scales α\alpha as (λ/550nm)−qK(\lambda/550\ {\mathrm{nm}})^{-q_{\mathrm{K}}}, with an exponent qKq_{\mathrm{K}} that describes the droplet size distribution: it is 1.6 above 50 km visibility, 1.3 for 6–50 km (the “clear air” of subsection 10.1), and falls to 0 below 500 m visibility. When qK=0q_{\mathrm{K}}=0, α\alpha no longer depends on wavelength, because fog droplets are much larger than the wavelength. Dense fog (visibility below 500 m, where qK=0q_{\mathrm{K}}=0) therefore attenuates 905 and 1,550 nm about equally [I, Kim, McArthur and Korevaar 2001], consistent with the <10% difference measured by Duthon et al. (§C4c). In light fog the model still favours 1,550 nm slightly: at 1 km visibility α=3.05\alpha=3.05 /km at 905 nm against 2.33 /km at 1,550 nm. A signal-limited lidar with 200 m clear-air range at 10% reflectance reaches the range where R2e2αRR^2e^{2\alpha R} equals its clear-air value [E]:
Visibility VV α\alpha at 905 nm Two-way loss at 50 m Reach of a 200 m (clear-air) lidar Reach / VV
1,000 m (fog, at the haze boundary; qK=0.5q_{\mathrm{K}}=0.5) 3.0 /km 1.3 dB ≈133 m 0.13
200 m (fog) 19.6 /km 8.5 dB ≈61 m 0.30
50 m (thick fog) 78 /km 34 dB ≈26 m 0.52
20 m (very thick fog) 196 /km 85 dB ≈13.7 m 0.69
  • How the numbers are derived [E]:
    • Extinction: Kim’s model gives α=(3.912/V)(λ/550nm)−qK\alpha=(3.912/V)\,(\lambda/550\ {\mathrm{nm}})^{-q_{\mathrm{K}}}, evaluated here at 905 nm. Between 0.5 and 1 km visibility the model sets qK=V−0.5q_{\mathrm{K}}=V-0.5 (with VV in km), which is 0.5 at 1 km. For V=1,000V=1{,}000 m with qK=0.5q_{\mathrm{K}}=0.5, α=(3.912/km)×(905/550)−0.5=3.912×0.78=3.05\alpha=(3.912/{\mathrm{km}})\times(905/550)^{-0.5}=3.912\times0.78=3.05 /km at 905 nm, and 3.912×(1,550/550)−0.5=3.912×0.596=2.333.912\times(1{,}550/550)^{-0.5}=3.912\times0.596=2.33 /km at 1,550 nm. Below 500 m visibility qK=0q_{\mathrm{K}}=0, so α=3.912/V\alpha=3.912/V: 19.6 /km at 200 m, 78 /km at 50 m and 196 /km at 20 m.
    • Two-way loss at 50 m: 10log⁡10e2αR=4.343×2αR10\log_{10}e^{2\alpha R}=4.343\times2\alpha R dB, where 4.343=10/ln⁡10=10log⁡10e4.343=10/\ln10=10\log_{10}e converts natural-log units into decibels. For 200 m visibility this is 4.343×2×0.0196m−1×50m=8.54.343\times2\times0.0196\ {\mathrm{m^{-1}}}\times50\ {\mathrm{m}}=8.5 dB; the other rows scale with α\alpha (1.3, 34 and 85 dB).
    • Reach: a signal-limited lidar still detects while e−2αR/R2e^{-2\alpha R}/R^2 is at least its clear-air value at 200 m, 1/(200m)21/(200\ {\mathrm{m}})^2. The reach is therefore the root of R2e2αR=(200m)2R^2e^{2\alpha R}=(200\ {\mathrm{m}})^2, found numerically. For 200 m visibility, R=61R=61 m gives 612×e2×0.0196×61=3,721×10.93=4.07×10461^2\times e^{2\times0.0196\times61}=3{,}721\times10.93=4.07\times10^4 m², within 2% of (200m)2=4.0×104(200\ {\mathrm{m}})^2=4.0\times10^4 m², as required (61 m is the root rounded from 60.8 m).
    • Reach / VV is that reach divided by the visibility, e.g. 61/200=0.3061/200=0.30 and 13.7/20=0.6913.7/20=0.69.
  • Reach relative to visibility rises as fog thickens: about 0.5–0.7 V for visibilities of 20–50 m in this model. A reach of 0.6 V therefore needs visibility below about 30 m, and reach equals V only near 4 m visibility, where αR=3.912\alpha R=3.912 [E: with qK=0q_{\mathrm{K}}=0 the reach solves R2e2αR=(200m)2R^2e^{2\alpha R}=(200\ {\mathrm{m}})^2, i.e. R=200m×e−αRR=200\ {\mathrm{m}}\times e^{-\alpha R}; a reach of 0.6 V means αR=0.6×3.912=2.35\alpha R=0.6\times3.912=2.35, so R=200m×e−2.35=19R=200\ {\mathrm{m}}\times e^{-2.35}=19 m and V=19/0.6=32V=19/0.6=32 m, while a reach of 1 V gives R=200m×e−3.912=4.0R=200\ {\mathrm{m}}\times e^{-3.912}=4.0 m]. The ratio rises because at a shorter reach the 1/R21/R^2 spreading loss is smaller, so the lidar can afford a larger fog optical depth αR\alpha R. Below 500 m visibility, where α=3.912/V\alpha=3.912/V, reach divided by visibility is that optical depth divided by 3.912.
  • Clutter and multiple scattering. Backscatter from droplets near the sensor adds clutter and can saturate SPADs. Multiple scattering returns some forward-scattered light and slightly extends real reach beyond this single-scattering estimate.
  • Rain. The empirical free-space-optics law γrain≈1.076Rr0.67\gamma_{\mathrm{rain}}\approx1.076\,R_r^{0.67} dB/km gives the specific attenuation γrain\gamma_{\mathrm{rain}}, the loss per kilometre of path, for a rain rate RrR_r in mm/h; 1.076 and 0.67 are Carbonneau’s fitted coefficients, as used with ITU-R P.1814, a recommendation of the International Telecommunication Union’s radiocommunication sector (ITU-R). The law yields 3.2, 9.3 and 23.5 dB/km at 5, 25 and 100 mm/h (for example, 1.076×50.67=1.076×2.94=3.21.076\times5^{0.67}=1.076\times2.94=3.2 dB/km). At 200 m range the light travels 0.4 km out and back, so the loss is only 3.2×0.4=1.33.2\times0.4=1.3, 9.3×0.4=3.79.3\times0.4=3.7 and 23.5×0.4=9.423.5\times0.4=9.4 dB [P, ITU-R P.1814; E for the 200 m losses]. Raindrops are far larger than the wavelength, so in this law the loss barely depends on it; one comparison cited in §C4c nevertheless found 905 nm reaching ≈2× farther than 1,550 nm at 25 mm/h [S, Wojtanowski et al. 2014, relayed by a survey]. In practice rain hurts more through:
    • water films on the window, which cost 9.4 dB round trip per millimetre at 1,550 nm but almost nothing at 905 nm (§C4c);
    • spray from other vehicles and splash near the sensor, which produce spurious near points;
    • wet roads, which turn specular, return little from the road surface and create mirrored ghosts.
  • Snow and sleet scatter strongly and unevenly. On K-Radar’s heavy-snow split (the heavy-snow subset of the K-Radar driving dataset), lidar-only 3D detection fell from 52.3 to 29.7 AP (average precision, a 0–100 score of object-detection accuracy), while radar-only detection fell only from 49.9 to 44.5 [I, K-Radar, NeurIPS 2022; §E4].

9. Amplitude-modulated (phase) ranging

A third way to measure range is to modulate the brightness of the light and measure how far the returning modulation has shifted in phase. This subsection explains that principle, which runs ToF cameras, surveying rangefinders and phase-based laser scanners. It also explains why the same physics gives millimetre precision at hundreds of metres in a surveying scanner but only about 10 m in a camera. The products themselves, the chips inside them and where the boundary of “lidar” is drawn are surveyed in §C1a. For cars, the conclusion is that phase ranging (indirect ToF, iToF) suits the cabin, while exterior sensing uses pulsed dToF or FMCW.

Principle. An amplitude-modulated continuous-wave (AMCW) ranger modulates the intensity of its light at a radio frequency fmf_m (Hz). It then measures the phase φ\varphi (rad) of the modulation envelope that comes back. This is indirect ToF (iToF), “indirect” because the delay is inferred from a phase rather than timed. The round trip 2R2R takes 2R/c2R/c, during which the modulation advances by a phase φ=2πfm(2R/c)\varphi=2\pi f_m\,(2R/c). Solving for RR gives the first relation in Eq. (36):

R=cφ4πfm,Ramb=c2fm,σR=c4πfmσφ.R=\frac{c\,\varphi}{4\pi f_m},\qquad R_{\mathrm{amb}}=\frac{c}{2f_m},\qquad \sigma_R=\frac{c}{4\pi f_m}\,\sigma_\varphi .(36)

Here RambR_{\mathrm{amb}} is the unambiguous range, the range at which φ\varphi reaches 2π2\pi and the phase starts to repeat, and σR\sigma_R is the range noise produced by an rms phase noise σφ\sigma_\varphi (rad).

  • Detection is incoherent. The phase of the optical carrier is thrown away, so laser linewidth does not matter, but every ambient photon adds shot noise.
  • FMCW (subsection 2) is the coherent counterpart. It sweeps the optical frequency and mixes the return with a local oscillator, which gives velocity directly and near-immunity to sunlight.
  • The phase repeats every RambR_{\mathrm{amb}}. Instruments therefore combine frequencies: a high one sets precision, and low ones count whole cycles.
  • Shot-noise scaling. Texas Instruments’ ToF design guide gives σR∝cne+nT2/(nmfmCd)\sigma_R\propto c\sqrt{n_e+n_T^2}/(n_m f_m C_d) [P, TI SBAU219D], i.e. by Eq. (36) a phase noise σφ∝ne+nT2/(Cdnm)\sigma_\varphi\propto\sqrt{n_e+n_T^2}/(C_d\,n_m). Here:
    • nmn_m is the number of modulated signal electrons;
    • nen_e is all electrons, including those from ambient light;
    • nTn_T is the pixel’s read noise (rms electrons);
    • CdC_d is the demodulation contrast, the fraction of the signal that the pixel actually separates by phase (between 0 and 1).
    The numerator is the noise: shot noise ne\sqrt{n_e} from every electron collected, plus read noise. The denominator is the useful phase signal. Ambient light therefore raises the noise without adding signal, and a higher fmf_m or contrast lowers the range noise directly.

The table evaluates Eq. (36) for typical modulation frequencies, at an assumed phase noise of 0.02 rad [E], i.e. a phase signal-to-noise ratio of 1/0.02=501/0.02=50.

fmf_m RambR_{\mathrm{amb}} c/(4πfm)c/(4\pi f_m) σR\sigma_R at σφ=0.02\sigma_\varphi=0.02 rad [E]
≈500 MHz (Kern Mekometer class) 0.3 m 0.048 m/rad ≈1 mm
100 MHz 1.5 m 0.24 m/rad ≈5 mm
20 MHz 7.5 m 1.2 m/rad ≈2.4 cm
3 MHz 50 m 8.0 m/rad ≈16 cm
≈0.41 MHz (implied by Z+F’s 365 m unambiguous range) 365 m 58 m/rad used only to count cycles

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Unambiguous range: Ramb=c/(2fm)R_{\mathrm{amb}}=c/(2f_m), e.g. 3.0×108/(2×100×106)=1.53.0\times10^8/(2\times100\times10^6)=1.5 m at 100 MHz; the same gives 0.3 m at 500 MHz, 7.5 m at 20 MHz and 50 m at 3 MHz.
  • Range per radian: c/(4πfm)c/(4\pi f_m), e.g. 3.0×108/(4π×100×106)=0.243.0\times10^8/(4\pi\times100\times10^6)=0.24 m/rad at 100 MHz, and likewise 0.048, 1.2 and 8.0 m/rad at 500, 20 and 3 MHz.
  • Precision: σR=[c/(4πfm)]σφ\sigma_R=[c/(4\pi f_m)]\,\sigma_\varphi with an assumed phase noise of σφ=0.02\sigma_\varphi=0.02 rad, e.g. 0.24m/rad×0.02rad=4.80.24\ {\mathrm{m/rad}}\times0.02\ {\mathrm{rad}}=4.8 mm ≈ 5 mm at 100 MHz; the other rows give 0.048×0.02=0.960.048\times0.02=0.96 mm, 1.2×0.02=2.41.2\times0.02=2.4 cm and 8.0×0.02=0.168.0\times0.02=0.16 m.
  • Z+F’s lowest frequency: Z+F’s datasheet calls its 365 m unambiguous range the “ambiguity interval”. Setting Ramb=365R_{\mathrm{amb}}=365 m in Ramb=c/(2fm)R_{\mathrm{amb}}=c/(2f_m) gives fm=3.0×108/(2×365)Hz=0.41f_m=3.0\times10^8/(2\times365)\ {\mathrm{Hz}}=0.41 MHz, and c/(4πfm)=Ramb/(2π)=365/(2π)=58c/(4\pi f_m)=R_{\mathrm{amb}}/(2\pi)=365/(2\pi)=58 m/rad.

Products. Surveying rangefinders (electronic distance meters, EDMs), phase-based laser scanners and iToF cameras all use this principle. §C1a compares them, describes the two pixel architectures of ToF chips (iToF and dToF) and sets out where usage draws the line of “lidar”.

Same physics, different photon budgets [E]. A phase scanner ranges to 365 m, with 0.3–3.7 mm noise at 50–100 m, while a ToF camera stops near 10 m. Three differences account for most of the gap.

  1. Ambient light per unit signal. Let Ω\Omega be the solid angle one detector or pixel sees (sr). Take a scanner at 10 mW average power that dwells 7.3 µs per point, the inverse of Z+F’s 136,719 pts/s: 10−2W×7.3×10−6s=7310^{-2}\ {\mathrm{W}}\times7.3\times10^{-6}\ {\mathrm{s}}=73 nJ per point. Its detector sees a matched 0.6 mrad full angle, twice the Z+F beam’s 0.3 mrad half-angle, so Ω=π×(0.3×10−3)2≈2.8×10−7\Omega=\pi\times(0.3\times10^{-3})^2\approx2.8\times10^{-7} sr. Take a VGA camera flooding 70° × 55° with 1 W for a 10 ms exposure: 1W×0.01s/307,200=331\ {\mathrm{W}}\times0.01\ {\mathrm{s}}/307{,}200=33 nJ per pixel, with Ω≈(1.222×0.960)/307,200≈3.8×10−6\Omega\approx(1.222\times0.960)/307{,}200\approx3.8\times10^{-6} sr per pixel. Here 70° and 55° are 1.222 and 0.960 rad, and their product, 1.17 sr, approximates the field’s solid angle; the exact solid angle of a 70° × 55° rectangular field, 1.07 sr, would give 3.5×10−63.5\times10^{-6} sr and lower the ratio below by about 9%.
    • The laser energy per point is similar.
    • Ambient light collected per unit signal scales as ΩTexp/Ept\Omega\,T_{\mathrm{exp}}/E_{\mathrm{pt}}, where TexpT_{\mathrm{exp}} is the time the detector integrates light for that point (the dwell of the scanner or the exposure of the camera; s) and EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} the laser energy spent on that point (J). That is 3.8×10−6×0.01/(33×10−9)≈1.23.8\times10^{-6}\times0.01/(33\times10^{-9})\approx1.2 sr·s/J for the camera against 2.8×10−7×7.3×10−6/(73×10−9)≈2.8×10−52.8\times10^{-7}\times7.3\times10^{-6}/(73\times10^{-9})\approx2.8\times10^{-5} sr·s/J for the scanner. TexpT_{\mathrm{exp}} cancels, because EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} is the laser power times TexpT_{\mathrm{exp}} (shared among the pixels, for the camera), so each figure is the solid angle over which the laser’s power is spread, divided by that power: 1.17sr/1W=1.171.17\ {\mathrm{sr}}/1\ {\mathrm{W}}=1.17 sr·s/J for the camera and 2.83×10−7sr/0.01W=2.83×10−52.83\times10^{-7}\ {\mathrm{sr}}/0.01\ {\mathrm{W}}=2.83\times10^{-5} sr·s/J for the scanner. The camera therefore collects about 4×1044\times10^4 times more sunlight per unit signal (1.17/(2.83×10−5)≈4.1×1041.17/(2.83\times10^{-5})\approx4.1\times10^4).
    • The cause is parallelism. The flood divides the laser energy among the pixels, but each pixel collects its own background for the whole exposure. A scanner’s detector looks at each direction only while the beam is there.
  2. Receiver aperture. Signal and background both scale with the receive-aperture area ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}}, so when background dominates, SNR scales as Arx\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}} (signal ∝Arx\propto A_{\mathrm{rx}} over noise ∝Arx\propto\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}, as in subsection 1). A scanner’s receiver is tens of millimetres across; a camera lens is a few millimetres [U].
  3. Modulation frequency and gain. Noise per radian scales as 1/fm1/f_m. A discrete APD with radio-frequency electronics can work at hundreds of MHz with near-full contrast. In-pixel demodulators run at tens of MHz up to about 200 MHz, with contrast below one; ST’s VD55H1 claims more than 85% at 200 MHz [T].

The scanner pays for all this in time: its scene must stay still for minutes. A camera must image a live scene in milliseconds, so it parallelizes and accepts the sunlight penalty.

Why long-range sensing uses pulses. Pulsed dToF (subsection 1) gates out ambient light the way a scanner’s short dwell does. Its precision is set by the pulse width and timing jitter, averaged over the detected photons, rather than by a modulation frequency that also fixes the unambiguous range. A histogram also separates multiple returns.

  • iToF’s own limits: it adds all paths into one phasor per pixel (a single amplitude and phase), so light bouncing off a floor or into a corner biases the depth instead of producing a second echo. The four or more sub-frames it needs also smear fast motion.
  • The split is the same everywhere. Precision surveying keeps phase ranging for millimetre accuracy at tens to hundreds of metres, and long-range scanners mostly use pulsed or waveform-digitizing ToF [U]. In cars, iToF works inside the cabin (gesture, driver and occupant monitoring; §B8), and exterior sensing is pulsed dToF or FMCW.

Sources: https://www.ti.com/lit/ug/sbau219d/sbau219d.pdf ; https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/time-of-flight-depth-image-sensor-has-0-5-megapixels/ ; https://www.imagesensors.org/Past%20Workshops/2024%20ISSW/Papers/R06.1.pdf ; https://geo3d.hr/sites/default/files/2018-06/Z+F%20IMAGER%205016_Datasheet.pdf ; https://www.zofre.de/en/laser-scanners/3d-laser-scanner ; https://www.slac.stanford.edu/econf/C8907312/papers/013.PDF

10. Link budget: loss versus range, the detection level, and how range scales

How far can a lidar see with a given laser energy per point and a given lens, and how much of that range survives a darker target, a dirty window or bad weather? This subsection answers both questions with one model. The model is built in three steps and then applied in three ways.

The three steps.

  1. How much light comes back (10.2). The link loss ℒ(R)\mathcal{L}(R) is the fraction of the transmitted light that the receiver can use from a target at range RR. It is derived for direct detection (the ToF receivers) and for coherent detection (FMCW), and plotted against range in Figure C0.10a.
  2. How much light is needed (10.3). Detection statistics give nreqn_{\mathrm{req}}, the mean number of signal photoelectrons per point that each receiver needs for a required detection probability at a fixed false-alarm rate (Figure C0.10b).
  3. Where the two meet (10.4). Converting nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} into a detection level ℒdet\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}, the smallest usable fraction, gives the maximum range as the crossing ℒ(Rmax)=ℒdet\mathcal{L}(R_{\max})=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}. These are the dashed lines and dots of Figure C0.10a.

The three applications. 10.5 shows what more energy per point, or a larger aperture, buys in range (Figure C0.10c). 10.6 asks how much margin each design keeps at shorter ranges, and what a darker target, a dirty or wet window, fog and rain then do to its range (Figure C0.10d). 10.7 turns that question around: it asks how much stronger than the weakest return the strongest returns get, and what that dynamic range does to each receiver. 10.8 tests the model against published systems, and 10.9 lists what the model leaves out. Before all of this, 10.1 states the assumptions and defines the symbols.

Part Question it answers Figure
10.1 Model, assumptions and symbols What is assumed, and what does each symbol mean? —
10.2 Link loss How much of the transmitted light can the receiver use? C0.10a (the curves)
10.3 Detection statistics How many photoelectrons does a reliable detection need? C0.10b
