Main results [E]:

  • Direct detection collects a fraction proportional to D2/R2D^2/R^2 at every range (10.2), with DD the aperture diameter and RR the range. A coherent (FMCW) receiver collects only the light in one spatial mode, so its collected fraction is flat out to the beam’s Rayleigh range and falls beyond it.
  • Equal apertures, constant gap (10.5). When each of the FMCW receiver’s two apertures (its four looks are two polarizations on each of two spatial modes, §C7a) is as large as the ToF lens and sized optimally for the coherent beam at each range, FMCW needs about 3.2 times the energy per point of SPAD ToF, whatever the range. Against the fixed 25 mm ToF lens of §C7a the factor is 4.1 at 200 m (10.5), close to the ≈4.2× of §C7a (0.303/0.0720.303/0.072 µJ, for a 20 mm FMCW beam and without clear-air loss). An ungated FMCW transmitter also emits during the two round trips of each point, 1.27 times its useful light at 200 m (10.1), so in emitted light §C7a’s ratio is 5.3× (0.384/0.0720.384/0.072).
  • The flat near field leaves FMCW little margin at short range (10.6). A direct-detection design that just reaches 200 m on a 10% target has 26 dB to spare at 10 m, while the best FMCW design has 3 dB. An extra 3 dB of loss, from a dirty window or a 5% target, therefore cuts that FMCW design’s reach to 27 m, and anything beyond 3.1 dB blinds it at every range. In fog of 200 m visibility its reach falls to 18 m, against 61 m for ToF. In heavy rain behind a wet window it falls to 50 m, against 147 m.
  • A smaller aperture buys the margin back with energy (10.6). An FMCW design that tolerates dark targets and fog as well as ToF does (a 7 mm aperture) needs five times the energy of the best FMCW design: 1.5 µJ per point against 303 nJ, or about twenty times the 74 nJ of the 25 mm ToF design (1,522/74=20.61{,}522/74=20.6). The best FMCW design already needs 4.1 times ToF’s energy here (303/74303/74), not 3.2 times, because the ToF lens (25 mm) is larger than FMCW’s 22 mm optimum. A wet window still costs it range, because water absorbs at 1,550 nm. What FMCW keeps in fog is its rejection of the backscatter from droplets near the sensor.
  • The same flat near field shrinks FMCW’s dynamic-range burden (10.7). Between a 10% target at 200 m and a retroreflective sign or white target at short range, the ToF design must span 56–82 dB of optical signal; a linear ToF receiver, whose photocurrent is proportional to optical power, would see twice that in dB at its amplifier. The best FMCW design must span about 45 dB, and because its beat current is proportional to the optical field, the square root of power, the electrical span stays 45 dB. This is why ToF vendors publish fixes for retroreflector blooming, ghosts and range bias, and why China’s lidar standard tests high-reflectivity ghosts.
  • The model agrees with published systems (10.8). Its coherent link equation reproduces Waymo’s design point to 0.1 dB and Pointcloud’s measured SNR to about 1 dB, and three measured systems show its flat near field. Its weakest input is efficiency: measured coherent chains reach 0.06–0.17, against the 0.25 used. For ToF no product publishes both laser energy and aperture; the published research sensors are consistent with the model given f/1-class lenses of 10–30 mm.

Figures and data. The script build/figures/link_budget_scaling.py draws the four figures and writes the numbers quoted here to link_budget_scaling_tables.txt. All numbers are [E], for a Lambertian target that fills the illuminated spot, at normal incidence and in clear air unless stated otherwise. The subsection joins subsections 1 (photon budget), 2 (FMCW), 7 (detection statistics) and 8 (weather) into one picture.

10.1 Model, assumptions and symbols

Assumptions. Every result below rests on the following conditions; 10.9 notes what changes when they fail.

  • Lambertian target. The target is perfectly diffuse, with a bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF, the ratio of reflected radiance to incident irradiance) of ρ/π\rho/\pi in every direction. This is invalid for glossy paint and for retroreflectors (signs, number plates), which return far more or far less toward the sensor, depending on angle.
  • Exponential (Rayleigh) speckle statistics. For coherent detection, the power in a single spatial mode is exponentially distributed from one look to the next (Rayleigh amplitude). Summing NspN_{\mathrm{sp}} independent speckles narrows the distribution (10.3).
  • Shot-noise-limited LO receiver. The coherent receiver’s noise is the shot noise of its local oscillator, with thermal (amplifier) noise and dark current neglected. This holds only approximately at the 105–125 °C of automotive temperature ratings; §C4c gives 82–94% of the shot-noise limit for Ge photodiodes at 125 °C. A receiver below the limit needs correspondingly more signal photoelectrons, which 10.6 treats as a fixed extra loss.
  • Ideal Gaussian beams. Transmit beam and LO are ideal TEM00 Gaussians (the fundamental, single-lobed transverse mode; M2=1M^2=1, where M2M^2 is the beam-quality factor, not the APD gain), with perfect mode matching and alignment between them. Real beams and misalignment lower the coherent signal below the computed value (10.9).
  • No turbulence. Atmospheric turbulence would distort the wavefront and lower heterodyne efficiency at long range (Frehlich and Kavaya 1991) [I].
  • Depolarizing target. The factor ½ in the coherent result assumes the target scrambles polarization, so only half its return lies in the LO’s polarization. A retroreflector largely preserves polarization, so the factor then differs.
  • Clear air and normal incidence. The target faces the sensor and fills the illuminated spot. The air is clear, except in 10.6, which adds fog and rain (subsection 8 treats weather for direct detection alone).

Symbols. Each symbol is also defined again where it is first used.

  • RR: range to the target. λ\lambda: wavelength. Eph=hν=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=h\nu=hc/\lambda: photon energy, with hh Planck’s constant and ν\nu the optical frequency (2.11×10−192.11\times10^{-19} J at 940 nm, 1.28×10−191.28\times10^{-19} J at 1,550 nm).
  • EptE_{\mathrm{pt}}: optical energy transmitted toward one point, summed over all shots of a point (ToF) or over the integration time TintT_{\mathrm{int}} of the up–down chirp pair (FMCW; subsection 2), i.e. Ept=PchTintE_{\mathrm{pt}}=P_{\mathrm{ch}}T_{\mathrm{int}} for a channel of constant optical power PchP_{\mathrm{ch}}. An ungated FMCW transmitter also emits during the two round trips, EptTdwell/TintE_{\mathrm{pt}}T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}} in all: for the §C7a central case at 200 m, 30 mW for Tdwell=12.67T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=12.67 µs, i.e. 0.30μJ×12.67/10=0.380.30\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times12.67/10=0.38 µJ. The link budget counts only EptE_{\mathrm{pt}}, the light that falls within the integration windows.
  • ρ\rho: Lambertian reflectance, here 0.1. A Lambertian surface that intercepts power PP radiates ρP/π\rho P/\pi per steradian along its normal.
  • DD: diameter of the receive lens (direct detection), or of the shared transmit–receive aperture (monostatic coherent). Arx=πD2/4A_{\mathrm{rx}}=\pi D^2/4.
  • PtxP_{\mathrm{tx}}: transmitted optical power. PhetP_{\mathrm{het}}: the signal a coherent receiver collects in its local oscillator’s (LO’s) spatial mode and polarization, expressed as an equivalent optical power.
  • AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}: the mode-equivalent collecting area of a coherent receiver (m²).
    • Definition. It is the area of an ideal direct-detection lens that would collect, from the same Lambertian target, the same signal power as the coherent receiver collects in its single LO mode. It takes the place of ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} in the link budget: Phet=PtxρAmode/(πR2)P_{\mathrm{het}}=P_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\rho A_{\mathrm{mode}}/(\pi R^2) before atmospheric loss.
    • Not a physical area. It depends on the range and on the beam, and is usually much smaller than the aperture: 63 mm² at 1,550 nm against the 491 mm² of a 25 mm aperture at 200 m. 10.2 derives it (Eqs. (39)–(41)).
  • Tatm=e−αRT_{\mathrm{atm}}=e^{-\alpha R}: one-way atmospheric transmission with extinction coefficient α\alpha (subsection 8; fog and rain in 10.6).
    • In clear air (Kim model, visibility 23 km, where the model’s exponent is qK=1.3q_{\mathrm{K}}=1.3), α=0.085\alpha=0.085 /km at 940 nm and 0.044 /km at 1,550 nm.
    • Tatm2T_{\mathrm{atm}}^2 then costs only 0.15 and 0.08 dB at 200 m.
  • η\eta: end-to-end efficiency from photons at the aperture to signal photoelectrons: optics × detector, and for coherent detection also × mixing. For a SPAD in sunlight the detector term includes the dead-time live fraction: η=0.5×0.37×0.885=0.164\eta=0.5\times0.37\times0.885=0.164 in the bright sun of 10.3. The coherent receiver’s mode and polarization factors are kept out of η\eta and put into AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}.
    • The FMCW value, 0.25, is a design value about 1.5× above the best coherent chain measured so far. Waymo’s lab chain measured 0.112 end to end, or 0.168 without its Hann window (Piggott et al. 2025, App. A) [P], and Pointcloud’s integrated array 0.057 once its amplifier noise is counted (Settembrini et al. 2026) [P]. With those values FMCW needs 1.5–2.2× (discrete fibre chain) or about 4.4× (integrated array) the energy per point quoted in this report.
  • nreqn_{\mathrm{req}}: mean signal photoelectrons per point needed for the required detection probability (10.3).
  • n‾\bar n: the mean number of signal photoelectrons actually obtained per point.
  • Coherent beam parameters:
    • w0w_0: the 1/e² intensity radius of the Gaussian beam at the aperture, its waist for a collimated beam; here w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D (10.2 explains the choice).
    • w(R)w(R): the 1/e² radius at the target.
    • zR=πw02/λz_R=\pi w_0^2/\lambda: the Rayleigh range, the distance over which a collimated Gaussian beam stays roughly its launched size before spreading.
    • t=1−e−2(D/2)2/w02=1−e−2×1.235=0.915t=1-e^{-2(D/2)^2/w_0^2}=1-e^{-2\times1.235}=0.915: the aperture-truncation factor, the fraction of the Gaussian’s power that passes a hard aperture of diameter DD. With w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D, (D/2)2/w02=0.25/0.2025=1.235(D/2)^2/w_0^2=0.25/0.2025=1.235. §C10.3b uses the same factor.

10.2 How much light comes back: the link loss (Figure C0.10a)

This step computes, for each receiver, the share of the transmitted light that it can use. Direct detection is simple: the lens collects whatever light from the lit spot falls on it. Coherent detection is subtler, because the receiver responds only to light in one spatial mode; the mode-equivalent area AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} puts the two receivers on the same footing. Figure C0.10a, at the end of this part, plots the results.

Definition of the link loss. The link loss ℒ\mathcal{L} is the fraction of the transmitted energy that reaches the receiver in a form it can use, before the detector efficiency. The mean signal per point is then n‾=ηEptEphℒ(R),\bar n=\frac{\eta\,E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}\,\mathcal{L}(R),(37) where Ept/EphE_{\mathrm{pt}}/E_{\mathrm{ph}} is the number of photons transmitted per point, ℒ(R)\mathcal{L}(R) the share of them the receiver can use and η\eta the share of those that become photoelectrons. The link loss in dB is −10log⁡10ℒ-10\log_{10}\mathcal{L}, so a larger number of dB means less light. Where the text says that a loss rises or falls, it means this dB value.

Direct detection: the lens collects the whole spot. The lit spot intercepts all the transmitted light and radiates ρEpt/π\rho E_{\mathrm{pt}}/\pi per steradian toward the sensor. A lens of area ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} subtends Arx/R2A_{\mathrm{rx}}/R^2 sr, so ℒDD(R)=ρArxπR2Tatm2=ρD24R2Tatm2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DD}}(R)=\frac{\rho\,A_{\mathrm{rx}}}{\pi R^2}\,T_{\mathrm{atm}}^2=\frac{\rho\,D^2}{4R^2}\,T_{\mathrm{atm}}^2 .(38) This is Eq. (31) of subsection 1 written as a fraction, with Arx=πD2/4A_{\mathrm{rx}}=\pi D^2/4.

  • Scope. This holds whatever the spot size, as long as the pixel sees the whole spot. It depends on wavelength only through TatmT_{\mathrm{atm}}.
  • Worked example: D=25D=25 mm and R=200R=200 m give 0.1×0.0252/(4×2002)=3.9×10−100.1\times0.025^2/(4\times200^2)=3.9\times10^{-10}, i.e. 94.1 dB. Clear air at 940 nm adds 0.15 dB, for 94.2 dB.

Coherent detection: one spatial mode and the mode-equivalent area. A heterodyne receiver responds only to light in the spatial mode (and polarization) of its local oscillator (LO). Three standard results give its effective collecting area.

  1. Antenna theorem [I: A. E. Siegman, Appl. Opt. 5, 1588 (1966)]. A single-mode receiver has an effective area Aeff(Ω)A_{\mathrm{eff}}(\Omega) for light arriving from direction Ω\Omega, with dΩd\Omega an element of solid angle (sr). It obeys ∫AeffdΩ=λ2\int A_{\mathrm{eff}}\,d\Omega=\lambda^2 per polarization: a single-mode receiver can have a large area or a wide field of view, but not both. This is the AΩ≈λ2A\Omega\approx\lambda^2 rule of §C7.
  2. Back-propagated LO [I: Siegman 1966; B. J. Rye, Appl. Opt. 18, 1390 (1979); R. G. Frehlich and M. J. Kavaya, Appl. Opt. 30, 5325 (1991)]. The angular pattern of AeffA_{\mathrm{eff}} is the LO mode propagated backwards from the detector, through the optics, to the target.
    • Let ĨB(𝐫)\tilde I_B(\mathbf r) be that back-propagated irradiance in the target plane, normalized so that ∫ĨBd2r=1\int\tilde I_B\,d^2r=1 (units m⁻²). Here 𝐫\mathbf r is the position in the target plane, measured from the beam axis, and d2rd^2r an element of target area.
    • Light from target point 𝐫\mathbf r arrives within a solid angle dΩ=d2r/R2d\Omega=d^2r/R^2 and sees Aeff(𝐫)=λ2R2ĨB(𝐫)A_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf r)=\lambda^2R^2\,\tilde I_B(\mathbf r).
    • This is consistent with result 1: ∫AeffdΩ=λ2∫ĨBd2r=λ2\int A_{\mathrm{eff}}\,d\Omega=\lambda^2\int\tilde I_B\,d^2r=\lambda^2.
  3. Diffuse target: patches add in power. A rough surface randomizes the optical phase from patch to patch, so on average over speckle their heterodyne powers add.
    • A patch d2rd^2r lit by irradiance IT(𝐫)I_T(\mathbf r) (the transmitted power per unit area arriving at the target, W/m²) radiates (ρ/π)ITd2r(\rho/\pi)\,I_T\,d^2r per steradian.
    • The receiver collects this over the area Aeff(𝐫)A_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf r) at distance RR, i.e. over Aeff/R2A_{\mathrm{eff}}/R^2 steradians.
    • Summing all patches, with Aeff/R2=λ2ĨBA_{\mathrm{eff}}/R^2=\lambda^2\tilde I_B from result 2: Phet=ρπλ2∫IT(𝐫)ĨB(𝐫)d2r.P_{\mathrm{het}}=\frac{\rho}{\pi}\,\lambda^2\int I_T(\mathbf r)\,\tilde I_B(\mathbf r)\,d^2r .(39)

Eq. (39) says that the coherent signal is the overlap of the transmitted spot with the receiver’s back-propagated mode. Writing the result in the direct-detection form, Phet=PtxρAmode/(πR2)P_{\mathrm{het}}=P_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\rho A_{\mathrm{mode}}/(\pi R^2), defines the mode-equivalent collecting area Amode=λ2R2∫IT(𝐫)PtxĨB(𝐫)d2r.A_{\mathrm{mode}}=\lambda^2R^2\int\frac{I_T(\mathbf r)}{P_{\mathrm{tx}}}\,\tilde I_B(\mathbf r)\,d^2r .(40)

Why the beam is launched with w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D. A Gaussian beam launched through a circular aperture of radius a=D/2a=D/2 faces a trade-off. A wide beam fills the aperture and diffracts least, but its edges are clipped; a narrow beam passes whole but spreads faster. The standard way to settle this is to maximize the far-field on-axis intensity at a fixed launched power. The launched field is E0e−r2/w02E_0e^{-r^2/w_0^2}, where rr is the distance from the beam axis and E0∝P/w0E_0\propto\sqrt{P}/w_0 for a beam of power PP. The far-field on-axis amplitude is the integral of this field over the aperture: ∫0aE0e−r2/w022πrdr=πw02E0(1−e−a2/w02)\int_0^aE_0e^{-r^2/w_0^2}\,2\pi r\,dr=\pi w_0^2E_0\,(1-e^{-a^2/w_0^2}). At fixed PP it therefore scales as w0(1−e−a2/w02)w_0\,(1-e^{-a^2/w_0^2}). Setting its derivative with respect to w0w_0 to zero gives ex2=1+2x2e^{x^2}=1+2x^2 with x=a/w0x=a/w_0. The solution is a/w0=1.12a/w_0=1.12, i.e. w0=0.89a≈0.45Dw_0=0.89a\approx0.45D. At the optimum the aperture passes 1−e−2(a/w0)2≈92%1-e^{-2(a/w_0)^2}\approx92\% of the power, or 91.5% (t=0.915t=0.915) at exactly 0.45D0.45D. By reciprocity the same choice maximizes the on-axis response of the matched single-mode receiver, so one value serves transmit and receive.

In a monostatic system (one aperture shared by transmitter and receiver) the transmitted beam and the back-propagated LO are the same Gaussian at the target, g(r)=2πw2e−2r2/w2g(r)=\frac{2}{\pi w^2}e^{-2r^2/w^2} (normalized to unit power), where r=|𝐫|r=\lvert\mathbf r\rvert and w=w(R)w=w(R) is the beam’s 1/e² radius at the target. Then ∫g2d2r=4π2w4⋅πw24=1πw2\int g^2\,d^2r=\frac{4}{\pi^2w^4}\cdot\frac{\pi w^2}{4}=\frac{1}{\pi w^2}. Two further factors complete the result:

  • the aperture passes a fraction tt of the Gaussian on transmit and again on receive, t2t^2 in all;
  • a depolarizing target sends only half its light into the LO’s polarization, a factor ½.

Amode(R)=t2λ2R22πw(R)2,ℒcoh(R)=ρAmodeπR2Tatm2=ρt2λ22π2w(R)2Tatm2.\boxed{A_{\mathrm{mode}}(R)=\frac{t^2\,\lambda^2R^2}{2\pi\,w(R)^2}},\qquad \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coh}}(R)=\frac{\rho\,A_{\mathrm{mode}}}{\pi R^2}\,T_{\mathrm{atm}}^2=\frac{\rho\,t^2\lambda^2}{2\pi^2\,w(R)^2}\,T_{\mathrm{atm}}^2 .(41)

This is the monostatic link equation of Piggott et al. (Waymo) [P], written as an area. §C7b (subsection 1(b)) and §C10.3b use it, and so do the report’s scripts.

  • What it assumes (see the assumptions in 10.1): perfect alignment and mode matching, truncation treated to first order as a power factor on each pass, no atmospheric turbulence (which reduces heterodyne efficiency at long range; Frehlich and Kavaya 1991 [I]), and a fully depolarizing Lambertian target.
  • Physical reading. The single-mode receiver collects the target’s radiance times λ2\lambda^2. Concentrating the light on a smaller spot raises the radiance, and with it the signal.

A collimated beam: flat near field, D2/R2D^2/R^2 far field and a best aperture. A collimated beam (waist at the aperture) spreads as w(R)2=w02[1+(R/zR)2].w(R)^2=w_0^2\,[1+(R/z_R)^2] .(42) With Eq. (42), ℒcoh\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coh}} in Eq. (41) has three regimes:

  • Near field (R≪zRR\ll z_R): w≈w0w\approx w_0, so ℒcoh→ρt2λ2/(2π2w02)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coh}}\to\rho t^2\lambda^2/(2\pi^2w_0^2), independent of range. The spot does not grow, so its radiance, and what one mode collects, stays constant. Here a larger aperture is worse (∝1/D2\propto1/D^2) and a longer wavelength better (∝λ2\propto\lambda^2).
  • Far field (R≫zRR\gg z_R): w→λR/(πw0)w\to\lambda R/(\pi w_0), so ℒcoh→ρt2w02/(2R2)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coh}}\to\rho t^2w_0^2/(2R^2). This is the direct-detection D2/R2D^2/R^2 law, reduced by a factor 2t2(0.45)2=0.342t^2(0.45)^2=0.34 (−4.7 dB). The factor is the ratio of ρt2w02/(2R2)\rho t^2w_0^2/(2R^2) to ρD2/(4R2)\rho D^2/(4R^2) from Eq. (38), with w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D.
  • Best collimated aperture at each range. w2=w02+(λR/πw0)2w^2=w_0^2+(\lambda R/\pi w_0)^2 is smallest, at 2λR/π2\lambda R/\pi, when w02=λR/πw_0^2=\lambda R/\pi, i.e. when the Rayleigh range equals the target range. Hence ℒenv(R)=ρt2λ4πRTatm2,Dopt(R)=λR/π0.45.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{env}}(R)=\frac{\rho\,t^2\lambda}{4\pi R}\,T_{\mathrm{atm}}^2,\qquad D_{\mathrm{opt}}(R)=\frac{\sqrt{\lambda R/\pi}}{0.45}.(43) Here ℒenv\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{env}} is the envelope, the best link loss any collimated aperture can reach at range RR, and DoptD_{\mathrm{opt}} the aperture that reaches it; dividing the optimal waist λR/π\sqrt{\lambda R/\pi} by 0.45 converts it into a diameter, because w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D.
    • This envelope falls only as 1/R1/R.
    • At the optimum, Amode=t2λR/4=t2(0.45)2Arx=0.17ArxA_{\mathrm{mode}}=t^2\lambda R/4=t^2(0.45)^2A_{\mathrm{rx}}=0.17\,A_{\mathrm{rx}}.

Worked numbers at 1,550 nm, D=25D=25 mm:

  • w0=0.45×25mm=11.25w_0=0.45\times25\ {\mathrm{mm}}=11.25 mm and zR=π(0.01125)2/1.55×10−6=257z_R=\pi(0.01125)^2/1.55\times10^{-6}=257 m. The factor 0.838 below is t2=0.91532t^2=0.9153^2.
  • The near-field level is 0.1×0.838×(1.55×10−6)2/(2π2×0.011252)=8.1×10−110.1\times0.838\times(1.55\times10^{-6})^2/(2\pi^2\times0.01125^2)=8.1\times10^{-11}, i.e. 100.9 dB.
  • At 200 m, w=11.251+(200/257)2=14.3w=11.25\sqrt{1+(200/257)^2}=14.3 mm, so Amode=63A_{\mathrm{mode}}=63 mm² and ℒcoh=0.1×6.3×10−5/(π×2002)=5.0×10−11\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coh}}=0.1\times6.3\times10^{-5}/(\pi\times200^2)=5.0\times10^{-11}: 103.0 dB, or 103.1 dB with clear air.
  • Envelope at 200 m: 0.1×0.838×1.55×10−6/(4π×200)=5.2×10−110.1\times0.838\times1.55\times10^{-6}/(4\pi\times200)=5.2\times10^{-11} (102.9 dB), with Dopt=1.55×10−6×200/π/0.45=22D_{\mathrm{opt}}=\sqrt{1.55\times10^{-6}\times200/\pi}/0.45=22 mm.

Figure C0.10a. Link loss versus range for a 10% Lambertian target in clear air; a larger number of dB means less light. The shaded band marks 200–300 m, the long-range window that §C7a examines.

  • (a) Direct detection with 10, 25 and 50 mm lenses.
  • (b) Coherent detection with collimated monostatic beams of 10, 25 and 50 mm at 1,550 nm, and 25 mm at 1,310 nm. The dash-dot curve is the best collimated aperture at each range, and the grey line the 25 mm direct-detection reference.
  • In both panels the dashed horizontal lines are the detection levels derived in 10.4 (Eq. (49)), and the dots mark where the curves cross them, i.e. the maximum ranges. 10.4 reads the crossings.

Reading Figure C0.10a: the shapes of the curves [E]:

  • Direct detection is a straight line on these axes, rising 20 dB per decade of range for every lens. Doubling the lens diameter lowers the loss by 6 dB at every range; going from 10 to 25 mm gains 20log⁡102.5=8.020\log_{10}2.5=8.0 dB (at 10 m, 76.0 against 68.1 dB).
  • Coherent detection is flat, then rises. Each curve is level out to about its Rayleigh range (41, 257 and 1,026 m for 10, 25 and 50 mm) and rises 20 dB per decade beyond it, 4.7 dB above (worse than) the direct-detection line of the same aperture.
  • In the near field a smaller aperture collects more. The plateaus lie at 93.0, 100.9 and 107.0 dB for 10, 25 and 50 mm: the loss grows as D2D^2. Two collimated apertures collect equally where their beams have the same radius, which by Eq. (42) happens at R=πw0,1w0,2/λ=zR,1zR,2R=\pi w_{0,1}w_{0,2}/\lambda=\sqrt{z_{R,1}z_{R,2}}. That is 103 m for 10 and 25 mm, and 513 m for 25 and 50 mm, just beyond the plot. Below that range the smaller aperture wins.
  • The envelope touches each curve at that aperture’s Rayleigh range, where the aperture is optimal. Its loss rises only 10 dB per decade (1/R1/R), because the best aperture grows as R\sqrt R.
  • At 1,310 nm the 25 mm plateau is 1.5 dB higher (102.4 dB), because the near-field level scales as λ2\lambda^2.

10.3 How much light is needed: detection statistics (Figure C0.10b)

A detection is a decision made in one range bin (ToF) or one frequency bin (FMCW): the signal there must cross a threshold that noise alone crosses only rarely. This part finds how many signal photoelectrons per point, on average, make that decision succeed with a given probability, with both receivers held to the same rule.

The detection rule. A point must be detected with probability PD=0.9P_D=0.9, and noise may produce at most PFA,pt=10−3P_{FA,{\mathrm{pt}}}=10^{-3} false points per point, counted over the whole range the receiver searches (0–300 m here).

  • Why per point, not per bin. The two receivers search different numbers of cells. A ToF histogram has 2,000 time bins over 300 m, while an FMCW receiver searches ≈2,450 frequency bins in one chirp ramp and a further window in the other. A common per-bin false-alarm probability would give them different false-point rates. Subsection 7 uses the same per-point budget, but with 1,000 bins (so 10−610^{-6} per bin) and a daylight background of one count per bin, for which an ideal counter needs ≈13 signal counts. The 2,000 bins and the 1.62 background counts per bin of the §C7a model raise this to 15.0 here.
  • What it allows. At 10 Mpts/s, 10−310^{-3} per point is 10410^{4} false points per second before any filtering; products remove most of them with neighbour-consistency checks (subsection 7).
  • Per-bin probability. The per-bin false-alarm probability pp then follows from the number of bins each receiver searches.

Photon counting (SPAD histogram). A pixel that sums hundreds of speckles sees a non-fading signal, so signal and background counts are Poisson.

  • Rule: the histogram has Nbins=2,000N_{\mathrm{bins}}=2{,}000 bins of 1 ns over 0–300 m, so each bin may false-alarm with probability p=PFA,pt/Nbins=5×10−7p=P_{FA,{\mathrm{pt}}}/N_{\mathrm{bins}}=5\times10^{-7}. With background mean bb per bin, the threshold nthn_{\mathrm{th}} is the smallest count with P(N≥nth∣b)≤pP(N\ge n_{\mathrm{th}}\mid b)\le p. Here P(N≥n∣μ)P(N\ge n\mid\mu) is the probability that a Poisson count NN of mean μ\mu is at least nn, and ss is the mean signal count in the echo’s bin. Then PD=P(N≥nth∣s+b)=γ(nth,s+b)Γ(nth).P_D=P(N\ge n_{\mathrm{th}}\mid s+b)=\frac{\gamma(n_{\mathrm{th}},\,s+b)}{\Gamma(n_{\mathrm{th}})}.(44) The special functions are:
    • Γ(n)=∫0∞un−1e−udu\Gamma(n)=\int_0^\infty u^{n-1}e^{-u}\,du, the gamma function, which equals (n−1)!(n-1)! for a whole number nn;
    • γ(n,x)=∫0xun−1e−udu\gamma(n,x)=\int_0^x u^{n-1}e^{-u}\,du, the lower incomplete gamma function, the same integral stopped at xx;
    • their ratio γ(n,x)/Γ(n)\gamma(n,x)/\Gamma(n), the regularized lower incomplete gamma function, which rises from 0 to 1 as xx grows. It equals the Poisson tail P(N≥n∣x)P(N\ge n\mid x), which is why it appears here.
  • Night, b=0.01b=0.01: P(N≥2∣0.01)=5.0×10−5P(N\ge2\mid0.01)=5.0\times10^{-5} is too high and P(N≥3∣0.01)=1.7×10−7P(N\ge3\mid0.01)=1.7\times10^{-7} passes, so nth=3n_{\mathrm{th}}=3.
  • Bright sun, b=1.62b=1.62: P(N≥11∣1.62)=1.15×10−6P(N\ge11\mid1.62)=1.15\times10^{-6} fails and P(N≥12∣1.62)=1.54×10−7P(N\ge12\mid1.62)=1.54\times10^{-7} passes, so nth=12n_{\mathrm{th}}=12.
  • Where b=1.62b=1.62 comes from [E]. It is the bright-sun background of the §C7a ToF model, built from the equations of §C6(d):
    • Eq. (89) gives rbg=2.97×108r_{\mathrm{bg}}=2.97\times10^{8} counts per second per macro-pixel for a fully sunlit scene of reflectance 0.9, at 940 nm behind a 10 nm filter and at PDE 0.3. The macro-pixel sees 0.05° × 0.05° (Ωpix=7.62×10−7\Omega_{\mathrm{pix}}=7.62\times10^{-7} sr, the IMX479 grid of subsection 5), and §C6(d) takes E⊙≈0.39E_\odot\approx0.39 W m⁻² nm⁻¹ at 940 nm, so with Eph=2.11×10−19E_{\mathrm{ph}}=2.11\times10^{-19} J and the 25 mm aperture Eq. (89) reads (0.39/2.11×10−19)×10×(0.9/π)×7.62×10−7×4.91×10−4×0.5×0.3=2.97×108(0.39/2.11\times10^{-19})\times10\times(0.9/\pi)\times7.62\times10^{-7}\times4.91\times10^{-4}\times0.5\times0.3=2.97\times10^{8} s⁻¹. The same SPADs count background and signal, so at the model’s PDE of 0.37 the rate is 2.97×108×0.37/0.3=3.66×1082.97\times10^{8}\times0.37/0.3=3.66\times10^{8} s⁻¹.
    • The central case takes half of that, rbg=1.83×108r_{\mathrm{bg}}=1.83\times10^{8} s⁻¹: a sunlit scene of reflectance ≈0.45, or a pixel whose view is only half filled by bright surfaces. The full value is the model’s high case.
    • Eq. (90) gives the dead fraction. The model treats Sony’s SPADs as paralyzable [E]. The development chip’s measured ceiling of 60 Mcps matches the 1/(eτd)=611/(e\tau_d)=61 Mcps of a paralyzable counter with a 6 ns dead time (ee is Euler’s number), the behaviour of passive recharge; the IMX459 press release, however, says active recharge, and the product may differ from the development chip (§C5a). A paralyzable SPAD is live only if no photon arrived during the last τd\tau_d, its dead time. Each of the macro-pixel’s nine SPADs (a 3×3 group, §C5a) counts r=1.83×108/9=2.03×107r=1.83\times10^{8}/9=2.03\times10^{7} s⁻¹, so rτd=0.122r\tau_d=0.122 for τd=6\tau_d=6 ns, the live fraction is e−0.122=0.885e^{-0.122}=0.885 and fdead=0.115f_{\mathrm{dead}}=0.115. A non-paralyzable SPAD would instead be dead a fraction 0.122/1.122=0.1090.122/1.122=0.109 of the time (the other form of Eq. (90)), i.e. live 0.891. That would raise bb only to 1.83×108×10−9×10×0.891=1.631.83\times10^{8}\times10^{-9}\times10\times0.891=1.63 and leave the threshold at 12 counts, so an ideal counter would need 14.97 signal counts rather than 14.98. Its larger live fraction would lower the energy per point by under 1% (0.885/0.891=0.9930.885/0.891=0.993).
    • Eq. (105) of §C7b, multiplied by the live fraction 1−fdead1-f_{\mathrm{dead}}, gives the counts in one bin of width Δtbin=1\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}=1 ns, summed over the Nshots=10N_{\mathrm{shots}}=10 shots of a point: b=rbgΔtbinNshots(1−fdead)=1.83×108×10−9×10×0.885=1.62b=r_{\mathrm{bg}}\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}\,N_{\mathrm{shots}}\,(1-f_{\mathrm{dead}})=1.83\times10^{8}\times10^{-9}\times10\times0.885=1.62.
    • A macro-pixel listens 20.8 µs per point, the column period of a scan of 2,400 columns at 20 frames per second (Sony’s IMX479, §C6). That leaves time for about ten shots of 2.08 µs, each longer than the 2 µs round trip to 300 m (§C6, §C7a). Over those 20.8 µs the same rate gives 1.83×108×20.8×10−6×0.885≈3,3701.83\times10^{8}\times20.8\times10^{-6}\times0.885\approx3{,}370 background events; with the 21.7 signal counts of 10.4 that is ≈3,390 events per point, the event count of the §C7a electronics budget.
    • The dead time blinds the SPADs to signal photons as well: only the live fraction 0.885 of the echo can be counted, so the §C7a model multiplies the SPAD’s signal efficiency by it: optics transmission 0.5 × PDE 0.37 × live fraction 0.885, i.e. 0.5×0.37×0.885=0.1640.5\times0.37\times0.885=0.164.

Coherent detection in one frequency bin (FMCW building blocks). After the FFT, the power in one frequency bin is compared with a threshold.

  • Normalization: the noise (LO shot noise) is set to unit mean, so noise-only power in a bin is exponential and exceeds a threshold xx with probability e−xe^{-x}. A per-bin false-alarm probability pp therefore sets the threshold xth=−ln⁡px_{\mathrm{th}}=-\ln p. In a shot-noise-limited receiver the mean signal-to-noise ratio equals n‾\bar n (subsection 2), so n‾\bar n is also the signal power in these units.
  • This noise is quantum, not background. It is the shot noise of heterodyne detection: every FFT bin searched carries about one photoelectron of it, whereas a ToF bin at night holds 0.01 background counts.
  • Steady, non-fading target: PD=Q1(2n‾,2xth),P_D=Q_1\!\left(\sqrt{2\bar n},\sqrt{2x_{\mathrm{th}}}\right),(45) where Q1(u,v)Q_1(u,v) is Marcum’s Q function: the probability that the envelope of a steady tone of amplitude uu plus Gaussian noise (unit variance per quadrature) exceeds a threshold vv. The factors of 2 convert the unit-mean power scale into that amplitude scale.
  • One speckle (Rayleigh amplitude, exponential intensity; Swerling I, Eq. (35) of subsection 7 with SNR¯=n‾\overline{\mathrm{SNR}}=\bar n): PD=p1/(1+n‾).P_D=p^{1/(1+\bar n)} .(46)
  • NspN_{\mathrm{sp}} independent speckles summed incoherently (polarization, wavelength or spatial diversity; each is one look, taken by its own coherent receiver. The model’s four looks are two polarizations on each of two spatial modes, received through two equal apertures, so each collects the full ℒcoh\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coh}} from the same transmitted energy, §C7a), with n‾\bar n split equally among them:
    • the noise-only sum is Gamma-distributed, so the threshold xNspx_{N_{\mathrm{sp}}} solves Q(Nsp,xNsp)=pQ(N_{\mathrm{sp}},x_{N_{\mathrm{sp}}})=p, where Q(n,x)=1−γ(n,x)/Γ(n)Q(n,x)=1-\gamma(n,x)/\Gamma(n) is the regularized upper incomplete gamma function, the probability that a sum of nn independent unit-mean exponential variables exceeds xx;
    • each speckle’s power, signal plus noise, is then exponential with mean 1+n‾/Nsp1+\bar n/N_{\mathrm{sp}}, so PD=Q(Nsp,xNsp1+n‾/Nsp).P_D=Q\!\left(N_{\mathrm{sp}},\,\frac{x_{N_{\mathrm{sp}}}}{1+\bar n/N_{\mathrm{sp}}}\right).(47)

An FMCW point: both ramps, over the whole range. Eqs. (45)–(47) put all the photons in one bin. An FMCW point needs more, because a triangular chirp measures it with an up-ramp and a down-ramp (subsection 2): range and radial velocity follow only when the echo’s peak is found in both, at fup=fb−fDf_{\mathrm{up}}=f_b-f_D and fdown=fb+fDf_{\mathrm{down}}=f_b+f_D, where fbf_b is the beat frequency set by range and fDf_D the Doppler shift (subsection 2).

  • The photons are split. Each ramp collects half of the point’s photoelectrons, n‾/2\bar n/2.
  • The fading is common. Target and beam do not change within the 12.67 µs dwell of the two ramps (10 µs of integration plus the two 1.33 µs round trips at 200 m, subsection 2), so both see the same speckle and only their noise is independent. A fade therefore removes the peak from both ramps at once; it does not average out between them.
  • Two searches. The up-ramp peak must be found among all NbN_b bins the beat can occupy, and the down-ramp peak within the window of NwN_w bins around it that the velocity range allows. For the §C7a chirp (1 GHz swept over the 5 µs useful window of each ramp, up and down, so 200 kHz bins; 300 m; ±70 m/s):
    • Nb=(fb,max+fD,max)Tu=2,450N_b=(f_{b,\max}+f_{D,\max})\,T_u=2{,}450, where Tu=5T_u=5 µs is the useful window of one ramp, fb,max=400f_{b,\max}=400 MHz the range beat at 300 m and fD,max=90f_{D,\max}=90 MHz the Doppler shift at 70 m/s. Equivalently Nb=(300m)/ΔR+fD,maxTu=2,000+450N_b=(300\ {\mathrm{m}})/\Delta R+f_{D,\max}T_u=2{,}000+450, where ΔR=c/(2B)=0.15\Delta R=c/(2B)=0.15 m is the range resolution of the chirp’s bandwidth B=1B=1 GHz. §C7a’s digitizer takes 2.5 samples per bin in each ramp, so its Eq. (102) counts NADC=5Nb≈12,300N_{\mathrm{ADC}}=5N_b\approx12{,}300 samples per point.
    • Nw=4fD,maxTu=1,800N_w=4f_{D,\max}T_u=1{,}800: the down-ramp peak sits 2fD2f_D from the up-ramp peak, and 2fD2f_D spans ±180 MHz.
  • False points and detection. A false point needs noise to cross the threshold in the up-ramp search (probability p1p_1 per bin) and again in the down-ramp window (p2p_2 per bin). The false-point rate and the detection probability are then PFA,pt≈Nbp1Nwp2,PD=∫0∞[QNsp(n‾G/Nsp,2x)]2GNsp−1e−GΓ(Nsp)dG.\begin{aligned}P_{FA,{\mathrm{pt}}}&\approx N_b\,p_1\,N_w\,p_2,\\ P_D&=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\left[Q_{N_{\mathrm{sp}}}\!\left(\sqrt{\bar nG/N_{\mathrm{sp}}},\,\sqrt{2x}\right)\right]^2\dfrac{G^{N_{\mathrm{sp}}-1}e^{-G}}{\Gamma(N_{\mathrm{sp}})}\,dG .\end{aligned}(48)
    • Thresholds. Splitting the budget evenly gives p1=p2=p=PFA,pt/(NbNw)=10−3/(2,450×1,800)=1.5×10−5p_1=p_2=p=\sqrt{P_{FA,{\mathrm{pt}}}/(N_bN_w)}=\sqrt{10^{-3}/(2{,}450\times1{,}800)}=1.5\times10^{-5}; the best uneven split changes the results by less than 0.1%. The threshold xx in each ramp solves Q(Nsp,x)=pQ(N_{\mathrm{sp}},x)=p, as in Eq. (47): x=−ln⁡p=11.1x=-\ln p=11.1 for one look and 18.2 for four.
    • Symbols. GG is the speckle power gain summed over the NspN_{\mathrm{sp}} looks, each look’s gain being exponential with unit mean; the sum is Gamma-distributed with the density shown, which for one look is e−Ge^{-G}. Each ramp then holds a signal power n‾G/(2Nsp)\bar nG/(2N_{\mathrm{sp}}) spread over its NspN_{\mathrm{sp}} looks. QN(a,b)Q_N(a,b) is the generalized Marcum Q function: the probability that the summed power of NN bins of unit-mean noise, carrying a total signal power a2/2a^2/2, exceeds b2/2b^2/2. Eq. (48) uses it with N=NspN=N_{\mathrm{sp}}, one bin per look; for N=1N=1 it is the Q1Q_1 of Eq. (45).
    • Reading. The square is the two ramps’ independent noise, and the integral averages over their common fading. A steady target does not fade, so for it PD=[Q1(n‾,2x)]2P_D=[Q_1(\sqrt{\bar n},\sqrt{2x})]^2 with x=−ln⁡px=-\ln p.

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Method: each entry solves the matching PDP_D expression numerically (script): Eq. (44) for photon counting, with n‾=s\bar n=s, and Eq. (48) for the FMCW rows, with the thresholds above.
  • Worked check, bright sun: s=14.98s=14.98 puts the total mean at s+b=14.98+1.62=16.60s+b=14.98+1.62=16.60, and a Poisson count of mean 16.60 reaches 12 with probability 0.90.
  • Worked check, one look: in Eq. (48) the common fade dominates. Both ramps cross their thresholds roughly when the speckle gain exceeds 2x/n‾2x/\bar n, which for one look happens with probability e−2x/n‾e^{-2x/\bar n}. Setting that to 0.9 gives n‾≈2×11.1/0.105=211\bar n\approx2\times11.1/0.105=211; the noise in each ramp raises the exact value to 259.
  • More looks: eight looks need 82.4 photoelectrons. The requirement approaches the steady target’s 39.1 only slowly as the number of looks grows.

Figure C0.10b. Detection probability versus mean signal photoelectrons per point, with at most 10−310^{-3} false points per point over a 0–300 m search.

  • Solid: photon counting at night and in bright sun (2,000 bins, Eq. (44)). Dashed: FMCW with the echo’s peak found in both chirp ramps (Eq. (48)), for a steady target, four summed looks and one look.
  • Dots and numbers mark PD=0.9P_D=0.9. The dotted verticals are the photoelectron counts used in the §C7a model: 21.7 for ToF (10.4) and 120 for FMCW (four looks).

Reading Figure C0.10b [E]:

  • ToF: the model’s 21.7 counts keep a ×1.45 implementation margin over the 15.0 that an ideal counter needs in bright sun (nreq=1.45×14.98=21.7n_{\mathrm{req}}=1.45\times14.98=21.7). The dead time is not part of this margin, because it is counted in the SPAD’s efficiency (the live fraction above, §C7a(a)). The margin covers a return spread over about two bins, which needs 18.1 counts summed over both (×1.21: the two bins hold 2b=3.242b=3.24 background counts, which raises the threshold to 16), and leaves ×1.20 for pile-up distortion (§C6) and other implementation losses. In the model’s high case, a fully sunlit scene of reflectance 0.9 (rbg=3.66×108r_{\mathrm{bg}}=3.66\times10^{8} s⁻¹, live fraction 0.784, b=2.87b=2.87, nth=15n_{\mathrm{th}}=15), the ideal counter needs 17.3.
  • FMCW: the model’s 120 photoelectrons over four looks carry a 1.36× margin over the ideal 88.5, close to ToF’s 1.45×. They give PD=0.96P_D=0.96 with four looks, 0.90 with two and 0.80 with one.
  • Waymo’s figure is a one-ramp figure. Waymo’s 50 photons per detection, 45 photoelectrons at its quantum efficiency of 0.9, for 90% detection with four averaged speckles at 10−610^{-6} per bin [P] match one ramp searched in full, which needs 47.3 under the rule here (10−310^{-3} false points over 2,450 bins, i.e. 4.1×10−74.1\times10^{-7} per bin) and 44.9 at Waymo’s own 10−610^{-6} per bin (10.8). Requiring the peak in both ramps raises this to 88.5.
  • Where FMCW’s extra photons go (four looks, 88.5 against the counter’s 15.0 in bright sun):
    • the noise floor, ×1.5: even a steady target in one fully searched ramp needs 21.9, 1.46 times the counter in bright sun (21.9/15.021.9/15.0). Each of the 2,450 bins carries one photoelectron of shot noise, and the threshold must clear the largest of them; the counter’s threshold only has to clear the Poisson tail of 1.62 counts;
    • both ramps, ×1.8: splitting the photons and passing two thresholds raises the steady target to 39.1;
    • fading, ×2.3: four looks raise it to 88.5. One look would raise it to 259, ×6.6.
  • Curve shapes: photon counting has the steepest curves. Once the mean clears the threshold, a non-fading Poisson signal almost always crosses it. Speckle fading makes the coherent curves shallow: the median (PD=0.5P_D=0.5) is 36–39 photoelectrons with one, two or four looks, but reaching 90% costs up to 7× the median (259 against 38.2 with one look). At the median more looks do not help: two looks need 36.2 and four need 39.0, against 38.2 for one, because the summed noise of four looks needs a higher threshold (18.2 against 11.1), which offsets their narrower fading.

The FFT is nearly the limit [E]. For a tone of unknown frequency and phase in white noise, the peak of the FFT power spectrum (the periodogram) is the maximum-likelihood, or generalized likelihood-ratio, detector [I: S. M. Kay, Fundamentals of Statistical Signal Processing, Vol. II: Detection Theory (Prentice Hall, 1998)]. No algorithm extracts more from one ramp without prior information. Two costs remain:

  • Straddle (scalloping) loss. A beat that falls between FFT bins loses signal: 1.1 dB on average and 3.9 dB at worst with a rectangular window, and 0.3 and 0.9 dB with twofold zero padding. This belongs to the 1.36× implementation margin.
  • The search. The threshold rises with the logarithm of the number of cells searched. A joint search, neighbour checks or a tracking window lower the requirement by 8–33%, for both receivers:
Search (FMCW: four looks; ToF: bright sun) FMCW n‾\bar n for PD=0.9P_D=0.9 ToF ss for PD=0.9P_D=0.9
Full search (the rule above) 88.5 15.0
Joint search over all NbNw=4.4×106N_bN_w=4.4\times10^{6} up–down pairs, summing both ramps 77.8 —
10−210^{-2} false points per point, pruned by neighbour checks 81.6 13.8
Tracking window of 20 bins per ramp around a predicted return 59.6 11.4
Known cell (no search; the ideal bound) 32.2 10.2
  • What the table shows. The joint search is the optimal detector for an unknown range and velocity, and the two-stage search of Eq. (48) needs only 14% more. Even a known cell needs 32.2 photoelectrons with four looks (13.8 for a steady target, 77.1 for one look), well above the counter’s 10.2. Fading and heterodyne shot noise are physics, not algorithm. The model therefore uses the full search for both receivers and treats these gains as sensitivities.

What this means for the comparison [E]. Under one rule, a SPAD ToF receiver in bright sun needs 15–22 counts per point (the ideal 15.0 and the model’s 21.7), and an FMCW receiver 88–120 photoelectrons with four looks (259 with one). The coherent receiver’s freedom from background does not lower its photon requirement: even a steady coherent target needs more (39.1) than an ideal counter in bright sun (15.0), and speckle fading adds to that. 10.4 turns the model’s counts, 21.7 for SPAD ToF and 120 for FMCW (30 in each of four looks), into detection levels.

10.4 Where they meet: the detection level and the maximum range (Figure C0.10a)

This step turns the photoelectron requirement of 10.3 into a level on the link-loss axis of Figure C0.10a. The maximum range can then be read off the figure as the range where a loss curve crosses that level.

The detection level. Setting the mean signal n‾\bar n equal to the required nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} in Eq. (37) gives the largest loss a point can tolerate, ℒdet=nreqEphηEpt,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}=\frac{n_{\mathrm{req}}\,E_{\mathrm{ph}}}{\eta\,E_{\mathrm{pt}}},(49) and the maximum range RmaxR_{\max} solves ℒ(Rmax)=ℒdet\mathcal{L}(R_{\max})=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}. “Largest loss” means the smallest usable fraction: a link with ℒ\mathcal{L} below ℒdet\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}} delivers fewer than nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} photoelectrons. The level moves by 10 dB for every factor of 10 in EptE_{\mathrm{pt}}. The table gives it for the three receivers compared in this report; these are the dashed lines of Figure C0.10a.

10.5 How range scales with energy per point and aperture (Figure C0.10c)

(49), with Tatm≈1T_{\mathrm{atm}}\approx1 in the closed forms. The answer tells a designer what an extra joule per point, or a larger lens, buys in range. (70), the range-weighted point-rate figure of merit of §C3b, which assumes signal-limited detection. A lidar can then trade points per second for range, but not raise both, without more power or a larger lens. The product ṄRmax⁡2\dot N R_{\max}^2 then shifts by about 21–23% per factor of two in point rate (15.0/12.2=1.2315.0/12.2=1.23 and 18.1/15.0=1.2118.1/15.0=1.21), part of the way toward the ṄR4\dot N R^4 of sunlight-limited detection (§C3b).
  • Coherent, fixed collimated aperture: nothing is detected below a minimum energy per point EminE_{\min}, the energy at which even the near-field plateau ℒcoh(0)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coh}}(0) just reaches the detection level: Emin=nreqEphηℒcoh(0)=2π2nreqEphw02ηρt2λ2.E_{\min}=\frac{n_{\mathrm{req}}E_{\mathrm{ph}}}{\eta\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coh}}(0)}=\frac{2\pi^2\,n_{\mathrm{req}}\,E_{\mathrm{ph}}\,w_0^2}{\eta\,\rho\,t^2\lambda^2}.(51)
    • This is 0.031, 0.19 and 0.76 µJ for D=10D=10, 25 and 50 mm.
    • Above it, Rmax=zREpt/Emin−1R_{\max}=z_R\sqrt{E_{\mathrm{pt}}/E_{\min}-1}, which becomes the Ept\sqrt{E_{\mathrm{pt}}} law once Rmax≫zRR_{\max}\gg z_R.
    • Worked (25 mm): 2π2×30×1.28×10−19×0.011252/(0.25×0.1×0.838×(1.55×10−6)2)=9.6×10−21/5.0×10−14=1.9×10−72\pi^2\times30\times1.28\times10^{-19}\times0.01125^2/(0.25\times0.1\times0.838\times(1.55\times10^{-6})^2)=9.6\times10^{-21}/5.0\times10^{-14}=1.9\times10^{-7} J.
  • Coherent, best collimated aperture at each range: setting the envelope of Eq. (43) equal to the detection level gives Rmax=ρt2ληEpt4πnreqEph∝Ept,ṄRmax=const.R_{\max}=\frac{\rho\,t^2\lambda\,\eta\,E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{4\pi\,n_{\mathrm{req}}E_{\mathrm{ph}}}\ \propto E_{\mathrm{pt}},\qquad \dot N\,R_{\max}=\text{const}.(52)
    • Worked: 0.1×0.838×1.55×10−6×0.25×3×10−7/(4π×30×1.28×10−19)=9.7×10−15/4.8×10−17=2020.1\times0.838\times1.55\times10^{-6}\times0.25\times3\times10^{-7}/(4\pi\times30\times1.28\times10^{-19})=9.7\times10^{-15}/4.8\times10^{-17}=202 m (198 m with clear air).
    • Doubling the energy doubles the range, but only if the aperture grows as R\sqrt R. The footprint area then grows only as RR (πw2=2λR\pi w^2=2\lambda R at the optimum, 10.2), while a cell of fixed angular pitch θcell\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} grows as R2R^2. The beam therefore covers a share πw2/(Rθcell)2=2λ/(Rθcell2)\pi w^2/(R\theta_{\mathrm{cell}})^2=2\lambda/(R\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}^2) of the cell, which shrinks as 1/R1/R: 4.1% at 100 m for a 0.05° cell (§C10.3a, item 3).
  • Equal apertures, constant gap. At D=Dopt(R)D=D_{\mathrm{opt}}(R), with each FMCW aperture as large as the ToF lens, the ratio of the energies per point needed by FMCW and SPAD ToF does not depend on range: EFMCWESPAD=ncEph,c/ηcndEph,d/ηd⋅ArxAmode=0.55×1t2(0.45)2=0.55×5.9=3.2.\frac{E_{\mathrm{FMCW}}}{E_{\mathrm{SPAD}}}=\frac{n_{\mathrm{c}}E_{\mathrm{ph,c}}/\eta_{\mathrm{c}}}{n_{\mathrm{d}}E_{\mathrm{ph,d}}/\eta_{\mathrm{d}}}\cdot\frac{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}{A_{\mathrm{mode}}}=0.55\times\frac{1}{t^2(0.45)^2}=0.55\times5.9=3.2 .(53)
    • The subscripts c and d mark the coherent and direct-detection cases: nc=30n_{\mathrm{c}}=30 (per look) and nd=21.7n_{\mathrm{d}}=21.7 are their values of nreqn_{\mathrm{req}}, Eph,cE_{\mathrm{ph,c}} and Eph,dE_{\mathrm{ph,d}} their photon energies (1,550 and 940 nm), and ηc\eta_{\mathrm{c}}, ηd\eta_{\mathrm{d}} their efficiencies.
    • The second factor is the ratio of the direct-detection lens area to the coherent mode-equivalent area at the optimum, Amode=t2(0.45)2ArxA_{\mathrm{mode}}=t^2(0.45)^2A_{\mathrm{rx}} from 10.2; 0.45 is again the ratio w0/Dw_0/D.
    • The first factor is (30×1.28×10−19/0.25)/(21.7×2.11×10−19/0.164)=1.54×10−17/2.79×10−17=0.55(30\times1.28\times10^{-19}/0.25)/(21.7\times2.11\times10^{-19}/0.164)=1.54\times10^{-17}/2.79\times10^{-17}=0.55.
    • With clear-air loss the ratio is 3.1–3.2 (3.21 at 100 m, 3.11 at 500 m), because clear air costs slightly more at 940 nm than at 1,550 nm.
  • Against a fixed 25 mm SPAD receiver, the gap per point closes as 1/R1/R, because the optimal coherent aperture grows: 8.2× at 100 m, 4.1× at 200 m, 2.7× at 300 m and 1.6× at 500 m (150, 303, 458 and 778 nJ against 18.2, 74.2, 169.7 and 487.7 nJ, with clear air).
  • Linear APD against SPAD with the same lens: (890×1.28×10−19/0.40)/(21.7×2.11×10−19/0.164)=2.85×10−16/2.79×10−17=10.2(890\times1.28\times10^{-19}/0.40)/(21.7\times2.11\times10^{-19}/0.164)=2.85\times10^{-16}/2.79\times10^{-17}=10.2. That is about ten times the energy per point at every range, which the 1,550 nm eye-safety limits can pay for at low point rates (§C4c).

  • The top axis converts energy per point into points per second per watt of light, 1/Ept1/E_{\mathrm{pt}} (1 µJ per point is 1 Mpts/s per W).
  • (a) Direct detection: SPAD at 940 nm with 10, 25 and 50 mm lenses, and a linear APD at 1,550 nm with 25 mm.

Reading Figure C0.10c [E]:

  • Direct-detection range grows as Ept\sqrt{E_{\mathrm{pt}}} (Eq. (50)): a factor of 10=3.2\sqrt{10}=3.2 per decade of energy, and doubling the lens diameter doubles the range. The linear APD with a 25 mm lens runs below the 10 mm SPAD, because with the same lens it needs 10.2 times the SPAD’s energy (10.5), more than the factor 2.52=6.252.5^2=6.25 between the 10 and 25 mm SPAD lenses; at equal energy it reaches 6.25/10.2=0.78\sqrt{6.25/10.2}=0.78 of the 10 mm SPAD’s range.
  • Each fixed coherent aperture starts at its minimum energy EminE_{\min} (Eq. (51)): 0.031, 0.19 and 0.76 µJ for 10, 25 and 50 mm. Its range climbs steeply through the near field and then follows the same Ept\sqrt{E_{\mathrm{pt}}} law beyond its Rayleigh range.
  • The best collimated aperture’s range grows as EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} (Eq. (52)), and touches each fixed-aperture curve at the range equal to that aperture’s Rayleigh range.
  • Against the 25 mm SPAD reference the FMCW energy gap closes as 1/R1/R (10.5), from 4.1× at 200 m to 1.6× at 500 m, so the two lines cross near 780 m, at about 1.2 µJ per point [E: the 1/R1/R law alone gives 500×1.59≈800500\times1.59\approx800 m; clear air, which costs more at 940 nm than at 1,550 nm, brings the crossing in to ≈780 m].

10.6 Margin at short range: dark targets, dirty windows, fog and rain (Figure C0.10d)

The crossings of 10.4 say how far a sensor sees one 10% target in clear air, through a clean window. In service it also meets darker targets, dirty or wet windows, fog and rain. Each of these multiplies the returned light by a factor below one. This part asks what that factor costs in range. The answer depends on the shape of the loss curve (10.2). Direct detection gains signal steeply as the target comes closer, so a design sized for 200 m has light to spare at short range. A collimated coherent beam does not gain signal, so it has almost none to spare.

The designs compared. To compare like with like, each design gets just enough energy per point to reach R0=200R_0=200 m on a 10% target in clear air: its detection level equals its own link loss at 200 m, ℒdet=ℒ(R0)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}=\mathcal{L}(R_0). By Eq. (49) that energy is Ept=nreqEph/[ηℒ(R0)]E_{\mathrm{pt}}=n_{\mathrm{req}}E_{\mathrm{ph}}/[\eta\,\mathcal{L}(R_0)], with nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} and η\eta from the table in 10.4.

  • SPAD ToF at 940 nm with a 25 mm lens needs 74 nJ per point: the 0.1 µJ of 10.4, which reaches 232 m, scaled by (200/232)2=0.743(200/232)^2=0.743. Without the 0.15 dB of clear-air loss this is the ≈72 nJ of §C7a subsection 2(a) and §C7b subsection 1 (74.2nJ/100.15/10=71.774.2\ {\mathrm{nJ}}/10^{0.15/10}=71.7 nJ).
  • FMCW at 1,550 nm with the best collimated aperture for 200 m (Dopt=22D_{\mathrm{opt}}=22 mm, Eq. (43)) needs 303 nJ in its integration windows; ungated, it emits 303×12.67/10=384303\times12.67/10=384 nJ (10.1). This is close to the ≈0.30 µJ of §C7b subsection 1, which uses a 20 mm beam and no atmospheric loss. With a 25 mm aperture it needs 312 nJ.
  • FMCW with smaller apertures (16, 13, 10 and 7 mm) needs more energy, because at 200 m these beams are in their far field and collect less (10.2). Eq. (56) below gives the price.

Margin. The margin ℳ(R)\mathcal{M}(R) of a design at range RR is the extra loss, in dB, that it can absorb there and still detect the target: ℳ(R)=10log⁡10ℒ(R)ℒdet,ℳDD(R)=20log⁡10R0R,ℳcoh(R)=10log⁡101+(R0/zR)21+(R/zR)2.\begin{aligned}\mathcal{M}(R)&=10\log_{10}\dfrac{\mathcal{L}(R)}{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}},\\ \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{DD}}(R)&=20\log_{10}\dfrac{R_0}{R},\\ \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{coh}}(R)&=10\log_{10}\dfrac{1+(R_0/z_R)^2}{1+(R/z_R)^2} .\end{aligned}(54) The direct-detection form follows from Eq. (38), and the coherent form from Eqs. (41) and (42), both with ℒdet=ℒ(R0)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}=\mathcal{L}(R_0). Both neglect clear-air extinction, which changes the margins by at most 0.15 dB here.

  • Direct detection gains 6 dB for every halving of range. At 10 m the margin is 20log⁡10(200/10)=26.020\log_{10}(200/10)=26.0 dB, or 26.2 dB with clear air: the design receives 400 times the light it needs.
  • The coherent margin saturates. As R→0R\to0, ℳcoh\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{coh}} rises only to the plateau margin ℳ0=10log⁡10[1+(R0/zR)2]\mathcal{M}_0=10\log_{10}[1+(R_0/z_R)^2], because the near-field loss is flat. For the best aperture zR=R0z_R=R_0, so ℳ0=10log⁡102=3.0\mathcal{M}_0=10\log_{10}2=3.0 dB: at 10 m the design receives only twice the light it needs. For 25 mm, zR=257z_R=257 m and ℳ0=10log⁡10[1+(200/257)2]=2.1\mathcal{M}_0=10\log_{10}[1+(200/257)^2]=2.1 dB.

A fixed extra loss: darker targets and dirty or wet windows. Let XX be an extra two-way loss, in dB, that does not depend on range. Examples:

  • A darker target. Both link losses are proportional to the reflectance (Eqs. (38) and (41)). A target of reflectance ρ\rho instead of ρ0=10%\rho_0=10\% therefore acts as X=10log⁡10(ρ0/ρ)X=10\log_{10}(\rho_0/\rho): 3.0 dB for a 5% target and 7.0 dB for a 2% target.
  • A water film on the window, crossed on the way out and again on the way back. Liquid water costs 9.4 dB per millimetre round trip at 1,550 nm (§C4c), so a 0.2 mm film costs 0.2×9.4=1.88≈1.90.2\times9.4=1.88\approx1.9 dB. At 940 nm water absorbs tens of times more weakly, and the film is neglected.
  • Dust, mud, salt or droplets on the window, which scatter light out of the beam at every wavelength.
  • A receiver below its design point, for example a Ge photodiode at 125 °C that reaches only 82–94% of the shot-noise limit (§C4c; 0.3–0.9 dB), or a stricter detection requirement than the model assumes (10.3).

A target is still detected wherever ℳ(R)≥X\mathcal{M}(R)\ge X. Solving Eq. (54) for the range gives the maximum range with the extra loss: Rmax⁡,DD(X)=R010−X/20,Rmax⁡,coh(X)=zR[1+(R0/zR)2]10−X/10−1for X<ℳ0.R_{\max,{\mathrm{DD}}}(X)=R_0\,10^{-X/20},\qquad R_{\max,{\mathrm{coh}}}(X)=z_R\sqrt{\left[1+(R_0/z_R)^2\right]10^{-X/10}-1}\quad\text{for }X<\mathcal{M}_0 .(55)

  • Direct detection degrades gracefully. A 3 dB loss costs 29% of the range (200×10−3/20=142200\times10^{-3/20}=142 m), 6 dB halves it (101 m), and 10 dB still leaves 64 m.
  • A coherent design falls off a cliff at X=ℳ0X=\mathcal{M}_0. Beyond it the square root has no real value: the design detects nothing at any range, because even its near-field plateau no longer reaches the detection level. The best-aperture design reaches 111 m behind a 0.2 mm water film (X=1.88X=1.88 dB), 27 m with X=3X=3 dB and nothing beyond 3.1 dB. The 25 mm design reaches 61 m behind the film and nothing beyond 2.1 dB.
  • The darkest target detectable at any range follows from X=ℳ0X=\mathcal{M}_0. For a coherent design it is ρmin=ρ0/[1+(R0/zR)2]\rho_{\min}=\rho_0/[1+(R_0/z_R)^2]: 4.9% for the best aperture and 6.1% for 25 mm (with clear air). Direct detection has no such floor, since ρmin(R)=ρ0(R/R0)2\rho_{\min}(R)=\rho_0(R/R_0)^2 keeps falling as the target comes closer: 0.024% at 10 m.

What margin costs a coherent design. Shrinking the aperture shortens the Rayleigh range and raises the plateau margin. But the narrower beam spreads more by 200 m, so more energy is needed to get there. Write u=zR/R0u=z_R/R_0 for the Rayleigh range in units of the design range. The energy needed is proportional to 1/ℒcoh(R0)1/\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coh}}(R_0), i.e. to w(R0)2w(R_0)^2 (Eq. (41)). Eq. (42) with w02=λzR/πw_0^2=\lambda z_R/\pi gives w(R0)2=w02+(λR0/πw0)2=(λR0/π)(u+1/u)w(R_0)^2=w_0^2+(\lambda R_0/\pi w_0)^2=(\lambda R_0/\pi)(u+1/u). The best aperture has u=1u=1, so relative to its energy per point EbestE_{\mathrm{best}} EptEbest=12(u+1u),ℳ0=10log⁡10(1+1u2),i.e.u=(10ℳ0/10−1)−1/2.\frac{E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{E_{\mathrm{best}}}=\frac12\left(u+\frac1u\right),\qquad \mathcal{M}_0=10\log_{10}\left(1+\frac1{u^2}\right),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad u=\left(10^{\mathcal{M}_0/10}-1\right)^{-1/2} .(56)

  • Plateau margins of 6.7, 9.7, 13.9 and 20.0 dB (apertures of 16, 13, 10 and 7 mm) cost 1.21, 1.61, 2.54 and 5.02 times the energy.
  • For large margins Ept/Ebest≈1210ℳ0/20E_{\mathrm{pt}}/E_{\mathrm{best}}\approx\tfrac12\,10^{\mathcal{M}_0/20}, so every further 6 dB of margin doubles the energy. Direct detection gets its short-range margin free.

The margins at 10 m in the table differ slightly from the plateau margins ℳ0\mathcal{M}_0 given above (3.0, 6.7, 9.7, 13.9 and 20.0 dB). Each design is sized against the clear-air loss at 200 m, little of which remains at 10 m; at 1,550 nm that adds about 0.07 dB, which lifts the best design to 3.1 dB. For the 10 and 7 mm designs, 10 m is also a sizeable fraction of the Rayleigh range (41 and 20 m), which costs 10log⁡10[1+(10/41)2]=0.2510\log_{10}[1+(10/41)^2]=0.25 dB and 10log⁡10[1+(10/20)2]=0.9710\log_{10}[1+(10/20)^2]=0.97 dB, hence 13.8 and 19.1 dB.

Fog. Fog multiplies ℒ\mathcal{L} by e−2αRe^{-2\alpha R}, where α\alpha is the extinction coefficient of the Kim model of subsection 8, α=(3.912/V)(λ/550nm)−qK\alpha=(3.912/V)(\lambda/550\ {\mathrm{nm}})^{-q_{\mathrm{K}}} for meteorological visibility VV. Below 500 m visibility qK=0q_{\mathrm{K}}=0, so fog then attenuates 940 and 1,550 nm equally. Unlike a dirty window, this loss grows with range: it is 10log⁡10e2αR=8.686αR10\log_{10}e^{2\alpha R}=8.686\,\alpha R dB, where 8.686=20/ln⁡108.686=20/\ln10. A design therefore detects out to the range at which its margin just pays for the fog: ℳ(Rmax)=8.686αRmax(dB).\mathcal{M}(R_{\max})=8.686\,\alpha\,R_{\max}\quad({\mathrm{dB}}) .(57)

  • For direct detection this is the condition R2e2αR=R02R^2e^{2\alpha R}=R_0^2 of subsection 8.
  • For a coherent design the left side never exceeds ℳ0\mathcal{M}_0, so the reach can never exceed ℳ0/(8.686α)\mathcal{M}_0/(8.686\,\alpha). In fog of 200 m visibility (α=19.6\alpha=19.6 /km) the best-aperture design is limited to 3.1/(8.686×0.0196m−1)=183.1/(8.686\times0.0196\ {\mathrm{m^{-1}}})=18 m, which is the reach the script finds.

The reason is that the Kim model gives 1,550 nm less extinction than 940 nm there: at 1 km, qK=0.5q_{\mathrm{K}}=0.5 and α1550/α940=(1550/940)−0.5=0.78\alpha_{1550}/\alpha_{940}=(1550/940)^{-0.5}=0.78.

The 7 mm design matches ToF to within 2 m, at about twenty times its energy (1,522/74=20.61{,}522/74=20.6).

Rain and a wet window. Raindrops are much larger than the wavelength, so rain extinguishes 940 and 1,550 nm almost equally. Subsection 8’s empirical law gives the specific attenuation γrain=1.076Rr0.67\gamma_{\mathrm{rain}}=1.076\,R_r^{0.67} dB/km for a rain rate RrR_r in mm/h: 3.2, 9.3 and 23.5 dB/km at 5, 25 and 100 mm/h. The light crosses range RR twice, so the loss is 2γrainR2\gamma_{\mathrm{rain}}R with RR in km, e.g. 1.9 dB at 100 m in 25 mm/h rain. Like fog, rain is a loss that grows with range, so Eq. (57) applies with 8.686αR8.686\,\alpha R replaced by 2γrainR2\gamma_{\mathrm{rain}}R. In rain the window is usually wet as well, which adds a fixed loss (Eq. (55)) at 1,550 nm only.

  • Rain alone costs every design range, and the large-aperture FMCW designs the most. Heavy rain of 25 mm/h leaves ToF 147 m and the best FMCW design 106 m.
  • A wet window then hits FMCW a second time. With a 0.2 mm film in 25 mm/h rain, the best-aperture FMCW design reaches 50 m and the 25 mm design 13 m. The ToF design keeps its 147 m, because water barely absorbs at 940 nm. Even the 7 mm FMCW design loses 23 m to the film (146 → 123 m).
  • Film thickness is the uncertain input. It depends on the window’s tilt, coating, heating and wiping, none of which is modelled here. Figure C0.10d(d) therefore plots range against film thickness at a fixed 25 mm/h.
  • Rain is often not the worst of it. Spray and splash from other vehicles, and wet, mirror-like roads, affect both receivers and are not modelled (subsection 8).

Fog also sends light back: backscatter clutter. Fog droplets scatter some of the light back toward the sensor, from every range. Two numbers decide whether this matters: how strong the fog return is in the target’s own range bin, and how strong it is close to the sensor.

  • Symbols. β\beta is the fog’s volume backscatter coefficient (m⁻¹ sr⁻¹). A slab of fog of thickness ΔR\Delta R sends βΔR\beta\,\Delta R per steradian back toward the sensor, per unit of power crossing it. It is tied to the extinction by the lidar ratio SL=α/βS_{\mathrm{L}}=\alpha/\beta, here 18 sr [E]; O’Connor et al. (2004) give 18.8 sr for water clouds at 905 nm [I]. ΔR\Delta R is the range-bin length, here 0.15 m: a 1 ns ToF bin, or the c/2Bc/2B resolution of an FMCW chirp of bandwidth B=1B=1 GHz.
  • In the target’s own bin. The Lambertian target returns ρ/π\rho/\pi per steradian, and both returns reach the receiver through the same geometry. So PfogPtgt=πβΔRρ(direct detection),PfogPtgt=2πβΔRρ(coherent).\frac{P_{\mathrm{fog}}}{P_{\mathrm{tgt}}}=\frac{\pi\beta\,\Delta R}{\rho}\ \ \text{(direct detection)},\qquad \frac{P_{\mathrm{fog}}}{P_{\mathrm{tgt}}}=\frac{2\pi\beta\,\Delta R}{\rho}\ \ \text{(coherent)} .(58)
    • The factor 2 for the coherent receiver arises because spherical droplets keep the polarization: all of their return lies in the LO’s polarization, while the model’s depolarizing target puts only half of its return there (the ½ in Eq. (41)).
    • In fog of 200 m visibility, β=19.6km−1/18sr=1.09×10−3\beta=19.6\ {\mathrm{km^{-1}}}/18\ {\mathrm{sr}}=1.09\times10^{-3} m⁻¹ sr⁻¹. Then πβΔR/ρ=π×1.09×10−3×0.15/0.1=5.1×10−3\pi\beta\Delta R/\rho=\pi\times1.09\times10^{-3}\times0.15/0.1=5.1\times10^{-3}, i.e. −22.9 dB, and −19.9 dB for coherent detection. At 50 m visibility the ratios are −16.9 and −13.9 dB.
    • So in the target’s own bin the fog is weak for both receivers.
  • Near the sensor. Here the receivers differ, because they collect nearby light differently. A direct-detection lens collects Arx/r2A_{\mathrm{rx}}/r^2 from range rr, so fog a few metres away returns far more per bin than fog near the target. A coherent receiver collects Amode(r)/r2=t2λ2/[2πw(r)2]A_{\mathrm{mode}}(r)/r^2=t^2\lambda^2/[2\pi w(r)^2] (Eq. (41)), which is flat inside the Rayleigh range. Relative to the echo of a 10% target at range RtR_t, the fog in the bin at range rr returns Pfog(r)Ptgt(Rt)={πβΔRρ(Rtr)2e2α(Rt−r)direct detection,2πβΔRρw(Rt)2w(r)2e2α(Rt−r)coherent,\frac{P_{\mathrm{fog}}(r)}{P_{\mathrm{tgt}}(R_t)}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\pi\beta\,\Delta R}{\rho}\left(\dfrac{R_t}{r}\right)^2e^{2\alpha(R_t-r)} & \text{direct detection},\\ \dfrac{2\pi\beta\,\Delta R}{\rho}\,\dfrac{w(R_t)^2}{w(r)^2}\,e^{2\alpha(R_t-r)} & \text{coherent},\end{cases}(59) where the exponential is the extra extinction on the target’s longer path. The direct-detection form assumes that the receiver sees the whole beam from rr onward (full overlap); a biaxial design, with separate transmit and receive apertures, sees less of the first metres.

The table gives the fog return in one bin relative to the echo of a 10% target at 50 m, in fog of 200 m visibility, from Eq. (59). The reach in each column heading is that design’s maximum range in this fog, from the fog table above; the 13 and 25 mm designs would not detect the 50 m target at all.

How the numbers are derived [E], worked for the bin at 2 m:

  • Direct detection, 2 m: −22.9dB+20log⁡10(50/2)+8.686×0.0196×48=−22.9+28.0+8.2=+13.2-22.9\ {\mathrm{dB}}+20\log_{10}(50/2)+8.686\times0.0196\times48=-22.9+28.0+8.2=+13.2 dB.
  • FMCW 7 mm, 2 m: zR=20z_R=20 m, so w(50)2/w(2)2=[1+(50/20.1)2]/[1+(2/20.1)2]=7.19/1.01=7.1w(50)^2/w(2)^2=[1+(50/20.1)^2]/[1+(2/20.1)^2]=7.19/1.01=7.1, i.e. 8.5 dB, and −19.9+8.5+8.2=−3.2-19.9+8.5+8.2=-3.2 dB.

What the clutter means [E]:

  • Direct detection. The fog in the first metres returns more light per bin than the target itself (+13 dB at 2 m). Summed over the 200 bins between 20 and 50 m, it returns 5.8 times the target’s photons.
    • The target echo still arrives later, so a linear receiver can reject the fog by its arrival time, provided the fog does not saturate its front end.
    • A SPAD, however, is dead for a few nanoseconds after each count, and a first-photon design records only one count per shot. The early fog counts then block part of the target echo (pile-up, §C6). This is the SPAD saturation noted in subsection 8.
    • Range gating and a biaxial layout cut the near fog, at the price of a blind zone near the car.
  • Coherent detection. Fog near the sensor is no brighter per bin than the target, even for the 7 mm design (−3 dB at 2 m), and it arrives at other beat frequencies. The strong LO keeps the receiver linear, so the fog adds a weak noise floor in the near-range bins and, at the target’s frequency, only the in-bin fog return of Eq. (58) (−19.9 dB at 200 m visibility). This is FMCW’s real advantage in fog: it rejects the clutter, although it gains no signal.
  • Doppler separates moving targets from fog, but not static ones: the droplets drift with the air, so they share the Doppler shift of the road and of parked cars.
  • Multiple scattering. A single-mode receiver accepts light only within about λ/(πw0)\lambda/(\pi w_0) of its axis (44 µrad for 25 mm at 1,550 nm), whereas a direct-detection pixel typically accepts a milliradian or more. The coherent receiver therefore rejects multiply scattered light, which arrives from wider angles. That removes clutter, but also the small gain in real reach that subsection 8 notes for direct detection.

Figure C0.10d. Maximum range on a 10% target for five designs that all reach 200 m in clear air. The designs are SPAD ToF at 940 nm with a 25 mm lens (red, dashed) and FMCW at 1,550 nm with collimated apertures of 25, 22 (the best for 200 m), 13 and 7 mm (cool colours). Each design’s energy per point, given in the legend, is set to reach exactly 200 m.

  • (a) Range versus an extra fixed two-way loss XX (Eq. (55)). The top axis gives the equivalent target reflectance behind a clean window, and the dotted line marks a 0.2 mm water film at 1,550 nm. A range of zero means no detection at any range.
  • (b) Range versus meteorological visibility, with fog extinction from the Kim model (Eq. (57)). Fog is visibility below 1 km; the shaded band is 200 m to 1 km, and thick fog is 50–200 m (international visibility code; Kim et al. 2001).
  • (c) Range versus rain rate, with a clean window (Carbonneau law, subsection 8). The rain classes are those of the Canadian observing manual MANOBS (light below 2.5 mm/h, moderate to 7.6, heavy, shaded, to 50, violent above); the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) notes that there is no agreed international definition.
  • (d) Range in 25 mm/h rain versus the thickness of a water film on the window. The top axis gives the film’s two-way loss at 1,550 nm; the film is neglected at 940 nm.

Reading Figure C0.10d [E]:

  • Panel (a) is Eq. (55). The ToF curve falls smoothly. Each FMCW curve drops to zero at its plateau margin ℳ0\mathcal{M}_0: 2.1 dB for 25 mm, 3.1 dB for 22 mm and 9.7 dB for 13 mm.
  • Only the 7 mm design follows the ToF curve. Its Rayleigh range (20 m) is far below 200 m, so over most of the range it is in its far field, where the fraction it collects falls as 1/R21/R^2 (its loss rises 20 dB per decade), as for direct detection.
  • Panel (b) shows the same ordering in fog, whose extinction adds a loss that grows with range. ToF and the 7 mm FMCW design keep about 60 m at 200 m visibility.
  • Panels (c) and (d) show rain costing every design range. The water film then adds a fixed loss for FMCW only, which pushes the large-aperture designs over their cliff.

What this means for design [E]:

  • A range specification at 10% in clear air says little about robustness. The same “200 m at 10%” describes a ToF design with 26 dB to spare at 10 m and an FMCW design with 3 dB. A coherent sensor’s datasheet should therefore also give its plateau margin, or equivalently the darkest target it detects at any range, ρ0/[1+(R0/zR)2]\rho_0/[1+(R_0/z_R)^2], together with its range at 5% and in 200 m fog.
  • Robustness costs a coherent design energy, not a ToF design.
    • A 13 mm aperture (1.6× the best FMCW energy) gives 9.7 dB of plateau margin: 133 m on a 5% target, 48 m in 200 m fog, and 115 m in heavy rain behind a 0.2 mm film.
    • A 7 mm aperture matches ToF’s tolerance of dark targets and fog. It needs 5.0× the best FMCW energy, i.e. 1.5 µJ per point, about twenty times ToF’s 74 nJ.
    • The eye-safety limits at 1,550 nm leave room for that energy (§C4c), but the laser power and channel count of §C7b subsection 1 grow in proportion.
  • The wet window remains a 1,550 nm problem at any aperture, because water absorbs there (§C4c). Window heating, water-repellent coatings and wiping matter more for FMCW than for 905 or 940 nm ToF.

10.7 Dynamic range: strong returns, blooming and blinding

10.6 asked how much light a design has to spare for weak returns. The same excess light appears as a burden for strong ones. A receiver must detect the weakest return it is specified for and still range the strongest one correctly. In between it must stay linear, or at least saturate gracefully, recover quickly and not spill light into neighbouring pixels. This part sizes that span for the designs of 10.6, describes the failure modes documented for ToF receivers, and says what coherent detection changes and what it does not. The problem is well studied. Vendors publish firmware fixes for it, China’s national lidar standard tests one of its artefacts, and open benchmarks have found it in production sensors.

How large the span is. Let the dynamic range a design must handle be the ratio of the link loss of the strongest return that must still be ranged correctly, ℒmax\mathcal{L}_{\max}, to the detection level: 𝒟=ℒmaxℒdet,10log⁡10𝒟=10log⁡10ρmaxρ0+ℳ(Rmin).\mathcal{D}=\frac{\mathcal{L}_{\max}}{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}},\qquad 10\log_{10}\mathcal{D}=10\log_{10}\frac{\rho_{\max}}{\rho_0}+\mathcal{M}(R_{\min}) .(60) Here ρmax\rho_{\max} is the effective reflectance of the strongest target, RminR_{\min} the shortest range at which it must be measured, ρ0=10%\rho_0=10\% the reflectance the design is sized for, and ℳ\mathcal{M} the margin of Eq. (54). The second form holds because both link losses are proportional to reflectance (Eqs. (38) and (41)). In words: the span a receiver must handle is the reflectance span plus the short-range margin of 10.6. The excess light that protects direct detection against dirt and fog is the same excess light its receiver must survive, and FMCW has little of either.

Retroreflectors as effective reflectances. A retroreflector is specified by its coefficient of retroreflection RAR_A (cd·lx⁻¹·m⁻²): the intensity it returns per unit illuminance and per unit area, in units of sr⁻¹. A Lambertian surface of reflectance ρ\rho returns ρ/π\rho/\pi in the same units, so the retroreflector acts like a Lambertian surface of reflectance ρeq=πRA.\rho_{\mathrm{eq}}=\pi R_A .(61)

  • Road-sign sheeting. White sheeting of ASTM D4956 Types I and III has RA=70R_A=70 and 250 at 0.2° observation and −4° entrance, i.e. ρeq≈220\rho_{\mathrm{eq}}\approx220 and 790 [P]. New sheeting of EN 12899-1 class RA2 measured 414–769, i.e. ρeq=\rho_{\mathrm{eq}}= 1,300–2,400 [I].
  • Licence plates. ISO 7591 specifies 30–45 at 0.2° observation, with a maximum of 250 [P].
  • These are floors for lidar. They are measured in visible light at observation angles of 0.2–0.33°, while a monostatic lidar looks back at nearly 0°, where retroreflection is stronger.
  • Measured at a lidar wavelength. In the 1,310 nm coherent array of Settembrini et al. (2026), a retroreflector at 7.2 m returned 31.8 dB more than a 50% Lambertian target [P]. By Eq. (61), treating the retroreflector as depolarizing like the reference target, that is ρeq=0.5×103.18≈760\rho_{\mathrm{eq}}=0.5\times10^{3.18}\approx760, i.e. RA=760/π≈240R_A=760/\pi\approx240, close to Type III sheeting. If it preserves polarization, it appears up to 3 dB stronger in a single-polarization coherent receiver (see “Polarization” below the table), and RAR_A may then be as low as ≈120.
  • Overall span. Waymo puts real scenes at more than 50 dB of reflectance: a retroreflector can exceed 1,000× a Lambertian target, and a wet dark car can fall below 1% (Piggott et al. 2025) [P].
  • Value used below. As in §C10.2, item 4, a bright sign is taken as RA=500R_A=500, i.e. ρeq=1,571\rho_{\mathrm{eq}}=1{,}571, 42.0 dB above a 10% target.

The table evaluates Eq. (60) for four of the designs of 10.6, in dB above each design’s weakest detectable return.

White 90% target at 0.3 m 66.2 dB 12.6 dB 19.3 dB 29.6 dB
