Why InGaAs SPAD arrays do not rescue 1,550 nm ToF: noise, afterpulsing and count rate. A SPAD is biased above its breakdown voltage, so one absorbed photon triggers a self-sustaining avalanche that is counted as a single event. The table compares an InGaAs/InP SPAD with a silicon one on four properties.

  • Dark count rate (DCR) is the rate of avalanches with no light at all, triggered by thermally generated carriers. It is quoted in counts per second (cps) per µm² of active area and rises steeply with temperature.
  • Afterpulsing is a false count caused by charge trapped in the material during one avalanche and released shortly after, triggering another. The cure is a hold-off: after each count the SPAD is held below breakdown long enough for the traps to empty. The dead time is the total interval after a count during which the SPAD cannot count again.
  • The maximum count rate follows from the hold-off or dead time: a SPAD that is blind for about 1 µs after each count cannot register much more than 10⁶ counts per second (1 Mcps).
  • Detection efficiency, or photon detection efficiency (PDE), is the fraction of incident photons that produce a count. It rises with the excess bias, the voltage by which the SPAD is biased above breakdown, but so does the dark count rate.
Parameter InGaAs/InP SPAD, 10 µm (Telesca et al., ISSW 2024) [I] Si SPAD, 10 µm (Sony) [I/P]
Dark count rate 38–255 cps/µm² at 225 K (at 37–51% efficiency); ≈2.5×10³–6×10⁴ cps/µm² at 300 K; ≈5–6× lower per 25 K of cooling ≈20 cps/µm² at 60 °C (2,007 cps per 10 µm pixel, Sony device paper); 34 cps/µm² typical in the IMX560 datasheet
Afterpulsing ≈8% at 1 µs hold-off, <3% at 10 µs, <0.01% beyond 50 µs 0.1%, 6 ns dead time
Maximum count rate ≈1 Mcps at 1 µs hold-off (≈0.1 Mcps at 10 µs) ≈60 Mcps per SPAD
Detection efficiency 51% at 1,550 nm (cooled) 22–37% at 905/940 nm
  • The decisive number is sunlight. A 1,550 nm pixel receives ≈3.4×10⁸ background counts/s in bright sun (subsection 2 table above), about 340× the ≈10⁶ counts/s an InGaAs SPAD can sustain with a 1 µs hold-off, which still leaves ≈8% afterpulsing [E: 3.4×108/106≈3403.4\times10^{8}/10^{6}\approx340]. The 10 µs hold-off needed for <3% afterpulsing lowers the ceiling to ≈10⁵ counts/s, ≈3,400× below the sunlight rate [E: 3.4×108/105≈3,4003.4\times10^{8}/10^{5}\approx3{,}400]. A silicon 3×3 macro-pixel (nine SPADs whose counts are pooled into one ranging pixel) at 940 nm stays below its ceiling, at about half to two-thirds of it [E: nine SPADs at 60 Mcps each sustain 5.4×1085.4\times10^{8} counts/s; 2.84×108/(5.4×108)=0.532.84\times10^{8}/(5.4\times10^{8})=0.53 with this subsection’s band-averaged irradiance, and 3.66×108/(5.4×108)=0.683.66\times10^{8}/(5.4\times10^{8})=0.68 with the higher irradiance of §C6(d), at the same PDE of 0.37].
  • 1,550 nm direct ToF is therefore built with linear-mode APDs. That is fine for a few channels but forfeits the monolithic line scaling of the SPAD-SoC, a silicon SPAD array stacked on its own timing and processing logic as one system-on-chip, whose channel count grows with chip area (§C5, §C6).

How the numbers are derived [E] (SPAD comparison table above):

  • InGaAs dark counts per area. Telesca et al.’s SPAD has a 10 µm active diameter, π(5µm)2=78.5µm2\pi(5\ {\mathrm{µm}})^2=78.5\ {\mathrm{µm^2}}. Their 3 kcps (at 37% PDE) and 20 kcps (at 51%) at 225 K give 3,000/78.5=383{,}000/78.5=38 and 20,000/78.5=25520{,}000/78.5=255 cps/µm². Their 300 K (room-temperature) curve (Fig. 5 of the paper) runs from ≈2×10⁵ cps at 3 V to ≈5×10⁶ cps at 11 V excess bias, i.e. 2×105/78.5≈2.5×1032\times10^{5}/78.5\approx2.5\times10^{3} to 5×106/78.5≈6×1045\times10^{6}/78.5\approx6\times10^{4} cps/µm². The same figure gives the ≈5–6× step per 25 K (at 3 V: ≈2×10⁵, 3.5×10⁴, 6×10³ and 1.2×10³ cps at 300, 275, 250 and 225 K).
  • Si dark counts per area. The Sony pixel is 10 µm square, so 2,007cps/100µm2=202{,}007\ {\mathrm{cps}}/100\ {\mathrm{µm^2}}=20 cps/µm²; the IMX560’s 3.5 kcps over the 10.082=101.6µm210.08^2=101.6\ {\mathrm{µm^2}} pitch is 3,500/101.6=343{,}500/101.6=34 cps/µm².
  • What the comparison means. At room temperature the InGaAs SPAD has far more dark counts per µm² than the silicon one (2.5×10³–6×10⁴ against ≈20–34 cps/µm²) and a much lower count-rate ceiling (≈1 against ≈60 Mcps). Cooling reduces the dark counts, but the ceiling is set by the afterpulsing hold-off, and it is the ceiling that sunlight exposes.

4. Ge-on-Si for coherent receivers with a strong local oscillator (LO): yes, with one cold-temperature caveat

A coherent (FMCW) receiver mixes the weak return with a strong local oscillator (LO), a copy of the transmitted laser light, on a photodiode. The photocurrent then contains a beat tone whose frequency encodes range and velocity. Because the beat amplitude grows with the square root of the LO power (mixing gain), the strong LO lifts the weak signal above the electronic noise, and the receiver needs no avalanche gain. The question is whether the ordinary germanium photodiodes that silicon-photonics foundries build on silicon wafers (Ge-on-Si) are good enough at 1,550 nm over the automotive temperature range. Foundry Ge photodiodes suffice even at 125 °C; the open issue is responsivity at −40 °C. This matters because Ge-on-Si lets the whole coherent receiver be made in a silicon foundry rather than in InGaAs.

Performance on foundry platforms [I]. Responsivity is the photocurrent per watt of light (A/W). Dark current is the current a reverse-biased photodiode passes in total darkness, from thermally generated carriers; it adds noise and rises with temperature. It is quoted at a reverse bias such as −1 V. Bandwidth is the highest signal frequency the photodiode follows. “PIN” is a p-i-n diode, whose undoped (intrinsic) Ge layer between p- and n-doped contacts absorbs the light. The O-band and C-band are the telecom bands around 1,310 and 1,550 nm. “Saturation” is the photocurrent above which the response stops being linear.

Platform / work Responsivity (at 1,550 nm unless stated) Dark current Bandwidth Notes
AIM Photonics (American Institute for Manufacturing Integrated Photonics), APSUNY process design kit (PDK, from Analog Photonics and SUNY Polytechnic Institute), vertical PIN >1 A/W at −1 V — ≈50 GHz —
imec, 1.8 × 15 µm² 0.9 A/W ≈15 nA at −1 V >50 GHz —
GlobalFoundries, OFC 2025 0.95 A/W (O-band) <30 nA ≈60 GHz —
Fudan / Zhangjiang Lab / Innolight, ultra-thin Ge >0.8 A/W (C-band) <20 nA up to 100 GHz —
FMCW receiver engine (Moore and More, 2025) 1.01–1.09 A/W over 18 PDs (photodiodes) 3.6 nA — Saturation photocurrent 6.3 mA

When dark current matters. Any DC photocurrent II carries shot noise, the fluctuation due to the random arrival of individual electrons. Its current noise density is in=2qIi_n=\sqrt{2qI} in A Hz⁻¹ᐟ², where q=1.602×10−19q=1.602\times10^{-19} C is the electron charge; equivalently, its mean-square noise current per hertz is 2qI2qI (A² Hz⁻¹). Here ini_n is a density, not the band-integrated mean square ⟨in2⟩\langle i_n^2\rangle of Eq. (34) (§C0 subsection 6). An ideal coherent receiver is limited only by the shot noise of the LO photocurrent ILOI_{\mathrm{LO}}, because that noise grows with LO power at the same rate as the beat signal, so more LO power cannot improve on it. Two other noise sources compete with it. One is the shot noise of the dark current IdI_d. The other is the input noise of the transimpedance amplifier (TIA), the amplifier that converts the photocurrent into a voltage; its input-referred current noise density is ithi_{\mathrm{th}} (A Hz⁻¹ᐟ², mostly thermal). The receiver is therefore LO-shot-noise limited when 2qILO2qI_{\mathrm{LO}} exceeds the amplifier’s input noise ith2i_{\mathrm{th}}^2 and Id≪ILOI_d\ll I_{\mathrm{LO}}.

  • With a 3 pA Hz⁻¹ᐟ² TIA, parity (LO shot noise equal to amplifier noise, 2qILO=ith22qI_{\mathrm{LO}}=i_{\mathrm{th}}^2) needs ILO=ith2/2q=(3×10−12AHz−1/2)2/(2×1.602×10−19C)=28I_{\mathrm{LO}}=i_{\mathrm{th}}^2/2q=(3\times10^{-12}\ {\mathrm{A\,Hz^{-1/2}}})^2/(2\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\mathrm{C}})=28 µA of LO photocurrent, and a 10× margin needs ≈0.3 mA [E].
  • Shot noise is in=2qIi_n=\sqrt{2qI}, so it grows only as the square root of the current. Dark current of 15 nA contributes 2×1.602×10−19×15×10−9=6.9×10−14\sqrt{2\times1.602\times10^{-19}\times15\times10^{-9}}=6.9\times10^{-14}, i.e. 69 fA Hz⁻¹ᐟ²; even 1 µA contributes only 0.57 pA Hz⁻¹ᐟ², against 2×1.602×10−19×10−3=1.79×10−11\sqrt{2\times1.602\times10^{-19}\times10^{-3}}=1.79\times10^{-11}, i.e. 17.9 pA Hz⁻¹ᐟ², from 1 mA of LO [E].
  • Hot-end data from Chen et al., JAP 2016: bulk leakage (dark current through the volume of the Ge) rises ≈30–40× from 25 to 125 °C [I]. A 15 nA diode then reaches 15 nA × 30–40 ≈ 0.45–0.6 µA, still ≈450–2,000× below the 0.27–0.9 mA photocurrent of a 0.3–1 mW LO (≈0.9 A/W) [E]: 0.9A/W×0.3mW=0.270.9\ {\mathrm{A/W}}\times0.3\ {\mathrm{mW}}=0.27 mA and 0.9×1mW=0.90.9\times1\ {\mathrm{mW}}=0.9 mA, and 0.27mA/0.6µA=4500.27\ {\mathrm{mA}}/0.6\ {\mathrm{µA}}=450 while 0.9mA/0.45µA=2,0000.9\ {\mathrm{mA}}/0.45\ {\mathrm{µA}}=2{,}000.

Shot-noise efficiency. A balanced detector uses two photodiodes whose photocurrents are subtracted, so that noise on the LO’s own intensity cancels while the beat signal adds. Its shot-noise efficiency ηsn\eta_{\mathrm{sn}} is the fraction of the ideal, LO-shot-noise-limited signal-to-noise ratio that the real receiver achieves, i.e. the LO shot noise divided by the total noise. Writing every noise term as the DC current that would produce the same shot noise gives

ηsn=ILOILO+2Id+ith2/2q\eta_{\mathrm{sn}}=\frac{I_{\mathrm{LO}}}{I_{\mathrm{LO}}+2I_d+i_{\mathrm{th}}^2/2q}(76)

where ILOI_{\mathrm{LO}} is the total LO photocurrent of the pair, 2Id2I_d the dark current of the two diodes together, and ith2/2qi_{\mathrm{th}}^2/2q the TIA noise expressed as an equivalent current. The assumptions are that LO intensity noise cancels perfectly in the balanced pair and that the signal photocurrent is negligible next to the LO.

In the companion figure below, a balanced Ge pair holds 82–94% of the ideal shot-noise limit at 0.3–1 mW of LO even at 125 °C, and 91–97% at 25 °C [E]. With ILO=0.9A/W×0.3mW=270I_{\mathrm{LO}}=0.9\ {\mathrm{A/W}}\times0.3\ {\mathrm{mW}}=270 µA, the TIA’s ith2/2q=28.1i_{\mathrm{th}}^2/2q=28.1 µA and the figure’s deliberately pessimistic 125 °C dark current of 15.8 µA per diode (50 nA at 25 °C, 0.5 eV activation energy) [E: Id(T)=Id(T0)(T/T0)3e−(Ea/kB)(1/T−1/T0)I_d(T)=I_d(T_0)\,(T/T_0)^3\,e^{-(E_a/k_B)(1/T-1/T_0)}, with Id(T0)=50I_d(T_0)=50 nA at T0=298.15T_0=298.15 K, activation energy Ea=0.5E_a=0.5 eV and Boltzmann’s constant kB=8.617×10−5k_B=8.617\times10^{-5} eV/K; at T=398.15T=398.15 K, (T/T0)3=2.38(T/T_0)^3=2.38 and e5,803K×(1/298.15−1/398.15)K−1=e4.89=133e^{5{,}803\ {\mathrm{K}}\times(1/298.15-1/398.15)\ {\mathrm{K^{-1}}}}=e^{4.89}=133, so Id≈50nA×2.38×133=15.8I_d\approx50\ {\mathrm{nA}}\times2.38\times133=15.8 µA], Eq. (76) gives ηsn=270/(270+2×15.8+28.1)=0.82\eta_{\mathrm{sn}}=270/(270+2\times15.8+28.1)=0.82; at 1 mW it is 900/(900+31.6+28.1)=0.94900/(900+31.6+28.1)=0.94, and at 25 °C (0.05 µA per diode) it is 270/298=0.91270/298=0.91 and 900/928=0.97900/928=0.97. Up to ≈105 °C TIA noise, not dark current, sets the shortfall (at 105 °C, 2Id=12.52I_d=12.5 µA against 28.1 µA). At 125 °C this pessimistic model’s dark current contributes about as much as the TIA (31.6 against 28.1 µA); with the measured 30–40× rise above, the 125 °C dark term 2Id2I_d is 0.9–1.2 µA (two diodes at 0.45–0.6 µA each), 23–31 times below the TIA term. In engineering terms, with realistic diodes the dark current at 125 °C is small next to the amplifier noise, so heat does not rule out foundry Ge receivers.

Figure C4c. (a) Shot-noise efficiency ηsn=ILO/(ILO+2Id+ith2/2q)\eta_{\mathrm{sn}}=I_{\mathrm{LO}}/(I_{\mathrm{LO}}+2I_d+i_{\mathrm{th}}^2/2q), Eq. (76), for a balanced Ge pair (0.9 A/W). Dark current is scaled from 50 nA at 25 °C with 0.5 eV activation (a cube-of-absolute-temperature prefactor times an Arrhenius factor, the usual law for thermally generated carriers); the yellow band marks 0.3–1 mW of LO. (b) Model estimate of the Ge direct-gap absorption edge versus temperature: Varshni form (an empirical fit of band gap against temperature) plus ≈−0.11 eV per 1% biaxial tensile strain. The edge marks where strong direct absorption begins, not a responsivity cut-off. Script: build/figures/ge_coherent_receiver.py.

How LO power is chosen in practice [I]:

  • Rogers et al. (Nature 2021) reached shot-noise parity at 5 µW of LO per pixel. They used foundry-standard Ge PIN balanced detectors in GlobalFoundries CMS90WG (a 90 nm silicon-photonics process with electronics on the same chip), with 1.5 fF parasitics (stray capacitance at the amplifier input) and a 20 kΩ TIA (its transimpedance, i.e. output voltage per unit input current), and note that telecom coherent receivers “typically require ~10–100× more LO power”. At 0.9 A/W, 5 µW gives 4.5 µA of LO photocurrent, so parity at that current implies an amplifier input noise of 2qILO=2×1.602×10−19×4.5×10−6≈1.2\sqrt{2qI_{\mathrm{LO}}}=\sqrt{2\times1.602\times10^{-19}\times4.5\times10^{-6}}\approx1.2 pA Hz⁻¹ᐟ², about 2.5 times quieter than the 3 pA Hz⁻¹ᐟ² assumed above [E]. The 0.3–1 mW used above therefore buys margin with a noisier amplifier; it is not a physical minimum.
  • A discrete FMCW engine uses 1–2 mW per balanced detector.
  • Coherent telecom transceivers have used Ge photodiodes on silicon since at least a 2014 single-chip 100 Gb/s demonstration.
  • SiLC describes “germanium detectors” on its chip [T]. Aurora says its “custom-designed photodiode achieves 25% higher sensitivity than… foundry library components”, without naming the material [P].

The caveat is cold, not heat. Germanium absorbs strongly only photons whose energy exceeds its direct band gap, the “direct edge”; in Ge-on-Si that edge lies just longward of 1,550 nm at room temperature. Ge grown on silicon is under biaxial tensile strain (stretched in the wafer plane: on cooling from the growth temperature it would contract more than the silicon beneath it, which holds it stretched), and this lowers that gap and moves the edge to longer wavelengths. Band gaps widen as temperature falls, so in the cold the edge moves to shorter wavelengths, toward 1,550 nm.

  • Tensile-strained Ge-on-Si has its direct edge near 1,600–1,625 nm at room temperature; the companion model puts it at 1,590 nm at 25 °C for 0.2% strain. The edge moves to shorter wavelengths as temperature falls: ≈0.54 nm/K for the SPAD cut-off in Vines et al., and ≈0.86 nm/K for the direct gap in the model, which puts the edge at 1,534 nm at −40 °C for 0.2% strain, so (1,590−1,534)nm/65K=0.86(1{,}590-1{,}534)\ {\mathrm{nm}}/65\ {\mathrm{K}}=0.86 nm/K.
  • Measured (the absorption coefficient is the fractional loss of light per cm of Ge; responsivity falls with it): at 1,550 nm, one device’s responsivity fell from 0.87 A/W at room temperature to 0.34 A/W at 200 K, and the extracted absorption coefficient from ≈1,100 to 248 cm⁻¹ [I, Liu et al., Micromachines 2025].
  • At −40 °C (233 K) a 1,550 nm receiver therefore loses roughly 40% of its responsivity unless it compensates [E: interpolating linearly between Liu et al.’s 0.87 A/W at room temperature, taken as 295 K, and 0.34 A/W at 200 K gives 0.34+(0.87−0.34)×(233−200)/(295−200)=0.34+0.53×0.347≈0.520.34+(0.87-0.34)\times(233-200)/(295-200)=0.34+0.53\times0.347\approx0.52 A/W at 233 K, i.e. 1−0.52/0.87≈40%1-0.52/0.87\approx40\% lower]; the model puts the direct edge at 1,534–1,544 nm at −40 °C for 0.20–0.25% strain, already short of 1,550 nm. Options: heat the photonic integrated circuit (PIC), as automotive lidars already heat windows; lengthen the absorber; operate nearer 1,530 nm; use 1,310 nm, far from the edge at all temperatures (the band Pointcloud chose, §C10.4), where the retinal factor C7=8+100.04(λ−1250)=259C_7=8+10^{0.04(\lambda-1250)}=259 (with C4=5C_4=5) makes the small-source Class 1 retinal limit for long exposures 3.9×10−4C4C7=0.513.9\times10^{-4}C_4C_7=0.51 W, so lenient that the binding limits become the 0.5 W cap at the Class 3B level, which IEC 60825-1:2014 imposes on Class 1 over 1,250–1,400 nm [P, Tables 8 and 9 via TCVN 12670-1:2020; I, Seibersdorf], and, in Europe, the A11 corneal limit for 1,250–1,400 nm, 0.1 W for exposures of 0.35 s or more [I, Seibersdorf] (subsection 1); or bond InGaAs photodiodes to the PIC.
  • Datacom (short-reach data communication) Ge photodiodes are mostly O-band (1,310 nm) and specified for 0–70 °C or −5 to 85 °C, so automotive C-band operation at −40 °C is a qualification item, not a solved one.

Ge for direct detection is a different matter.

  • Ge-on-Si SPADs are not ready for automotive 1,550 nm ToF. Artilux’s room-temperature device: dark count 19 kcps/µm², 12% PDE at 1,310 nm [I]. Vines et al. needed 125 K for 38% at 1,310 nm [I]; for 1 µm-thick Ge, detection at 1,550 nm needs operation at or above ≈245 K, because cooling moves the absorption edge to wavelengths shorter than 1,550 nm [I/E].
  • Sony’s IEDM 2025 (International Electron Devices Meeting) 10 µm Ge-on-Si SPAD reports 23.3% PDE at 1,550 nm; its dark count rate (DCR) and operating temperature were not read (§C5a) [I].
  • Coherent detection sidesteps the problem. It needs no avalanche gain, so ordinary foundry Ge photodiodes suffice.

5. Water, rain and fog

Water absorbs near-infrared light more and more strongly toward longer wavelengths, so this subsection asks how much a wet window, a wet target, fog and rain cost in each band. Liquid water on windows and targets is the main weather penalty at 1,550 nm; fog treats the bands almost equally, because fog droplets are larger than all these wavelengths and scatter them about the same. The practical consequence is that a 1,550 nm lidar depends more on keeping its window dry.

Effect Numbers Tag
Liquid-water absorption coefficient 905 nm 0.07; 940 nm 0.18–0.29; 1,310 nm 1.2–1.6; 1,550 nm 10.8–11.9 cm⁻¹ [I, Segelstein; Hale & Querry; Kou]
1 mm water film (window or target) Transmits 99.3% at 905 nm but 34% at 1,550 nm (−4.7 dB one-way, −9.4 dB round trip); a 0.1 mm film costs 0.47 dB one way at 1,550 nm [E]
Fog Extinction differs by <10% between 905 and 1,550 nm (a ratio of 1.0–1.1); light of 1,000–2,400 nm, including 1,550 nm, is ≈10% more attenuated than visible light, which 905 nm matches, only in very dense fog (<30 m visibility), especially advection fog [I, Duthon et al. 2019]
Rain 905 nm reaches ≈2× farther than 1,550 nm at 25 mm/h [S, Wojtanowski et al. 2014, relayed by a survey]

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Film transmission follows the Beer–Lambert law, Tfilm=e−αabsdfilmT_{\mathrm{film}}=e^{-\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}d_{\mathrm{film}}}. Here TfilmT_{\mathrm{film}} is the fraction of light transmitted through the film, αabs\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}} the absorption coefficient of liquid water from the table (cm⁻¹, the fractional loss per cm of path), and dfilmd_{\mathrm{film}} the film thickness in cm. The law assumes normal incidence and absorption only, with no scattering or reflection at the film’s surfaces. The lower absorption coefficient of each range is used. For a 1 mm film (dfilm=0.1d_{\mathrm{film}}=0.1 cm) at 905 nm, Tfilm=e−0.07×0.1=0.993T_{\mathrm{film}}=e^{-0.07\times0.1}=0.993. At 1,550 nm, Tfilm=e−10.8×0.1=e−1.08=0.34T_{\mathrm{film}}=e^{-10.8\times0.1}=e^{-1.08}=0.34, which is 10log⁡100.34=−4.710\log_{10}0.34=-4.7 dB one way and 2×(−4.7)=−9.42\times(-4.7)=-9.4 dB for the two passes of a round trip. A 0.1 mm film gives 10log⁡10e−0.108=−0.4710\log_{10}e^{-0.108}=-0.47 dB. With the upper coefficient, 11.9 cm⁻¹, the 1 mm film transmits 30% (−5.2 dB one way). Because the light crosses the film twice, the 1 mm film leaves 0.3420.34^2 of the dry-window signal at 1,550 nm, which costs range just as a much darker target would.
  • Terms in the table. Extinction is the total loss of the beam by absorption plus scattering. Advection fog forms when moist air flows over a colder surface, and “visibility” is the distance at which a dark object can still be made out.

6. Verdict by band [E]

Putting subsections 1–5 together, each band wins or loses on a different constraint. The summary below is what a sensor architect would take from them.

  • 905 nm is the incumbent: VCSEL columns in the Hesai AT128/ATX and edge-emitting lasers (EELs) in the RoboSense M1/M1P/MX (§C3). It has the highest silicon absorption of the three bands but the worst sunlight. Where the source is an EEL, its drift (the shift of the emission wavelength as the laser warms) forces wide filters, which admit more sunlight.
  • 940 nm (VCSEL plus a back-side-illuminated (BSI) SPAD, lit through the thinned back of the chip so that wiring does not shade it) wins new designs. It has 17.5% more C4C_4 allowance and the lowest photon background (0.46× 905 nm, band-averaged). Its VCSEL drift of ≈0.07 nm/K allows 10 nm filters (0.07nm/K×145K≈100.07\ {\mathrm{nm/K}}\times145\ {\mathrm{K}}\approx10 nm over −40 to +105 °C, §C4 item 4). And light-trapped SPADs, whose surface textures lengthen the light’s path in the silicon, recover PDE to 37–45% despite silicon’s weaker absorption (45% is RoboSense’s claim, §C4b).
  • 1,550 nm pulsed ToF gains 10²–10³× in allowed pulse energy for scanned beams (≈460–950× in the scanned-raster row of subsection 1). It pays with fibre lasers; with linear InGaAs APDs, because InGaAs SPAD arrays are ≈340–3,400× over their count-rate ceiling in sunlight (subsection 3); with array costs of 10–100× silicon per mm² (processed InGaAs at 1–10 €/mm² against ≈$0.1 per mm² for the silicon of a Sony SPAD die, $17–44 over 244 mm², §C5a); and with a ≈9 dB round-trip penalty through a 1 mm water film. It survives where range at low point rate is worth that price (§C4).
  • 1,550 nm FMCW is the natural pairing. The eye-safety allowance covers watts of CW light; telecom lasers, semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs) and modulators exist; and ordinary Ge photodiodes suffice once the LO sets the noise floor. Its constraints are heat, parallelism (how many coherent channels can run at once) and cold-start responsivity (§C7a, this section), not the detector material.

C4d. Mechanical beam steering in numbers: speed limits, vibration qualification, scanner designs and what shipped

This section asks why lidars still steer their beams mechanically, which mechanisms survived automotive qualification, and why. Every long-range automotive lidar in series production still moves something. The designs that won keep the mechanism slow and put the speed in silicon. A mirror turning at 200 rpm in front of 128 or more laser–detector channels (Hesai), or a rotating four-sided prism (Huawei), has shipped in the millions. A single-beam 2-D MEMS mirror (micro-electro-mechanical systems: a millimetre-scale silicon mirror etched with its own torsion springs and actuators) must sweep 1,000–3,000 times a second [E] (subsection 2(a): 1,250 sweeps/s for the RoboSense M1 and 2,400–2,560 for InnovizOne). MEMS lidars shipped in hundreds of thousands, and their largest user is retiring them. Polygon-plus-galvo scanners grew with 1,550 nm and are now declining with it; Risley prisms and flexure scanners have not gone beyond their first programmes. This section works through the physics of speed (subsection 2), vibration and qualification (subsection 3) and the deployed trade-offs (subsection 4). Evidence tags are as elsewhere ([P] primary document, [I] independent source, [T] trade press, [E] my own estimate or calculation, [U] unverified); [D] deployed, [NT] near-term and [R] research mark deployment status.

The scanner vocabulary used below.

  • A polygon is a mirror with several flat facets that spins continuously; each facet sweeps the beam once across the field.
  • A galvo (galvanometer scanner) is a mirror on a limited-rotation motor with position feedback, so it can be pointed at any angle, held there, or swept at a chosen speed.
  • A Risley prism pair is two thin wedge prisms rotating about the beam axis; each deflects the beam by a fixed angle, and their changing relative orientation traces a rosette pattern.
  • A flexure is a spring-like structure that moves by bending rather than on bearings; a voice coil is the moving-coil motor of a loudspeaker, used as an actuator.
  • A resonant axis oscillates sinusoidally at its mechanical resonance, which gives large angles for little power but a fixed frequency. A quasi-static axis is driven below resonance and can follow an arbitrary waveform, such as a slow linear ramp.
  • The fast axis is swept once per line, the slow axis once per frame; “pts/s” is points (range measurements) per second.

1. The families: what moves, and where the parallelism sits

Livox Mid-40: 18° wedges, n=1.51n=1.51, −4,664 and 7,294 rpm on brushless DC motors; 38.4° circular field; 100,000 pts/s [P, Brazeal et al. 2021]. Deviation per prism ≈(n−1)αwedge=9.2°\approx(n-1)\alpha_{\mathrm{wedge}}=9.2°, so the pair reaches ≈18° off-axis [E] One or a few channels; the pattern fills the field over time Livox HAP on the Xpeng P5 (2021, two per car, $1,599) [P]. Its launch release calls it “rotating-mirror technology”, so its internals may differ from the Mid-40 [U]. No later Livox automotive programme was found after Xpeng went lidar-free (Nov 2024, §C3) [D, exited] Through the prisms; aperture can be large
Focal-plane flexure (Cepton MMT) Emitters and detectors on voice-coil-driven flexures behind fixed lenses (§C3a): “frictionless, mirrorless, rotation-free” [P]. A Cepton patent scans both axes fast and nearly equally, for example 200 Hz horizontally and 210 Hz vertically, a Lissajous pattern that repeats at the 10 Hz difference, on counter-moving tuning-fork flexures that cancel reaction forces, to keep both axes away from road-bump frequencies [P, US 12,313,784 B2; a patent embodiment, not a product value] Few Vista-X90: 90° × 25°, 200 m at 10%, 0.13°, <12 W, <900 g, ASIL-B [P]. InnovizOne on the BMW 7 Series (2023); InnovizTwo on the VW ID. Buzz AD [D]. Blickfeld, AEye, MicroVision MAVIN, Pioneer: no car series [R/NT] Coaxial through the mirror (Blickfeld: two resonant mirrors >10 mm [P]) or separate (AEye: mirror <1 mm [P])

Research systems (Yoo et al. 2022) [R] Staring: the receiver does not look through the mirror
Coherent (FMCW) scanners Mostly undisclosed; patents and one product show the pattern. Aurora (Blackmore-origin patents): one or two polygons, e.g. ≈1,000–5,000 and ≈200–1,000 rpm (US 10,838,045 B2), or a refracting polygon (US 11,822,010 B2). Aeva: a galvo-driven slow axis with a diffractive fast axis (US 11,372,105 B1) [P, patents]. Voyant Carbon: one axis steered on chip plus a slow mirror (§C10.4) [P] Few: one to tens of coherent channels (Mobileye’s ended design was specified with 184 lines, §C3, §C7a), because each channel needs its own local oscillator (LO), balanced detector and GS/s digitizer for a 100–400 MHz beat (§C7, §C7a) Aurora FirstLight on ≈20–25 driverless trucks [D]; Aeva on Daimler Truck from 2027 [NT]; Voyant in industrial sales; no passenger-car series (§C7) Monostatic through the scanner, so walk-off and scanner-induced Doppler must be compensated: Aeva’s lag-angle receive waveguides and mirror-Doppler patents (§C7) [P]

Terms in the table: an electronic column is a vertical line of laser and detector channels fired electronically, so the mechanism only has to scan one (horizontal) axis. A VCSEL (vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser) emits from the chip surface, which makes dense laser arrays on one chip easy. A SPAD (single-photon avalanche diode) is a photodiode biased above breakdown, so that a single photon can trigger a detectable avalanche, and a SiPM (silicon photomultiplier) is an array of SPADs whose outputs are summed into one analogue signal. FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous-wave) lidar is the coherent kind: it sweeps its laser frequency and measures range and velocity from the beat between the return and the local oscillator. A coaxial or monostatic receiver looks back through the same optics, here the same scanner, that sent the beam out. A GS/s digitizer is an analogue-to-digital converter taking 10⁹ samples per second or more. ASIL-B is level B of the four Automotive Safety Integrity Levels of ISO 26262, from A (least demanding) to D (most). Walk-off and scanner-induced Doppler are explained in subsection 2(c).

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Spinning-head speed. A head that makes one revolution per frame turns at 60fframe60f_{\mathrm{frame}} rpm, where fframef_{\mathrm{frame}} is the frame rate in Hz, so 5–20 Hz is 60×5=30060\times5=300 to 60×20=1,20060\times20=1{,}200 rpm.
  • Risley deviation. A thin wedge of apex angle αwedge\alpha_{\mathrm{wedge}} (the angle between its two faces) and refractive index nn deviates a ray by ≈(n−1)αwedge=(1.51−1)×18°=9.2°\approx(n-1)\alpha_{\mathrm{wedge}}=(1.51-1)\times18°=9.2°; the thin-prism approximation assumes small angles and near-normal incidence. When the two wedges line up the deviations add, 2×9.2°=18.4°2\times9.2°=18.4°, so the pattern reaches ≈18° off-axis, a ≈37° cone, close to the quoted 38.4° field.

2. Speed: what limits each family

This subsection asks how fast each scanner must move and what physics stops it going faster. Five limits appear: (a) the sweep rate that the line count demands, (b) the pulse rate a single channel can use without range ambiguity, (c) the angle the scanner turns while the light is in flight, (d) the trade-off between mirror size, angle and frequency in MEMS, and (e) the collecting area of a mirror that also receives. Item (f) adds the eye-safety consequence. Together they explain why many slow channels beat one fast beam.

(a) The mechanism’s speed is set by the channel count. Consider a frame of NlinesN_{\mathrm{lines}} lines (rows of points, each drawn along the fast axis and stacked along the slow axis), repeated at the frame rate fframef_{\mathrm{frame}} (Hz), with NparN_{\mathrm{par}} channels imaging different lines at once. Assuming each line takes one full fast-axis sweep and no line is scanned twice, the scanner needs

S=NlinesfframeNparS=\frac{N_{\mathrm{lines}}\,f_{\mathrm{frame}}}{N_{\mathrm{par}}}(77)

fast-axis sweeps per second (SS in s⁻¹). A bidirectional resonant mirror makes two sweeps per cycle (one each way), so its oscillation frequency must be fmirror=S/2f_{\mathrm{mirror}}=S/2. Examples [E]:

  • AT128: 128×10/128=10128\times10/128=10 sweeps/s, which is one facet per frame at 200 rpm (3facets×200/60revs−1=103\ {\mathrm{facets}}\times200/60\ {\mathrm{rev\,s^{-1}}}=10 facets/s). ATX (256 channels): also 256×10/256=10256\times10/256=10 per second at 10 Hz. HDL-64E: 64×10/64=1064\times10/64=10, one revolution per frame.
  • Seyond Falcon K1: its manual gives 1,520 “vertical scanning lines” per second at 10 frames/s, configurable from 5 to 20 frames/s [P]. That is 152 lines per frame, close to the 144 implied by the manual’s resolution table (4.8°/0.08°=604.8°/0.08°=60 lines inside the region of interest and (25°−4.8°)/0.24°≈84(25°-4.8°)/0.24°\approx84 outside) [E], so a “vertical scanning line” is one horizontal sweep per beam. A teardown of a 2022 Falcon shows a five-facet polygon fed by a one-to-four fibre split, i.e. four beams scanning four lines at once [I]. The polygon therefore makes 1,520/4=3801{,}520/4=380 facet sweeps per second and turns at 1,520/(4×5)=761{,}520/(4\times5)=76 rev/s, i.e. 4,560 rpm [E]. Each facet can sweep the beam over at most 2×360°/5=144°2\times360°/5=144°, so the 120° field uses 120/144=83%120/144=83\% of each sweep.
  • RoboSense M1 (125 lines at 10 Hz [P, user guide]; RoboSense’s January 2020 launch release gave 15 Hz for the pre-series unit): each of its five modules carries one laser (a teardown confirms one laser per module [I]) and scans every line of its own horizontal tile, so that Npar=1N_{\mathrm{par}}=1 per tile in Eq. (77), the mirror makes S=125×10/1=1,250S=125\times10/1=1{,}250 sweeps/s, a resonant fast axis near fmirror=S/2=0.63f_{\mathrm{mirror}}=S/2=0.63 kHz. The point rate fits: 750,000/(125×10)=600750{,}000/(125\times10)=600 points per line, one every 0.2° over 120° [P/E].
  • InnovizOne (256 lines at 10 frames/s, or 160 at 15 [P]) uses four 905 nm lasers and four silicon detectors behind one large in-house MEMS mirror [P, the chief executive in a call transcript filed with the SEC, Mar 2021]. With Npar=4N_{\mathrm{par}}=4 in Eq. (77), the mirror makes 256×10/4=640256\times10/4=640 or 160×15/4=600160\times15/4=600 sweeps/s, a resonant fast axis near fmirror=S/2=0.30f_{\mathrm{mirror}}=S/2=0.30–0.320.32 kHz [E]. A single-beam design would need 2,4002{,}400–2,5602{,}560 sweeps/s, i.e. 1.2–1.3 kHz.
  • This is the core of why one mechanical axis won (§C4, item 6). The column puts the parallelism in silicon, so the mirror runs about 100–300× slower than a single-beam 2-D mirror (10 sweeps/s against 1,000–3,000, i.e. 1,000/10=1001{,}000/10=100 to 3,000/10=3003{,}000/10=300; 1,250/10=1251{,}250/10=125 for the M1 and 2,560/10=2562{,}560/10=256 for a single-beam InnovizOne; figure panel d). InnovizOne softens the problem by sharing each sweep among four lasers, at 600–640 sweeps/s [P/E].

(b) Each channel has a time-of-flight rate limit. If a channel fires its next pulse before the previous echo can have returned from the farthest target, it cannot tell which pulse an echo belongs to (range ambiguity). Without range ambiguity a channel can therefore fire at most once per round trip:

PRFch≤c2Rmax\text{PRF}_{\mathrm{ch}}\le\frac{c}{2R_{\max}}(78)

where PRFch\text{PRF}_{\mathrm{ch}} is the channel’s pulse repetition frequency, cc the speed of light and RmaxR_{\max} the maximum range. That is 3×108ms−1/(2×200m)=7503\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}/(2\times200\ {\mathrm{m}})=750 kHz for a 200 m maximum range, 600 kHz for 250 m and 300 kHz for 500 m [E]. Pulse coding (giving successive pulses distinguishable patterns) can relax the bound, at a cost in processing and interference robustness (§C9). A sensor’s point rate divided by this per-channel limit is the minimum number of channels that must fire in parallel, at one pulse per point; several pulses per point multiply that minimum by their number. Examples [E]:

  • InnovizOne’s 2.8 M native pts/s [P] with a 250 m maximum range need at least 2.8×106/(6×105)=4.72.8\times10^{6}/(6\times10^{5})=4.7, i.e. five, channels firing in parallel. With four lasers [P], each would fire at 2.8×106/4=7002.8\times10^{6}/4=700 kHz, above the 600 kHz limit, so each pulse probably yields more than one point, for example through a small detector array per laser [E/U].
  • Falcon K1’s 900,000 pts/s with a 500 m maximum [P] need at least 9×105/(3×105)=39\times10^{5}/(3\times10^{5})=3, consistent with a four-way split source.
  • RoboSense M1 Plus’s 787,500 pts/s [P] would just exceed one channel’s limit at 200 m (787,500/750,000=1.05787{,}500/750{,}000=1.05). Across five modules each fires at 787,500/5≈160787{,}500/5\approx160 kHz.
  • AT128 and ATX measure only 12–15 kpts/s per channel (1.536 M pts/s over 128 channels and 3.84 M/256). At one pulse per point that is also each channel’s pulse rate, roughly 40–60 times below Eq. (78)’s 600–750 kHz (600/15=40600/15=40 to 750/12≈63750/12\approx63). The ATX_S01 configuration spreads 1.74×1061.74\times10^{6} pts/s over 64 physical receive channels (§C4b), 1.74×106/64≈271.74\times10^{6}/64\approx27 kpts/s each; if the 256-line version kept 64 channels, each would handle 3.84×106/64=603.84\times10^{6}/64=60 kpts/s, still about a tenth of the limit [P/T/E]. The dominant designs are far from this limit; single-beam scanners run into it.

(c) Walk-off during the round trip. If the return comes back through the moving scanner, the scanner keeps turning during the round-trip time 2R/c2R/c, so by the time the echo arrives the receiver is looking in a slightly different direction from the one the pulse was sent in. The angular offset, the walk-off, is

Δθ=2Rθ̇c\Delta\theta=\frac{2R\,\dot\theta}{c}(79)

where RR is the target range, cc the speed of light and θ̇\dot\theta the optical angular speed, i.e. the rate at which the outgoing beam direction sweeps (for a mirror, twice its mechanical rotation rate θ̇m\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}, because reflection doubles angles). With θ̇\dot\theta in °/s, Δθ\Delta\theta comes out in degrees; with θ̇\dot\theta in rad/s, in radians. The formula assumes that θ̇\dot\theta is constant during the flight time. This is the time-of-flight (ToF) counterpart of the coherent lag angle in §C10.3a (item 6). The table evaluates it at each scanner’s peak optical angular speed θ̇\dot\theta, against a 0.1° receive pixel [E]:

Scanner Optical angular speed Walk-off at 200 m Against a 0.1° pixel
360° spin at 10 Hz 3,600°/s 0.005° Negligible
AT128 mirror at 200 rpm (reflection doubles the angle) 2,400°/s 0.003° Negligible
Polygon, Falcon K1: five facets, four beams, 2×360°×762\times360°\times76 rev/s [I/E]; §C7 and §C7b use the lower bound 120°×380=45,600120°\times380=45{,}600°/s 54,720°/s 0.073° (0.091° at 250 m) About one 0.09° region-of-interest (ROI) step: the receive field must be elongated or offset along the scan
Resonant MEMS, 1 kHz, ±30° optical (illustrative; peak speed, mid-sweep) 188,500°/s 0.25° 2.5 pixels: a coaxial receiver loses the return unless its field is widened, which admits more sunlight
Resonant 1-D MEMS, 1.5 kHz, 180° field 848,000°/s 1.1° The receiver must stare, as in Yoo et al.’s line-laser system

How the numbers are derived [E] (companion script):

  • Optical angular speed. A 10 Hz spin is 360°×10=3,600360°\times10=3{,}600°/s. The AT128 mirror turns at θ̇m=200/60×360°=1,200\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}=200/60\times360°=1{,}200°/s, doubled on reflection to θ̇=2,400\dot\theta=2{,}400°/s. Each of its three facets turns through 120° per frame and so sweeps the beam through 240°, of which the 120° field uses half; the frame-average rate 120°×10Hz=1,200120°\times10\ {\mathrm{Hz}}=1{,}200°/s used for a column sweep in §C10.3a (item 6) is therefore half this active rate. The Falcon K1 polygon turns at 76 rev/s (subsection 2(a)), so θ̇=2×360°×76s−1=54,720\dot\theta=2\times360°\times76\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=54{,}720°/s, the value in the table; the lower bound used in §C7 and §C7b, 120°×380s−1=45,600120°\times380\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=45{,}600°/s, assumes that the 120° field fills each facet’s whole sweep time. A resonant mirror scanning θ(t)=(Θpp/2)sin⁡2πfmirrort\theta(t)=(\Theta_{\mathrm{pp}}/2)\sin2\pi f_{\mathrm{mirror}}t, where θ(t)\theta(t) is the optical beam angle at time tt, Θpp\Theta_{\mathrm{pp}} the peak-to-peak optical scan angle and fmirrorf_{\mathrm{mirror}} the resonant frequency, moves fastest mid-sweep. Its time derivative peaks there at θ̇max=πfmirrorΘpp\dot\theta_{\max}=\pi f_{\mathrm{mirror}}\Theta_{\mathrm{pp}}: π×1,000Hz×60°=188,500\pi\times1{,}000\ {\mathrm{Hz}}\times60°=188{,}500°/s for ±30°, and π×1,500Hz×180°=848,000\pi\times1{,}500\ {\mathrm{Hz}}\times180°=848{,}000°/s for the 180° 1-D mirror.
  • Walk-off is Δθ=2Rθ̇/c\Delta\theta=2R\dot\theta/c, Eq. (79). At 200 m and 3,600°/s, Δθ=2×200m×3,600°/s/(3×108ms−1)=0.0048°\Delta\theta=2\times200\ {\mathrm{m}}\times3{,}600°{\mathrm{/s}}/(3\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}})=0.0048°. The same step gives 0.0032° (AT128), 0.073° (polygon at 54,720°/s; 0.091° at 250 m, and 0.061° at the 45,600°/s lower bound), 0.25° (1 kHz MEMS, 0.25/0.1=2.50.25/0.1=2.5 pixels) and 1.13° (1.5 kHz 1-D MEMS).
  • Polygon row. The entry uses the teardown geometry of subsection 2(a): each of the five facets sweeps the beam through 2×360°/5=144°2\times360°/5=144°, of which the 120° field uses 83%, so the active sweep is faster than the lower bound. The “ROI step” is the finest angular spacing Falcon K1 uses inside its region of interest, the part of the field it samples more densely (0.09°, subsection 4).

Walk-off is why fast resonant mirrors either work at short range or pair with a staring receiver, while slow rotating mirrors can share one large aperture for transmit and receive (figure panel b). For a coherent receiver the moving mirror also spreads and shifts the optical frequency (a Doppler effect, because different parts of the mirror move toward or away from the light), by about Δfscan≈θ̇D/λ\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}\approx\dot\theta D/\lambda per pass. Here θ̇\dot\theta is the optical angular speed in rad/s, DD the beam diameter on the scanner and λ\lambda the wavelength. A chirp (the FMCW frequency sweep) longer than about 1/Δfscan=λ/(θ̇D)1/\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}=\lambda/(\dot\theta D) is smeared, so that time caps the chirp; it is also the time the beam takes to sweep through one diffraction-limited beamwidth, λ/D\lambda/D. For a 5 mm beam at 1,550 nm and the Falcon polygon’s lower-bound 45,600°/s (796 rad/s), Δfscan=796s−1×5×10−3m/(1.55×10−6m)≈2.6\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}=796\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times5\times10^{-3}\ {\mathrm{m}}/(1.55\times10^{-6}\ {\mathrm{m}})\approx2.6 MHz, which caps the chirp near 1/(2.6MHz)≈0.391/(2.6\ {\mathrm{MHz}})\approx0.39 µs (§C7, scanner-induced Doppler). ToF is immune, because it measures arrival time, not optical frequency.

(d) The MEMS bound: aperture × angle × frequency. A lidar wants a MEMS mirror that is large (to carry a wide beam and collect light), scans a wide angle and moves fast. For a given technology these three pull against each other, so their product is a useful figure of merit (FoM).

  • Figure of merit. Wang, Watkins & Xie (Micromachines 2020) define

    FoM=θedefe{\mathrm{FoM}}=\theta_e\,d_e\,f_e(80)

    in mm·rad·kHz. Here θe\theta_e is the optical field (full scan angle) in radians; de=4Amirror/πd_e=\sqrt{4A_{\mathrm{mirror}}/\pi} the effective mirror size in mm, i.e. the diameter of a circle with the same area as the mirror of area AmirrorA_{\mathrm{mirror}}; and fef_e the resonance in kHz. Their minimum for self-driving cars is a 25° field, a 2 mm mirror, a 0.8 kHz resonance and FoM 0.7; for blind-spot sensing, 120°, 1 mm and 0.5 kHz [P, review]. With 25°=0.43625°=0.436 rad, the car case is 0.436×2×0.8=0.700.436\times2\times0.8=0.70.

  • Measured examples [P]:

    • Mirrorcle’s quasi-static gimbal-less mirrors (both axes driven directly, without a separate gimbal frame for the second axis): 2.0 mm / ±10° optical / 1,300 Hz first resonance; 3.0 mm / ±16° / 400 Hz; 5.0 mm / ±11° / 350 Hz; 6.4 mm / ±5° / 300 Hz. These give FoM 0.3–0.9 [E], taking θe\theta_e as the full optical field: 0.349rad(20°)×2.0mm×1.3kHz=0.910.349\ {\mathrm{rad}}\ (20°)\times2.0\ {\mathrm{mm}}\times1.3\ {\mathrm{kHz}}=0.91; 0.559×3.0×0.4=0.670.559\times3.0\times0.4=0.67; 0.384×5.0×0.35=0.670.384\times5.0\times0.35=0.67; 0.175×6.4×0.3=0.340.175\times6.4\times0.3=0.34.
    • Fraunhofer’s resonant 1-D mirror: 2 × 4 mm, 180°, 1.5 kHz, FoM ≈13 [E]: the ellipse, with semi-axes of 1 and 2 mm, has Amirror=π×1×2=6.28mm2A_{\mathrm{mirror}}=\pi\times1\times2=6.28\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}, so de=4Amirror/π=2.83d_e=\sqrt{4A_{\mathrm{mirror}}/\pi}=2.83 mm and Eq. (80) gives FoM =πrad×2.83mm×1.5kHz=13.3=\pi\ {\mathrm{rad}}\times2.83\ {\mathrm{mm}}\times1.5\ {\mathrm{kHz}}=13.3.
    • Hua et al.’s electromagnetic 2-D Φ5 mm (5 mm diameter) mirror: a 30° fast axis at 1.2–1.3 kHz (FoM ≈3.3 [E]: 0.524rad×5mm×1.25kHz=3.30.524\ {\mathrm{rad}}\times5\ {\mathrm{mm}}\times1.25\ {\mathrm{kHz}}=3.3 at mid-band, 3.1–3.4 over 1.2–1.3 kHz) and a 20° slow axis with a 136 Hz resonance.

  • Resonance buys an order of magnitude in FoM. The price is a fixed, sinusoidal fast axis that must track its own resonance (subsection 3).

  • Why the bound exists. Three effects limit a larger, faster mirror.

    • Inertia against stiffness. The mirror’s moment of inertia about its rotation axis grows as J∝ρmtmD4J\propto\rho_{\mathrm{m}}t_{\mathrm{m}}D^4, where ρm\rho_{\mathrm{m}} is the density of the mirror material, tmt_{\mathrm{m}} the mirror thickness and DD its diameter (mass ∝ρmtmD2\propto\rho_{\mathrm{m}}t_{\mathrm{m}}D^2, times the square of a lever arm ∝D\propto D). The resonant frequency is set by the torsion spring’s stiffness kθk_\theta (torque per radian of twist) against that inertia, fmirror∝kθ/Jf_{\mathrm{mirror}}\propto\sqrt{k_\theta/J}, so a bigger mirror needs a much stiffer spring to stay fast.
    • Spring stress. A stiffer spring twisted through a large angle is more highly stressed, and the stress runs into silicon’s fracture strength.
    • Dynamic deformation. The mirror bends as it accelerates, because its outer parts must be pushed hardest. The angular acceleration of a sinusoidal scan peaks at the turning points, where the mirror is flexed most.

  • Brosens’ formula for that dynamic deformation is

    δmax=0.217ρmfmirror2D5θmechEtm2\delta_{\max}=\frac{0.217\,\rho_{\mathrm{m}}f_{\mathrm{mirror}}^2D^5\theta_{\mathrm{mech}}}{E\,t_{\mathrm{m}}^2}(81)

    [I, as reproduced with its variable definitions by Urey (Proc. SPIE 4773, 2002) from P. J. Brosens, Appl. Opt. 11, 2987 (1972); the 1972 original is paywalled and was not read]. Here δmax\delta_{\max} is the peak departure of the mirror surface from flat (m); ρm\rho_{\mathrm{m}} the density (kg/m³); fmirrorf_{\mathrm{mirror}} the scan frequency (Hz); DD the mirror diameter (m); θmech\theta_{\mathrm{mech}} the mechanical scan amplitude, i.e. the peak rotation of the mirror from rest (rad), which is half the optical amplitude; EE the material’s Young’s modulus (Pa); and tmt_{\mathrm{m}} the thickness (m). Here fmirrorf_{\mathrm{mirror}} is in hertz, not the angular frequency 2πfmirror2\pi f_{\mathrm{mirror}}; DD is strictly the width across the rotation axis, and δmax\delta_{\max} the largest departure of the bent cross-section from the chord through the axis and the edges. A cantilever-strip estimate reproduces the coefficient [E]: each half of a mirror held along its axis, bent by the inertial load of the peak angular acceleration (2πfmirror)2θmech(2\pi f_{\mathrm{mirror}})^2\theta_{\mathrm{mech}}, gives δmax=0.226(1−ν2)ρmfmirror2D5θmech/(Etm2)\delta_{\max}=0.226\,(1-\nu^2)\rho_{\mathrm{m}}f_{\mathrm{mirror}}^2D^5\theta_{\mathrm{mech}}/(E\,t_{\mathrm{m}}^2), where ν\nu is Poisson’s ratio. That equals 0.217 for ν=0.2\nu=0.2, and 0.208–0.215 for silicon (ν=0.22\nu=0.22–0.28), within 1–4%. The formula assumes a flat plate of uniform thickness and elastic, small deflections. The steep D5D^5 and tm−2t_{\mathrm{m}}^{-2} dependences are what make large, thin, fast mirrors impractical. Worked examples for silicon (ρm=2,330\rho_{\mathrm{m}}=2{,}330 kg/m³, E≈169E\approx169 GPa, a typical value for silicon’s direction-dependent stiffness), θmech=15°\theta_{\mathrm{mech}}=15° [E]:

    • 3 mm, 100 µm thick, 1.5 kHz: in SI units with θmech=15°=0.26\theta_{\mathrm{mech}}=15°=0.26 rad, Eq. (81) gives δmax=0.217×2,330×1,5002×(3×10−3)5×0.26/[169×109×(10−4)2]=4.25×10−8\delta_{\max}=0.217\times2{,}330\times1{,}500^2\times(3\times10^{-3})^5\times0.26/[169\times10^{9}\times(10^{-4})^2]=4.25\times10^{-8} m, i.e. 42.5 nm.
    • 5 mm, 100 µm, 1.5 kHz: (5/3)5=12.86(5/3)^5=12.86 times the 3 mm value, 12.86×42.5nm=54712.86\times42.5\ {\mathrm{nm}}=547 nm ≈ 0.55 µm, six times λ/10\lambda/10 at 905 nm (90.5 nm; 547/90.5=6.0547/90.5=6.0). Here λ/10\lambda/10, a surface flat to a tenth of the wavelength, is the usual flatness requirement for optics that must not degrade a diffraction-limited beam. At 250 µm thickness the deformation falls by (250/100)2=6.25(250/100)^2=6.25 to 88 nm.
    • 10 mm at the same frequency: 25=322^5=32 times worse, 32×0.547=17.532\times0.547=17.5 µm at 100 µm. Since δmax∝tm−2\delta_{\max}\propto t_{\mathrm{m}}^{-2}, meeting λ/10\lambda/10 would take tm=100µm×17,500/90.5≈1.4t_{\mathrm{m}}=100\ {\mathrm{µm}}\times\sqrt{17{,}500/90.5}\approx1.4 mm of silicon, whose inertia would pull the resonance far below 1.5 kHz (figure panel c).

  • How flat is flat enough for lidar? λ/10\lambda/10 is a diffraction-limited imaging criterion. A 905 nm ToF beam is 0.05–0.1° wide, 5–10 times the 0.01° diffraction limit of a 5 mm mirror (λ/D=905nm/5mm=0.18\lambda/D=905\ {\mathrm{nm}}/5\ {\mathrm{mm}}=0.18 mrad). What matters is therefore not wavefront error against λ/10\lambda/10 but whether deformation tilts the reflected rays by a sizeable fraction of the beam width; that tilt is roughly 10δmax/D10\,\delta_{\max}/D [E, order of magnitude]. The factor 10 is a rough allowance, not a derived constant: the local surface slope of a bent mirror is several times its average slope δmax/D\delta_{\max}/D, and reflection doubles any tilt of the surface. That gives 10×0.55µm/5mm=1.110\times0.55\ {\mathrm{µm}}/5\ {\mathrm{mm}}=1.1 mrad ≈0.06° for the 5 mm, 100 µm, 1.5 kHz case, already comparable with a 0.1° pixel. A 10 mm mirror 250 µm thick at 1.5 kHz (δmax=17.5µm/6.25=2.8\delta_{\max}=17.5\ {\mathrm{µm}}/6.25=2.8 µm) gives 10×2.8µm/10mm=2.810\times2.8\ {\mathrm{µm}}/10\ {\mathrm{mm}}=2.8 mrad ≈0.16°. A coherent receiver, which must match the return to a single optical mode (the LO’s wavefront), is held to the stricter λ/10\lambda/10 class (§C10.3a). In practice, then, a ToF mirror may be less flat than λ/10\lambda/10, but a 5 mm, 100 µm mirror at 1.5 kHz already blurs the beam by an amount comparable with a pixel.

(e) Receive aperture: the mirror that also receives sets the collecting area. Compare a coaxial MEMS mirror with the ≈25 mm (491 mm²) lens of a scanned one-axis unit (§C10.3a, item 7). Range scales as Arx\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}} when signal-limited and as Arx1/4A_{\mathrm{rx}}^{1/4} when background-limited, where ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} is the receive-aperture area (the caveats of §C10.3a, item 7) [E]. The reasons are as follows, for a target that fills the beam and returns light as 1/R21/R^2, with everything else (pixel field, filter, clear air) unchanged.

  • Signal-limited means that detection needs a fixed number of signal photons. That number scales as Arx/R2A_{\mathrm{rx}}/R^2, so the range at which it is reached scales as Arx\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}.
  • Background-limited means that the noise is the shot noise of the sunlight background. The background itself grows in proportion to ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} (Eq. (75)), so the signal-to-noise ratio scales as (Arx/R2)/Arx=Arx/R2(A_{\mathrm{rx}}/R^2)/\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}=\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}/R^2, and range as Arx1/4A_{\mathrm{rx}}^{1/4}.
Coaxial mirror Area at normal incidence Area ratio Range factor, signal-limited Range factor, background-limited
10 mm (Blickfeld class) 78.5 mm² 1/6.3 0.40 0.63
5 mm 19.6 mm² 1/25 0.20 0.45
2 × 4 mm ellipse 6.3 mm² 1/78 0.11 0.34
2 mm 3.1 mm² 1/156 0.08 0.28
  • At an angle of incidence θinc\theta_{\mathrm{inc}} (between the incoming light and the mirror’s normal) the projected area falls by a further cos⁡θinc\cos\theta_{\mathrm{inc}} (0.71 at 45°).
  • Mirrorcle’s own architecture study reaches the same conclusion from the vendor side [P]. A coaxial rangefinder reaching beyond 100 m “may need” a mirror of 3–5 cm, and even ≥10 mm is needed for 30 m in a concentric design (transmit and receive paths nested on the same axis). Smaller, faster mirrors belong in biaxial designs, whose separate receiver sits beside the transmitter.
  • Blickfeld’s Cube 1 (two resonant mirrors >10 mm, 70° × 30°, 0.4° divergence) has a typical range of 1.5–75 m [P], consistent with the table: applied to the ≈200 m of a one-axis unit such as the AT128, its factors give roughly 80 m when signal-limited (0.40×2000.40\times200 m) and ≈126 m when background-limited (0.63×2000.63\times200 m). If its receive field matches its 0.4° divergence, it spans about (0.4/0.1)2=16(0.4/0.1)^2=16 times the solid angle of a 0.1° pixel, and that extra background favours the lower figure [E].
  • Production MEMS lidars therefore either tile several transceivers under one mirror (RoboSense M1’s five modules [I]) or receive through separate optics, which brings back part of the staring-receiver penalty of §C6 [E].

How the numbers are derived [E] (aperture table above):

  • Areas and ratios. A circular mirror of diameter DD has Arx=πD2/4A_{\mathrm{rx}}=\pi D^2/4: the 25 mm lens has π×12.52=491mm2\pi\times12.5^2=491\ {\mathrm{mm^2}} and the 10 mm mirror π×52=78.5mm2\pi\times5^2=78.5\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}, a ratio of 491/78.5=6.25491/78.5=6.25. The ellipse, with semi-axes a=1a=1 mm and b=2b=2 mm, has πab=π×1×2=6.28mm2\pi ab=\pi\times1\times2=6.28\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}, and 491/6.28=78491/6.28=78.
  • Range factors are (Arx/Alens)1/2(A_{\mathrm{rx}}/A_{\mathrm{lens}})^{1/2} and (Arx/Alens)1/4(A_{\mathrm{rx}}/A_{\mathrm{lens}})^{1/4}, where Alens=491A_{\mathrm{lens}}=491 mm² is the 25 mm lens. For the 10 mm mirror they are (1/6.25)1/2=0.40(1/6.25)^{1/2}=0.40 and (1/6.25)1/4=0.63(1/6.25)^{1/4}=0.63; for the 2 mm mirror, (1/156)1/2=0.080(1/156)^{1/2}=0.080 and (1/156)1/4=0.28(1/156)^{1/4}=0.28.

(f) Eye safety of a small, fast scanner. A few-mm mirror emits a beam narrower than the 7 mm pupil, so a whole pulse can enter the eye (§C4c). A stalled scanner also concentrates pulses in one direction.

  • IEC 60825-1 requires the class to hold “under reasonably foreseeable single fault failure conditions” [P, via a test house].
  • A scanned Class 1 design therefore needs scan monitoring interlocked with the laser, i.e. a circuit that switches the laser off if the scan stops or slows. Mirrorcle: Class 1 on a continuously scanned beam “requires that the scan is reliably monitored” [P]. The system in the Fraunhofer paper uses an Infineon AURIX safety controller (an automotive safety microcontroller) that monitors the mirror, its driver and the receiver [P, abstract via a search extract].
  • Spinning heads and rotating mirrors need the same interlock (motor speed, encoder). Their larger exit apertures spread each pulse over more area, so less of it can enter a 7 mm pupil [E].

3. Vibration, shock and qualification

A part mounted on a car must survive years of road vibration and occasional shocks, and it must pass standard tests before a carmaker will buy it. This subsection lists what those tests demand, where each scanner family is exposed, and why MEMS mirrors, though mechanically strong, are vulnerable in a way that slow motor-driven mirrors are not. The short answer is that the road’s vibration energy sits mostly below 400 Hz, exactly where the slow axis of a MEMS mirror of 3 mm or more resonates.

What the tests require. Random-vibration tests are specified by a power spectral density (PSD) of acceleration, Ga(f)G_a(f) in (m/s²)²/Hz: the mean-square acceleration per hertz of bandwidth at frequency ff. Integrating it over frequency gives the total mean-square acceleration, whose square root is the “rms” (root-mean-square) level. Shock and vibration levels are also quoted in units of g=9.81g=9.81 m/s², the acceleration due to gravity.

  • ISO 16750-3 (mechanical loads) [P, 2012 edition, public preview of the standard]:

    • Test IV, passenger car sprung masses (the body, which sits on the suspension springs), is random vibration to IEC 60068-2-64: 8 h per plane at 27.1 m/s² rms. The PSD falls from 30 (m/s²)²/Hz at 10 Hz to 0.2 at 400 Hz and stays flat to 1,000 Hz.

    • By integration, 84% of the mean-square acceleration lies below 400 Hz, and nothing lies above 1 kHz [E]. Between 10 and 400 Hz the PSD falls as a power law, a straight line on log–log axes between the two breakpoints (the usual way such profiles are specified):

      Ga(f)=30(m/s2)2Hz−1×(f10Hz)−γ,γ=ln⁡(30/0.2)ln⁡(400/10)=1.358G_a(f)=30\ {\mathrm{(m/s^2)^2\,Hz^{-1}}}\times\left(\frac{f}{10\ {\mathrm{Hz}}}\right)^{-\gamma},\qquad \gamma=\frac{\ln(30/0.2)}{\ln(400/10)}=1.358(82)

      where −γ-\gamma is the slope on log–log axes (the PSD falls as f−γf^{-\gamma}). So ∫10400Gadf=30×10/(1−γ)×(401−γ−1)=614(m/s2)2\int_{10}^{400}G_a\,df=30\times10/(1-\gamma)\times(40^{1-\gamma}-1)=614\ {\mathrm{(m/s^2)^2}}; the flat part adds 0.2×600=1200.2\times600=120. The total, 734, gives 734=27.1\sqrt{734}=27.1 m/s² rms, and 614/734=84%614/734=84\%.

    • Test V (unsprung masses, i.e. wheel mounts) is 107.3 m/s² rms.

    • The current edition, ISO 16750-3:2023, splits the body test by component size. Test IV covers small and lightweight devices under test (DUTs) on passenger-car sprung masses (§4.1.8), and Test XIV, taken from ISO 19453-3:2018, covers large and heavy DUTs on hybrid-electric and fully electric cars (§4.1.10) [P, official preview]. Its foreword says the vibration profiles were changed “where necessary due to extended datasets of and experience from vehicle measurements”. The 2023 breakpoints and the mass threshold between the two classes are not in the public preview, so the 2012 profile is used here, and placing a 0.36–1.75 kg lidar in the small class is an assumption [U].

    • Mechanical shock: 500 m/s² (≈50 g), 6 ms half-sine (a single acceleration pulse shaped like half a sine wave, 6 ms long), 10 shocks per direction [P, Bosch datasheet citing ISO 16750-3].

  • LV 124 (the German carmakers’ common component specification) includes M-01 free fall, M-04 vibration and M-05 mechanical shock among its tests M-01 to M-09 [T]. Yoo et al. drove their MEMS lidar with a wideband profile based on LV 124 [P].
  • OEM group standards (a carmaker’s, or original equipment manufacturer’s, own test specifications).
    • InnovizOne’s series datasheet lists “MEMS: AECQ and BMW GS 950324-3-1” as printed. BMW’s environmental standard for components is usually cited as GS 95024-3-1 [U].
    • At system level it lists DIN/EN/IEC 60068-2, ISO 16750, ISO 20653 (IP6K6K, IP6K9K, IP6K7) and ISO 26262 ASIL B(D) [P]. ISO 20653 defines the IP (ingress protection) codes: the first digit rates dust (“6K” is dust-tight), the second water (7 is temporary immersion, 9K high-pressure, high-temperature jets, 6K powerful jets). ISO 26262 is the functional-safety standard, and ASIL B(D) denotes a part developed to ASIL B as one share of a safety goal rated ASIL D, the highest level.
  • Component qualification. The Automotive Electronics Council (AEC) publishes stress-test qualifications for components.
    • AEC-Q100 covers integrated circuits (ICs) and AEC-Q102 discrete optoelectronics such as lasers and photodiodes. AEC-Q103 covers only MEMS pressure sensors (-002) and microphones (-003) [P].
    • No AEC document covers MEMS mirrors or scanner motors. Suppliers therefore cite AEC-Q100 for the MEMS chip (RoboSense: MEMS module AEC-Q100, tested by SGS [P]) or an OEM test (Innoviz).
  • System-level examples [P]:
    • Falcon K1: IEC 60068-2-27 shock and IEC 60068-2-64 vibration; IP67 body and IP69K window; −40 to +85 °C; 1.75 kg.
    • ATX: ASIL B product certification; IP6K7 and IP6K9K; 360 g.
    • M1 Plus: ASIL B; AEC-Q100; IP67 and IP6K9K; −40 to +85 °C.
    • InnovizOne: 15 years, 300,000 km or 8,000 operating hours. It operates from −15 to +85 °C “with airflow/cooling solution (depending on configuration, mounting position and environment)”, and is stored at −40 to +105 °C. A −15 °C operating floor is narrow for a car part; the datasheet gives no reason [U].

Where each family is exposed [E unless tagged]. The table rates each mechanism against shock, road vibration, wear and temperature. The wear column counts revolutions or oscillation cycles over the 8,000 operating hours that InnovizOne’s datasheet specifies as its life.

Family Shock Road vibration (10–1,000 Hz) Wear over 8,000 operating hours Temperature
Spinning head Largest moving mass: bearings, balance, alignment of the rotating optics Rotor modes and bearing loads; roof mount 10 Hz gives 2.9 × 10⁸ revolutions Motor, power and data transfer across the rotor
One-axis rotating mirror Small rotor Mirror and rotor modes far above the band; speed held by an encoder AT128 at 200 rpm gives 9.6 × 10⁷ revolutions Motor, lubricant
Polygon plus galvo Two mechanisms; heavier (Falcon K1 1.75 kg [P]) The galvo servo must out-run the disturbance; polygon speed stability The 76 rev/s of subsection 2(a) gives 2.2 × 10⁹ revolutions Motors, bearings
Risley pair Two motors and glass prisms Continuous rotation, no reversal 7,294 rpm gives 3.5 × 10⁹ revolutions. Livox alternates the two prism speeds between power cycles, which Brazeal et al. suggest extends motor life [P] Motors
MEMS Intrinsically strong [P, Mirrorcle]: 500 g / 1 ms for integrated 2 mm devices and 300 g / 1 ms for larger bonded ones; 20 g sine over 20–2,000 Hz (MIL-STD-883) The weak point: a slow axis whose resonance lies inside the band, and a fast axis that must hold phase 1–1.5 kHz gives 2.9–4.3 × 10¹⁰ cycles. Vendor tests report “billions of cycles (2500+ hours)” without mechanical failures; a die-attach epoxy failure was found and fixed [P, Mirrorcle] Resonance drifts ≈−30 ppm/K in uncompensated silicon, −3,750 ppm over −40 to 85 °C [P]. Vacuum packaging raises Q and protects the mirror (Fraunhofer)

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Revolutions or cycles are rate × 8,000 h × 3,600 s/h, i.e. rate × 2.88×1072.88\times10^{7} s. A 10 Hz head makes 10×2.88×107=2.9×10810\times2.88\times10^{7}=2.9\times10^{8} revolutions; the AT128 at 200/60=3.33200/60=3.33 rev/s makes 9.6×1079.6\times10^{7}; the Risley’s 7,294/60=1227{,}294/60=122 rev/s makes 3.5×1093.5\times10^{9}; a 1–1.5 kHz mirror makes 2.9×10102.9\times10^{10} to 4.3×10104.3\times10^{10} cycles.
  • Polygon. The ≈380 sweeps/s of subsection 2(a), already divided by the four beams, need 380/5=76380/5=76 rev/s from the five-facet polygon of the teardown (one sweep per facet), and 76×2.88×107=2.2×10976\times2.88\times10^{7}=2.2\times10^{9}.
  • Resonance drift. −30ppm/K×125K=−3,750-30\ {\mathrm{ppm/K}}\times125\ {\mathrm{K}}=-3{,}750 ppm over −40 to 85 °C (ppm/K is parts per million of the frequency per kelvin). Silicon’s stiffness falls slightly as it warms, so an uncompensated resonance drifts downward with temperature.
  • Terms in the table. “Modes” are a structure’s natural patterns of vibration, each with its own resonant frequency. The quality factor QQ of a resonance is its frequency divided by its bandwidth; a lightly damped resonance also amplifies a drive at that frequency roughly QQ times. Vacuum packaging removes air damping and so raises QQ. A servo is a feedback-controlled actuator, and “hold phase” means keeping the oscillation in step with the scan timing. MIL-STD-883 is the US military test-method standard for microelectronics, and the die attach is the adhesive that fixes the chip in its package.

The MEMS vibration problem in numbers [E unless tagged]

  • Why the resonance must sit high. In ISO Test IV the PSD at 136 Hz (Hua’s slow-axis resonance) is, from Eq. (82), 30×(136/10)−1.358=0.8730\times(136/10)^{-1.358}=0.87 (m/s²)²/Hz, 0.87/0.2=4.30.87/0.2=4.3 times its value at 1 kHz. Miles’ approximation estimates how much a resonance responds to such random vibration:

    xrms≈(π/2)fnQGa(fn)(2πfn)2x_{\mathrm{rms}}\approx\frac{\sqrt{(\pi/2)\,f_n\,Q\,G_a(f_n)}}{(2\pi f_n)^2}(83)

    Here xrmsx_{\mathrm{rms}} is the rms relative displacement of the resonating part (m), fnf_n its natural (resonant) frequency (Hz), QQ its quality factor and Ga(fn)G_a(f_n) the input PSD at that frequency ((m/s²)²/Hz). The square root is the rms acceleration of the resonant response (m/s²); dividing by (2πfn)2(2\pi f_n)^2 turns acceleration into displacement for motion at fnf_n. The approximation assumes a single, lightly damped (Q≫1Q\gg1) resonance and an input PSD that is roughly flat across the resonance’s bandwidth. Q=50Q=50 below is an assumed, illustrative value.

    • On that model a Q = 50 mode at 136 Hz moves ≈40 times more than one at 1 kHz: 132 µm against 3.2 µm equivalent displacement. At 136 Hz, xrms=(π/2)×136×50×0.87/(2π×136)2=96ms−2/(7.3×105s−2)=1.3×10−4x_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{(\pi/2)\times136\times50\times0.87}/(2\pi\times136)^2=96\ {\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}}/(7.3\times10^{5}\ {\mathrm{s^{-2}}})=1.3\times10^{-4} m; at 1 kHz, (π/2)×1,000×50×0.2/(2π×1,000)2=125/(3.9×107)=3.2×10−6\sqrt{(\pi/2)\times1{,}000\times50\times0.2}/(2\pi\times1{,}000)^2=125/(3.9\times10^{7})=3.2\times10^{-6} m; the ratio is 41. It is a single-degree-of-freedom model (one mass on one spring); the angular error depends on how the mode couples to tilt.
    • A mode above 1 kHz is outside the body profile altogether.
    • This is the physics behind the “>0.8 kHz” requirement (Wang et al.), and behind Mirrorcle’s remark that smaller, higher-resonance mirrors are “more robust to shock and vibration” [P].

  • A resonant fast axis cannot be placed at will. The line budget sets it: fmirror=S/2f_{\mathrm{mirror}}=S/2 with SS from Eq. (77), which gives 0.30–0.63 kHz for the products above. For the M1 that is 0.63 kHz at its 10 Hz frame rate, about half the 1.2–1.3 kHz at which the maker of its module mirror rates the fast axis [I]; that rating matches the 20 Hz to which the M1’s GAZE function can switch (125×20/2=1,250125\times20/2=1{,}250 Hz) [P/E]. For InnovizOne, whose four lasers share each sweep, it is 0.30–0.32 kHz [P/E]. The frequency also drifts with temperature.

    • At Q = 1,000 (an illustrative value for a resonant mirror) its bandwidth is fmirror/Q=fmirror/1,000f_{\mathrm{mirror}}/Q=f_{\mathrm{mirror}}/1{,}000, i.e. 0.1% of fmirrorf_{\mathrm{mirror}}, while −40 to +85 °C moves it by 30ppm/K×125K=0.375%30\ {\mathrm{ppm/K}}\times125\ {\mathrm{K}}=0.375\%: 0.375/0.1=3.750.375/0.1=3.75, nearly four bandwidths. A drive left at a fixed frequency would fall off the resonance and lose most of its amplitude.
    • The drive must therefore track the resonance with a phase-locked loop (PLL, a feedback loop that keeps the drive frequency locked to the measured phase of the mirror’s motion) and sense the mirror angle. Wang et al. make the same point: non-resonant scanning is “more robust against ambient temperature variations” [P].

  • Measured [P]:

    • Yoo et al. (J. Optical Microsystems 2022) tested a 1-D resonant MEMS lidar under a wideband LV 124-based profile. It used a multichannel horizontal line laser, a 10° × 11° field and frame rates up to 29 Hz. In open loop (drive without feedback), vibration caused “wobbly distortion along the scan angle”. PLL control cut the mean and standard deviation of the point-to-surface error (the distance of measured points from the true surface) by up to 69.3% and 90.0%.
    • Hua et al. (Micromachines 2021) shook a Φ5 mm electromagnetic 2-D mirror at 0.8–1.2 g below 200 Hz. The vibration response superposed linearly on the drive and peaked at the 136 Hz slow-axis resonance. A feed-forward sliding-mode controller (a robust nonlinear feedback scheme, plus a term that anticipates the known drive) beat PID control (the standard proportional–integral–derivative feedback).

  • The conclusion for 2-D MEMS. The quasi-static slow axis that makes a raster must be driven at the frame rate (10–30 Hz) with a resonance well above its drive harmonics (the multiples of the frame rate contained in its ramp-like waveform), so that the ramp is reproduced without ringing. Raising that resonance needs stiffer springs, which cut the quasi-static angle for a given actuator (the FoM bound, Eq. (80)). Mirrors of 3 mm and more therefore sit at about 100–400 Hz (Hua et al.’s 5 mm mirror at 136 Hz; Mirrorcle’s 3–6.4 mm mirrors at 300–400 Hz), the most energetic part of the road spectrum. Only small mirrors escape it, such as Mirrorcle’s 2 mm mirror at 1.3 kHz, at the cost of the collecting area of subsection 2(e). A 1-D resonant mirror with an electronic second axis avoids that axis altogether, and so does a one-axis macro-mirror with a column.

4. What shipped, and the trade-offs that decided it

This subsection turns from physics to the market record: which scanner families reached series production, what each delivered, and what it cost. The one-axis mirror with an electronic column won on volume, while MEMS, polygon-plus-galvo and Risley designs retreated to niches or left the car market. In the table, “10%” means a target of 10% reflectance, the usual benchmark for quoting range; “klx” is kilolux of ambient illuminance (100 klx is bright sunlight); a “robotaxi” is a driverless taxi; and L3 is SAE driving-automation level 3, where the car drives itself within a defined domain and the driver takes over on request.

Even robotaxis now use forward one-axis units as the primary lidar: four AT128 on Pony.ai’s seventh generation [P] and on Baidu’s Yichi 06 [T]

Other terms in the table: Yole is a market-research firm; “roof crown” mounting places the lidar in a bump on the roof above the windscreen; “pixel summation” pools the returns of neighbouring pixels to reach farther at coarser resolution; “behind-fascia” means hidden behind the car’s front bodywork; and Chapter 11 is US bankruptcy reorganization.

5. What this adds up to [E]

  1. Channel count sets mechanical speed, and silicon made channels cheap. Sweep rate is lines × frame rate / parallel channels (Eq. (77)). With 128–256 channels a mirror needs about 10 sweeps a second, so an ordinary motor, encoder and mirror suffice and the mechanism is nowhere near a limit. A single-beam MEMS asks its mirror for 1,000–3,000 sweeps a second and meets four limits at once: the FoM bound (Eq. (80)), D5D^5 deformation (Eq. (81)), walk-off (Eq. (79)) and the per-channel ToF rate (Eq. (78)).
  2. In series production so far, “slow moving parts” has proved a more successful target than “no moving parts”. Motor-driven mirrors proved qualifiable (Valeo since 2017; Hesai and Huawei by the million), so the premise that macroscopic motion could not pass automotive vibration and lifetime tests did not hold. The MEMS mirror’s shock strength (300–500 g) was never its problem. Its fast-axis tracking, low slow-axis resonance and small aperture were.
  3. Aperture follows the mechanism. Anything that receives through its scanner inherits the scanner’s aperture, and only slow macro-mirrors could afford a 25 mm-class coaxial path. MEMS designs had to tile modules or receive separately, which re-imports part of the staring-receiver penalty (§C6).
  4. Programmable ROI did not need MEMS. A galvo-scheduled ROI (Falcon) and an electronic ROI (denser channels in the column) delivered the “gaze” benefit that was one of MEMS’s selling points.
  5. What could reverse this. Two developments could: a large-aperture receive-side steerer (a device that steers the field of view of a large receiving aperture, §C6, §C10), or MEMS mirrors with FoM of order 10 at ≥5 mm and robust closed-loop control at car cost. The Fraunhofer 1-D mirror (FoM ≈13) shows that the resonant 1-D route has headroom; its remaining problem is the staring receiver it requires.

C5. SPAD-SoC receivers in Chinese lidars: design origin and foundries

This section asks which receiver chips in Chinese lidars are the makers’ own designs and which are bought-in Sony parts, and whether their manufacturing sites have been disclosed. A SPAD-SoC (SPAD system-on-chip) is a single stacked chip that combines an array of single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) with the timing, histogramming and processing logic of a direct time-of-flight (dToF) receiver, which times each photon’s round trip. SPAD-SoCs in Chinese lidars follow two patterns: (a) Sony parts described generically as “SPAD-SoCs” and (b) distinct designs. No foundry (contract chip manufacturer) is publicly named for any of the lidar makers’ own distinct designs; the one named foundry is Tower, for Fortsense’s merchant FL6031. The answer matters for judging how much of the lidar’s key silicon Chinese makers design themselves.

The line-count shortcut. “Line count” in this class is the receiver’s long-axis dToF pixel count after 3×3 binning (grouping 3 × 3 SPADs into one ranging pixel). Sony’s two automotive parts bin to 192 and 520 lines, so a product with exactly one of these counts is a first candidate for a Sony part (details in §C5a). The two Sony reference parts are described below. “Pitch” is the centre-to-centre spacing of the SPADs. “Cu–Cu bonded” means that the SPAD wafer and the logic wafer are joined face to face through direct copper-to-copper contacts, so each pixel connects straight to circuitry beneath it. “90 nm” and “40 nm” are the process generations (nodes) of the two wafers, and ISSCC is the International Solid-State Circuits Conference.

  • Sony IMX459: 597×168 SPADs, 10.08 µm pitch, back-side-illuminated (BSI) SPAD wafer Cu–Cu bonded to a logic wafer (a 90 nm SPAD process [I] and, per trade press only, 40 nm logic [T]; §C5a), PDE (photon detection efficiency, the share of arriving photons that are counted) 24% at 905 nm [P]. Binned: about 192 lines [P].
  • Sony IMX479: 105×1,568 SPADs, 10.08 µm, 520 dToF pixels at 0.05° vertical, PDE 37% at 940 nm, about 98% on-chip data reduction and 25 Mpts/s [P]; 3 GHz equivalent-time sampling [I, §C5a]. Equivalent-time sampling builds a finely sampled waveform from many repeated measurements with shifted sampling instants, here equivalent to a 3 GHz sampling rate; Mpts/s is millions of points per second.

The table lists, for each Chinese lidar or receiver chip, what teardowns or vendor documents establish and what is only inferred; Hesai’s two SiPM-based units, AT128 and ATX, are included for contrast.
