First row: 2-fold 36×2×(7.32×106)2×10−9=3.9×10636\times2\times(7.32\times10^{6})^2\times10^{-9}=3.9\times10^{6}; 3-fold 84×3×(7.32×106)3×10−18=9.9×10484\times3\times(7.32\times10^{6})^3\times10^{-18}=9.9\times10^{4}, which is 6.59×107/(9.9×104)≈6706.59\times10^{7}/(9.9\times10^{4})\approx670 times below the singles; 4-fold 126×4×(7.32×106)4×10−27=1.4×103126\times4\times(7.32\times10^{6})^4\times10^{-27}=1.4\times10^{3}. The second row, with r=2.965×108/9=3.29×107r=2.965\times10^{8}/9=3.29\times10^{7} s⁻¹, gives 7.8×1077.8\times10^{7}, 9.0×1069.0\times10^{6} (a factor 2.965×108/(9.0×106)≈332.965\times10^{8}/(9.0\times10^{6})\approx33 below the singles) and 5.9×1055.9\times10^{5} (a factor 2.965×108/(5.9×105)≈5002.965\times10^{8}/(5.9\times10^{5})\approx500).
  • Little gain in the third row: rτc=1.22×108×10−9=0.12r\tau_c=1.22\times10^{8}\times10^{-9}=0.12 is not small, so Eq. (92) is only a rough guide there. It gives 2-fold accidentals of 72×(1.22×108)2×10−9=1.1×10972\times(1.22\times10^{8})^2\times10^{-9}=1.1\times10^{9}, about the singles rate, so a 2-fold rule rejects almost nothing; 3- and 4-fold rules give 252×(1.22×108)3×10−18=4.6×108252\times(1.22\times10^{8})^3\times10^{-18}=4.6\times10^{8} and 504×(1.22×108)4×10−27=1.1×108504\times(1.22\times10^{8})^4\times10^{-27}=1.1\times10^{8}, only ≈2× and ≈10× below the singles.

What the coincidence numbers teach:

  • Lesson 1: coincidence works only once optics have made rτc≪1r\tau_c\ll1. In the brightest case (rτc≈0.12r\tau_c\approx0.12) a 2-fold rule does nothing and even a 4-fold rule gains only ≈10×, against ≈500× at 940 nm behind a 10 nm filter (rτc≈0.033r\tau_c\approx0.033), so Layer 1 has to come first.
  • Lesson 2: coincidence costs sensitivity at long range, because it needs at least nthn_{\mathrm{th}} signal photons within τc\tau_c. Let n‾\bar n be the mean number of detected signal photons per shot (the per-pulse count Ns,1N_{s,1} of §C0 Eq. (31)). With Poisson photon statistics, the probability of detecting at least nth=3n_{\mathrm{th}}=3 is one minus the probability of detecting zero, one or two: P(≥3)=1−e−n‾(1+n‾+n‾2/2)P(\ge3)=1-e^{-\bar n}(1+\bar n+\bar n^2/2). A mean of n‾=5\bar n=5 detected photons per shot gives 1−e−5×18.5=0.881-e^{-5}\times18.5=0.88; a mean of 2 gives only 1−e−2×5=0.321-e^{-2}\times5=0.32. At 200 m on a 10% target, (c) gives ≈21–33 photons per point, i.e. n‾≈2.1\bar n\approx2.1–3.3 per shot over the ≈10 shots of a point, so a 3-fold requirement would catch only 1−e−2.1×5.305=0.351-e^{-2.1}\times5.305=0.35 to 1−e−3.3×9.745=0.641-e^{-3.3}\times9.745=0.64 of the shots.
  • Hence adaptive thresholds: raise nthn_{\mathrm{th}} in bright sun; lower it in darkness and for weak far returns. RoboSense’s multi-threshold TDC (time-to-digital converter) applies this idea [T/I]. IMX479’s pixel-level threshold control is a different mechanism: it sets the comparator level at which a pulse counts as an avalanche, which keeps the dead time stable (§C5a).
  • Shorter dead time (active recharge). An active recharge circuit resets the SPAD quickly after each avalanche instead of letting it recover through a resistor, and makes it non-paralyzable (Eq. (90), right-hand form). In the bright 940 nm/10 nm case (r=2.965×108/9=3.29×107r=2.965\times10^{8}/9=3.29\times10^{7} s⁻¹ per SPAD, so rτd=0.20r\tau_d=0.20 at 6 ns) a passively recharged SPAD with Sony’s 6 ns is dead 1−e−0.20=18%1-e^{-0.20}=18\% of the time, as in (d). With active recharge it is dead 17% at 6 ns (0.20/1.200.20/1.20), 9% at 3 ns (0.099/1.0990.099/1.099) and 40% at 20 ns (rτd=0.66r\tau_d=0.66, and 0.66/1.66=0.400.66/1.66=0.40). The trade-off is more afterpulsing: carriers trapped during one avalanche are released after a fast reset and trigger a false count.
  • More SPADs per channel. Larger macro-pixels, up to the SiPM limit of hundreds to about a thousand cells (§C4b), add parallel cells, so some are always armed when the return arrives. The price is resolution.

Layer 4 — statistics and processing

  • Multi-shot time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) histograms accumulate photon arrival times over many shots. Matched filtering correlates the histogram with the expected pulse shape. Constant-false-alarm-rate (CFAR) peak detection sets the detection threshold from the measured noise floor, so that false alarms stay at a fixed rate. The background forms a flat floor that grows in proportion to NshotsN_{\mathrm{shots}}, the number of laser shots accumulated into one histogram, while its relative fluctuation falls as 1/Nshots1/\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{shots}}}; the signal-to-noise ratio of the return therefore grows as Nshots\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{shots}}}.
  • Pile-up correction. Coates’ correction (1968) reconstructs the true arrival histogram from the first-photon-biased one. Research methods go further: asynchronous or shifted gating, and deliberately attenuating flux to the optimal level (Gupta et al., CVPR 2019 / ICCV 2019, two computer-vision conferences) [U].
  • Point-level confidence and spatio-temporal filtering drop low-confidence returns caused by sunlight noise, using the fact that real surfaces persist between neighbouring points and successive frames while noise does not.

Layer 5 — system architecture

  • Adaptive exposure within eye safety. Concentrate energy on each region of interest (ROI), or trade point rate and frame rate for more energy per point in bright conditions. Hesai’s AT128 prospectus describes ASIC-driven (application-specific integrated circuit) addressable laser channels with “dynamic exposure” [P].
  • SiPM receivers tolerate sunlight better per channel, because background is spread over about 10310^3 cells (§C4b), so a background count blinds only a small fraction of the channel.
  • 1550 nm ToF: about 10× the eye-safe average power and 2.6–3× less solar irradiance, at 2–3× the cost. On the ±10 nm band averages of §C4c, 1,550 nm has 0.270/0.693=0.390.270/0.693=0.39 of the 905 nm solar irradiance (≈2.6× less). Counted in photons per nm, which is what sets the background count, that is 0.39×1,550/905=0.670.39\times1{,}550/905=0.67 of the 905 nm value (≈1.5× less), because each 1,550 nm photon carries less energy. At the exact wavelengths the two ratios are 0.270/0.817=0.330.270/0.817=0.33 (3× less) and 0.33×1,550/905=0.570.33\times1{,}550/905=0.57.
  • FMCW coherent detection strongly suppresses broadband sunlight at the detected beat frequency. In FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous-wave) lidar the laser frequency is swept, and the return is mixed on the detector with a local oscillator (LO), a copy of the outgoing light. The range appears as a beat frequency in the intermediate-frequency (IF) signal. Only light in the local oscillator’s spatial mode and IF bandwidth contributes coherently; detector saturation and other interference mechanisms can still matter.
    • Example: a sunlit ρ = 0.5 surface at 1550 nm, in one spatial mode (ArxΩ≈λ2A_{\mathrm{rx}}\Omega\approx\lambda^2: the étendue of a single mode, aperture area times accepted solid angle) and a 200 MHz IF bandwidth (Δλ≈1.6\Delta\lambda\approx1.6 pm), contributes only about 10310^3 photons/s.
    • The IF bandwidth Δf\Delta f converts to an optical bandwidth as Δλ=λ2Δf/c=(1.55×10−6)2×2×108/(3×108)=1.6×10−12\Delta\lambda=\lambda^2\Delta f/c=(1.55\times10^{-6})^2\times2\times10^{8}/(3\times10^{8})=1.6\times10^{-12} m.
    • With the ASTM G173 irradiance of 0.27 W m⁻² nm⁻¹ at 1,550 nm (§C4c), the in-band irradiance is 0.27Wm−2nm−1×1.6×10−3nm=4.3×10−4Wm−20.27\ {\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,nm^{-1}}}\times1.6\times10^{-3}\ {\mathrm{nm}}=4.3\times10^{-4}\ {\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}}. One mode collects this irradiance times the Lambertian factor ρ/π\rho/\pi times the single-mode étendue λ2\lambda^2: 4.3×10−4×(0.5/π)×λ2=4.3×10−4×0.159×2.4×10−12≈1.7×10−164.3\times10^{-4}\times(0.5/\pi)\times\lambda^2=4.3\times10^{-4}\times0.159\times2.4\times10^{-12}\approx1.7\times10^{-16} W. Dividing by the 1,550 nm photon energy Eph=1.28×10−19E_{\mathrm{ph}}=1.28\times10^{-19} J gives ≈1.3×103\approx1.3\times10^{3} photons/s (about half that in one polarization).
    • That is 5–6 orders of magnitude below a ToF macro-pixel’s 10810^8–10910^9/s (108/(1.3×103)≈8×10410^{8}/(1.3\times10^{3})\approx8\times10^{4} to 109/(1.3×103)≈8×10510^{9}/(1.3\times10^{3})\approx8\times10^{5}), and negligible against local-oscillator shot noise (the photon-counting noise of the strong LO beam itself).
    • The price is FMCW’s cost and point-rate penalties (§C7).

How it shows up in specs. Vendors quote range at a stated ambient level: Seyond Falcon K2 gives 250 m @10% at 100 klx with PdP_d (probability of detection) > 90% [P]; Sony’s ISSCC 2021 receiver gives 150 m on a 10% target and 200 m on a 95% target under 117 klx [P] (§C5a). The sun directly in the field of view still blinds affected columns for a moment; systems blank or flag those regions and rely on other sensors meanwhile.

(e) Histogram memory. Each pixel read out in parallel needs its own histogram, so memory grows with the number of simultaneously active pixels.

  • A full 300 m / 5 cm histogram is 300/0.05=6,000300/0.05=6{,}000 bins × 10 bits (an assumed 10-bit counter per bin) = 60 kbit per pixel. One 520-pixel column needs about 520×60kbit=31520\times60\ {\mathrm{kbit}}=31 Mbit, manageable in a scanned column. A staring 520k-pixel array needs about 31 Gbit (5.2×105×60kbit5.2\times10^{5}\times60\ {\mathrm{kbit}}), impractical as full, simultaneous on-sensor storage in a cost-limited automotive device.
  • The answers are equivalent-time sampling plus compression (Sony, about 98%), partial histograms, peak tracking (following a known return from frame to frame so only a small window is stored) and zone multiplexing (reading different zones in turn).

(f) Avalanche power. Every count, whether from signal or sunlight, dumps a small charge through the biased SPAD, so bright sunlight costs electrical power.

  • Each avalanche costs about CVex(Vbd+Vex)≈1.6C\,V_{\mathrm{ex}}(V_{\mathrm{bd}}+V_{\mathrm{ex}})\approx1.6–3.9 pJ. Here CC is the capacitance of the diode plus its circuit node, VexV_{\mathrm{ex}} the excess bias and VbdV_{\mathrm{bd}} the breakdown voltage. The avalanche discharges the node by VexV_{\mathrm{ex}}, so a charge CVexCV_{\mathrm{ex}} passes, and recharging draws it from the total bias Vbd+VexV_{\mathrm{bd}}+V_{\mathrm{ex}}.
  • The numbers take Sony’s supplies as Vbd=20.5V_{\mathrm{bd}}=20.5 V and Vex=3.3V_{\mathrm{ex}}=3.3 V (§C5a) and assume 20–50 fF of diode plus node capacitance. C=20C=20 fF gives 20×10−15×3.3×23.8=1.620\times10^{-15}\times3.3\times23.8=1.6 pJ and C=50C=50 fF gives 3.9 pJ.
  • In sunlight a scanned column dissipates about 0.13–0.33 W in the model’s central case (0.24–0.58 W in full sun); a staring VGA (640 × 480) SPAD array about 5–12 W. The avalanche power is Pav=NpixravEavP_{\mathrm{av}}=N_{\mathrm{pix}}\,r_{\mathrm{av}}\,E_{\mathrm{av}}, where NpixN_{\mathrm{pix}} is the number of active pixels, ravr_{\mathrm{av}} the avalanche rate per pixel (s⁻¹) and EavE_{\mathrm{av}} the energy per avalanche (J).
    • Roughly, only photons that find a SPAD armed trigger a full avalanche, so the avalanche rate is close to the recorded count rate (Eq. (84) for paralyzable SPADs) rather than the incident photon rate. The column figure takes the 1.83×108×0.885=1.62×1081.83\times10^{8}\times0.885=1.62\times10^{8} avalanches/s recorded in each of 520 macro-pixels in the model’s central case of (d) [E]: 520×1.62×108s−1×1.6pJ=0.13520\times1.62\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times1.6\ {\mathrm{pJ}}=0.13 W, and 0.33 W at 3.9 pJ. In full sun the recorded rate is 3.66×108×0.784=2.87×1083.66\times10^{8}\times0.784=2.87\times10^{8} s⁻¹, which gives 0.24 W and 0.58 W.
    • The VGA figure corresponds to about 10710^{7} avalanches/s in each of 640×480=3.1×105640\times480=3.1\times10^{5} pixels: 3.1×105×107s−1×1.6pJ=4.93.1\times10^{5}\times10^{7}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times1.6\ {\mathrm{pJ}}=4.9 W, and 12 W at 3.9 pJ. The 10710^{7} is the recorded rate of a staring 10 µm single-SPAD pixel behind an f/2.4 lens in the fully sunlit scene of (d). A pixel collects background in proportion to its étendue πp2/(4N2)\pi p^2/(4N^2), with pp the pixel pitch and NN the f-number: π×(10μm)2/(4×2.42)=1.36×10−11\pi\times(10\ \mu{\mathrm{m}})^2/(4\times2.4^2)=1.36\times10^{-11} m² sr, i.e. 0.036 of the 7.62×10−7sr×4.91×10−4m2=3.74×10−107.62\times10^{-7}\ {\mathrm{sr}}\times4.91\times10^{-4}\ {\mathrm{m^2}}=3.74\times10^{-10} m² sr of the macro-pixel in (d). That gives 2.965×108×0.036=1.08×1072.965\times10^{8}\times0.036=1.08\times10^{7} s⁻¹ incident (940 nm, 10 nm filter, reflectance 0.9, PDE 0.3) and, with 6 ns of paralyzable dead time, 1.08×107×e−0.065=1.0×1071.08\times10^{7}\times e^{-0.065}=1.0\times10^{7} s⁻¹ recorded. At f/2 the recorded rate is 1.4×1071.4\times10^{7} s⁻¹; an f/1.2 lens, with four times the étendue of f/2.4, gives 3.3×1073.3\times10^{7} s⁻¹ and about 3.3 times the power [E].
  • Enabling only the illuminated zone is one way to control this load; a true simultaneous flash instead needs a different power, gating and readout budget.

(g) Cost.

  • NE Times reports that SPAD-SoC receivers become cheaper than SiPM receivers above about 200 lines [T].
  • RoboSense claims about 50% cost reduction for its Phoenix, which puts the SPAD array and processing on one stacked chip rather than in separate parts [P].
  • The SPAD wafer stays on mature (older, cheaper) process nodes, while the logic wafer moves to finer nodes for SRAM and DSP [E].

Can a fully solid-state 2D addressable VCSEL × SPAD “electronic scan” reach long range over a wide field?

Shipping wide-field solid-state units reach about 30 m @10%, and every long-range product keeps one moving axis. Receive aperture is the likely first constraint.

To compare products with different fields, the table uses the descriptive figure of merit R10%2⋅FOVR_{10\%}^2\cdot\text{FOV}. Here R10%R_{10\%} is the quoted range on a 10%-reflectance target and FOV is the product of the horizontal and vertical field angles (deg²). The reasoning behind it: at fixed laser power, receiver and integration time, spreading the light over a larger field leaves fewer photons per direction, in proportion to 1/FOV1/{\mathrm{FOV}}, and signal-limited range scales as the square root of the photons per direction (the same argument as Eq. (87)). For one design, R2⋅FOVR^2\cdot{\mathrm{FOV}} therefore stays roughly constant, and a larger value marks a more capable design. Selected shipping products [P vendor specifications, E figure of merit]:

Product FOV Range @10% R2⋅R^2\cdotFOV (m²·deg²)
Hesai FTX-140 (solid-state) 140°×105° 30 m 1.3×10⁷
RoboSense E1 (solid-state) 120°×90° 30 m 9.7×10⁶
Seyond Hummingbird D1 (solid-state) 140°×100° 30 m 1.26×10⁷
Opsys ALTOS 70 / 150 / 300 (same design, different optics) 80°×22° / 45°×13° / 22.5°×6.5° 55 / 100 / 200 m 5.3 / 5.85 / 5.85 ×10⁶ (constant)
Hesai ATX (1 scan axis) 120°×20° 230 m 1.3×10⁸
Seyond Falcon K2 (1550 nm, 2-axis) 120°×25° 250 m 1.9×10⁸
RoboSense EM4 (1 scan axis) 120°×27° [P]; the lens, not the IMX479-class chip, sets this field (Sony’s 120° × 26° is its own test system at 0.05°) 300 m (basis unclear) about 2.9×10⁸

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • The figure of merit is the square of the quoted 10% range times the product of the horizontal and vertical fields in degrees. Example: Hesai FTX-140 gives 302×140×105=900×14,700=1.3×10730^2\times140\times105=900\times14{,}700=1.3\times10^{7} m²·deg²; Hesai ATX gives 2302×120×20=52,900×2,400=1.3×108230^2\times120\times20=52{,}900\times2{,}400=1.3\times10^{8}.

  • Opsys variants: 552×80×22=5.3×10655^2\times80\times22=5.3\times10^{6}, 1002×45×13=5.85×106100^2\times45\times13=5.85\times10^{6} and 2002×22.5×6.5=5.85×106200^2\times22.5\times6.5=5.85\times10^{6}, a spread of 5.85/5.3=1.105.85/5.3=1.10.

  • Opsys keeps R2⋅R^2\cdotFOV constant to within about 10% across its own variants, as the figure of merit predicts for one design behind different optics. Scaling that same design to 120°×25° suggests about 44 m @10%, if power, integration time and detection threshold are held fixed [E: R=5.85×106/(120×25)=1,950≈44R=\sqrt{5.85\times10^{6}/(120\times25)}=\sqrt{1{,}950}\approx44 m].

  • Across manufacturers, the metric does not hold those conditions fixed, so it cannot establish a universal solid-state limit.

The physics behind it: receive étendue and silicon area [E]. Étendue is the product of a receiver’s aperture area and the solid angle it accepts. Optics cannot increase it, so it caps how much light the receiver can gather from a scene of given brightness. A wide staring field forces a short focal length onto a fixed-size sensor, and at a given f-number (focal length divided by aperture diameter) that means a small aperture.

  • Aperture. Take IMX479’s 15.8 mm array at f/1.2. With a rectilinear lens (one that maps straight lines to straight lines, image height ftan⁡θf\tan\theta), half the array length must subtend half the field, f=(L/2)/tan⁡(Θ/2)f=(L/2)/\tan(\Theta/2), where ff is the focal length, LL the array length and Θ\Theta the full field angle along it. At f/1.2 the entrance aperture diameter is D=f/1.2D=f/1.2. Covering a 26° axis (scanned column) needs f=7.9mm/tan⁡13∘≈34f=7.9\ {\mathrm{mm}}/\tan13^\circ\approx34 mm and aperture D=34.2/1.2≈28.5D=34.2/1.2\approx28.5 mm; staring over 120° needs f=7.9mm/tan⁡60∘≈4.6f=7.9\ {\mathrm{mm}}/\tan60^\circ\approx4.6 mm and D=4.56/1.2≈3.8D=4.56/1.2\approx3.8 mm. That is about 1.8% of the collecting area ((3.8/28.5)2=0.018(3.8/28.5)^2=0.018). Because range scales as the square root of the collected photons (signal-limited, extended target), and the collected photons scale as D2D^2, that means roughly 7.5× less range for the same photons (28.5/3.8=7.528.5/3.8=7.5).
  • Illustrative staring-array size. 120°×26° sampled at 0.05° needs about 2,400×520 = 1.25 million effective angular cells. At a 30.24 µm macro-pixel pitch (IMX479’s 3×3 unit), an equiangular image-plane mapping (image position proportional to field angle, so every cell spans the same angle) gives about 72.6×15.7 mm (1,140 mm²) of active pixels (2,400×30.24μm=72.62{,}400\times30.24\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=72.6 mm by 520×30.24μm=15.7520\times30.24\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=15.7 mm): about 68× IMX479’s active area (1,140/16.7≈681{,}140/16.7\approx68), and too long for one conventional exposure field. This is a projection-dependent lower-order sizing example, not the inevitable sensor size: a rectilinear 120° lens at the same on-axis angular pitch would be wider still, while deliberate angular nonuniformity can redistribute samples. Circuits, margins and bonding add area beyond the array.
  • Smaller pitch. A 5 µm physical SPAD pitch with the same 3×3 grouping (15 µm macro-pixels) shrinks the equiangular array to about 36×7.8 mm (2,400×15μm2{,}400\times15\ \mu{\mathrm{m}} by 520×15μm520\times15\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}), still wider than a 33 mm field before periphery; at 4 µm (12 µm macro-pixels) it is about 29×6.2 mm (2,400×12μm=28.82{,}400\times12\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=28.8 mm by 520×12μm=6.2520\times12\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=6.2 mm), nominally within one field. But smaller pixels do not preserve the photon budget automatically. At a fixed 0.05° angular pitch the focal length, f=pmp/θlinef=p_{\mathrm{mp}}/\theta_{\mathrm{line}} as in the IMX479 check above, shrinks in proportion to the macro-pixel pitch pmpp_{\mathrm{mp}}, and so does the entrance aperture at a given f-number. In the same f/1.2 example the entrance aperture falls from about 28.5 to 11.5 mm at 4 µm pitch (f=12μm/(8.73×10−4rad)=13.8f=12\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(8.73\times10^{-4}\ {\mathrm{rad}})=13.8 mm and D=13.8/1.2=11.5D=13.8/1.2=11.5 mm; at 5 µm pitch, f=17.2f=17.2 mm and D=14.3D=14.3 mm); preserving it requires faster optics, a different projection or a different architecture.
  • The emitter is not the bottleneck: addressable VCSEL zones concentrate energy as well as a scanner does.
  • Likely binding constraints for the architecture modeled here: (1) receive étendue and aperture; (2) silicon area and yield; (3) histogram memory for parallel readout; (4) background avalanche power. The order can change with tiling, gating, coherent detection, frame rate and cost target.
  • A mechanical one-axis scanner appears to be the cheapest proven optical multiplexer at current automotive volumes. An optical multiplexer here means a way of sharing one detector among many viewing directions. The scanner shares one small column across about 2,400 horizontal positions while keeping a large aperture. A matched total-system-cost comparison with new solid-state architectures has not been presented.
  • Industry evidence: every long-range SPAD-SoC (“digital”) product shipping or announced keeps one moving axis (Hesai ETX, RoboSense EM4 and Phoenix-based units, Seyond Robin E2). So do the SiPM-based Hesai ATX and the Huawei 896-line, whose detector type is undisclosed (§C5).

What could break this [E]. Four developments could change this conclusion:

  1. Tiling narrow-field solid-state modules (about 20× ALTOS 300 to cover 120°×25°: (120×25)/(22.5×6.5)=3,000/146≈20.5(120\times25)/(22.5\times6.5)=3{,}000/146\approx20.5), which is a cost problem.
  2. Smaller SPAD pitch (5 µm) with high NIR PDE on stitched or three-layer stacks.
  3. Non-mechanical steering of the receive path, feeding a small detector from a large aperture: an optical phased array (OPA, which steers light by controlling the phase across many emitting elements), liquid-crystal (LC) metasurfaces (Lumotive), LC polarization gratings, or wavelength steering (a grating sends each wavelength in a different direction). This is one attractive missing capability, not the only route.
  4. Coherent (FMCW) detection, which removes the sunlight and pile-up problem but brings back 1550 nm and the same steering need.

C7. FMCW and non-mechanical beam steering

This section asks whether frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) lidar and non-mechanical beam steering are ready for cars, and what physics limits them. An FMCW lidar sweeps (chirps) the optical frequency of a continuous laser and measures range, and radial velocity through the Doppler shift, from the beat between the returned light and a local copy of the transmitted light, the local oscillator (LO). A time-of-flight (ToF) lidar instead times short pulses. Non-mechanical steering points the beam with no moving parts, for example with an optical phased array (OPA), by tuning the wavelength, or with a liquid-crystal metasurface.

The short answer is that FMCW has no passenger-car series production, and trucks are its only commercial foothold. The physics below shows what holds it back technically: FMCW’s per-channel throughput and its single-mode light collection, not its laser coherence, are what limit point rate and cost.

Commercial status

The first passenger-car programme starts in 2028, and several steering start-ups have entered insolvency or put their assets up for sale, and others sell mainly to industrial users.

  • Passenger cars: zero series production. Yole (a market-research firm) had said FMCW would not enter automotive “before 2028” [T]. The first passenger-car design win is Aeva with an unnamed top-10 European OEM, L3, SOP 2028 (announced 3 Dec 2025) [P]. Here OEM means a carmaker, L3 is SAE driving-automation level 3 (the car drives itself in a defined domain and the driver takes over on request), and SOP is start of production.
  • Trucks, the only foothold:
    • Aurora FirstLight:
      • Aurora has run a driverless commercial service since 1 May 2025. Since May 2025 a person Aurora describes as an observer has ridden in the cab: truck maker Paccar asked for a person back on board less than three weeks after the first driverless runs. Aurora counts these as driverless miles [T, NYT, 17 Mar 2026]. Aurora ran 10 driverless trucks in December 2025 and reduced that fleet in early 2026 to prepare a second-generation fleet [P, Q4 2025 shareholder letter]. It launched that fleet in late July 2026 and expected 20–25 second-generation driverless trucks by the end of September [P, Q2 2026 shareholder letter]; CNBC reported 20 on the road on 22 Sep 2026 [T]. It targets more than 200 by year-end 2026, which it says translates to a revenue run-rate of about $80 M a year for its Transportation-as-a-Service business [P, Q2 2026 shareholder letter].
      • Aurora reports more than 500k driverless miles since commercial launch. At its 23 Sep 2026 investor day Aurora said it is “fully allocated” to exit 2026 with 200 driverless trucks. It targets more than 30,000 by 2030 and has a 500-truck Driver-as-a-Service order (Aurora supplies the self-driving system as a service rather than as hardware) from Hirschbach, with deliveries from 2027 [P] (release).
      • Gen 2 claims 1,000 m detection. Its fiber-free photonic engine uses silicon-nitride (SiN) waveguides, a III-V (compound-semiconductor) laser, custom semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs) and custom photodiodes; Fabrinet, a contract manufacturer, builds the kit [P].
      • Gen 3 follows in 2027, built by Aumovio (Continental’s automotive business, spun off in September 2025), “for tens of thousands of trucks” [P].
      • In Q2 2026 Aurora reported $2 M of revenue, a $270 M net loss and about $1.2 B of cash [P].
    • Aeva:
      • Aeva is the exclusive long-range lidar supplier for Daimler Truck/Torc. It delivered C-samples (near-production prototypes, the last of the automotive A/B/C sample stages) in May 2026 [P], began production in 2026 on a fully automated final-assembly line at the contract manufacturer Jabil in North America, which it expects to reach 100,000 systems a year [P, Aeva earnings calls of 26 Feb and 12 Aug 2026], and the programme plans Daimler Truck’s production ramp for 2027 [P, Aeva–Daimler Truck release, 9 Jan 2024].
      • It also works with Bendix on L2+ truck ADAS (advanced driver-assistance systems at level 2+, where the driver still supervises).
      • Its Atlas Ultra reaches 250 m at 10% reflectance over up to 150° of horizontal field of view (FOV), and is specified to ASIL-B(D). ASIL is the ISO 26262 Automotive Safety Integrity Level (A lowest, D highest); B(D) denotes ASIL B obtained by decomposing an ASIL-D safety requirement. Wavelength and scanner type are not disclosed [P].
  • Attrition:
    • Mobileye ended its FMCW programme on Intel silicon photonics (SiPh) in Sep 2024, citing progress of its EyeQ6 vision chip, in-house imaging radar and “better-than-expected cost reductions in third-party time-of-flight lidar” [P].
    • Scantinel went insolvent in Aug 2025; its assets went to MicroVision [P] (§C3a).
    • Baraja (wavelength steering) cut staff 75% in 2023 [T] and put its patents up for sale in 2025 [P] (§C3a).
    • Quanergy (optical phased array, OPA) filed Chapter 11 (US bankruptcy reorganization) in 2022 [P] (§C3a).
    • Analog Photonics (OPA with electro-optic phase shifters; its ≈60° phase-steered field implies a pitch of about 1.5 µm [E]) has no production award found. Its 2025 FS-4S datasheet specifies 200 m at 10% in a 20°×10° region of interest (ROI) mode (80 m over 60°×14°), at 35 W [P] (§C10.2b). It is funded mainly by US defence contracts (≈$45 M of federal prime awards, §C3a).
  • Industrial and security sales, the route Yole predicted:
    • SiLC sells its Eyeonic line for industrial and security uses and claims more than 1 km for its Eyeonic Vista [P/T] (§B8). Honda invested in it through its venture arm, Honda Xcelerator Ventures, in September 2024, for an undisclosed amount [P].
    • Voyant sells its Carbon for $1,490 a unit [P], with one axis steered on chip and the other by a slow mirror (§B8). Its Helium, announced as “coming soon”, is a 2D solid-state focal-plane array (FPA), i.e. a chip with a grid of switchable emitters and receivers, one per look direction.
    • LightIC builds its Lark lidar on the silicon-photonics foundry platform of Tower Semiconductor [P, Tower Semiconductor, 5 Jan 2026], with a system-on-chip (SoC) that LightIC describes as custom and whose published description matches indie Semiconductor’s iND83301 “Surya” [E] (§D7).
  • China:
    • LuminWave’s “Raptor” engine (Sep 2024) is a fully integrated III-V-on-Si chip (compound-semiconductor laser material on silicon photonics) with more than 10 GHz of FM bandwidth, i.e. optical frequency sweep [P, LuminWave, 10 Sep 2024]. Its heavy-truck nomination of 8 July 2025 (selection for a truck programme) does not name the product, customer or start of production, or state that the product is FMCW [P, LuminWave, 8 Jul 2025] (§D7).
    • No FMCW product from Hesai, RoboSense or Huawei, although Hesai holds FMCW, OPA and metasurface patents.
  • Non-mechanical steering in production:
    • flash solid-state units with single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) receivers, which illuminate the whole field at once (used for blind-spot coverage);
    • Lumotive LCM (Light Control Metasurface, a liquid-crystal beam steerer) in an industrial ToF sensor (Hokuyo YLM-10LX, 2024, 10 m at 10%; 180°×140° platform at ≤50 m, 2026; §C10.5).
    • No OPA or wavelength-steered scanner is in automotive series production.

Physics constraints for FMCW [E]

This subsection goes through the physical requirements an FMCW lidar must meet, one at a time, and says which are hard. Coherence length and target Doppler are manageable. The hard limits are per-channel throughput and single-mode collection:

  • Throughput is set by the dwell (the time spent measuring one point) and by the load on the analog-to-digital converter (ADC).
  • Single-mode collection is limited by étendue (the area × solid-angle product of the light a receiver accepts) and by speckle (the random interference pattern of light scattered from a rough surface).

A mechanical scanner adds a Doppler shift of its own, which ties scan rate, aperture and chirp length together (below). The practical consequence is that FMCW point rate is bought with parallel coherent channels, not with a faster scanner.

Coherence. A laser with a Lorentzian line of full width Δν\Delta\nu (Hz) has a coherence length, the path difference over which its phase stays correlated, of roughly Lc=c/(πΔν)L_c=c/(\pi\Delta\nu), with cc the speed of light. Requiring LcL_c to exceed the 600 m round trip to a 300 m target gives Δν≲c/(π×600m)=3×108/1,885≈160\Delta\nu\lesssim c/(\pi\times600\ {\mathrm{m}})=3\times10^{8}/1{,}885\approx160 kHz. That condition marks where detection becomes marginal, not a design point. At the round-trip delay τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c, only a fraction e−2πΔντe^{-2\pi\Delta\nu\tau} of the beat power stays in the coherent FFT peak, so Lc=2RL_c=2R keeps e−2≈14%e^{-2}\approx14\%, an 8.7 dB loss. Holding the loss to 1–3 dB needs ≈18–55 kHz at 300 m (§C7b subsection 2(e)). Practical FMCW sensitivity also depends on chirp linearity, dwell time and processing.

Beat frequency and ADC load. A linear chirp of bandwidth BB (Hz) swept in a time TcT_c returns from a target at range RR delayed by 2R/c2R/c. By then the LO has moved on in frequency, so the photodiode sees a beat tone at

fb=2BRcTcf_b=\frac{2BR}{cT_c}(93)

This beat frequency fbf_b sets the bandwidth each receive channel must digitize. For B=1B=1 GHz (range resolution c/2B=15c/2B=15 cm), Tc=10T_c=10 µs and R=300R=300 m, Eq. (93) gives fb=2×109×300/(3×108×10−5)≈200f_b=2\times10^{9}\times300/(3\times10^{8}\times10^{-5})\approx200 MHz per channel.

Doppler. A target closing at radial speed vrv_r shifts the return by fD=2vr/λf_D=2v_r/\lambda, where λ\lambda is the wavelength. At 1,550 nm this is ≈1.29 MHz per m/s (2/(1.55×10−6m)=1.29×1062/(1.55\times10^{-6}\ {\mathrm{m}})=1.29\times10^{6}). A 50 m/s closing speed adds about 50×1.29≈6550\times1.29\approx65 MHz to the beat tone. A single chirp cannot tell this shift from range, so the sensor needs up/down chirps or other disambiguation: the Doppler shift moves the up-chirp and down-chirp beat tones in opposite directions while range moves them together, so a pair separates the two.

Scanner-induced Doppler (mechanical scanning) [E unless tagged]. A moving scan mirror shifts the optical frequency of the light it reflects. ToF, which does not measure optical frequency, is immune. The result below is that fast mechanical scanning smears the FMCW beat tone and adds a false velocity, so coherent scanners must scan slowly, use small apertures or short chirps, or correct the effect digitally.

  • Mechanism. Let the mirror rotate at mechanical angular rate θ̇m\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}} (rad/s). A point on the mirror a distance ss from the rotation axis, measured across the tilt direction, moves along the mirror normal at vn=θ̇msv_n=\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}s. One reflection at angle of incidence θi\theta_i (measured from the mirror normal) shifts the light’s frequency by 2vncos⁡θi/λ2v_n\cos\theta_i/\lambda, where λ\lambda is the wavelength. A monostatic scanner (one that transmits and receives through the same optics) reflects the outgoing and the returning light off the same moving face, so the two shifts add.

  • Spread across the beam. The two edges of the beam’s footprint on the mirror move in opposite directions, so different parts of the beam are shifted by different amounts. Let θ̇\dot\theta be the optical scan rate, the rate at which the beam direction sweeps (rad/s; for one mirror reflection it is twice the mechanical rate, θ̇=2θ̇m\dot\theta=2\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}), and DD the beam diameter on the scanner. The frequency spread Δfscan\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}} across the beam, per pass, is then

    Δfscan≈θ̇Dλ\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}\approx\frac{\dot\theta D}{\lambda}(94)

    This is the inverse of the time the beam takes to sweep across its own angular width θb≈λ/D\theta_b\approx\lambda/D (its diffraction divergence, rad). That crossing time θb/θ̇\theta_b/\dot\theta is also the speckle-decorrelation time of the return. The received beat is therefore broadened by about Δfscan\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}} over the round trip, not by 2Δfscan2\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}: the outgoing and returning shifts add for the mean shift of Eq. (96) below, but the width is set by how fast the return decorrelates, once per crossing time [E]. Afocal optics after the mirror (a telescope that enlarges the beam also slows its angular sweep by the same factor) conserve θ̇D\dot\theta D, so for a given field-scan rate the spread grows with the output aperture.

    • Let TcT_c be the chirp duration of Eq. (93), over which one fast Fourier transform (FFT) integrates the beat tone. If TcT_c outlasts θb/θ̇\theta_b/\dot\theta, the beat tone spreads over ≈Tcθ̇D/λ=TcΔfscan\approx T_c\,\dot\theta D/\lambda=T_c\,\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}} FFT bins. Its peak falls by that factor (roughly half as much in dB with incoherent combining across bins), and the velocity estimate blurs by ≈λΔfscan/2=θ̇D/2=θ̇mD\approx\lambda\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}/2=\dot\theta D/2=\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}D, the difference between the normal velocities of the two edges of the beam’s footprint on the mirror.

    • Equivalently, a coherent aperture can integrate a whole chirp only if

      D≲λθ̇TcD\lesssim\frac{\lambda}{\dot\theta T_c}(95)

  • Offset: a mean Doppler bias. If the rotation axis does not pass through the beam centre, the whole return shifts, not just its edges. With s‾\bar s the distance of the beam centre from the rotation axis (across the tilt direction), the shift over the round trip is

    fbias≈4θ̇ms‾cos⁡θiλf_{\mathrm{bias}}\approx\frac{4\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}\bar s\cos\theta_i}{\lambda}(96)

    The factor 4 is two reflections (out and back) times the factor 2 of each reflection. The velocity estimator reads this as a false radial velocity λfbias/2=2θ̇ms‾cos⁡θi\lambda f_{\mathrm{bias}}/2=2\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}\bar s\cos\theta_i.

    • Galvanometer mirrors (galvos) and MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical) mirrors are pivoted near the beam centre, so their bias comes from centring error. A polygon facet is never pivoted at the beam: s‾\bar s runs across the facet as it turns, so the bias sweeps with scan angle and differs from facet to facet.
    • A single-slope chirp would also read the bias as range. A beat frequency ff maps to range cf/(2κ)cf/(2\kappa), where κ=B/Tc\kappa=B/T_c is the chirp rate in Hz/s, so the range error is ΔRbias=cfbias/2κ\Delta R_{\mathrm{bias}}=cf_{\mathrm{bias}}/2\kappa. Up/down chirp pairs cancel it to first order, because the bias adds to one beat tone and subtracts from the other.

The table evaluates Eq. (94) and Eq. (95) for four scanners at 1,550 nm, from a slow column sweep to a fast resonant MEMS mirror.

Example at 1,550 nm Optical scan rate θ̇\dot\theta Beam DD Spread Δfscan\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}} (per pass; ≈ the round-trip broadening) Beam-crossing time FFT bins spread in a 10 µs chirp Largest DD for a 10 µs / 1 µs chirp
Slow column sweep (the §C10.3a example) 1,200°/s 20 mm 0.27 MHz 3.7 µs ≈3 7.4 / 74 mm
Aeva’s threshold (below), read as an optical rate, with a 5 mm beam assumed [E] 5,000°/s 5 mm 0.28 MHz 3.6 µs ≈3 1.8 / 18 mm
Polygon at a Falcon-class sweep (§C4d) 45,600°/s 5 mm 2.6 MHz 0.39 µs ≈26 (−14 dB peak) 0.19 / 1.9 mm
Resonant MEMS, 1 kHz, ±30° optical (peak) 188,500°/s 5 mm 10.6 MHz 94 ns ≈106 (−20 dB peak) 0.05 / 0.5 mm

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Spread per pass: Δfscan=θ̇D/λ\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}=\dot\theta D/\lambda (Eq. (94)) with θ̇\dot\theta in rad/s. Polygon row: 45,600∘/s×π/180=79645{,}600^\circ/{\mathrm{s}}\times\pi/180=796 rad/s, so Δfscan=796×5×10−3/(1.55×10−6)=2.6\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}=796\times5\times10^{-3}/(1.55\times10^{-6})=2.6 MHz. The other rows use 1,200°/s = 20.9 rad/s and 5,000°/s = 87.3 rad/s.

  • Beam-crossing time: θb/θ̇=λ/(Dθ̇)=1/Δfscan\theta_b/\dot\theta=\lambda/(D\dot\theta)=1/\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}; for the polygon, 1/(2.6MHz)=0.391/(2.6\ {\mathrm{MHz}})=0.39 µs.

  • FFT bins spread: TcΔfscanT_c\,\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}} for Tc=10T_c=10 µs, e.g. 10μs×2.6MHz≈2610\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}\times2.6\ {\mathrm{MHz}}\approx26. An FFT over a chirp of length TcT_c has bins 1/Tc1/T_c wide, so a tone spread over Δfscan\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}} occupies TcΔfscanT_c\,\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}} bins. The coherent peak falls by that factor, 10log⁡1026≈1410\log_{10}26\approx14 dB.

  • Largest coherent aperture: Dmax=λ/(θ̇Tc)D_{\max}=\lambda/(\dot\theta T_c) (Eq. (95)); for the polygon, 1.55×10−6/(796×10−5)=0.191.55\times10^{-6}/(796\times10^{-5})=0.19 mm at 10 µs and 1.9 mm at 1 µs.

  • Resonant MEMS peak rate: a sinusoidal scan of optical amplitude Θ0\Theta_0 (rad) at scan frequency fmirrorf_{\mathrm{mirror}} (Hz) peaks at θ̇=2πfmirrorΘ0=2π×1,000×0.524rad=3,290\dot\theta=2\pi f_{\mathrm{mirror}}\Theta_0=2\pi\times1{,}000\times0.524\ {\mathrm{rad}}=3{,}290 rad/s, i.e. 188,500°/s. Here Θ0=30∘=0.524\Theta_0=30^\circ=0.524 rad.

  • Bias examples. These put numbers into Eq. (96) for a polygon and a MEMS mirror, and compare the result with a pedestrian’s walking speed.

    • A polygon with facets 20 mm from its axis, turning at 3,000 rpm and used over ±30° mechanical (120° optical) at 30° incidence: s‾\bar s reaches ±11.5 mm, a false radial velocity of up to ±6.3 m/s (±8.1 MHz). A single 1 GHz / 10 µs chirp would read that as ≈12 m of range; an up/down pair cancels all but the bias’s drift within the pair, ≈3–4 cm here.
      • The arithmetic [E]: the mechanical rate is θ̇m=3,000×2π/60=314\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}=3{,}000\times2\pi/60=314 rad/s. Let ϕ\phi be the facet’s mechanical rotation angle from scan centre and h=20h=20 mm the facet distance (the perpendicular distance from the rotation axis to the facet plane; not Planck’s constant). At angle ϕ\phi the beam meets the facet s‾=htan⁡ϕ\bar s=h\tan\phi from the foot of the perpendicular from the axis: 20mm×tan⁡30∘=11.520\ {\mathrm{mm}}\times\tan30^\circ=11.5 mm at the scan edge. The false velocity is therefore 2θ̇ms‾cos⁡θi=2×314×0.0115×0.866=6.32\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}\bar s\cos\theta_i=2\times314\times0.0115\times0.866=6.3 m/s, and fbias=2vr/λ=2×6.3/(1.55×10−6)=8.1f_{\mathrm{bias}}=2v_r/\lambda=2\times6.3/(1.55\times10^{-6})=8.1 MHz, with vrv_r the false radial velocity. With chirp rate κ=B/Tc=109/10−5=1014\kappa=B/T_c=10^{9}/10^{-5}=10^{14} Hz/s, a single chirp’s range error is cfbias/2κ=3×108×8.1×106/(2×1014)≈12cf_{\mathrm{bias}}/2\kappa=3\times10^{8}\times8.1\times10^{6}/(2\times10^{14})\approx12 m.
      • The bias drifts because ds‾/dt=hθ̇msec⁡2ϕd\bar s/dt=h\,\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}\sec^2\phi (with sec⁡ϕ=1/cos⁡ϕ\sec\phi=1/\cos\phi), which is 6.3 m/s at scan centre and 8.4 m/s at ±30°. The bias frequency therefore changes at (4θ̇mcos⁡θi/λ)ds‾/dt(4\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}\cos\theta_i/\lambda)\,d\bar s/dt, 4.4×1094.4\times10^{9} Hz/s at the centre and 5.9×1095.9\times10^{9} Hz/s at the edge. Let δ\delta be the change in fbiasf_{\mathrm{bias}} over the 10 µs between the up- and down-chirp centres: δ=44\delta=44–59 kHz. The pair’s range estimate, which averages the two beat frequencies, is then off by cδ/(4κ)=3.3c\,\delta/(4\kappa)=3.3–4.4 cm, because only the part of the bias that differs between the two chirps survives the averaging.
    • A 1 kHz MEMS mirror swinging ±15° mechanically (±30° optical, the table’s MEMS row), centred to 0.2 mm (s‾=0.2\bar s=0.2 mm), shows a false velocity of up to ±0.57 m/s that oscillates at the scan frequency. The peak mechanical rate is θ̇m=2π×1,000×0.262rad=1,645\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}=2\pi\times1{,}000\times0.262\ {\mathrm{rad}}=1{,}645 rad/s (15∘=0.26215^\circ=0.262 rad), so at the same 30° incidence 2θ̇ms‾cos⁡θi=2×1,645×2×10−4×0.866=0.572\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}\bar s\cos\theta_i=2\times1{,}645\times2\times10^{-4}\times0.866=0.57 m/s.
    • A walking pedestrian moves at ≈1.4 m/s, so the bias must be calibrated per facet, speed and temperature to a few per cent of itself: holding the residual to a tenth of walking speed, 0.14 m/s, for example, is 0.14/6.3≈2%0.14/6.3\approx2\% of the polygon’s 6.3 m/s bias.

  • The industry treats this as a real constraint [P, patents]:

    • Aeva holds three patents (priority Oct 2020) on compensating “mirror Doppler spreading”: by convolution (US 11,262,437 B1), matched filtering (US 11,327,158 B1) and power spectral density (US 11,366,200 B2). The convolution patent states that “the mirror-induced Doppler shift may broaden the received signal bandwidth”, lowering detection probability and raising range, velocity and reflectivity errors. It places the problem at mirror speeds above about 5 kdeg/s, with “little impact” below. The table treats this as an optical scan rate and assumes a 5 mm beam [E]; if the patent means the mirror’s mechanical rate, the optical rate is 10,000°/s and the spread doubles to 0.56 MHz.
    • A Blackmore patent now held by Aurora (US 10,838,061, priority Jul 2019) says speckle evolution “can limit the scanning speed to a value on the order one diffraction limited divergence angle per CPI” (coherent processing interval), and that compensating the broadening digitally allows faster scanning. That is the D≲λ/(θ̇Tc)D\lesssim\lambda/(\dot\theta T_c) condition of Eq. (95): one diffraction-limited angle λ/D\lambda/D per coherent processing interval TcT_c.
    • Insight LiDAR’s patent quantifies the related walk-off: the coherent signal falls by ≈10 dB when the transmit and receive spots are one spot diameter apart (US 11,366,203 B1).

  • Consequence. Scanner-induced Doppler is the companion of walk-off (§C0 subsection 2, §C7a subsection 2(d), §C10.3a). Both compare the angle the beam turns with its width λ/D\lambda/D: walk-off over the round trip 2R/c2R/c, Doppler spreading over the chirp TcT_c (Eq. (95)). Both scale with scan rate, and both push coherent scanners toward slow mechanical axes with parallel on-chip channels, short chirps (which raise the ADC load, §C7a), small apertures, digital compensation or step-and-stare steering. It effectively rules out fast resonant MEMS mirrors for µs-chirp FMCW (§C4d).

Point rate. A coherent channel measures one point at a time, so point rate scales with the number of channels, not with scanner speed.

  • Each point needs a dwell Tdwell=Tint+2τT_{\mathrm{dwell}}=T_{\mathrm{int}}+2\tau (several µs to tens of µs; §C7b, Eq. (111)). Here TintT_{\mathrm{int}} is the useful integration time of an up-chirp and a down-chirp, which together separate range from Doppler, and τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c is the round trip that each of the two ramps loses before its echo arrives. With NchN_{\mathrm{ch}} parallel coherent channels, the point rate Ṅ\dot N (points per second) is

    Ṅ≈NchTdwell\dot N\approx\frac{N_{\mathrm{ch}}}{T_{\mathrm{dwell}}}(97)

  • Reaching 2–4 Mpts/s (million points per second) therefore needs tens of parallel coherent channels. Each digitizes 100–400 MHz of beat bandwidth, sampled at ≈2.5× the highest beat plus Doppler frequency: ≈1.2 GS/s (gigasamples per second) for 5 µs chirps at 300 m (§C7a subsection 2(c)). The §C7a model integrates a 5 µs up-chirp plus a 5 µs down-chirp, whose beat at 300 m is 400 MHz rather than the 200 MHz of the 10 µs example above. At its 200 m design range the two round trips add 2τ=2×2×200m/(3×108ms−1)=2.672\tau=2\times2\times200\ {\mathrm{m}}/(3\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}})=2.67 µs, so Tdwell=10+2.67=12.67T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=10+2.67=12.67 µs. At that dwell, Nch=ṄTdwell=2×106s−1×12.67×10−6s=25N_{\mathrm{ch}}=\dot N\,T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=2\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times12.67\times10^{-6}\ {\mathrm{s}}=25 channels, and 51 for 4 Mpts/s.

  • Shorter chirps reduce the channel count, though never below the round-trip share 2τṄ2\tau\dot N, but raise the beat frequency, fb∝1/Tcf_b\propto1/T_c by Eq. (93), and with it the ADC rate.

  • This throughput problem is why photonic integration, with many LO-matched receivers on one photonic integrated circuit (PIC), is the main route to higher FMCW point rates [E].

Single-mode étendue (antenna theorem). A coherent receiver collects one spatial mode per channel, which ties its collecting area to its angular cell. The mixing with the LO only produces a beat for light that matches the LO’s spatial mode, so light arriving in any other mode is lost.

  • A single coherent spatial mode has an area–angle product (étendue) of order

    AmodeΩmode∼λ2A_{\mathrm{mode}}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{mode}}\sim\lambda^2(98)

    per polarization, with beam-shape factors of order one. Here AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} is the mode’s effective collecting area (the area over which the receiver captures power from a plane wave matched to that mode, m²) and Ωmode\Omega_{\mathrm{mode}} is the solid angle from which the mode accepts light (sr).

  • For a nominal mode angular area of a 0.1° cell (Ωmode≈(0.1×π/180)2=3×10−6\Omega_{\mathrm{mode}}\approx(0.1\times\pi/180)^2=3\times10^{-6} sr), Eq. (98) gives Amode∼(1.55μm)2/(3×10−6)≈8×10−7A_{\mathrm{mode}}\sim(1.55\ \mu\text{m})^2/(3\times10^{-6})\approx8\times10^{-7} m². That is an equivalent collecting diameter of about 1 mm (4Amode/π=4×7.9×10−7/π≈1.0\sqrt{4A_{\mathrm{mode}}/\pi}=\sqrt{4\times7.9\times10^{-7}/\pi}\approx1.0 mm) before beam-shape and polarization factors. Matching the mode’s solid angle to the cell’s does not make its response uniform: a round, Gaussian-shaped mode responds weakly near the corners of a square cell.

  • A larger coherent aperture narrows one mode’s angular acceptance, so the same field needs more angular samples or parallel modes. The 1 mm diameter (0.8 mm²) is therefore an illustrative size for a mode that fills a 0.1° cell, not a prohibition on larger FMCW telescopes. §C7a takes the other branch: a 20 mm aperture whose mode collects Amode≈64A_{\mathrm{mode}}\approx64 mm² at 200 m, with a beam that covers only ≈2% of a 0.05° cell (§C7b subsection 1(b), §C10.3a).

  • Direct-detection ToF can accept many spatial modes per pixel and use a larger aperture at the same pixel-defined instantaneous field, although its optics still obey ordinary étendue conservation.

  • An LO can lift a weak coherent signal above electronic noise and reject much broadband background. It cannot restore signal photons rejected by poor spatial-mode overlap.

Speckle. Light scattered from a rough target interferes with itself into a random pattern of bright and dark speckles. Single-mode detection samples one speckle, whose amplitude is Rayleigh-distributed (its intensity is exponentially distributed), so the return often fades deeply. High detection probability therefore needs polarization, wavelength or spatial diversity, i.e. several independent speckles averaged. Multimode ToF receivers average over many speckle cells automatically.

Benefits.

  • per-point radial velocity, which lowers prediction latency because motion is known from a single frame;
  • intrinsic rejection of sunlight and other lidars, because only LO-matched light within the IF bandwidth (the intermediate-frequency band of beat tones the receiver digitizes) mixes; this is not absolute, since FMCW interference modes exist;
  • no retroreflector blooming, i.e. no smearing of very bright returns into neighbouring pixels: Aeva, Mobileye, SiLC and Voyant claim it [P], none has been tested independently, and Settembrini et al. (2026) saw no noticeable blooming beside a retroreflector whose measured SNR was 37.7 dB above that of a 5% target, ≈42 dB in reflectance terms [P/E] (§C0 subsection 10.7).

OPA arithmetic [E]. An optical phased array steers a beam by setting the phase of each emitter in a row of emitters spaced at pitch dd. Wide fields need sub-µm pitch, and fine beams need hundreds to thousands of calibrated elements.

  • If the pitch is too large, copies of the main beam (grating lobes) appear at other angles. In this simple array model the field ±arcsin⁡(λ/2d)\pm\arcsin(\lambda/2d) about the array normal is free of grating lobes: while the main beam steers to any angle θs\theta_{\mathrm{s}} inside it (measured from the array normal), the nearest grating lobe stays outside, reaching the opposite edge when θs\theta_{\mathrm{s}} reaches the edge. The usable steering range is therefore

    |θs|≤arcsin⁡(λ2d)\lvert\theta_{\mathrm{s}}\rvert\le\arcsin\!\left(\frac{\lambda}{2d}\right)(99)

    where arcsin\arcsin is the inverse sine. At d=1.5d=1.5 µm that is ±arcsin⁡(1.55/3.0)=±arcsin⁡0.517≈±31∘\pm\arcsin(1.55/3.0)=\pm\arcsin0.517\approx\pm31^\circ, which matches Analog Photonics’ “about 60°”.

  • Covering ±60° at 1,550 nm with this simple array model needs d≲λ/(2sin⁡60∘)=1.55/1.732≈0.90d\lesssim\lambda/(2\sin60^\circ)=1.55/1.732\approx0.90 µm instead. Antenna-pattern and nonuniform-array designs can change the usable field, but the 1.5 µm-pitch example does not supply 120° horizontal coverage.

  • The beam’s angular width θb\theta_b (rad) is set by the array’s total length NeldN_{\mathrm{el}}d, roughly θb≈λ/(Neld)\theta_b\approx\lambda/(N_{\mathrm{el}}d), so the element count needed for a beamwidth θb\theta_b is

    Nel≈λdθbN_{\mathrm{el}}\approx\frac{\lambda}{d\,\theta_b}(100)

    This is about 590 elements for 0.1° and about 1,200 for 0.05°, each with calibrated phase control. At d=1.5d=1.5 µm and θb=0.1∘=1.745×10−3\theta_b=0.1^\circ=1.745\times10^{-3} rad, Nel=1.55/(1.5×1.745×10−3)≈592N_{\mathrm{el}}=1.55/(1.5\times1.745\times10^{-3})\approx592; halving θb\theta_b doubles it to ≈1,180.

  • The orthogonal axis is usually wavelength-steered with grating emitters, whose emission angle θ\theta changes with wavelength by about dθ/dλ=0.1d\theta/d\lambda=0.1–0.2°/nm in Si. That needs tens to hundreds of nm of tuning alongside the chirp: covering a vertical field Θv\Theta_{\mathrm{v}} takes Δλ=Θv/(dθ/dλ)\Delta\lambda=\Theta_{\mathrm{v}}/(d\theta/d\lambda), which is 50–100 nm for a 10° vertical field and 125–250 nm for 25° (§C10.2 item 2 gives 64 and 160 nm at 0.155°/nm).

  • Receive-side OPA efficiency and aperture are the hard part.

Reticle constraint on an FMCW transmitter is architecture-specific. The reticle is the largest area a lithography tool patterns in one exposure (one “field”), so it bounds the size of a single unstitched chip. A coherent transmitter does not need one physical emitter per far-field range pixel. Continuous OPA steering reuses one small aperture; a switched focal-plane array needs one cell per look direction. Whether the reticle binds therefore depends on which of the two is used.

Continuously steered one-dimensional OPA:

  • The 0.1° and 0.05° beamwidth examples above imply apertures D∼λ/θbD\sim\lambda/\theta_b of about 0.9 and 1.8 mm at 1,550 nm (1.55μm/(1.745×10−3)=0.891.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(1.745\times10^{-3})=0.89 mm and 1.55μm/(8.73×10−4)=1.781.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(8.73\times10^{-4})=1.78 mm; the numerical beamwidth convention changes the coefficient).
  • These are transmit diffraction examples, not sufficient receive collection areas or proofs of long-range sensitivity.
  • Phase shifters, splitters, routing, driver bonds, pads, laser and amplifier can use much more die area than the optical aperture. Optical loss, power handling, heat, phase calibration and the packaging of the CMOS electronics with the PIC can bind before the reticle.
  • Analog Photonics’ published 8,192-element, 1 µm-pitch coherent OPA, a research device distinct from the 1.5 µm-pitch OPA under Commercial status, has an ≈8.2 mm transmit aperture (8,192×1μm=8.28{,}192\times1\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=8.2 mm), well inside one ≈26×33 mm reticle field (§C6(a)) [P, Poulton et al., 2022]. This research demonstrator is evidence of integration scale, not of automotive cost or long-range performance.

Focal-plane switch array (a separate addressable antenna per look direction):

  • A published 128×128 array at 55 µm pitch uses a 7×7 mm active array on a 10×11 mm PIC. It reports 0.6° address spacing versus 0.05° beam divergence over 70°×70° [P, Zhang et al., 2022]. Address spacing and divergence must not be interchanged.
  • Extending that same 55 µm cell pitch to 2,400×520 distinct addresses would span roughly 132×29 mm (2,400×55μm=1322{,}400\times55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=132 mm by 520×55μm=28.6520\times55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=28.6 mm) before routing, so field size and packaging become severe.
  • Only 128×96 cells of the 128×128 FMCW demonstrator were experimentally bonded, because of package-pin limits: a constraint other than reticle size.

External steering and the receive path:

  • An FMCW system can steer with an external mirror and set its final transmitting aperture with external optics; that aperture need not fit on the PIC.
  • For long-range FMCW, the more consequential sizing question may be the receive path: how many coherent modes or parallel channels collect sufficient target light over the desired field, at acceptable loss and cost.
  • Stitching can extend photonic waveguides across fields [P, imec]. A stitched, actively phased automotive transmit/receive aperture has additional control and qualification demands, and passive-waveguide stitching is not proof those are solved.

Advances that would change the FMCW and OPA assessment

This subsection lists the advances that would change the verdict above, and the cost they would have to meet. One high-value technical advance, for both ToF and FMCW, would be a large-aperture, low-loss, fast, non-mechanical steerer usable on receive. Its value depends on insertion loss, angular coverage, temperature qualification, cost, and whether tiled or parallel-receiver architectures advance faster. Other advances:

  • coherent focal-plane arrays with many parallel LO-matched pixels (the Voyant Helium direction), which fix point rate;
  • integrated narrow-linewidth chirped lasers + SOAs on SiN or thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) at automotive cost;
  • speckle diversity built into the PIC, so that each point averages several independent speckles and fades less.

The cost bar is about $300–500 for trucks and L3 and about $200 for passenger L2++ (driver-supervised assistance with extended features such as navigation-guided highway driving) [E]. SPAD ToF performance is also rising: RoboSense’s 2,160-beam EM4 reaches 41 Mpts/s [P] (§C7a subsection 1), and RoboSense claims a 45% photon detection efficiency (PDE) for its Phoenix SPAD chip [P, unverified] (§C5).

C7a. FMCW and ToF maturity compared: point rate, pixels, readout and power in numbers

This section asks whether coherent FMCW lidar (frequency-modulated continuous wave, which measures range and velocity from the beat with a local oscillator, LO) can match direct-detection time-of-flight (ToF) lidar with single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) receivers. It answers with an energy budget per point: optical energy, laser electrical energy and receiver electronics, for a 200 m, 10%-reflectance target. The answer matters because energy per point sets a lidar’s heat, point rate and cost, which decide whether FMCW can compete in passenger cars or only in trucks.

Short answer.

  • Point rate per watt: very probably not. Point rate per watt at long range is the metric that Chinese vendors’ line-count race (their competition on the number of scan lines) rewards. On it, FMCW is behind for structural reasons that, in this model, engineering narrows but does not remove.
    • The model below gives about 12× more electrical energy per point than 940 nm SPAD ToF in 2026 (4.90/0.415≈11.84.90/0.415\approx11.8), counting the light the FMCW laser emits for its whole dwell on a point, round trips included. This narrows to about 6× in an optimistic 2032 projection (1.74/0.280≈6.21.74/0.280\approx6.2; totals from the subsection 3 table). Both receivers are held to the same detection rule (§C0 subsection 10.3). With the lower FMCW efficiencies measured so far (subsection 2(a) below), the 2026 gap is ≈15–19× for a discrete fibre chain and ≈33× for an integrated array.
    • That comparison is per sample, and FMCW’s sample is sparse: its beam footprint covers about 2% of a 0.05° cell at 200 m (§C10.3b, Result 2).
  • Automotive product maturity: about even odds by 2030 (≈50–60%, subsection 6), in a narrower segment. Series production, qualification and ≥100k units a year are plausible by about 2028–2030, mainly in trucks and L3 (SAE level 3, where the car drives itself in a defined domain). There FMCW would be a “fewer, richer points” sensor with per-point velocity and immunity to sunlight and other lidars.

The companion script build/figures/fmcw_tof_system_budget.py writes the figure and fmcw_tof_system_budget_tables.txt. Numbers are [E] unless tagged. Deployability tags:

  • [D]: shipping or qualified product;
  • [NT]: product-oriented, with a plausible automotive path within about 5 years;
  • [R]: research-stage, very unlikely to reach automotive lidars within 5 years.

Figure C7a.

  • (a) Modelled sensor electrical power (3 W overhead + point rate × electrical energy per point) for a 200 m, 10% extended target. The 3 W is an assumed fixed overhead for scanner motor, the sensor’s system-on-chip (SoC), heaters and power conversion, the same for both sensor types. Bands span the low/high parameter sets, and the yellow band marks the 8–25 W typical of shipping automotive lidars; the parity target of §C7b subsection 5 is ≤15 W.
    • Product markers show published point rate and power. They are at different ranges, so they are sanity checks, not fits; subsection 1 derives the implied rates:
      • Hesai ATX: 3.84 Mpts/s (million points per second), 8 W, 230 m at 10% [P];
      • Hesai ETX: ≈15 Mpts/s implied, <13 W, 300 m at 10% [P/E];
      • LuminWave F1: 128 lines at 0.1° and 10 Hz, ≈1.5 Mpts/s implied, <45 W, 250 m at 10% [P/E].
  • (b) Electrical energy per point in the central case, for ToF and FMCW in 2026 and 2032, split into the emitted optical energy, the loss in the laser, semiconductor optical amplifier (SOA) and driver, and the receiver electronics. The totals are 0.42, 0.28, 4.90 and 1.74 µJ. FMCW’s emitted energy includes the light its transmitter sends while it stays on through the round trips (an ungated transmitter), Tdwell/Tint=12.67/10=1.27T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}=12.67/10=1.27 times its useful energy (subsection 2(d)).
  • (c) Parallel coherent channels (transmit beams) needed (Ṅ×Tdwell\dot N\times T_{\mathrm{dwell}}, point rate times dwell per point) for 4, 10 and 20 µs of integration plus the two round trips at 200 m, 2τ=2.672\tau=2.67 µs, i.e. dwells of 6.7, 12.7 and 22.7 µs. The note gives the raw ADC data at 10 bits per sample over the useful windows, counting the four receivers of each channel: at the model’s 12.7 µs dwell, 2, 10 and 25 Mpts/s need 25, 127 and 317 channels and produce 0.98, 4.9 and 12 Tb/s (subsection 2(d)).

1. Published FMCW products and results (vendor figures unless tagged)

This subsection collects what FMCW vendors and research groups have published, so the model below can be checked against it. Only one FMCW vendor publishes point rate, range and power for the same configuration: Analog Photonics, whose FS-4S datasheet gives 90 kpts/s at 200 m on a 10% target in a 20° × 10° region-of-interest mode at 35 W, i.e. ≈390 µJ per point [P] (§C0 subsection 10.8, §C3b). The automotive FMCW vendors do not publish all three, and those three numbers together are what the energy-per-point comparison needs.
