2. The limits, one by one

This subsection computes the energy one point costs, stage by stage, for both lidar types. FMCW pays more at every stage: single-mode collection and detection statistics (speckle fading, and a peak needed in both chirp ramps) raise the optical energy, a continuous-wave (CW) laser that stays on through the round trips emits 27% more light than it uses (Tdwell/Tint=12.67/10T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}=12.67/10), CW amplification limits wall-plug efficiency (electrical-to-optical conversion efficiency), and dense digitization in four receivers per point dominates the receiver.

(a) Optical energy per point: ≈72 nJ for ToF against ≈300 nJ (0.30 µJ) for FMCW.

Assumptions of the model. The budget holds under these conditions:

  • Lambertian target. The target is a perfectly diffuse reflector of reflectance ρ\rho that fills the sample (the beam footprint, or the ToF pixel’s cell), at normal incidence and in clear air (no atmospheric loss). A Lambertian surface scatters a fraction ρ\rho of the incident power into a radiance of ρ/π\rho/\pi times the irradiance, so a receiver of aperture area ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} at range RR collects the fraction ρArx/(πR2)\rho A_{\mathrm{rx}}/(\pi R^2) of the transmitted power. Glossy paint and retroreflectors are not Lambertian: they return far more or far less toward the sensor, depending on angle, so the budget does not describe them.
  • FMCW receiver: four looks per point. Each coherent receiver collects only the light that matches its LO in polarization and spatial mode. The central design gives every beam four such receivers, one per polarization on each of two spatial modes (for example two receive apertures side by side), so each point is seen in four independent speckles, four looks.
  • Rayleigh speckle. Each look sees one speckle, whose intensity is exponentially distributed (Rayleigh amplitude), so detection needs extra signal margin against fades; summing the four looks narrows the spread but does not remove it. The ToF pixel sums hundreds of speckles and does not fade.
  • One detection rule for both receivers: 90% detection per point with at most 10−310^{-3} false points per point over the whole 0–300 m search (§C0 subsection 10.3).
  • Shot-noise-limited LO. The coherent receiver is limited by the LO’s shot noise, with thermal and dark-current noise neglected. At 105–125 °C this holds only approximately: §C4c gives 82–94% of the shot-noise limit for Ge at 125 °C, so the FMCW optical energy would rise somewhat when hot.
  • SPAD dead time 6 ns, the state of the art: Sony’s IMX479 specifies “approx. 6 ns” with 3×3 SPADs per macro-pixel, and its IMX459 predecessor measured 6 ns, a 60 Mcps (million counts per second) count-rate ceiling and 0.1% afterpulsing [P]. The model treats its SPADs as paralyzable [E], as passive recharge would make them, although the IMX459 press release says active recharge (§C5a): a SPAD is live only if no photon arrived during the last dead time τd=6\tau_d=6 ns. A paralyzable counter counts at most 1/(eτd)=1/(2.718×6ns)=611/(e\tau_d)=1/(2.718\times6\ {\mathrm{ns}})=61 Mcps, with ee Euler’s number, which matches the measured 60 Mcps ceiling (§C5a, Eq. (84)); a non-paralyzable counter would instead approach 1/τd=1671/\tau_d=167 Mcps. Each macro-pixel sees a 0.05° × 0.05° field, one cell of the IMX479 grid (2,400 × 520 cells over 120° × 26°), i.e. a solid angle Ωpix=(0.05∘×π/180)2=(8.727×10−4)2=7.615×10−7\Omega_{\mathrm{pix}}=(0.05^\circ\times\pi/180)^2=(8.727\times10^{-4})^2=7.615\times10^{-7} sr. In the model’s central “bright sun” case, half the background of a fully sunlit scene of reflectance 0.9 (the model’s high case; §C0 subsection 10.3), the macro-pixel counts rbg=1.83×108r_{\mathrm{bg}}=1.83\times10^{8} s⁻¹ (subsection 2(c)), so each of its nine SPADs counts r=1.83×108/9=2.03×107r=1.83\times10^{8}/9=2.03\times10^{7} s⁻¹, rτd=0.122r\tau_d=0.122, and each SPAD is dead a fraction 1−e−0.122=11.5%1-e^{-0.122}=11.5\% of the time (Eq. (90)). A SPAD that is dead when the echo arrives misses it, so the live fraction 0.885 multiplies the signal efficiency as well as the background. In the fully sunlit high case the rate doubles, rτd=0.244r\tau_d=0.244, and the dead fraction is 1−e−0.244=21.6%1-e^{-0.244}=21.6\% (live fraction 0.784).
  • 20 mm apertures for FMCW: each spatial mode is received through a 20 mm aperture in the mode of a Gaussian beam, one of them the monostatic aperture that also transmits; the ToF receiver uses one 25 mm aperture.
  • FMCW efficiency η=0.25\eta=0.25, checked against Waymo’s estimate (details below) rather than built up from component data.

Under these assumptions, the optical energy each point needs is

Ept=nreqEphπR2ρAeffηE_{\mathrm{pt}}=\frac{n_{\mathrm{req}}\,E_{\mathrm{ph}}\,\pi R^2}{\rho\,A_{\mathrm{eff}}\,\eta}(101)

where:

  • EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} is the useful optical energy per point (J), the light whose echo the receiver integrates: all of a ToF point’s light, whereas an ungated FMCW laser emits Tdwell/TintT_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}} times more, because it stays on through the round trips (subsection 2(d));
  • nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} is the number of detected counts (ToF) or photoelectrons (FMCW) needed for reliable detection;
  • Eph=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda is the photon energy (J);
  • RR is the range (m) and ρ\rho the target’s diffuse reflectance (0.1 here);
  • AeffA_{\mathrm{eff}} is the effective collecting area (m²): the area that, in the Lambertian fraction ρAeff/(πR2)\rho A_{\mathrm{eff}}/(\pi R^2), gives the power the receiver actually collects into its detection path, before the losses counted in η\eta;
  • η\eta is the receive efficiency, the fraction of that collected light that becomes counts or photoelectrons.

Eq. (101) simply inverts the Lambertian link: the detected number is Ept/EphE_{\mathrm{pt}}/E_{\mathrm{ph}} photons times ρAeffη/(πR2)\rho A_{\mathrm{eff}}\eta/(\pi R^2), and it is set equal to nreqn_{\mathrm{req}}.

  • ToF: Aeff=ArxA_{\mathrm{eff}}=A_{\mathrm{rx}} is the whole 25 mm receive aperture (491 mm²), and the pixel sums hundreds of speckle modes. An ideal counter needs 15.0 counts in the model’s bright sun (14.98; §C0 subsection 10.3); the model applies a ×1.45 implementation margin to it [E], nreq=1.448×14.98=21.7n_{\mathrm{req}}=1.448\times14.98=21.7 counts, and its low and high cases apply ×1.16 and ×2.03 (17.4 and 30.4 counts). At 940 nm, 37% PDE (photon detection efficiency of the SPAD) and the bright-sun live fraction of 0.885 the result is ≈72 nJ (51–113). With nreq=21.7n_{\mathrm{req}}=21.7 (central), Eph=2.11×10−19E_{\mathrm{ph}}=2.11\times10^{-19} J, πR2=π×2002=1.26×105\pi R^2=\pi\times200^2=1.26\times10^{5} m², ρ=0.1\rho=0.1 and η=0.5×0.37×0.885=0.164\eta=0.5\times0.37\times0.885=0.164 (optics transmission × PDE × live fraction): Ept=21.7×2.11×10−19×1.26×105/(0.1×4.91×10−4×0.164)=5.77×10−13/(8.05×10−6)≈7.2×10−8E_{\mathrm{pt}}=21.7\times2.11\times10^{-19}\times1.26\times10^{5}/(0.1\times4.91\times10^{-4}\times0.164)=5.77\times10^{-13}/(8.05\times10^{-6})\approx7.2\times10^{-8} J. The low case is night (17.4 counts, no dead time, η=0.185\eta=0.185): 51 nJ. The high case is the fully sunlit scene (30.4 counts, live fraction 0.784, η=0.145\eta=0.145): 113 nJ.
  • FMCW:
    • Each look collects one polarization in one spatial mode, so its effective area is AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}, the mode-equivalent collecting area. It is the area that, placed in the Lambertian fraction ρAmode/(πR2)\rho A_{\mathrm{mode}}/(\pi R^2), gives the power actually coupled into the polarization and spatial mode that the LO selects. It therefore already includes the polarization and mode-shape factors. It rests on the antenna theorem of Eq. (98) in §C7, applied to a monostatic Gaussian beam rather than to a 0.1° cell (§C0 subsection 10.2):
      • §C0 Eq. (41) gives Amode=t2λ2R2/(2πw2)A_{\mathrm{mode}}=t^2\lambda^2R^2/(2\pi w^2), where ww is the beam’s 1/e² radius at the target, t2=0.84t^2=0.84 the aperture-truncation factor counted on transmit and on receive, and the 2 in the denominator the factor ½ for the single polarization the LO accepts.
      • A 20 mm aperture launches a beam of 1/e² radius w0=0.45×20mm=9w_0=0.45\times20\ {\mathrm{mm}}=9 mm, whose Rayleigh range is πw02/λ=π×(9×10−3m)2/(1.55×10−6m)≈164\pi w_0^2/\lambda=\pi\times(9\times10^{-3}\ {\mathrm{m}})^2/(1.55\times10^{-6}\ {\mathrm{m}})\approx164 m. At 200–250 m the target is only 1.2–1.5 Rayleigh ranges away, so the spot has not yet grown in proportion to range, and Amode∝R2/w2A_{\mathrm{mode}}\propto R^2/w^2 still rises with range. At 200 m, w=14.2w=14.2 mm and Amode=0.84×(1.55×10−6)2×2002/(2π×0.01422)≈64A_{\mathrm{mode}}=0.84\times(1.55\times10^{-6})^2\times200^2/(2\pi\times0.0142^2)\approx64 mm² (§C7b subsection 1(b), §C10.3b); at 250 m it is 74.5 mm², the value used in the Waymo check below.
      • Piggott et al. (Waymo) put one mode ≈6 dB below a direct-detection receiver of the same aperture (3 dB polarization, 3 dB aperture) [P]. In this model one mode collects 4.9× (6.9 dB) less than the 314 mm² of its own 20 mm aperture (314/64=4.9314/64=4.9).
      • The four looks together give Aeff=4Amode=255A_{\mathrm{eff}}=4A_{\mathrm{mode}}=255 mm².
    • Single-mode returns fade, so detection needs more signal, and an FMCW point must show its peak in both the up- and the down-ramp of its chirp. Under the report’s detection rule four looks need ≈88 photoelectrons in total for 90% detection, and one look ≈259 (§C0 subsection 10.3). The model uses nreq=120n_{\mathrm{req}}=120, 30 per look: a ×1.36 implementation margin, close to the ×1.45 that takes ToF from 15.0 to 21.7 counts. Waymo’s analysis uses 50 photons (45 photoelectrons at a quantum efficiency of 0.9) for 90% detection with four averaged speckles at a 10−610^{-6} false-alarm probability per frequency bin, and finds that with a single speckle 10–30 photoelectrons give only ≈50%, depending on the false-alarm probability [P]. Waymo’s 45 photoelectrons require the peak in one ramp only: the report’s rule gives 47 for that case and 88.5 when the peak must appear in both ramps (§C0 subsection 10.3).
    • For FMCW, η\eta is the product of optical transmission, detector quantum efficiency and heterodyne mixing efficiency. It excludes the mode and polarization factor, which AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} already contains.
    • Result: ≈0.30 µJ (0.15–0.88) for 120 photoelectrons over four looks. With Aeff=4×63.7=255A_{\mathrm{eff}}=4\times63.7=255 mm², Eph=1.28×10−19E_{\mathrm{ph}}=1.28\times10^{-19} J at 1,550 nm and η=0.25\eta=0.25, Eq. (101) gives Ept=120×1.28×10−19×1.26×105/(0.1×2.55×10−4×0.25)=1.93×10−12/(6.37×10−6)≈3.0×10−7E_{\mathrm{pt}}=120\times1.28\times10^{-19}\times1.26\times10^{5}/(0.1\times2.55\times10^{-4}\times0.25)=1.93\times10^{-12}/(6.37\times10^{-6})\approx3.0\times10^{-7} J. The low case uses 96 photoelectrons and η=0.40\eta=0.40 (0.15 µJ), the high case 168 and η=0.12\eta=0.12 (0.88 µJ).
    • Check against Waymo. Waymo’s “realistic” 10–20 W optical for their ADAS (advanced driver-assistance) case (12 Mpts/s, 250 m, 5%, 50 photons or 45 photoelectrons at a quantum efficiency of 0.9, 90% detection) is 10–20 W divided by 12×10612\times10^{6} points/s, i.e. 0.83–1.67 µJ per point. Eq. (101) for one receiver with Amode=74.5A_{\mathrm{mode}}=74.5 mm² (a 20 mm aperture at 250 m) and η=0.25\eta=0.25 gives 45×1.28×10−19×π×2502/(0.05×7.45×10−5×0.25)=1.2145\times1.28\times10^{-19}\times\pi\times250^2/(0.05\times7.45\times10^{-5}\times0.25)=1.21 µJ for one ramp. Waymo’s energy per point pays for two chirps of 50 photons each: its ideal 0.52 µJ is 2×50×1.28×10−19J/(2.45×10−11)2\times50\times1.28\times10^{-19}\ {\mathrm{J}}/(2.45\times10^{-11}), through a −106.1 dB worst-case link [P, Piggott et al. 2025, Table 1]. The like-for-like value is therefore 2×1.21=2.42\times1.21=2.4 µJ at η=0.25\eta=0.25, 1.5–2.9× Waymo’s range, or 1.35 µJ at η=0.45\eta=0.45, the efficiency of Waymo’s 3 dB case including its quantum efficiency of 0.9, which lies inside it [E]. One receiver is the right basis for the check, because Waymo takes all four speckles through one single-mode receiver: it sums the FFT spectra of successive acquisitions, between which the scanning beam has moved enough to decorrelate the speckle, and its 50 photons, 45 photoelectrons, are the total over the four acquisitions [P, Piggott et al. 2025, §3.2 and Fig. 8(b)]. The §C7a design takes its four looks through four receivers at once instead, which divides the energy for the same 45 photoelectrons by four, to 1.21/4≈0.301.21/4\approx0.30 µJ.
    • Measured efficiencies are lower. The FMCW value, 0.25, is a design value about 1.5× above the best coherent chain measured so far. Waymo’s lab chain measured 0.112 end to end, or 0.168 without its Hann window (Piggott et al. 2025, App. A), and Pointcloud’s integrated array 0.057 once its amplifier noise is counted (Settembrini et al. 2026) [P; §C0 subsection 10.1]. With those values FMCW needs 0.25/0.168=1.50.25/0.168=1.5 to 0.25/0.112=2.20.25/0.112=2.2 times (discrete fibre chain) or 0.25/0.057=4.40.25/0.057=4.4 times (integrated array) the optical energy per point quoted here: 0.45–0.68 µJ or 1.3 µJ instead of 0.30 µJ. The laser’s electrical energy (2.56 µJ, subsection 3) scales in the same way while the receiver electronics (2.34 µJ) do not, so the total per point rises from 4.90 µJ to 2.563×1.488+2.337=6.152.563\times1.488+2.337=6.15 µJ and 2.563×2.232+2.337=8.062.563\times2.232+2.337=8.06 µJ (15–19× ToF’s 0.415 µJ), or to 2.563×4.386+2.337=13.62.563\times4.386+2.337=13.6 µJ (≈33×). The model keeps 0.25 as its central value and carries these as a sensitivity.

FMCW therefore needs ≈4.2× more useful optical energy per point than ToF (0.303μJ/72nJ=4.20.303\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/72\ {\mathrm{nJ}}=4.2), and its ungated transmitter emits ≈5.3× more (0.384μJ/72nJ=5.30.384\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/72\ {\mathrm{nJ}}=5.3), because it also emits during the round trips (subsection 2(d)). The ≈4.2× ratio is the product of four factors, 1.93×5.53×0.606×0.656=4.21.93\times5.53\times0.606\times0.656=4.2:

  • collection (1.9×), the ToF aperture area over the four looks’ AeffA_{\mathrm{eff}} (491 mm² against 255 mm²);
  • detection statistics (5.5×), 120 required photoelectrons against 21.7 counts: speckle fading, a peak needed in both chirp ramps, and one photoelectron of shot noise in every FFT bin searched (§C0 subsection 10.3);
  • photon energy (0.61×), because a 1,550 nm photon carries less energy than a 940 nm one (1.28/2.111.28/2.11);
  • efficiency (0.66×), ToF’s 0.164, which includes the SPADs’ dead time in bright sun, against FMCW’s 0.25.

§C7b subsection 1 derives each factor. It also explains why pulsing matters to ToF (sunlight in the timing bin) but not to coherent detection, and extends the same budget to ToF with linear-mode avalanche photodiodes (APDs) and to full-cell FMCW coverage.

The 1,550 nm eye-safety allowance (§C4c) can pay for this optical energy. Items (b) and (c) give its electrical and thermal cost.

(b) Laser wall-plug efficiency and power handling. Heat, not eye safety, is the practical ceiling on FMCW point rate at 1,550 nm. Wall-plug efficiency ηwp\eta_{\mathrm{wp}} is the optical power out divided by the electrical power in, so the laser’s electrical energy per point is the light it emits per point divided by ηwp\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}: Ept/ηwpE_{\mathrm{pt}}/\eta_{\mathrm{wp}} for a pulsed ToF laser and EptTdwell/(Tintηwp)E_{\mathrm{pt}}T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/(T_{\mathrm{int}}\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}) for the ungated FMCW laser (subsection 2(d)). Everything not emitted becomes heat. Eye safety allows ≈9.1 W of scanned light over a 120° × 25° field at 1,550 nm (§C7b subsection 3a(b)). FMCW’s useful light at 200 m, 3.0 W at 10 Mpts/s and 7.6 W at 25 Mpts/s, fits within it if the transmitter is gated during the round trips. The model’s transmitter is ungated and emits Tdwell/Tint=12.67/10=1.27T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}=12.67/10=1.27 times as much, 3.8 W and 9.6 W, so at 25 Mpts/s it exceeds the allowance unless it is gated.

  • ToF emitters (multi-junction vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers, VCSELs, and edge-emitting lasers, EELs, with gallium-nitride (GaN) transistor drivers) reach ≈15–30% system wall-plug efficiency on short pulses [E]. The model spans this range and takes 20% as its 2026 central value (25% in 2032; subsection 3).
  • FMCW needs a narrow-linewidth, linearly chirped CW source plus amplification:
    • Aeva reports an SOA at >28 dBm (1028/1010^{28/10} mW ≈ 630 mW) with >20% wall-plug efficiency at ≤50 °C [P]; no data at 85–105 °C.
    • Silicon waveguides saturate near 16 mW from two-photon and free-carrier absorption [P, Pointcloud Methods], so the model’s 30 mW channels (subsection 2(e)), and brighter ones, need silicon-nitride (SiN) or III-V (compound-semiconductor) paths.
  • The model therefore uses 10–20% (central 15%) in 2026.
  • At 10 Mpts/s that means ≈3.0 W of useful light, ≈3.8 W emitted and ≈22 W of heat in the laser/SOA stage alone; at 25 Mpts/s, ≈7.6 W useful, ≈9.6 W emitted and ≈54 W of heat. The useful optical power is the point rate Ṅ\dot N times the optical energy per point, Popt=ṄEpt=107s−1×0.303μJ=3.03P_{\mathrm{opt}}=\dot N E_{\mathrm{pt}}=10^{7}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times0.303\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=3.03 W. The ungated laser emits for the whole dwell, PoptTdwell/Tint=3.03×12.67/10=3.84P_{\mathrm{opt}}T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}=3.03\times12.67/10=3.84 W (subsection 2(d)). The heat is the electrical input minus the light out, 3.84×(1/ηwp−1)=3.84×(1/0.15−1)=21.83.84\times(1/\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}-1)=3.84\times(1/0.15-1)=21.8 W; at 25 Mpts/s, 7.59×1.267×5.67=54.57.59\times1.267\times5.67=54.5 W, where 5.67=1/0.15−15.67=1/0.15-1.

(c) Digitization: FMCW pays for every range bin, photons or not. An FMCW receiver must sample its beat signal densely over the useful window of every chirp ramp and Fourier-transform it, whether or not a target is there, so its electronics energy per point is fixed by range and resolution rather than by the returned light.

The beat frequency is fb=2BR/(cTu)f_b=2BR/(cT_u), Eq. (93) with the useful window TuT_u of one chirp ramp in place of the chirp duration, where RR is the range and BB the bandwidth swept in the useful window. The useful window is the part of the ramp after the round trip τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c, once the echo beats with the LO; the ramp itself lasts Tu+τT_u+\tau, with τ\tau taken at the 200 m design range (§C7b, Eq. (110)), so the laser sweeps 1GHz×(5+1.33)/5=1.271\ {\mathrm{GHz}}\times(5+1.33)/5=1.27 GHz per ramp (§C7b, Eq. (114)). An echo from beyond 200 m arrives later and beats for less of the window, 4.33 µs instead of 5 µs at 300 m, which the model ignores because its design target sits at 200 m. On top of it comes the Doppler shift fD=2vr/λf_D=2v_r/\lambda of the fastest target, 2×70/(1.55×10−6)≈902\times70/(1.55\times10^{-6})\approx90 MHz at a closing speed vr=70v_r=70 m/s. The model samples at fs≈2.5(fb+fD)f_s\approx2.5(f_b+f_D), where fsf_s is the ADC sample rate and fbf_b is taken at the maximum range RmaxR_{\max}. The receiver must search the whole 0–300 m window even when the design target is at 200 m, so Rmax=300R_{\max}=300 m sets the digitization while 200 m sets the optical energy. The factor 2.5 is twice the highest beat frequency (the Nyquist rate for real sampling) times a 25% margin. Only the two useful windows, Tint=2TuT_{\mathrm{int}}=2T_u in all, are digitized, so the number of ADC samples per point is NADC=fs×2TuN_{\mathrm{ADC}}=f_s\times2T_u, which gives

NADC≈5RmaxΔR+5fDTuN_{\mathrm{ADC}}\approx 5\,\frac{R_{\max}}{\Delta R}\;+\;5\,f_D\,T_u(102)

samples per point, independent of how many photons return. Here ΔR=c/(2B)\Delta R=c/(2B) is the range resolution, so Rmax/ΔRR_{\max}/\Delta R is the number of range bins. The first term follows because fbTu=2BRmax/c=Rmax/ΔRf_bT_u=2BR_{\max}/c=R_{\max}/\Delta R at maximum range. Eq. (102) is Eq. (113) of §C7b with R=RmaxR=R_{\max}.

  • For 300 m, 15 cm resolution (2,000 range bins) and 5 µs useful windows: fs≈1.2f_s\approx1.2 GS/s and ≈12,000 samples per point. Step by step: B=c/(2ΔR)=1B=c/(2\Delta R)=1 GHz and Rmax/ΔR=300/0.15=2,000R_{\max}/\Delta R=300/0.15=2{,}000; fb=2×109×300/(3×108×5×10−6)=400f_b=2\times10^{9}\times300/(3\times10^{8}\times5\times10^{-6})=400 MHz; fs=2.5×(400+90)MHz=1.23f_s=2.5\times(400+90)\ {\mathrm{MHz}}=1.23 GS/s; NADC=fs×2Tu=1.23×109s−1×10−5s≈12,300N_{\mathrm{ADC}}=f_s\times2T_u=1.23\times10^{9}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times10^{-5}\ {\mathrm{s}}\approx12{,}300. Eq. (102) gives the same count, because fbTu=Rmax/ΔRf_bT_u=R_{\max}/\Delta R: NADC=5×2,000+5×(90×106)×(5×10−6)=10,000+2,250≈12,300N_{\mathrm{ADC}}=5\times2{,}000+5\times(90\times10^{6})\times(5\times10^{-6})=10{,}000+2{,}250\approx12{,}300.

  • Energy per sample. Each sample costs one analog-to-digital conversion plus its share of the digital processing:

    • ADC: the Walden figure of merit (FOM) is the energy per conversion step, so one conversion at an effective number of bits ENOB (the resolution left after noise and distortion) costs FOM × 2ENOB2^{\mathrm{ENOB}}. Research 1 GS/s ADCs reach 7–10 fJ/step, i.e. ≈7–20 mW at 10–11 ENOB [I, Murmann survey]; product ADCs are several times worse. The power is P=FOM×2ENOB×fsP={\mathrm{FOM}}\times2^{\mathrm{ENOB}}\times f_s: 7fJ×210×109s−1=7.27\ {\mathrm{fJ}}\times2^{10}\times10^{9}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=7.2 mW at the low end (10 ENOB) and 10fJ×211×109s−1=2010\ {\mathrm{fJ}}\times2^{11}\times10^{9}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=20 mW at the high end (11 ENOB).

    • Digital signal processing (DSP): the FFT, windowing and peak search take ≈70 operations per sample (a model assumption).

    • Together, the energy per sample is

      es=FOM×2ENOB+NopEope_s={\mathrm{FOM}}\times2^{\mathrm{ENOB}}+N_{\mathrm{op}}\,E_{\mathrm{op}}(103)

      with Nop≈70N_{\mathrm{op}}\approx70 DSP operations per sample and EopE_{\mathrm{op}} the energy per operation.

    • 2026 central: ≈37 pJ/sample (22–61). The model assumes an 8-bit effective resolution (ENOB = 8) at a product-grade FOM of 50 fJ/step (range 30–100), so the conversion costs 50fJ×28=12.850\ {\mathrm{fJ}}\times2^{8}=12.8 pJ. It adds 70 operations at 0.35 pJ each (range 0.2–0.5 pJ), 70×0.35=24.570\times0.35=24.5 pJ, for 37.3 pJ. The low case, still at 8 ENOB (28=2562^{8}=256), is 30fJ×256+70×0.2pJ=7.7+14=2230\ {\mathrm{fJ}}\times256+70\times0.2\ {\mathrm{pJ}}=7.7+14=22 pJ, and the high case 100fJ×256+70×0.5pJ=25.6+35=61100\ {\mathrm{fJ}}\times256+70\times0.5\ {\mathrm{pJ}}=25.6+35=61 pJ.

  • The analog front end adds ≈10 mW per receiver for the transimpedance amplifier (TIA), bias and drivers, drawn for the whole dwell. Each of the NL=4N_L=4 receivers of a point (one per look) digitizes and transforms its own beat, so the receiver electronics energy per point is

    Erx=NL(NADCes+PanTdwell)E_{\mathrm{rx}}=N_L\left(N_{\mathrm{ADC}}\,e_s+P_{\mathrm{an}}\,T_{\mathrm{dwell}}\right)(104)

    where ErxE_{\mathrm{rx}} is the receiver electronics energy per point, NLN_L the number of receivers (looks) per point, PanP_{\mathrm{an}} the analog power per receiver and TdwellT_{\mathrm{dwell}} the dwell per point. The dwell is the two useful windows plus the two round trips, Tdwell=2Tu+2τ=10+2.67=12.67T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=2T_u+2\tau=10+2.67=12.67 µs at the 200 m design range (§C7b, Eq. (111)). The ADC samples only the useful windows, but the analog front end stays on for the whole dwell. This gives ≈2.3 µJ per point (1.3–4.0): Erx=4×(12,300×37.3pJ+10mW×12.67μs)=4×(0.459+0.127)=2.34E_{\mathrm{rx}}=4\times(12{,}300\times37.3\ {\mathrm{pJ}}+10\ {\mathrm{mW}}\times12.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}})=4\times(0.459+0.127)=2.34 µJ. The low and high cases are 4×(12,300×22pJ+5mW×12.67μs)=1.34\times(12{,}300\times22\ {\mathrm{pJ}}+5\ {\mathrm{mW}}\times12.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}})=1.3 µJ and 4×(12,300×61pJ+20mW×12.67μs)=4.04\times(12{,}300\times61\ {\mathrm{pJ}}+20\ {\mathrm{mW}}\times12.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}})=4.0 µJ.

  • Waymo’s analysis reaches the same scale from the other direction: ≈1.1×10131.1\times10^{13} FLOPS (floating-point operations per second) for 12 Mpts/s, “comparable to a high-end desktop GPU” [P]. The model’s count for one receiver per point is the same, 12×106s−1×12,300×70≈1.0×101312\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times12{,}300\times70\approx1.0\times10^{13} operations/s; with four receivers per point it is ≈4×1013\approx4\times10^{13}.

  • ToF is event-driven. A SPAD-SoC (a SPAD array stacked on its own processing chip) spends energy per avalanche and histogram increment, a few pJ each, plus fixed clocking and readout. Its histogram also has ≈2,000 bins, but they are counted sparsely, not sampled and transformed densely.

    • Result: ≈57 nJ per point (20–102), calibrated to Sony’s 1.19 W development chip (§C5a).
    • Event count: background count rate × listening time × live fraction + signal counts, rbgtlisten(1−fdead)+nreq=1.83×108s−1×20.8μs×0.885+21.7≈3,369+22≈3,390r_{\mathrm{bg}}\,t_{\mathrm{listen}}\,(1-f_{\mathrm{dead}})+n_{\mathrm{req}}=1.83\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times20.8\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}\times0.885+21.7\approx3{,}369+22\approx3{,}390 events per point in bright sun. The inputs are:
      • the background count rate rbg=1.83×108r_{\mathrm{bg}}=1.83\times10^{8} s⁻¹ per 0.05° × 0.05° macro-pixel, half the fully sunlit 940 nm, 10 nm-filter case of §C6(d) (Eq. (89)) evaluated at the model’s PDE of 0.37. §C6(d) gives 2.965×1082.965\times10^{8} s⁻¹ at PDE 0.3, so rbg=0.5×2.965×108×0.37/0.3=1.83×108r_{\mathrm{bg}}=0.5\times2.965\times10^{8}\times0.37/0.3=1.83\times10^{8} s⁻¹, i.e. a sunlit scene of reflectance ≈0.45 or a pixel half filled by bright surfaces (§C0 subsection 10.3);
      • a listening time tlisten=20.8t_{\mathrm{listen}}=20.8 µs per point, a model input equal to one column period of a 520-line sensor at 25 Mpts/s (520/(25×106s−1)=20.8520/(25\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}})=20.8 µs);
      • the live fraction 0.885 that the paralyzable form of Eq. (90) gives at the per-SPAD rate r=rbg/9=2.03×107r=r_{\mathrm{bg}}/9=2.03\times10^{7} s⁻¹ (nine SPADs per 3×3 macro-pixel; subsection 2(a)): e−rτd=e−0.122=0.885e^{-r\tau_d}=e^{-0.122}=0.885, so each SPAD is blind 11.5% of the time;
      • nreq=21.7n_{\mathrm{req}}=21.7 signal counts (subsection 2(a)).
    • Cross-check: the same rate gives b=rbgΔtbinNshots(1−fdead)=1.83×108s−1×1ns×10×0.885=1.62b=r_{\mathrm{bg}}\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}\,N_{\mathrm{shots}}\,(1-f_{\mathrm{dead}})=1.83\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times1\ {\mathrm{ns}}\times10\times0.885=1.62 background counts per 1 ns bin, summed over the Nshots=10N_{\mathrm{shots}}=10 shots of a point, the value §C0 subsection 10.3 uses.
    • Energy: at 5 pJ per event plus a fixed 40 nJ per point, E=40nJ+3,390×5pJ=57E=40\ {\mathrm{nJ}}+3{,}390\times5\ {\mathrm{pJ}}=57 nJ.
    • Calibration: the 57 nJ total sits inside the 40–80 nJ per point that a 1–2 W IMX479-class chip implies at 25 Mpts/s (1W/(25×106s−1)=401\ {\mathrm{W}}/(25\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}})=40 nJ); Sony’s 1.19 W gives 48 nJ.
    • Range: from 20 nJ at night (20 nJ fixed, 4 pJ per event) to 60nJ+(3.66×108×20.8μs×0.784+30.4)×7pJ=10260\ {\mathrm{nJ}}+(3.66\times10^{8}\times20.8\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}\times0.784+30.4)\times7\ {\mathrm{pJ}}=102 nJ in the fully sunlit scene (live fraction 0.784).

(d) Channels and data: the parallelism problem. Each coherent channel measures one point per dwell, so a point rate Ṅ\dot N needs Nch=ṄTdwellN_{\mathrm{ch}}=\dot N\,T_{\mathrm{dwell}} parallel channels (Eq. (97) rearranged).

  • The dwell is the 10 µs of useful integration of (c), the 5 µs up-chirp plus the 5 µs down-chirp, plus the round trip that each of the two ramps loses, 2τ=2.672\tau=2.67 µs at 200 m: Tdwell=12.67T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=12.67 µs (the dwell of Eq. (104); §C7b, Eq. (111)). At that dwell, 2 Mpts/s needs Nch=2×106s−1×12.67×10−6s=25N_{\mathrm{ch}}=2\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times12.67\times10^{-6}\ {\mathrm{s}}=25 channels, 10 Mpts/s needs 127, and 25 Mpts/s needs 317. With four receivers per channel these are 101, 507 and 1,267 receivers. Integrating for 4 µs instead (2 µs useful windows) shortens the dwell only to 4+2.67=6.674+2.67=6.67 µs, a factor of 1.9 rather than 2.5, because the round trips stay: 13, 67 and 167 channels (53, 267 and 667 receivers). Meanwhile fsf_s and ADC energy rise: 2 µs chirps give fb=1.0f_b=1.0 GHz and fs=2.5×(1,000+90)MHz≈2.7f_s=2.5\times(1{,}000+90)\ {\mathrm{MHz}}\approx2.7 GS/s. The samples per point stay near 5Rmax/ΔR5R_{\max}/\Delta R (2.7×109×4×10−6≈10,9002.7\times10^{9}\times4\times10^{-6}\approx10{,}900), so the energy per point rises through the poorer figure of merit of faster converters rather than through more samples.
  • The central design is ungated: its laser stays on through the round trips, so it emits EptTdwell/Tint=0.303μJ×12.67/10=0.38E_{\mathrm{pt}}T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}=0.303\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times12.67/10=0.38 µJ per point (0.19–1.12 µJ across the cases), and the laser’s electrical energy is counted on that emitted light (subsections 2(b) and 3). A transmitter switched off during the last τ\tau of each ramp, whose echo would land in the next ramp’s discarded window, would save that extra light, 2τ/Tdwell=2.67/12.67=21%2\tau/T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=2.67/12.67=21\% of what the ungated laser emits (§C7b subsection 3a(b)).
  • Raw ADC output at 10 bits per sample is 0.98, 4.9 and 12 Tb/s respectively: NLṄNADC×10N_L\dot N N_{\mathrm{ADC}}\times10 bits with NL=4N_L=4 receivers per channel, e.g. 4×107s−1×12,300×10=4.9×10124\times10^{7}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times12{,}300\times10=4.9\times10^{12} b/s at 10 Mpts/s. This counts the useful windows only, as the ADC energy of (c) does; converters left running through the round trips would stream Tdwell/Tint=1.27T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}=1.27 times more, 6.2 Tb/s. The 10 bits are the converter’s output word; the energy model’s 8 effective bits (ENOB) are fewer because noise and distortion corrupt the lowest bits. This data stream cannot leave the chip economically, so FFT and peak extraction must sit beside the ADCs in a stacked electronic-photonic IC (EPIC): the same stacking step Sony made for SPAD-SoCs, with GS/s converters instead of counters.
  • Today’s merchant FMCW SoC, indie’s iND83301 “Surya”, provides 4 × 1 GS/s or 8 × 500 MS/s 12-bit ADCs with an FFT unit and four DSP cores; power is not published [P]. A 10 Mpts/s sensor would need roughly 120–130 such devices [E]. The aggregate sample rate is ṄNLNADC=107s−1×4×12,300≈4.9×1011\dot N N_LN_{\mathrm{ADC}}=10^{7}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times4\times12{,}300\approx4.9\times10^{11} samples/s, against 4×14\times1 GS/s per device, so 490/4≈123490/4\approx123 devices. Counting one ADC per receiver gives 507/4≈127507/4\approx127, but each 1 GS/s converter is then below the 1.23 GS/s a receiver needs during its useful windows, and the 8 × 500 MS/s mode (≈63 devices) is far too slow per receiver. Because NADC≈5Rmax/ΔRN_{\mathrm{ADC}}\approx5R_{\max}/\Delta R (Eq. (102)), the aggregate rate barely depends on the chirp length.
  • Pointcloud’s 2026 array still reads out through an RFSoC (a commercial FPGA with integrated RF data converters) and says an application-specific chip (ASIC) “is under development” [P].
  • Physics bounds the minimum dwell: each of the two ramps loses one round trip, τ=2R/c=2×250m/(3×108ms−1)=1.67\tau=2R/c=2\times250\ {\mathrm{m}}/(3\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}})=1.67 µs at 250 m, so even unlimited light leaves a dwell of at least 2τ=3.332\tau=3.33 µs (2.67 µs at 200 m; §C7b subsection 2(a)).
  • Walk-off bounds the scan rate. During the round trip 2R/c2R/c the beam direction turns by θ̇⋅2R/c\dot\theta\cdot2R/c, where θ̇\dot\theta is the beam’s optical scan rate (rad/s; for a spinning sensor, its rotation rate). At range RR the return therefore lands a lateral distance Δx≈2R2θ̇/c\Delta x\approx2R^2\dot\theta/c away from where the receiver now looks. For a 360°, 10 Hz spin (θ̇=2π×10s−1=62.8\dot\theta=2\pi\times10\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=62.8 rad/s) the lag angle 2Rθ̇/c2R\dot\theta/c is 2×100m×62.8s−1/(3×108ms−1)=4.2×10−52\times100\ {\mathrm{m}}\times62.8\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}/(3\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}})=4.2\times10^{-5} rad =0.0024∘=0.0024^\circ at 100 m and 0.006° at 250 m, against the 0.0036° 1/e² half-angle of a beam sized for 250 m (§C10.3a). Waymo says this makes 360°, 10 Hz spinning “impractical for target ranges much above 100 m” and pushes designs to step-and-stare fast axes (point, dwell, then jump) [P]; the lag angles above show why.
  • The scan also bounds the maximum dwell: a chirp that outlasts the beam’s crossing time θb/θ̇\theta_b/\dot\theta (with θb≈λ/D\theta_b\approx\lambda/D the beam’s angular width and DD its diameter) is spread by scanner-induced Doppler (§C7, Eq. (94)). At a Falcon-class 45,600°/s (the polygon row of the §C7 table), even the 1.67 µs round trip to 250 m exceeds the crossing time of any beam wider than ≈1.2 mm unless the broadening is compensated digitally [E: the crossing time λ/(Dθ̇)\lambda/(D\dot\theta) falls below 1.67 µs for D>λ/(θ̇×1.67μs)=1.55×10−6/(796×1.67×10−6)=1.2D>\lambda/(\dot\theta\times1.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}})=1.55\times10^{-6}/(796\times1.67\times10^{-6})=1.2 mm]. For any wider beam even the shortest ramp, one round trip long, outlasts the crossing time, so no chirp length works without digital compensation, as §C7b subsection 2(g) also finds for a 0.05° beam at 300 m.

(e) Pixel and resolution scaling. A “line” is one row of the lidar image, i.e. one vertical angular sample repeated across the horizontal field. A ToF line and an FMCW line cost very different amounts, which is why line count scales so differently for the two.

  • SPAD ToF: one more line is ≈30 µm of die (three 10 µm SPADs) plus a share of a time-to-digital converter and histogram, a few cents of silicon (§C5a economics: $17–44 of silicon per IMX479 die spread over 520 lines is 3–8 US cents per line). The laser energy is shared in time. This is why Chinese vendors’ line counts went 192 → 520 → 896 → 2,160 → 4,320 in under two and a half years, from Huawei’s 192-line D3, launched on 26 Dec 2023 [T], to Hesai’s ETX with up to 4,320 channels, shown on 17 Apr 2026 [P].
  • FMCW: every simultaneous line needs four receivers (one per look), each with an LO tap, a 90° hybrid (an optical mixer that yields in-phase and quadrature beats) or balanced Ge photodiode pair, a TIA, a GS/s ADC and an FFT pipe, plus its own CW optical power. Lines beyond the channel count come from stepping the beam, which costs dwell.
    • Light per channel: ≈30 mW in the central model at 200 m, the useful energy over the integration time, Pch=Ept/Tint=0.303μJ/10μs=30P_{\mathrm{ch}}=E_{\mathrm{pt}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}=0.303\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/10\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=30 mW. The channel emits it for the whole 12.67 µs dwell, 0.38 µJ per point (subsection 2(d)). The high-energy case needs 0.885μJ/10μs=880.885\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/10\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=88 mW.
    • With range: the power grows with the energy, Ept∝R2/AmodeE_{\mathrm{pt}}\propto R^2/A_{\mathrm{mode}} (Eq. (101)). For the model’s fixed 20 mm aperture, AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} is 63.7 mm² at 200 m, 74.5 mm² at 250 m (subsection 2(a)) and ≈82 mm² at 300 m, where w=9mm×1+(300/164)2≈18.8w=9\ {\mathrm{mm}}\times\sqrt{1+(300/164)^2}\approx18.8 mm and Amode=0.84×(1.55×10−6)2×3002/(2π×0.01882)≈82A_{\mathrm{mode}}=0.84\times(1.55\times10^{-6})^2\times300^2/(2\pi\times0.0188^2)\approx82 mm² (§C0 Eq. (41)). A channel therefore needs 30.3×(250/200)2×63.7/74.5=4030.3\times(250/200)^2\times63.7/74.5=40 mW at 250 m and 30.3×(300/200)2×63.7/82=5330.3\times(300/200)^2\times63.7/82=53 mW at 300 m. An aperture re-optimized at each range holds the growth to ∝R\propto R (§C7b subsection 1(f)): 30.3×250/200=3830.3\times250/200=38 mW and 30.3×300/200=4530.3\times300/200=45 mW.
  • Worked example: a 520-line, 10 Hz, 2,400-column FMCW image at 200 m (12.5 Mpts/s) implies ≈158 channels (≈630 receivers) at the 12.67 µs dwell, ≈3.8 W of useful light (4.8 W emitted), ≈27 W of laser heat and ≈29 W of receiver electronics under the central 2026 assumptions. That is about 64 W in total, against ≈8 W for a 520-line ToF unit in the same model, and each FMCW sample still covers only ≈2% of its cell (§C10.3b, Result 2). The arithmetic: Ṅ=520×2,400×10Hz=1.25×107\dot N=520\times2{,}400\times10\ {\mathrm{Hz}}=1.25\times10^{7} pts/s; Nch=1.25×107×12.67μs=158N_{\mathrm{ch}}=1.25\times10^{7}\times12.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=158; useful optical power 1.25×107×0.303μJ=3.81.25\times10^{7}\times0.303\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=3.8 W, emitted 1.25×107×0.384μJ=4.81.25\times10^{7}\times0.384\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=4.8 W; laser heat, the laser’s electrical energy per point minus the light it emits, 1.25×107×(2.56−0.38)μJ=271.25\times10^{7}\times(2.56-0.38)\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=27 W; receivers 1.25×107×2.34μJ=29.21.25\times10^{7}\times2.34\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=29.2 W. With the 3 W overhead, the total is 3W+1.25×107×4.90μJ≈643\ {\mathrm{W}}+1.25\times10^{7}\times4.90\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\approx64 W. The ToF unit is 3W+1.25×107×0.415μJ≈8.23\ {\mathrm{W}}+1.25\times10^{7}\times0.415\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\approx8.2 W.

(f) Coherence and chirp: solved as components, not yet as integrated automotive parts. The laser must have a narrow linewidth and a linear chirp; parts exist that do both, but not yet as integrated, qualified automotive components. §C7b subsection 2(d)–(h) derives the requirements; for 15 cm resolution at 300 m they are:

  • Linewidth. Laser phase noise leaves a fraction ηcoh=e−2πΔν⋅2R/c\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}=e^{-2\pi\Delta\nu\cdot2R/c} of the beat power in the coherent FFT peak (Eq. (118)); the rest is lost to detection. It does not limit how long a chirp can be (§C7b subsection 2(e)).
    • A 1 dB loss allows Δν≲18\Delta\nu\lesssim18 kHz at 300 m (27 kHz at 200 m), and 3 dB allows 55 kHz (83 kHz) (Eq. (119)). Waymo’s ≲60–120 kHz for 250 m [P] corresponds to a 2.7–5.5 dB loss [E].
    • Narrow-linewidth grades of commercial distributed-feedback lasers (DFBs) reach tens of kHz: AeroDIODE specifies its 20 mW and 40 mW 1550 nm butterfly DFBs at <50 kHz, measured by the phase-noise method at 1 MHz [P, AeroDIODE datasheets PN_A75 and PN_A79, 2026], and Waymo notes that several vendors offer DFBs with linewidths in the low tens of kHz [P, Piggott et al. 2025]. A standard commercial DFB measured by Bianconi et al. showed 802 kHz over 1 ms [I]. The integrated lasers below are quoted with linewidths over 1 ms, which slow frequency noise dominates. The SiN self-injection-locked laser (42 kHz over 1 ms) has a 3 Hz intrinsic linewidth [I, Voloshin et al. 2025], and the TFLN extended distributed Bragg reflector (E-DBR) laser (378 kHz over 1 ms) one of 2.8 kHz [I, Siddharth et al. 2025]. Taken as Lorentzian widths in Eq. (118), the 1 ms values would cost 2.3 dB and 21 dB at 300 m, but the lasers’ measured frequency-noise spectra in Eq. (117) give less than 0.01 dB and about 0.2–0.4 dB (up to ≈0.9 dB for a 16 µs useful window) [E].
  • Chirp. The laser must sweep more than the 1 GHz that 15 cm needs, continuously and without mode hops, because the first round trip τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c of each ramp yields no usable beat (Eq. (114)). At 300 m that is 1.14–1.27 GHz in 9.5–16 µs ramps at ≤30 mW per channel, and 1.89 GHz in 4.25 µs ramps at 100 mW (§C7b subsection 2(g)), repeated as a 30–120 kHz triangle. Its residual frequency error must stay below ≈c/(16R)=62.5c/(16R)=62.5 kHz (Eq. (116)), i.e. a chirp-rate error below ΔR/R=5×10−4\Delta R/R=5\times10^{-4}.
    • The ramp length is set by the photon budget, not by the laser. The implied chirp rate, 0.70.7–1.3×10141.3\times10^{14} Hz/s at ≤30 mW per channel (4.4×10144.4\times10^{14} Hz/s at 100 mW), is modest, and a faster laser does not raise the point rate at ≤30 mW per channel (§C7b subsection 2(g)).
  • Parts. Waymo’s thermally chirped DFB with pre-distortion holds its frequency error below 100 kHz over a 1 GHz sweep, a fractional error δν/B<10−4\delta\nu/B<10^{-4} [P]. Eq. (116) allows a peak deviation of 94 kHz at 200 m, 75 kHz at 250 m and 62.5 kHz at 300 m: read as a peak-to-peak bound (±50 kHz) the figure meets 200–250 m and is marginal at 300 m, while as a peak deviation it is marginal already at 200 m [E].
    • Integrated alternatives are SiN self-injection-locked lasers (42 kHz linewidth over 1 ms, 0.65% nonlinearity) and TFLN E-DBR lasers (378 kHz over 1 ms, 1.5%) [I, Bianconi et al. 2025]. Bianconi et al. define the nonlinearity σ\sigma as the RMS deviation of the laser frequency from a least-squares straight ramp, divided by the sweep excursion BB [I, Bianconi et al. 2025, Supplementary Eq. (4)]. The 0.65% belongs to an unpackaged self-injection-locked chip swept over 500 MHz, which reached 0.08% over 210 MHz once packaged [I, Voloshin et al. 2025]; the 1.5% was measured over a 10.5 GHz sweep [I, Siddharth et al. 2025]. For the parabolic bow of Eq. (116) the peak deviation from the chord is 35/2≈3.353\sqrt5/2\approx3.35 times the RMS deviation, so δνmax=3.35σB\delta\nu_{\max}=3.35\,\sigma B and ε=8δνmax/B=125σ≈27σ\varepsilon=8\delta\nu_{\max}/B=12\sqrt5\,\sigma\approx27\sigma. If the same fractions hold over a 1 GHz sweep, 0.65% and 1.5% give δνmax≈22\delta\nu_{\max}\approx22 and 50 MHz, or ε≈0.17\varepsilon\approx0.17 and 0.40: about 350× and 800× the 62.5 kHz (equivalently the 5×10−45\times10^{-4}) that Eq. (116) allows for 15 cm at 300 m. The packaged 0.08% is still about 43× too large. They need pre-distortion or resampling [E].
    • Snigirev et al.’s 12 PHz/s (1.2×10161.2\times10^{16} Hz/s) TFLN laser (500 MHz excursion; ranging with an EDFA at 4 mW to 3 m) is [R]. Its 500 MHz excursion alone limits the resolution to ≈0.3–0.4 m (§C7b subsection 2(g)).
  • Very fast chirps buy little: above ≈101710^{17} Hz/s, a 25 GHz detector bandwidth restricts ranging to short distances [P, Bianconi et al.]. With chirp rate κ=B/Tu\kappa=B/T_u (Hz/s), the beat frequency is κ×2R/c\kappa\times2R/c, the chirp rate times the round-trip delay. It must stay below the detector bandwidth fdetf_{\mathrm{det}}, so a 25 GHz detector limits range to R≤cfdet/(2κ)=3×108×2.5×1010/(2×1017)≈37R\le cf_{\mathrm{det}}/(2\kappa)=3\times10^{8}\times2.5\times10^{10}/(2\times10^{17})\approx37 m [E]. This limits the value of ultrafast chirps, one of TFLN’s advantages, for automotive ranging.
  • What is missing is not a part that does this on a bench but an integrated source, qualified at 105 °C, that does it while feeding watts of amplified CW light to hundreds of channels. At 10 Mpts/s and 300 m, producing the useful light alone takes ≈30 W of the sensor’s ≈68 W electrical draw (4.5 W of optical power at 15% wall-plug efficiency), and light emitted during the round-trip dead time takes ≈9 W more (§C7b subsection 3a(a)).

This table collects the budget of subsection 2 for a 200 m, 10%-reflectance target. FMCW needs about 12× ToF’s electrical energy per point in 2026 and about 6× in the optimistic 2032 case, but measures velocity on every point.

These are optimistic but not exotic. The residual ≈6× gap (1.74/0.280=6.21.74/0.280=6.2) comes from detection statistics and single-mode collection, SOA wall-plug efficiency, the light emitted during the round trips, and dense digitization in four receivers per point.

4. Maturity beyond physics

Physics is not the only gap. FMCW also trails ToF by about ten doublings of cumulative production volume, which matters because unit cost falls with every doubling, and it trails in automotive qualification.

  • Volume and learning.
    • Hesai alone shipped ≈200,000 lidars in Q1 2025 [P]. Aeva’s Q2 2026 product revenue was $2.5 M [P]; Aurora runs about 20–25 driverless trucks and plans 200 by end-2026, which it describes as “fully allocated” [P/T].
    • Cumulative automotive ToF volume is roughly 10710^7 units; FMCW’s is probably 10410^4 [E]. That is about ten doublings (log⁡2(107/104)=log⁡21,000≈10\log_2(10^{7}/10^{4})=\log_2 1{,}000\approx10).
    • The learning rate is the fractional cost reduction for each doubling of cumulative volume (the experience curve). At a 15–20% learning rate per doubling, experience alone predicts a ≈5–10× unit-cost gap at equal complexity [E]: each doubling multiplies cost by 0.80–0.85, so ten doublings give 1/0.8510≈5.11/0.85^{10}\approx5.1 to 1/0.8010≈9.31/0.80^{10}\approx9.3.
  • Qualification.
    • No AEC-Q102/Q100 qualification (the Automotive Electronics Council stress-test standards for discrete optoelectronic parts and for integrated circuits) of any FMCW laser, SOA or PIC was found [E, search].
    • Aeva claims an ISO 26262 (functional safety) ASIL-B(D) process, IP69K (protection against dust and high-pressure hot-water jets) and −40 to 85 °C at system level [P, claim].
    • Public laser and SOA ageing data were not found [E, search].
  • Attrition since 2022: Quanergy (Chapter 11, 2022), Mobileye (exited 2024), Insight LiDAR (Chapter 11, 2024), Baraja (IP sale 2025) and Scantinel (insolvency 2025) [P/T]; details under §C7 Commercial status and, for Insight LiDAR, §C3a.

5. What parity would need: the three conditions of §C7b subsection 5

This subsection summarizes the parity arithmetic of §C7b subsection 5. Parity means ≥15 Mpts/s in ≤15 W at 200 m on a 10% target, which leaves 0.8 µJ of electricity per point after the 3 W overhead (Eq. (128)); the 2026 SPAD ToF model meets it with 3+15×0.415=9.23+15\times0.415=9.2 W. The central 2026 FMCW model needs 4.90 µJ per point, i.e. 3+15×4.90=76.53+15\times4.90=76.5 W at 15 Mpts/s. Three conditions must land together; any two of them alone leave a 15 Mpts/s sensor at ≈23.5 W or more (§C7b subsection 5 table).

  1. A low-power coherent receiver chip, with the electronics and photonics stacked or monolithic: ≈2–3 mW per receiver including ≈1 GS/s ADCs and FFT, i.e. ≈0.10 µJ of receiver energy per point against the model’s 2.34 µJ, for 115–190 channels of four receivers each.
  2. CW lasers and amplifiers at ≥30% wall-plug efficiency at 105 °C, twice the model’s 15%.
  3. ≈0.15 µJ of optical energy per point at 200 m, half the model’s 0.30 µJ, which needs a receive efficiency η\eta near 0.5, or more looks per point, each with its own receiver.

With all three and the model’s ungated dwell (10 µs of integration, so 15 mW per channel and 190 channels), a point costs 0.150×1.267/0.30+0.10=0.730.150\times1.267/0.30+0.10=0.73 µJ, and a 15 Mpts/s sensor draws 3+15×0.73=14.03+15\times0.73=14.0 W: just inside the target, yet still 1.8× the electrical energy per point of the SPAD ToF model (0.73/0.4150.73/0.415). Channels brighter than ≈22 mW stay inside 15 W only with a gated transmitter: at 30 mW per channel the sensor draws 16 W ungated and 12 W gated (§C7b subsection 5). More power per channel is not a lever: it trades receivers against light wasted during the round trips, and the optimum is already ≈30–40 mW per channel (§C7b subsection 3a(a)). The energies also assume a laser narrow enough to lose little to phase noise: ≲27 kHz for a 1 dB coherent loss at 200 m, or ≲55 kHz for 3 dB at 300 m (Eq. (119); table in §C7b subsection 2(e)), with its residual chirp error inside Eq. (116), all qualified to automotive grade. Two gaps lie outside this per-watt definition: each sample covers only ≈2% of its cell (§C10.3b, Result 2), which more modes per sample would close at the price of more receivers (§C7b subsection 6, item 3), and the cost curve needs programmes of hundreds of thousands of units a year (subsection 4).

6. Verdict and probabilities (my judgement)

The likeliest outcome is series production in a truck or L3 niche; matching ToF on point rate per watt is unlikely.

Outcome By Probability
FMCW in series production (qualified, ≥100k units/yr) in at least one automotive segment, most likely trucks or L3 via Aeva, or Aurora’s gen 3 2030 ≈50–60%
An FMCW automotive sensor at ≤$500 with ≥2 Mpts/s at ≥200 m at 10% 2030 ≈35–45%
FMCW matching 2026 SPAD ToF on point rate per watt (≥15 Mpts/s in ≤15 W at 200 m on a 10% target, the three conditions of subsection 5) 2032 ≈3–7%
FMCW overtakes ToF as the main passenger-car lidar technology 2035 ≈5%

FMCW’s case is strongest when the metric is actionable information per point (instantaneous velocity at 250–400 m for trucks), and when interference or sunlight starts to hurt ToF measurably (§C9). It does not win a line-count race.
