C7b. FMCW against ToF: the binding constraint, what beam steering can and cannot do, and what would have to change

This section asks whether FMCW lidar can beat pulsed time-of-flight (ToF) lidar on a figure that weighs heavily in volume programmes: points measured per second per watt. FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous wave) lidar sweeps the frequency of a continuous laser in linear ramps (chirps), one up and one down per point, and mixes the echo with a copy of its own light, which gives range and radial velocity for every point. The answer is no, not with today’s parts. The limit is not beam steering: it is the cost of each parallel coherent receiver channel, which this section calls the channel tax. The point rate per watt matters because it sets how dense a long-range point cloud a car can afford within its power and heat budget.

Short answer [E unless tagged].

  • Per joule of useful light, FMCW buys ≈4.2× fewer sampled points than 940 nm SPAD ToF, and the reason is spatial, not temporal (subsection 1). A coherent receiver collects one spatial mode and one polarization of the echo, ≤65 mm² at 200 m for any collimated beam, and a single speckle that fades, whereas a direct-detection pixel sums the ≈491 mm² of a 25 mm lens and hundreds of speckles. An ungated CW channel, which also emits during the round trips, widens the gap to ≈5.3× per joule emitted, and the coherent efficiencies measured so far (0.057–0.168) widen it to 6–19× (subsection 1(c)).
  • Per covered cell the gap is ≈200× (subsection 1(d)). One FMCW sample, ≈0.30 µJ against ≈72 nJ per ToF point at 200 m on a 10% target, covers only ≈2% of a 0.05° × 0.05° cell, so covering the cell takes ≈15 µJ (48 samples).
  • Pulsing matters for direct detection, not for coherent detection (subsection 1(a) and (e)). ToF must pulse so that sunlight competes with the signal only inside a 1 ns bin; spread evenly in time, the same echo would need ≈13× more energy. In FMCW the local oscillator (LO) already rejects sunlight, so continuous-wave (CW) light costs no photons, apart from the 12–35% emitted during the last τ\tau of each ramp (21% in the §C7a central case), whose echo falls in a discarded window.
  • What CW light costs is hardware: the channel tax (subsections 2–3). A CW channel carries only tens of milliwatts, so it must dwell Ept/Pch+2τE_{\mathrm{pt}}/P_{\mathrm{ch}}+2\tau on each point, and 15 Mpts/s needs ≈190 channels, each a transmit beam with four complete coherent receivers drawing ≈385 mW against ≈20 mW for a SPAD-SoC macro-pixel.
  • Neither a better beam steerer nor a faster laser removes the tax (subsections 2(g) and 4). Mirrors already move each beam as fast as one channel can use, faster scanning adds scanner-induced Doppler and receive walk-off (§C7), and at ≤30 mW per channel photons, not the laser’s chirp rate or tuning range, set each ramp’s useful window (7.5–14 µs at 300 m).
  • At the sensor level most of the power is light (subsection 3a(a)). A 10 Mpts/s sensor at 300 m draws ≈68 W, ≈30 W of it to make the useful light, which no split among channels reduces; a 100 kHz laser raises the total to ≈160 W.
  • The 1,550 nm eye-safety allowance buys range, not watts per point (subsection 3a(b)). It allows ≈9.1 W of scanned light over a 120° × 25° field, enough for ≈470–600 m of eye-safe reach at 10 Mpts/s, but the ungated §C7a central transmitter exceeds it at 25 Mpts/s (9.6 W).
  • Parity with ToF, ≥15 Mpts/s in ≤15 W at 200 m and 10%, needs three things at once (subsection 5): a coherent receiver chip at ≈2–3 mW per receiver for 115–190 channels of four receivers, CW lasers and amplifiers at ≥30% wall-plug efficiency at 105 °C, and ≈0.15 µJ of light per point. With all three an ungated sensor draws ≈14 W at 15 Mpts/s, still 1.8× the electrical energy per point of the 2026 SPAD ToF reference (9.2 W); today’s central case draws ≈76.5 W.
  • FMCW can win a market, but not the point-rate race. Its market is buyers who pay for velocity on every point and for immunity to sunlight and other lidars at long range: trucks and highway L3. (L3 is SAE driving-automation Level 3: the car drives itself in a defined domain, and the driver takes over on request.) Through 2028 that market is projected at thousands of units a year, against millions for ToF (§B4).

1. How many points one joule of light buys, by architecture

This subsection asks how much emitted light each lidar architecture needs to measure one point at 200 m on a dark (10% reflectance) target, and therefore how many points one joule of light buys. A 940 nm SPAD time-of-flight sensor needs ≈72 nJ per point; a 1,550 nm FMCW sensor needs ≈0.30 µJ per sample, about 4.2× more. The gap comes from how much of the echo each receiver can collect, not from pulsed versus continuous light, which adds only the light an ungated CW channel emits during the round trips: 1.27× the useful energy in the §C7a central case (item (e)). It matters because the optical energy per point, multiplied by the point rate, sets the laser power, and so the heat, of the whole sensor.

One equation covers every architecture. A point is measured when the receiver collects enough signal photoelectrons, nreqn_{\mathrm{req}}, to pass its detection threshold.

  • Assumptions. The target is Lambertian (perfectly diffuse: its radiance is ρ/π\rho/\pi times the irradiance falling on it). It fills the illuminated sample and is seen at normal incidence. The air is clear, so atmospheric transmission is taken as 1. Glossy paint and retroreflectors are not Lambertian: depending on angle, they return far more or far less light toward the sensor. Fog and rain add loss on both legs of the path.
  • For such a target of reflectance ρ\rho at range RR, a fraction ρAeff/(πR2)\rho A_{\mathrm{eff}}/(\pi R^2) of the transmitted light reaches the receiver’s effective collecting area AeffA_{\mathrm{eff}}. AeffA_{\mathrm{eff}} is the area of an ideal lens that would collect the same signal. For direct detection it is the real lens area; for coherent detection it is the smaller mode-equivalent area AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} of (b).
  • A fraction η\eta of the arriving photons becomes photoelectrons. η\eta lumps together the optics transmission, the detector’s efficiency and, for coherent detection, the mixing efficiency.
  • The optical energy that must be sent out per point is therefore Eq. (101) of §C7a, Ept=nreqEphπR2/(ρAeffη)E_{\mathrm{pt}}=n_{\mathrm{req}}E_{\mathrm{ph}}\pi R^2/(\rho A_{\mathrm{eff}}\eta), where Eph=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda is the energy of one photon, hh Planck’s constant, cc the speed of light and λ\lambda the wavelength. One joule of light therefore buys 1/Ept1/E_{\mathrm{pt}} points.
  • The sensor’s average optical power is Popt=EptṄP_{\mathrm{opt}}=E_{\mathrm{pt}}\dot N, where Ṅ\dot N is the point rate (points per second). This holds whatever the time format of the light. At 15 Mpts/s:
    • SPAD ToF: 72nJ×15×106s−1=1.172\ {\mathrm{nJ}}\times15\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=1.1 W;
    • FMCW: 0.30μJ×15×106s−1=4.50.30\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times15\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=4.5 W of useful light, and 1.27 times as much, 5.7 W, from a transmitter that also emits during the round trips (item (e)).
  • A ToF pulse of a few hundred nJ at ≈100 W peak simply delivers its share of that average. It does so either by lighting a line of pixels at once or as one of several shots accumulated per point.

The architecture enters through AeffA_{\mathrm{eff}}, nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} and η\eta. How the light is distributed in time, and how it is distributed over the target, enter through different terms for the two detection principles. Items (a) and (b) take them in turn.

(a) Direct detection (SPAD, SiPM or APD ToF): the lens collects everything, and timing sets how many counts are needed. Direct detection registers the echo’s optical power, or its individual photons, without mixing it with a reference beam. A SiPM (silicon photomultiplier) is an array of SPAD microcells summed into one output. An APD (avalanche photodiode) in linear mode amplifies the photocurrent without counting single photons.

  • Collection. The pixel sums all the light its lens gathers from its cell. AeffA_{\mathrm{eff}} is therefore the lens area, however the transmitted light is spread over the cell: for a 25 mm lens, Aeff=π(12.5mm)2=491A_{\mathrm{eff}}=\pi(12.5\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2=491 mm². The pixel accepts hundreds of speckle modes at once (§C10.3a). Their fluctuations average out, so the echo does not fade.
  • Counts needed, and why pulses matter here. Sunlight reflected by the target reaches the pixel along with the signal. A direct detector can separate the two only by when photons arrive. So the only competition for the signal is the background that falls in the signal’s own time bin, n‾bg,bin=rbgΔtbinNshots,\bar n_{\mathrm{bg,bin}}=r_{\mathrm{bg}}\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}\,N_{\mathrm{shots}},(105) where n‾bg,bin\bar n_{\mathrm{bg,bin}} is the mean number of background counts in that bin, rbgr_{\mathrm{bg}} the pixel’s background count rate (counts per second), Δtbin\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}} the bin width and NshotsN_{\mathrm{shots}} the number of laser shots accumulated per point.
    • In the §C7a model: a macro-pixel (a group of SPADs read out as one pixel, here 3×3 SPADs viewing a 0.05° × 0.05° field) in bright sun counts rbg=1.83×108r_{\mathrm{bg}}=1.83\times10^{8} s⁻¹. That is half the fully sunlit case of §C6(d), 2.965×1082.965\times10^{8} s⁻¹ at a photon detection efficiency (PDE) of 0.3, scaled to the model’s PDE of 0.37: 2.965×108×(0.37/0.3)/2=1.83×1082.965\times10^{8}\times(0.37/0.3)/2=1.83\times10^{8} s⁻¹. It listens for the 20.8 µs column time per point (≈10 shots of ≈2 µs, §C6). Each of its nine SPADs counts r=1.83×108/9=2.03×107r=1.83\times10^{8}/9=2.03\times10^{7} s⁻¹. With the dead time τd=6\tau_d=6 ns this gives rτd=0.122r\tau_d=0.122, so each SPAD is dead (unable to count) for 1−e−0.122=11.5%1-e^{-0.122}=11.5\% of that time (Eq. (90), paralyzable form), and the macro-pixel is live for a fraction 0.885 of it. That gives 1.83×108×20.8×10−6×0.885≈3,3701.83\times10^{8}\times20.8\times10^{-6}\times0.885\approx3{,}370 background events per point. (§C7a(c) counts ≈3,390 because it adds the 21.7 signal counts.)
    • Per bin: these events are spread over the ≈2,080 histogram bins of 1 ns in each shot’s 2.08 µs listening window (≈300 m of range), so there are 3,370/2,080≈1.623{,}370/2{,}080\approx1.62 counts per bin. Eq. (105), with the 0.885 live fraction, gives the same: 1.83×108×10−9×10×0.885=1.621.83\times10^{8}\times10^{-9}\times10\times0.885=1.62. So the model’s 21.7 signal counts in one bin stand out clearly: the detection threshold is 12 counts (§C0 subsection 10.3).
    • The same energy spread evenly in time, as with CW light, would have to stand out against all ≈3,370 background events. Their random (Poisson) fluctuation is 3,370≈58\sqrt{3{,}370}\approx58 counts. At 5 standard deviations that takes 53,370≈2905\sqrt{3{,}370}\approx290 counts: 290/21.7≈13290/21.7\approx13 times the energy per point, before any requirement on ranging precision.
    • This is why direct-detection lidars pulse. It is also why AMCW ToF cameras stay short-range outdoors (§C0 subsection 9). (AMCW, amplitude-modulated continuous wave, is the indirect-ToF or iToF principle: range comes from the phase of a modulated light wave.) It also explains why flash designs lose range in sunlight: they light the whole scene at once and so accumulate many weak shots per point, raising NshotsN_{\mathrm{shots}}.
  • Amplifier noise (linear-mode APDs). A linear APD with a TIA adds electronic noise to every shot, so its threshold is set shot by shot. Splitting the energy across shots then costs sensitivity. Illustrative 1,550 nm case [E], with assumed parameters:
    • Assumptions. The APD gain (avalanche multiplication) is M=10M=10. The ionization ratio kk, the impact-ionization coefficient of the weaker-ionizing carrier divided by that of the stronger one (hole/electron in Si; electron/hole in InP), is 0.45; a smaller kk gives a quieter avalanche. The excess-noise factor F=F(M)F=F(M) is the factor by which the randomness of the avalanche multiplies the shot noise: F=kM+(1−k)(2−1M)=5.5.F=kM+(1-k)\left(2-\frac{1}{M}\right)=5.5 .(106) The TIA noise is 2pA/Hz2\ {\mathrm{pA/\sqrt{Hz}}} over an electrical bandwidth Δf=250\Delta f=250 MHz, so the rms input noise current is in=2pA/Hz×250MHz=32i_n=2\ {\mathrm{pA/\sqrt{Hz}}}\times\sqrt{250\ {\mathrm{MHz}}}=32 nA rms. The pulse lasts tp=4t_p=4 ns, and the required single-shot signal-to-noise ratio is 7. Sunlight and dark current are neglected.
    • Solve MIs=72qM2FIsΔf+in2,Is=nqtp,M I_s=7\sqrt{2qM^2F\,I_s\,\Delta f+i_n^2},\qquad I_s=\frac{nq}{t_p},(107) for nn. Here IsI_s is the primary (unmultiplied) signal photocurrent during the pulse, qq the elementary charge and nn the number of primary photoelectrons per pulse. The left side is the amplified signal current. Under the root, the first term is the amplified shot noise of the signal and the second the amplifier noise. Squaring Eq. (107) and dividing by M2M^2 gives a quadratic in IsI_s, Is2−98qFΔfIs−49in2/M2=0I_s^2-98\,qF\Delta f\,I_s-49\,i_n^2/M^2=0, with 98qFΔf=98×1.60×10−19C×5.5×2.5×108s−1=21.698\,qF\Delta f=98\times1.60\times10^{-19}\ {\mathrm{C}}\times5.5\times2.5\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=21.6 nA and 49in2/M2=49×(32nA)2/100=502nA249\,i_n^2/M^2=49\times(32\ {\mathrm{nA}})^2/100=502\ {\mathrm{nA^2}}. Its positive root is Is=(21.6+21.62+4×502)/2nA=35.7I_s=(21.6+\sqrt{21.6^2+4\times502})/2\ {\mathrm{nA}}=35.7 nA. Then n=Istp/q=35.7nA×4ns/(1.60×10−19C)≈890n=I_st_p/q=35.7\ {\mathrm{nA}}\times4\ {\mathrm{ns}}/(1.60\times10^{-19}\ {\mathrm{C}})\approx890 photoelectrons, some 41× the SPAD’s 21.7 counts.
    • Result: with quantum efficiency 0.8 and optics 0.5 (η=0.40\eta=0.40), Eq. (101) gives Ept≈0.73E_{\mathrm{pt}}\approx0.73 µJ at 200 m and 10%. It is 0.6–0.9 µJ for TIA noise of 1.5–3 pA/√Hz.
    • 1,550 nm ToF sensors make up for this with larger apertures and with the µJ-class pulses that 1,550 nm eye-safety limits allow (§C4c), not with more points per joule.

(b) Coherent detection (FMCW, or pulsed coherent): the LO removes the background, and the spot size sets the collection. A coherent receiver mixes the echo with the LO on a photodiode. It measures the beat between the two fields, so only light that matches the LO in direction, wavefront and polarization contributes.

  • Background. The receiver responds only to light in the LO’s spatial mode and polarization, within the beat bandwidth. Worked number:
    • Sunlight at 1,550 nm has a spectral irradiance Eλ≈0.27E_\lambda\approx0.27 W m⁻² nm⁻¹ (ASTM G173-03, §C4c) [P]. On a 10% target it gives a radiance L=ρEλ/π=0.1×0.27/π≈8.6×10−3L=\rho E_\lambda/\pi=0.1\times0.27/\pi\approx8.6\times10^{-3} W m⁻² sr⁻¹ nm⁻¹.
    • One spatial mode has étendue λ2=2.4×10−12\lambda^2=2.4\times10^{-12} m² sr. (Étendue is the product of collecting area and accepted solid angle; a single mode always occupies λ2\lambda^2.) A beat bandwidth Δfbeat=1\Delta f_{\mathrm{beat}}=1 GHz corresponds to an optical bandwidth Δλ=λ2Δfbeat/c=0.008\Delta\lambda=\lambda^2\Delta f_{\mathrm{beat}}/c=0.008 nm. Accepting one polarization halves the total.
    • Collected sunlight: 8.6×10−3×2.4×10−12×0.008×0.5≈8.3×10−178.6\times10^{-3}\times2.4\times10^{-12}\times0.008\times0.5\approx8.3\times10^{-17} W. Divided by the photon energy, 8.3×10−17W/(1.28×10−19J)8.3\times10^{-17}\ {\mathrm{W}}/(1.28\times10^{-19}\ {\mathrm{J}}), that is ≈650 photons per second, or 0.006 photons in the 10 µs that one point integrates (TintT_{\mathrm{int}}, subsection 2(b)). The LO’s own shot noise, by comparison, is equivalent to about one photon in every FFT bin.
    • So coherent detection gains nothing from concentrating light in time. CW light costs it no photons per point, apart from the dead time in (e).
  • Collection: one mode, and it depends on where the light lands. A single-mode receiver collects the target’s radiance times λ2\lambda^2. The smaller the illuminated spot, the higher the radiance, so the collecting area is set by the beam footprint, not by the lens. Consider a Gaussian beam of radius ww at the target. The mode-equivalent area of Eq. (41) (§C0 subsection 10.2; §C10.3b evaluates it), with truncation factor tt and one polarization, is Amode=t2λ2R2/(2πw2)A_{\mathrm{mode}}=t^2\lambda^2R^2/(2\pi w^2).
    • Variables and derivation. AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} is the mode-equivalent collecting area. It is the area of an ideal direct-detection lens that would collect the same signal, from the same target, as the coherent receiver collects in its single LO mode. It therefore replaces the lens area in the link budget. λ\lambda is the wavelength, RR the range and ww the beam’s 1/e² intensity radius at the target. t=0.915t=0.915 is the fraction of the Gaussian’s power that passes the aperture, counted once on transmit and once on receive (hence t2t^2). The factor 2 in the denominator is the ½ for the single polarization the LO accepts. §C0 subsection 10.2 derives Eq. (41) from the antenna theorem and the back-propagated-LO overlap (Siegman 1966; Rye 1979; Frehlich and Kavaya 1991) [I] and plots it against range (Figure C0.10a).
    • Assumptions of Eq. (41). The beams are ideal TEM00 Gaussians (beam-quality factor M2=1M^2=1; this MM is unrelated to the APD gain of (a)), with perfect mode matching and alignment between echo and LO, and no atmospheric turbulence. The target is depolarizing, so half the echo is in the accepted polarization; a retroreflector largely preserves polarization, so the factor then differs. Turbulence and misalignment would lower AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}.
    • A collimated 20 mm aperture (w0=9w_0=9 mm, t2=0.84t^2=0.84) spreads, by Eq. (42) (§C0 subsection 10.2), to w(200m)=14.2w(200\ {\mathrm{m}})=14.2 mm. Here w0w_0 is the beam’s 1/e² radius as it leaves the aperture. Then Amode=0.84×(1.55×10−6)2×2002/(2π×0.01422)=64A_{\mathrm{mode}}=0.84\times(1.55\times10^{-6})^2\times200^2/(2\pi\times0.0142^2)=64 mm², about 1/8 of the ToF lens area.
    • A bigger collimated aperture does not help.
      • A collimated Gaussian beam of starting radius w0w_0 spreads with range as w2=w02+(λR/πw0)2w^2=w_0^2+(\lambda R/\pi w_0)^2, Eq. (42) written out with the Rayleigh range zR=πw02/λz_R=\pi w_0^2/\lambda. At a given RR, w2w^2 is smallest, wmin⁡2=2λR/πw^2_{\min}=2\lambda R/\pi, when w0=λR/π=9.9w_0=\sqrt{\lambda R/\pi}=9.9 mm (a ≈22 mm aperture). A smaller beam diffracts faster; a larger one starts wider.
      • Inserting that minimum into Eq. (41) gives the ceiling Amode≤t2λR/4=65A_{\mathrm{mode}}\le t^2\lambda R/4=65 mm² at 200 m, the collecting-area form of the best-aperture envelope of Eq. (43). A 40 mm collimated aperture gives 36 mm², and an 80 mm one gives 10 mm², because their beams are wider at 200 m.
      • Only focusing on the target range raises the ceiling, and only near that range.
    • The price is coverage. The 14 mm beam’s footprint, πw2=6.3×10−4\pi w^2=6.3\times10^{-4} m², is 2.1% of a 0.05° cell at 200 m, whose area is (8.7×10−4×200m)2=0.030(8.7\times10^{-4}\times200\ {\mathrm{m}})^2=0.030 m² (§C10.3b, Result 2). (A cell is one angular resolution element of the point cloud; 0.05° is 8.7×10−48.7\times10^{-4} rad.) Widening the beam to fill the cell cuts AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} by the same factor of 48, to 1.3 mm². Covering the cell costs ≈15 µJ either way, as one wide sample or as 48 narrow ones of 0.30 µJ.
  • Counts needed. One mode means one speckle. A single speckle’s intensity is exponentially distributed (its field amplitude follows Rayleigh statistics), so many looks are much dimmer than the mean. Averaging NspN_{\mathrm{sp}} independent speckles narrows this spread; a direct-detection pixel averages hundreds, while each coherent receiver sees one. The §C7a design therefore gives each beam four receivers, one per polarization on each of two spatial modes, and sums their powers: four looks. Under the report’s detection rule (90% per point, at most 10−310^{-3} false points per point over the full search) and with the peak required in both the up- and the down-ramp, four looks need ≈88 photoelectrons in total and one look ≈259 (§C0 subsection 10.3). The model uses 120, a ×1.36 margin, close to the ×1.45 that takes ToF from the ideal 15.0 to 21.7 counts. Waymo’s 50 photons per detection with four averaged speckles, 45 photoelectrons at its quantum efficiency of 0.9 [P], are the corresponding one-ramp figure (≈47 by the same rule). These counts assume a receiver at the LO shot-noise limit, i.e. thermal and dark-current noise neglected. At 105–125 °C this holds only approximately: §C4c gives 82–94% of the shot-noise limit for Ge at 125 °C.

(c) Result: points per joule of light, 200 m, 10% target [E; §C7a parameters unless stated]

The table applies Eq. (101) to each architecture. (dToF is direct time-of-flight, which times each photon’s return; a line-flash design lights a whole line of the scene with each shot.) Every row shares the following assumptions:

  • a Lambertian target of 10% reflectance that fills the sample, at 200 m and normal incidence;
  • clear air, with no atmospheric loss;
  • for the coherent rows, a monostatic 20 mm beam (its transmit aperture also receives) and four looks per sample (two polarizations × two spatial modes), each with its own AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} (Eq. (41)), and a depolarizing target;
  • speckle and search: direct-detection pixels average hundreds of speckles, while each coherent look sees one exponentially fading speckle; with four looks, and the peak required in both ramps, a coherent sample needs 120 photoelectrons against 21.7 counts (§C0 subsection 10.3);
  • coherent receivers at the LO shot-noise limit, and the SPAD rows in the bright-sun background of (a).

If the target is glossy or retroreflective or smaller than the sample, or if it is seen through fog or rain, the energies in every row change.

Architecture Effective collecting area Photoelectrons needed η\eta Optical energy per point Points per optical joule
940 nm SPAD or SiPM dToF, scanned or line-flash, 25 mm lens 491 mm² (whole lens) 21.7 counts 0.164 72 nJ 1.4×1071.4\times10^{7}
1,550 nm pulsed ToF, linear InGaAs APD, same lens (illustrative, (a)) 491 mm² ≈890 0.40 ≈0.73 µJ 1.4×1061.4\times10^{6}
1,550 nm FMCW, collimated 20 mm monostatic beam, four looks, per sample 255 mm² (4 × 64 mm²) 120 0.25 0.30 µJ 3.3×1063.3\times10^{6}
FMCW at the parity target (subsection 5) — — — 0.15 µJ 6.7×1066.7\times10^{6}
FMCW with the beam widened, or 48 samples tiled, to cover a whole 0.05° cell 5.3 mm² (4 × 1.3 mm²) 120 0.25 ≈15 µJ 6.8×1046.8\times10^{4}
AMCW (iToF) camera outdoors at long range whole lens set by sunlight integrated over the exposure: ≈4×10⁴× a scanner’s sunlight per unit signal (§C0 subsection 9) — not viable —

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Energy column: Eq. (101), Ept=nreqEphπR2/(ρAeffη)E_{\mathrm{pt}}=n_{\mathrm{req}}E_{\mathrm{ph}}\pi R^2/(\rho A_{\mathrm{eff}}\eta), with πR2=1.26×105\pi R^2=1.26\times10^{5} m² at R=200R=200 m, ρ=0.1\rho=0.1, and Eph=2.11×10−19E_{\mathrm{ph}}=2.11\times10^{-19} J at 940 nm or 1.28×10−191.28\times10^{-19} J at 1,550 nm. Worked example (SPAD row): 21.7×2.11×10−19×1.26×105/(0.1×4.91×10−4×0.164)=7.2×10−821.7\times2.11\times10^{-19}\times1.26\times10^{5}/(0.1\times4.91\times10^{-4}\times0.164)=7.2\times10^{-8} J.
  • η\eta:
    • ToF: optics 0.5 × photon detection efficiency 0.37 × the bright-sun live fraction 0.885 (6 ns paralyzable dead time, (a) and §C7a(a)), i.e. 0.5×0.37×0.885=0.1640.5\times0.37\times0.885=0.164;
    • APD: optics 0.5 × quantum efficiency 0.8;
    • FMCW: 0.25, a design value for optics × detector × mixing, checked against Waymo’s estimate rather than built from component factors (§C7a(a)); the mode and polarization factors are in AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}.
  • Last column: 1/Ept1/E_{\mathrm{pt}}; for example 1/(7.2×10−8J)=1.4×1071/(7.2\times10^{-8}\ {\mathrm{J}})=1.4\times10^{7} points per joule.
  • Full-cell FMCW row: the energy scales inversely with AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}, so 0.30μJ×64/1.32=14.60.30\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times64/1.32=14.6 µJ.
  • AMCW row: an iToF camera integrates sunlight over its whole exposure rather than over a 1 ns bin, so at long range outdoors the background swamps the signal (§C0 subsection 9).
  • The FMCW efficiency is a design value. The FMCW value, 0.25, is a design value about 1.5× above the best coherent chain measured so far: Waymo’s lab chain measured 0.112 end to end, or 0.168 without its Hann window (a taper applied to the beat signal before the FFT, which cost Waymo 1.8 dB of SNR, §C0 subsection 10.7), and Pointcloud’s integrated array 0.057 [P] (§C0 subsection 10.1, §C7a(a)). With those values the FMCW rows need 1.5–2.2× or about 4.4× the energy shown, so FMCW buys 4.23×0.25/0.168=6.34.23\times0.25/0.168=6.3 to 4.23×0.25/0.112=9.44.23\times0.25/0.112=9.4 times (discrete fibre chain) or 4.23×0.25/0.057=18.64.23\times0.25/0.057=18.6 times (integrated array) fewer points per optical joule than SPAD ToF, instead of ≈4.2×. Here 4.23 is the unrounded ratio of Eq. (108), 0.303μJ/71.7nJ0.303\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/71.7\ {\mathrm{nJ}}.
  • Useful and emitted light: the FMCW rows count the light whose echo arrives inside the useful windows. An ungated CW transmitter also emits during the round trips (item (e)), 1.27 times as much in the §C7a central case: 0.384 µJ per sample, or 1/(3.84×10−7J)=2.6×1061/(3.84\times10^{-7}\ {\mathrm{J}})=2.6\times10^{6} samples per emitted joule.

(d) Why FMCW buys ≈4.2× fewer sampled points per joule than SPAD ToF. Let EFMCWE_{\mathrm{FMCW}} be the optical energy per FMCW sample (0.30 µJ) and EToFE_{\mathrm{ToF}} the optical energy per SPAD ToF point (72 nJ), both from Eq. (101). Their ratio splits term by term; each factor is the ratio of one term of that equation, FMCW over ToF, or its inverse: EFMCWEToF=491255⏟collection×12021.7⏟detection×9401,550⏟photonenergy×0.1640.25⏟efficiency=1.93×5.53×0.606×0.656≈4.2.\frac{E_{\mathrm{FMCW}}}{E_{\mathrm{ToF}}}=\underbrace{\frac{491}{255}}_{\mathrm{collection}}\times\underbrace{\frac{120}{21.7}}_{\mathrm{detection}}\times\underbrace{\frac{940}{1{,}550}}_{\mathrm{photon\ energy}}\times\underbrace{\frac{0.164}{0.25}}_{\mathrm{efficiency}}=1.93\times5.53\times0.606\times0.656\approx4.2.(108) The collection factor is the ratio of effective areas in mm², the detection factor the ratio of required photoelectrons, the photon-energy factor the wavelength ratio (since Eph=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda), and the efficiency factor the ratio of the two η\eta values.

  • Collection (1.9×):
    • 1.56× of this comes from the model’s larger ToF lens ((25/20)2(25/20)^2).
    • 1.23× compares the four looks’ 255 mm² with the full area of one 20 mm aperture, π(10mm)2=314\pi(10\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2=314 mm². Each look alone collects only Amode=64A_{\mathrm{mode}}=64 mm², 4.9× less than that area (314/64314/64), because it takes one polarization, in the Gaussian mode shape, of a 20 mm beam that has spread at 200 m; Waymo puts this single-mode penalty at ≈6 dB [P]. Two polarizations on each of two spatial modes recover a factor of four.
  • Detection statistics (5.5×): the four looks need 120 photoelectrons and ToF 21.7 counts; for the ideal requirements the ratio is 5.9 (88.5/15.088.5/15.0, §C0 subsection 10.3). Of the ideal 5.9, ×1.46 is the coherent receiver’s one photoelectron of shot noise in each of the ≈2,450 FFT bins it searches (15.0 → 21.9), ×1.79 is finding the peak in both ramps (21.9 → 39.1), and ×2.26 is speckle fading with four looks (39.1 → 88.5): 1.46×1.79×2.26=5.91.46\times1.79\times2.26=5.9.
  • 1,550 nm helps (0.61×): each 1,550 nm photon carries only 0.61× the energy of a 940 nm one, so a joule contains more of them.
  • Efficiency (0.66×): the FMCW model’s η=0.25\eta=0.25 is higher than the ToF model’s 0.164, the SPADs’ optics × PDE × live fraction in bright sun, which also helps FMCW.
  • Per fully covered cell the gap is ≈200× (14.6μJ/72nJ=20314.6\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/72\ {\mathrm{nJ}}=203).
  • Which figure to use: the per-sample figure is the fair one for objects larger than the sample spacing, such as cars. The per-cell figure applies to objects smaller than a cell, such as debris (§C10.3a).

(e) What CW light does cost FMCW in photons. Two things: a round-trip dead time, modest at today’s channel powers, and a coherence loss set by the laser’s linewidth and the range.

  • Round-trip dead time. The receiver discards the first τ\tau of each ramp (subsection 2(a)). The light a CW channel sends during the last τ\tau of each ramp returns in that discarded window of the next ramp and is wasted; the wasted transmission and the receiver’s dead time each last τ\tau per ramp, 2τ2\tau per point. Here τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c is the round-trip time (Eq. (109)), 1.33 µs at 200 m.
    • The transmitted energy per point is EptTdwell/TintE_{\mathrm{pt}}T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}. TdwellT_{\mathrm{dwell}} is the whole time the channel spends on one point. Tint=Ept/PchT_{\mathrm{int}}=E_{\mathrm{pt}}/P_{\mathrm{ch}} is the part of it that collects usable echo, where PchP_{\mathrm{ch}} is the channel’s CW optical power (subsection 2(b)).
    • At 16–30 mW per channel, a share 2τ/Tdwell2\tau/T_{\mathrm{dwell}} of 12–35% of the transmitted energy is emitted during the dead time and wasted (subsection 2 table).
    • The §C7a central case is ungated: Ept=0.303E_{\mathrm{pt}}=0.303 µJ at Pch=30P_{\mathrm{ch}}=30 mW gives Tint=10T_{\mathrm{int}}=10 µs and Tdwell=12.67T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=12.67 µs, so each point costs 0.303×12.67/10=0.3840.303\times12.67/10=0.384 µJ of emitted light, 21% of it wasted. Per joule emitted, FMCW therefore buys 0.384/0.072≈5.30.384/0.072\approx5.3 times fewer points than SPAD ToF, against the 4.2 of Eq. (108) for the useful light.
    • A pulsed laser stays dark while it waits.
  • Coherence loss. Laser phase noise does not cap how long a ramp can integrate. It removes a range-dependent share of the beat power from the coherent FFT peak and leaves ηcoh=e−2πΔντ\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}=e^{-2\pi\Delta\nu\,\tau} in it (subsection 2(e), Eq. (118)), where Δν\Delta\nu is the laser’s linewidth, the spread of its optical frequency caused by phase noise.
    • The energies of this subsection leave the loss out, so they hold for a laser narrow enough that ηcoh≈1\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}\approx1: ≲27 kHz for a 1 dB loss at 200 m (Eq. (119)).
    • Otherwise the requirement becomes Ept/ηcohE_{\mathrm{pt}}/\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}. A 100 kHz laser at 200 m keeps ηcoh=e−2π×105×1.33×10−6=e−0.84=0.43\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}=e^{-2\pi\times10^{5}\times1.33\times10^{-6}}=e^{-0.84}=0.43, so the central 0.30 µJ becomes 0.70 µJ. At 300 m it keeps 0.28, a 3.5× penalty.

(f) Range dominates everything. The required energy grows with range in both principles, but at different rates.

  • Direct detection: from Eq. (101) with a fixed lens, Ept∝R2/ρE_{\mathrm{pt}}\propto R^2/\rho. The same SPAD receiver needs only 72nJ×(10/200)2=0.1872\ {\mathrm{nJ}}\times(10/200)^2=0.18 nJ per point at 10 m, i.e. 400× more points per joule. This is why phone dToF (direct time-of-flight) modules and ToF cameras deliver many points for milliwatts (§B8, §C0 subsection 9).
  • Coherent: for a collimated beam at its optimum aperture, Amode∝RA_{\mathrm{mode}}\propto R (Eq. (43)), so Ept∝R2/Amode∝RE_{\mathrm{pt}}\propto R^2/A_{\mathrm{mode}}\propto R. The footprint’s share of a fixed angular cell, however, falls as 1/R1/R.
  • Consequence. FMCW’s photon handicap against ToF shrinks as 1/R1/R. At 300 m FMCW needs 0.30μJ×300/200=0.450.30\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times300/200=0.45 µJ per sample and SPAD ToF 72nJ×(300/200)2=0.1672\ {\mathrm{nJ}}\times(300/200)^2=0.16 µJ per point, so the ratio of Eq. (108) falls from 4.2 at 200 m to 0.45/0.16=2.80.45/0.16=2.8 at 300 m [E]. This assumes that the coherent aperture is re-optimized for each range while the ToF lens stays at 25 mm.

(g) What the pulse format does change: occupancy, not photons. A channel is busy for as long as it takes to deliver EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} at its peak power, plus the round trip. That sets how many channels must run in parallel (subsections 2–3). It does not set how many joules the scene needs. In engineering terms: the laser’s average power is fixed by the scene, but the number of receivers is fixed by how fast each channel can deliver its energy.

2. What sets the dwell of one FMCW point

This subsection asks how long one FMCW channel must stay on each point (its dwell), because the dwell fixes how many points per second one channel can deliver. At 200 m with 16–30 mW per channel, the photon budget dominates: emitting it takes 5–19 µs per point, and the round trip adds a fixed 2.67 µs, for a dwell of 8–21 µs. The ADC rate and the laser’s chirp rate and tuning range set further lower bounds on the chirp length, scanning sets an upper bound, and laser linewidth multiplies the energy each point needs (items (c)–(g)). Subsection 3a then adds up the electrical power of a whole sensor at 10 Mpts/s and 300 m and asks what the 1,550 nm eye-safety allowance buys. The dwell matters because, multiplied by the point rate, it gives the number of parallel channels the sensor needs (subsection 3).

Notation. An FMCW channel sweeps its optical frequency linearly over one “ramp” (chirp) of duration TcT_c. The chirp rate κ\kappa (Hz/s) is the rate of that sweep: the bandwidth swept divided by the time taken. The echo from a target at range RR returns after the round-trip time

τ=2Rc,τ(200m)=2×200m3×108m/s=1.33μs,\tau=\frac{2R}{c},\qquad \tau(200\ {\mathrm{m}})=\frac{2\times200\ {\mathrm{m}}}{3\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{m/s}}}=1.33\ \mu{\mathrm{s}},(109)

where cc is the speed of light. The standard measurement uses an up-ramp and a down-ramp, because the pair separates range from Doppler (§C0 subsection 2). One point therefore takes Tdwell=2TcT_{\mathrm{dwell}}=2T_c, the dwell.

(a) The round trip removes τ\tau from every ramp. The echo produces a clean beat with the LO only once it has arrived. During the first τ\tau of each ramp, what returns is the tail of the previous ramp, which has the opposite slope and is discarded. The useful window per ramp is therefore

Tu=Tc−τ.T_u=T_c-\tau .(110)

Two consequences follow.

  • Resolution comes from the useful window only.
    • The frequency swept while the beat exists is the effective bandwidth Beff=κTuB_{\mathrm{eff}}=\kappa T_u. The range resolution, the smallest separation at which two targets appear as separate peaks, is ΔR=c/(2Beff)\Delta R=c/(2B_{\mathrm{eff}}).
    • Keeping ΔR=15\Delta R=15 cm needs Beff=c/(2ΔR)=3×108/(2×0.15)=1B_{\mathrm{eff}}=c/(2\Delta R)=3\times10^{8}/(2\times0.15)=1 GHz within TuT_u.
    • The total sweep is larger: Btot=κTc=BeffTc/TuB_{\mathrm{tot}}=\kappa T_c=B_{\mathrm{eff}}\,T_c/T_u. For Tu=2T_u=2 µs, Tc=3.33T_c=3.33 µs and Btot=1GHz×3.33/2=1.67B_{\mathrm{tot}}=1\ {\mathrm{GHz}}\times3.33/2=1.67 GHz.
  • There is a hard ceiling on point rate per channel. Even with infinite laser power (Tu→0T_u\to0), Tdwell≥2τT_{\mathrm{dwell}}\ge2\tau. At 200 m that is 2.67 µs, i.e. at most 1/(2.67μs)≈3751/(2.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}})\approx375 kpts/s per channel.

(b) The photon budget sets the rest, and it is the binding term.

  • Energy needed. Subsection 1 gives an optical energy per point Ept=0.30E_{\mathrm{pt}}=0.30 µJ at 200 m and 10% for the central 2026 case; the parity energy of subsection 5 is 0.15 µJ.
  • Integration time. A channel transmitting a constant CW optical power PchP_{\mathrm{ch}} must integrate for Tint=Ept/PchT_{\mathrm{int}}=E_{\mathrm{pt}}/P_{\mathrm{ch}} of useful window, summed over both ramps: 2Tu=Tint2T_u=T_{\mathrm{int}}. With Tc=Tu+τT_c=T_u+\tau from Eq. (110), the dwell and the per-channel point rate Ṅch\dot N_{\mathrm{ch}} are Tdwell=2Tc=EptPch+2τ,Ṅch=1Tdwell.\boxed{\,T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=2T_c=\frac{E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{P_{\mathrm{ch}}}+2\tau\,},\qquad \dot N_{\mathrm{ch}}=\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{dwell}}}.(111) The first term is the time needed to emit the required energy; the second is the dead time of the two round trips.
  • Worked example: Ept=0.30E_{\mathrm{pt}}=0.30 µJ and Pch=30P_{\mathrm{ch}}=30 mW give Tint=0.30×10−6/0.030=10T_{\mathrm{int}}=0.30\times10^{-6}/0.030=10 µs. Then Tdwell=10+2.67=12.7T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=10+2.67=12.7 µs and Ṅch=1/12.7μs=79\dot N_{\mathrm{ch}}=1/12.7\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=79 kpts/s. This is the §C7a central case, whose 10 µs of integration are its two 5 µs useful windows.
  • What limits PchP_{\mathrm{ch}}. It cannot simply be raised:
    • Heat. CW sources plus semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs) run at ≈15–20% wall-plug efficiency (light out per electrical power in), so each watt of light costs 4–6 W of heat (§C7a(b)).
    • Waveguide power handling. Silicon waveguides saturate near 16 mW through two-photon and free-carrier absorption [P, Pointcloud Methods] (§C7a(b)). At high intensity silicon absorbs two photons at once, and the free carriers this creates absorb still more light. Higher power needs SiN (silicon nitride) or III-V (compound-semiconductor, e.g. InP) paths.
    • Per-beam eye safety at 1,550 nm. This is secondary; §C7a concludes that heat is the practical ceiling.
  • The wasted share of the laser’s energy, 2τ/Tdwell2\tau/T_{\mathrm{dwell}} (subsection 1(e)), is 2.67/12.7=21%2.67/12.7=21\% in the example.

The table evaluates Eq. (111) at 200 m for the two energy cases.

PchP_{\mathrm{ch}} TdwellT_{\mathrm{dwell}} at 0.30 µJ Per-channel rate Wasted share TdwellT_{\mathrm{dwell}} at 0.15 µJ Per-channel rate Wasted share
16 mW (silicon limit) 21.4 µs 47 kpts/s 12% 12.0 µs 83 kpts/s 22%
30 mW 12.7 µs 79 kpts/s 21% 7.7 µs 130 kpts/s 35%
100 mW 5.7 µs 176 kpts/s 47% 4.2 µs 240 kpts/s 64%
Unlimited → 2.67 µs → 375 kpts/s → 100% → 2.67 µs → 375 kpts/s → 100%

How the table is computed [E]:

  • Tdwell=Ept/Pch+2τT_{\mathrm{dwell}}=E_{\mathrm{pt}}/P_{\mathrm{ch}}+2\tau (Eq. (111)), with 2τ=2.672\tau=2.67 µs at 200 m.
  • Rate =1/Tdwell=1/T_{\mathrm{dwell}}; wasted share =2τ/Tdwell=2\tau/T_{\mathrm{dwell}}.
  • Example row (100 mW, 0.15 µJ): 0.15μJ/0.1W=1.50.15\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/0.1\ {\mathrm{W}}=1.5 µs, plus 2.67 µs, gives 4.17 µs. The rate is 1/4.17μs=2401/4.17\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=240 kpts/s, and the wasted share is 2.67/4.17=64%2.67/4.17=64\%.

At the powers realistic for integrated photonics (16–30 mW), the photon term is 2–7 times the round-trip term. The ratio Tint/2τT_{\mathrm{int}}/2\tau of the two terms of Eq. (111) is 3.7–7.0 at 0.30 µJ and 1.9–3.5 at 0.15 µJ. So the dwell mostly measures how much CW light one channel can carry.

(c) Readout bandwidth makes short chirps expensive but does not forbid them. The electronics must digitize the beat signal, and shorter chirps push the beat to higher frequencies.

  • Beat frequency. The largest beat, at maximum range and closing speed, is fb,max=κτ+fD=BeffTuτ+2vλ,f_{b,\max}=\kappa\tau+f_D=\frac{B_{\mathrm{eff}}}{T_u}\,\tau+\frac{2v}{\lambda},(112) where κ=Beff/Tu\kappa=B_{\mathrm{eff}}/T_u is the chirp rate, τ\tau the round-trip time, κτ\kappa\tau the beat produced by range, and fD=2v/λf_D=2v/\lambda the Doppler shift for a closing speed vv at wavelength λ\lambda. At 70 m/s and 1,550 nm, fD=2×70/(1.55×10−6)=90f_D=2\times70/(1.55\times10^{-6})=90 MHz.
  • Sampling rate. The ADC samples at fs≈2.5fb,maxf_s\approx2.5\,f_{b,\max}: twice the maximum beat frequency (the Nyquist rate for real sampling) plus a ≈25% margin. At R=200R=200 m and Beff=1B_{\mathrm{eff}}=1 GHz this gives:
Useful window TuT_u Chirp Tc=Tu+τT_c=T_u+\tau Total sweep BtotB_{\mathrm{tot}} Range beat Beffτ/TuB_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau/T_u fb,maxf_{b,\max} with Doppler Sampling rate fsf_s
10 µs 11.3 µs 1.13 GHz 133 MHz 223 MHz 0.56 GS/s
5 µs 6.3 µs 1.27 GHz 267 MHz 357 MHz 0.89 GS/s
2 µs 3.3 µs 1.67 GHz 667 MHz 757 MHz 1.9 GS/s
1 µs 2.3 µs 2.33 GHz 1,333 MHz 1,423 MHz 3.6 GS/s

Worked row (5 µs): 1GHz×1.33μs/5μs=2671\ {\mathrm{GHz}}\times1.33\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}/5\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=267 MHz; adding 90 MHz gives 357 MHz; ×2.5=0.89\times2.5=0.89 GS/s.

  • Samples per point barely depend on the chirp length. Sampling both useful windows at fs=2.5fb,maxf_s=2.5f_{b,\max} (Eq. (112)) gives the number of ADC samples per point, NADC=fs×2Tu=5Beffτ+5fDTu=5RΔR+5fDTu,N_{\mathrm{ADC}}=f_s\times2T_u=5B_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau+5f_DT_u=5\frac{R}{\Delta R}+5f_DT_u ,(113) using Beffτ=(c/2ΔR)(2R/c)=R/ΔRB_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau=(c/2\Delta R)(2R/c)=R/\Delta R. Here ΔR\Delta R is the range resolution, TuT_u the useful window per ramp and fDf_D the Doppler shift. The first term is five samples per range-resolution cell out to range RR; the second is the extra bandwidth reserved for Doppler.
    • At 200 m and 15 cm with Tu=5T_u=5 µs: NADC=5×200/0.15+5×90×106×5×10−6=6,670+2,260≈8,900N_{\mathrm{ADC}}=5\times200/0.15+5\times90\times10^{6}\times5\times10^{-6}=6{,}670+2{,}260\approx8{,}900 samples per point.
    • At 300 m (the §C7a case, with the same Tu=5T_u=5 µs), it is 5×300/0.15+2,260=10,000+2,260≈12,3005\times300/0.15+2{,}260=10{,}000+2{,}260\approx12{,}300. This is the count of §C7a’s Eq. (102): Eq. (113) becomes Eq. (102) when RR is the far end of the range searched, Rmax=300R_{\max}=300 m, and the chirp duration TT of Eq. (102) is read as the useful window TuT_u, since only the useful windows are digitized. The §C7a model digitizes this whole 0–300 m search for its 200 m design point; a sensor that searched only to 200 m would need the 8,900 samples above.
    • A faster ADC simply runs for a shorter time. The §C7a model’s central energy is ≈37 pJ per sample (ADC plus FFT). It assumes an 8-ENOB ADC (8 effective bits of resolution) at a product-grade 50 fJ per conversion step, 50fJ×28=12.850\ {\mathrm{fJ}}\times2^{8}=12.8 pJ per sample, plus ≈70 FFT, windowing and peak-search operations per sample at 0.35 pJ each. At that energy each receiver spends 8,900×37pJ≈0.338{,}900\times37\ {\mathrm{pJ}}\approx0.33 µJ per point at 200 m, and 12,300×37pJ≈0.4512{,}300\times37\ {\mathrm{pJ}}\approx0.45 µJ at 300 m, before TIA and bias power; the four receivers of the §C7a design spend four times as much, 1.3 and 1.8 µJ.
  • Why short chirps are still costly in practice:
    • ADC energy per conversion step worsens above about 1 GS/s (the Murmann ADC survey trend) [I].
    • Wider-band TIAs add noise and power [U].
    • All of this is replicated in every channel.
    • So the readout makes TuT_u below about 2 µs (≥1.9 GS/s per channel at 200 m) expensive at scale, but it is not a physical floor.

(d) The chirp the laser must deliver: tuning range, ramp time and linearity. A cost, not the floor. Three quantities specify the chirp: how far it sweeps, how long each ramp lasts, and how straight the sweep is. The chirp rate follows from the first two.

  • Tuning range. The range resolution is set by the frequency swept while the echo is present, Beff=c/(2ΔR)B_{\mathrm{eff}}=c/(2\Delta R) (item (a)): 1 GHz for ΔR=15\Delta R=15 cm, 3 GHz for 5 cm. The laser must sweep further than that, because it keeps sweeping through the round trip τ\tau at the start of each ramp, before any usable echo has arrived. The total continuous, mode-hop-free sweep per ramp (one without jumps between the laser cavity’s modes) is therefore

    Btot=κTc=BeffTu+τTu=Beff(1+τTu),B_{\mathrm{tot}}=\kappa\,T_c=B_{\mathrm{eff}}\,\frac{T_u+\tau}{T_u}=B_{\mathrm{eff}}\left(1+\frac{\tau}{T_u}\right),(114)

    where κ=Beff/Tu\kappa=B_{\mathrm{eff}}/T_u is the chirp rate, Tc=Tu+τT_c=T_u+\tau the ramp duration (Eq. (110)) and TuT_u the useful window.

    • The overhead cannot be avoided when one laser serves as both transmitter and LO. The echo that beats during the useful window [τ,Tc][\tau,T_c] was emitted during [0,Tc−τ][0,T_c-\tau], so the laser frequency must follow one straight line over the whole ramp [0,Tc][0,T_c].
    • The overhead is small for long useful windows (Tu≫τT_u\gg\tau) and grows without bound as Tu→0T_u\to0. At 300 m (τ=2.0\tau=2.0 µs, Eq. (109)) and 15 cm: Tu=7.5T_u=7.5 µs gives Btot=1GHz×(1+2/7.5)=1.27B_{\mathrm{tot}}=1\ {\mathrm{GHz}}\times(1+2/7.5)=1.27 GHz, and Tu=2.25T_u=2.25 µs gives 1GHz×(1+2/2.25)=1.891\ {\mathrm{GHz}}\times(1+2/2.25)=1.89 GHz.

  • Ramp time. TcT_c is not a free choice of the laser. It is Tu+τT_u+\tau, and TuT_u is set by how long the channel needs to collect its photons (item (g)). The laser then repeats the up–down triangle at a rate 1/(2Tc)1/(2T_c): 30–120 kHz in the cases of item (g).

  • Chirp rate follows: κ=Beff/Tu\kappa=B_{\mathrm{eff}}/T_u, e.g. 1GHz/7.5μs=1.3×10141\ {\mathrm{GHz}}/7.5\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=1.3\times10^{14} Hz/s, or 1GHz/1μs=10151\ {\mathrm{GHz}}/1\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=10^{15} Hz/s. It is a derived number, not a requirement in its own right. What the laser must do is cover BtotB_{\mathrm{tot}} within TcT_c, linearly, ramp after ramp.

  • Linearity: an absolute frequency tolerance set by range alone. Let δν(t)\delta\nu(t) be the laser frequency’s deviation from the ideal straight ramp. The beat is the LO frequency now minus the frequency of the echo emitted τ\tau earlier:

    fb(t)=ν(t)−ν(t−τ)≈κτ+τdδνdt,f_b(t)=\nu(t)-\nu(t-\tau)\approx\kappa\tau+\tau\,\frac{d\,\delta\nu}{dt},(115)

    which holds when δν\delta\nu changes little within τ\tau. The beat therefore wanders by τ\tau times the slope of the frequency error.

    • Take a smooth bow over the useful window, δν(t)=δνmax[1−(2t/Tu−1)2]\delta\nu(t)=\delta\nu_{\max}\,[1-(2t/T_u-1)^2] for 0≤t≤Tu0\le t\le T_u: zero at both ends and δνmax\delta\nu_{\max} at the centre. Its slope runs from +4δνmax/Tu+4\delta\nu_{\max}/T_u to −4δνmax/Tu-4\delta\nu_{\max}/T_u, so by Eq. (115) the beat sweeps over 8τδνmax/Tu8\tau\,\delta\nu_{\max}/T_u during the window.
    • The FFT resolves frequencies in bins 1/Tu1/T_u wide. The peak stays within one bin if 8τδνmax/Tu≤1/Tu8\tau\,\delta\nu_{\max}/T_u\le1/T_u, that is

    δνmax≲18τ=c16R.\delta\nu_{\max}\lesssim\frac{1}{8\tau}=\frac{c}{16R}.(116)

    • The tolerance depends on range only, not on the sweep bandwidth or the ramp time: 3×108/(16×300)=62.53\times10^{8}/(16\times300)=62.5 kHz at 300 m and 94 kHz at 200 m.
    • As a fractional peak-to-peak error in the chirp rate the same condition reads ε=8δνmax/Beff≤1/(τBeff)=ΔR/R\varepsilon=8\delta\nu_{\max}/B_{\mathrm{eff}}\le1/(\tau B_{\mathrm{eff}})=\Delta R/R, using Beffτ=R/ΔRB_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau=R/\Delta R (Eq. (113)). That is 5×10−45\times10^{-4} for 15 cm at 300 m and 1.7×10−41.7\times10^{-4} for 5 cm. It is the range-blur rule δR≈εR\delta R\approx\varepsilon R with the blur held inside one range bin: at 200 m, ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3} gives δR≈0.2\delta R\approx0.2 m, more than the 15 cm bin, and ε=10−4\varepsilon=10^{-4} gives 2 cm.
    • The tolerance applies to what remains after any correction. An auxiliary reference interferometer that measures the actual ramp, followed by resampling or digital correction of the beat, relaxes the laser requirement at the cost of one more optical and digital path per sensor.

  • Directly modulated DFB lasers (distributed-feedback laser diodes, chirped by modulating their drive current) tune through two competing effects: fast carrier tuning and slower thermal tuning. The two cross over at roughly 1–10 MHz of modulation frequency [U].

    • A linear ramp of a few µs has harmonic content up to tens of MHz, so pre-distortion (shaping the drive current so that the optical chirp comes out linear) or feedback must stay accurate across that crossover. It gets harder as TcT_c shrinks.
    • Waymo reports a pre-distorted DFB holding <100 kHz error over 1 GHz [P] (§C7a(f)), a fractional frequency error δν/Beff<10−4\delta\nu/B_{\mathrm{eff}}<10^{-4}. With the bow shape of Eq. (116) and δνmax=100\delta\nu_{\max}=100 kHz it would give ε=8×10−4\varepsilon=8\times10^{-4}, just outside the 94 kHz tolerance at 200 m. Read as a peak-to-peak bound (±50 kHz) it meets 200–250 m and is marginal at 300 m (62.5 kHz), so the margin depends on how the figure is defined and on the error’s shape [E].

  • Electro-optic chirping, in thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) or with single-sideband modulators, or an optical phase-locked loop (a feedback loop that locks the laser’s frequency sweep to a reference) reaches 101510^{15}–101610^{16} Hz/s linearly [U]. A TFLN laser has been chirped at 1.2×10161.2\times10^{16} Hz/s (Snigirev et al., §C7a(f)) [I]. The laser’s ability to chirp is therefore not the fundamental floor; it sets the cost of reaching short, linear chirps. Item (g) shows when that cost matters.

(e) Laser linewidth sets a range-dependent loss, not a cap on the chirp length.

  • Where the loss comes from. The LO and the echo are the same laser at two instants τ\tau apart. Their phase difference Δϕ(t)=ϕ(t)−ϕ(t−τ)\Delta\phi(t)=\phi(t)-\phi(t-\tau) therefore carries only the phase noise accumulated over τ\tau. Its variance is set by the laser’s frequency-noise spectrum:

    σΔϕ2≈∫1/Tu∞Sν(f)4sin⁡2(πfτ)f2df,\sigma^2_{\Delta\phi}\approx\int_{1/T_u}^{\infty}S_\nu(f)\,\frac{4\sin^2(\pi f\tau)}{f^2}\,df,(117)

    where Sν(f)S_\nu(f) is the one-sided power spectral density of the laser’s frequency fluctuations (Hz²/Hz) at Fourier frequency ff, and 4sin⁡2(πfτ)/f24\sin^2(\pi f\tau)/f^2 is the filter of the delay τ\tau.

    • Frequency noise slower than about 1/Tu1/T_u is left out: within one ramp it only shifts the beat’s phase, or its frequency by τdδν/dt\tau\,d\delta\nu/dt, which the FFT does not count as lost power [E].
    • For white frequency noise, Sν=Δν/πS_\nu=\Delta\nu/\pi, where Δν\Delta\nu is the Lorentzian (intrinsic) linewidth. With ∫0∞sin⁡2(af)/f2df=πa/2\int_0^\infty\sin^2(af)/f^2\,df=\pi a/2 and a=πτa=\pi\tau, the integral gives σΔϕ2=(Δν/π)×4×π2τ/2=2πΔντ\sigma^2_{\Delta\phi}=(\Delta\nu/\pi)\times4\times\pi^2\tau/2=2\pi\Delta\nu\,\tau (slightly less with the 1/Tu1/T_u lower limit).
    • So the specification that matters is the frequency-noise level at Fourier frequencies from about 1/Tu1/T_u (≈0.1 MHz) to a few 1/τ1/\tau (MHz), not a linewidth measured over milliseconds.

  • What it costs. With Δϕ\Delta\phi Gaussian, the beat splits into a sharp coherent tone that carries a fraction

    ηcoh≈e−σΔϕ2=e−2πΔντ\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}\approx e^{-\sigma^2_{\Delta\phi}}=e^{-2\pi\Delta\nu\,\tau}(118)

    of the beat power, and a pedestal that carries the rest (Richter et al., IEEE J. Quantum Electron. 22, 2070 (1986)) [I].

    • In the regime of automotive lidar, 2πΔντ≲12\pi\Delta\nu\tau\lesssim1, the pedestal spreads over roughly ±1/τ\pm1/\tau around the tone (±0.5 MHz at 300 m), not over 2Δν2\Delta\nu. That is about ±Tu/τ\pm T_u/\tau FFT bins, i.e. ±Tu/τ\pm T_u/\tau range bins, so it raises the floor near a strong return and can mask a weak target just behind it [E].

  • Why it does not cap the chirp. The coherent tone is a true spectral line: its FFT peak keeps growing as TuT_u lengthens, exactly as without phase noise. What linewidth removes is a fixed fraction of the signal, set by the range. It therefore enters the photon budget as a multiplier on the energy, Ept→E′=Ept/ηcohE_{\mathrm{pt}}\to E'=E_{\mathrm{pt}}/\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}, not as a limit on TuT_u. What does make long ramps harder is low-frequency noise (flicker noise, drift): as TuT_u grows, the lower limit 1/Tu1/T_u of Eq. (117) falls and lets more of that noise into σΔϕ2\sigma^2_{\Delta\phi}. Chirp nonlinearity (Eq. (116)) also makes long ramps harder. Both are specified separately from the linewidth.

  • Requirement. Allowing the coherent share to fall to no less than ηmin\eta_{\min} gives

    Δν≤ln⁡(1/ηmin)2πτ=cln⁡(1/ηmin)4πR.\Delta\nu\le\frac{\ln(1/\eta_{\min})}{2\pi\tau}=\frac{c\,\ln(1/\eta_{\min})}{4\pi R}.(119)

The table evaluates Eq. (119) for five allowed losses at 200, 250 and 300 m.

(119) with 2πτ=2π×2R/c2\pi\tau=2\pi\times2R/c, which is 8.38×10−68.38\times10^{-6} s at 200 m, 1.05×10−51.05\times10^{-5} s at 250 m and 1.26×10−51.26\times10^{-5} s at 300 m. Worked cell (3 dB at 300 m): ln⁡2/(1.26×10−5s)=0.693/(1.26×10−5s)=55\ln2/(1.26\times10^{-5}\ {\mathrm{s}})=0.693/(1.26\times10^{-5}\ {\mathrm{s}})=55 kHz. A loss of LL dB means ηmin=10−L/10\eta_{\min}=10^{-L/10}, so ln⁡(1/ηmin)=0.115\ln(1/\eta_{\min})=0.115, 0.230, 0.693, 1 and 2 for the five rows.

  • Lasers against the requirement at 300 m [E; linewidths as cited in §C7a(f)]. With 2πτ=1.26×10−52\pi\tau=1.26\times10^{-5} s:
    • 10 kHz: 2πΔντ=0.1262\pi\Delta\nu\tau=0.126, ηcoh=0.88\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}=0.88 (−0.5 dB), energy ×1.13;
    • 42 kHz, taken as a Lorentzian width (the SiN self-injection-locked laser’s linewidth over 1 ms; its measured frequency noise gives less than 0.01 dB, §C7a(f)): 0.528, ηcoh=0.59\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}=0.59 (−2.3 dB), energy ×1.7;
    • 100 kHz (within Waymo’s ≲60–120 kHz, §C7a(f); Pointcloud’s external DFB, §C10.4): 1.26, ηcoh=0.28\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}=0.28 (−5.5 dB), energy ×3.5;
    • 378 kHz, taken as a Lorentzian width (the TFLN E-DBR laser’s linewidth over 1 ms): 4.75, ηcoh=0.0087\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}=0.0087 (−21 dB), energy ×116. The laser itself does far better: its measured frequency noise, a 2.8 kHz white floor plus slower thermal noise, gives about 0.2–0.4 dB at 300 m through Eq. (117), with the noise data of §C7a(f) [E].
  • The energies of subsection 1 leave this loss out; at 200 m a 100 kHz laser more than doubles them (subsection 1(e)).
  • The coherence-length rule of thumb, Lc=c/(πΔν)≥2RL_c=c/(\pi\Delta\nu)\ge2R (§C7; Eq. (64) of §C3a, and §F6), where LcL_c is the coherence length (§C0 subsection 2; §C3a, Eq. (64)), is the condition 2πΔντ≤22\pi\Delta\nu\tau\le2. It keeps only e−2=14%e^{-2}=14\% of the beat in the coherent peak: a limit of detectability, not a design point.

(f) Scanning caps the chirp from above. The chirp must end before the beam sweeps across its own width (§C7): Tc≲θbθ̇,T_c\lesssim\frac{\theta_b}{\dot\theta},(120) where TcT_c is the chirp duration, θb\theta_b the angular width of one beam (rad) and θ̇\dot\theta the optical scan rate, the beam’s angular speed (rad/s).

  • For θb=0.05°=8.7×10−4\theta_b=0.05°=8.7\times10^{-4} rad and a 5 µs chirp, θ̇≲8.7×10−4/(5×10−6)=175\dot\theta\lesssim8.7\times10^{-4}/(5\times10^{-6})=175 rad/s ≈ 10410^4 °/s.
  • Target motion during a chirp is negligible: 50 m/s × 10 µs = 0.5 mm.
  • Eq. (120) caps each ramp. The up- and down-ramp of one point are paired to separate range from Doppler, and if both must see the same spot the condition becomes 2Tc≲θb/θ̇2T_c\lesssim\theta_b/\dot\theta, which halves the allowed scan rate (≈5×1035\times10^3 °/s for 0.05° and 5 µs chirps). Item (g) and subsection 4 use the per-ramp condition of Eq. (120), which lets the two ramps of a point fall on adjacent beam positions.

(g) Which floor sets the useful window: photons, ADC, chirp rate or tuning range. Items (a)–(f) combine into one rule. The useful window of each ramp must be long enough for four separate reasons, and the longest of the four wins:

Tu=max⁡{Tph,TADC,Tκ,TB},T_u=\max\{T_{\mathrm{ph}},\,T_{\mathrm{ADC}},\,T_\kappa,\,T_B\},(121)

subject to the scan limit Tu+τ≤θb/θ̇T_u+\tau\le\theta_b/\dot\theta (Eq. (120)). The dwell is then Tdwell=2(Tu+τ)T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=2(T_u+\tau). The four floors are:

  1. Photons, Tph=E′/(2Pch)T_{\mathrm{ph}}=E'/(2P_{\mathrm{ch}}). The two ramps together must collect the energy E′=Ept/ηcohE'=E_{\mathrm{pt}}/\eta_{\mathrm{coh}} (item (e)) at the channel’s CW optical power PchP_{\mathrm{ch}}; this is Eq. (111) with the coherent loss included.
  2. ADC, TADC=(R/ΔR)/(fs,max/2.5−fD)T_{\mathrm{ADC}}=(R/\Delta R)/(f_{s,\max}/2.5-f_D). The largest beat, κτ+fD=(R/ΔR)/Tu+fD\kappa\tau+f_D=(R/\Delta R)/T_u+f_D (Eq. (112), with Beffτ=R/ΔRB_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau=R/\Delta R), must fit a converter that samples at most at fs,maxf_{s,\max} under the 2.5× rule of item (c). Solving 2.5[(R/ΔR)/Tu+fD]≤fs,max2.5[(R/\Delta R)/T_u+f_D]\le f_{s,\max} for TuT_u gives the floor.
  3. Laser chirp rate, Tκ=Beff/κmaxT_\kappa=B_{\mathrm{eff}}/\kappa_{\max}. A laser that cannot chirp faster than κmax\kappa_{\max} needs at least this long to sweep BeffB_{\mathrm{eff}}.
  4. Laser tuning range, TB=τBeff/(Bmax−Beff)T_B=\tau B_{\mathrm{eff}}/(B_{\max}-B_{\mathrm{eff}}). Solving Beff(1+τ/Tu)≤BmaxB_{\mathrm{eff}}(1+\tau/T_u)\le B_{\max} (Eq. (114)) for TuT_u, where BmaxB_{\max} is the laser’s largest continuous, linear sweep at the required repetition rate. If Bmax≤BeffB_{\max}\le B_{\mathrm{eff}}, the resolution cannot be reached at all.

A better laser (a larger κmax\kappa_{\max} or BmaxB_{\max}) shortens the dwell only if TκT_\kappa or TBT_B is the largest floor. Otherwise it changes nothing.

It takes E′=0.45E'=0.45 µJ: the central 0.30 µJ at 200 m scaled in proportion to range for an aperture optimized at 300 m (subsection 1(f)), with a laser narrow enough to lose nothing to coherence (ηcoh≈1\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}\approx1).

  • TB=τBeff/(Bmax−Beff)T_B=\tau B_{\mathrm{eff}}/(B_{\max}-B_{\mathrm{eff}}): 2μs×1/(1.2−1)=102\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}\times1/(1.2-1)=10 µs; 2×1/0.5=42\times1/0.5=4 µs; 2×1/1=22\times1/1=2 µs; 2×1/4=0.52\times1/4=0.5 µs.

What the table shows [E]:

  • At ≤30 mW per channel, photons set the window: 7.5–14 µs. The laser then needs only 1.14–1.27 GHz of sweep in ramps of 9.5–16 µs, a chirp rate of 0.70.7–1.3×10141.3\times10^{14} Hz/s, with 0.14–0.27 GHz of headroom above BeffB_{\mathrm{eff}} (Eq. (114)). A faster or wider-tuning laser shortens nothing, and even a 1 GS/s converter does not bind.
  • The ADC binds next, not the laser. Photons stop setting the window once Tph<TADCT_{\mathrm{ph}}<T_{\mathrm{ADC}}, i.e. above Pch=E′/(2TADC)P_{\mathrm{ch}}=E'/(2T_{\mathrm{ADC}}). That is 0.45μJ/(2×6.45μs)=350.45\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/(2\times6.45\ \mu{\mathrm{s}})=35 mW with 1 GS/s converters (the class of indie Semiconductor’s Surya FMCW system-on-chip, §C7a(d)), 80 mW at 2 GS/s and 170 mW at 4 GS/s. Beyond that, more power per channel buys nothing unless the converters get faster too.
  • The laser binds only in photon-rich channels. At 100 mW per channel with converters of ≥2.5 GS/s (TADC=2,000/(9.1×108s−1)=2.2T_{\mathrm{ADC}}=2{,}000/(9.1\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}})=2.2 µs), the window falls to Tph=2.25T_{\mathrm{ph}}=2.25 µs. The laser must then sweep 1.89 GHz in 4.25 µs (4.4×10144.4\times10^{14} Hz/s). A DFB limited to 101410^{14} Hz/s, or to a 1.2 GHz sweep, would stretch the window back to 10 µs.
  • A fast but narrow sweep limits resolution instead. A laser with Bmax=0.5B_{\max}=0.5 GHz, like the 500 MHz excursion of the 12 PHz/s TFLN laser of §C7a(f), cannot reach 15 cm at all. With Tu=7.5T_u=7.5 µs at 300 m it gives Beff≤BmaxTu/(Tu+τ)=0.5×7.5/9.5=0.39B_{\mathrm{eff}}\le B_{\max}T_u/(T_u+\tau)=0.5\times7.5/9.5=0.39 GHz, i.e. ΔR≥3×108/(2×3.9×108)=0.38\Delta R\ge3\times10^{8}/(2\times3.9\times10^{8})=0.38 m.
  • Finer resolution is paid for in converters, not photons. Halving ΔR\Delta R doubles BeffB_{\mathrm{eff}}, BtotB_{\mathrm{tot}}, κ\kappa, the range beat and TADCT_{\mathrm{ADC}}, and doubles the range samples per point, 5R/ΔR5R/\Delta R (Eq. (113)). At 5 cm and 300 m, TADC=6,000/(3.1×108s−1)=19T_{\mathrm{ADC}}=6{,}000/(3.1\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}})=19 µs at 1 GS/s, so the converter, not photons, sets the window even at 16 mW. A surface that is deeper than ΔR\Delta R within the beam footprint (a road at grazing incidence) also spreads its echo over several range bins, so finer resolution can lower the peak signal.
  • Splitting a dwell into several shorter chirp pairs never helps. Each pair pays its own round trip, so kk pairs need Tdwell=E′/Pch+2kτT_{\mathrm{dwell}}=E'/P_{\mathrm{ch}}+2k\tau for the same energy. Short, fast chirps pay only when photons are plentiful or when the scan forces them.
  • So a faster or wider-tuning laser helps in three cases only:
    • photon-rich channels: ≳100 mW each at 300 m, or short range and bright targets, where TphT_{\mathrm{ph}} falls below the laser floors;
    • fast scanning, when θb/θ̇\theta_b/\dot\theta (Eq. (120)) forces the ramp below the photon window. The shorter window then also needs more power per channel, Pch≥E′/[2(θb/θ̇−τ)]P_{\mathrm{ch}}\ge E'/[2(\theta_b/\dot\theta-\tau)]. For a 0.05° beam at 10410^4 °/s (θb/θ̇=5\theta_b/\dot\theta=5 µs) at 300 m, that is 0.45μJ/(2×3μs)=750.45\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/(2\times3\ \mu{\mathrm{s}})=75 mW. At the 45,600°/s of a Falcon-class polygon (§C4d) the crossing time, 1.1 µs, is shorter than the 2 µs round trip, and no chirp fits;
    • finer range resolution, which needs a wider BeffB_{\mathrm{eff}}.
  • Linearity (Eq. (116)) and linewidth (Eq. (119)) always matter, because they blur every point or multiply every point’s energy.

Summary of the dwell.

  • At 200 m, with 16–30 mW per channel, the photon budget dominates: emitting it takes 5–19 µs per point, and the round trip adds a fixed 2.67 µs, for a dwell of 8–21 µs, i.e. 47–130 kpts/s per channel.
  • The round trip alone caps any channel at ≈375 kpts/s.
  • The useful window is the largest of four floors (Eq. (121)): photons, ADC rate, laser chirp rate and laser tuning range. At ≤30 mW per channel photons win, so a faster or wider-tuning laser does not raise the point rate; the ADC binds next (above ≈35 mW per channel with 1 GS/s converters at 300 m).
  • Scanning caps the ramp at θb/θ̇\theta_b/\dot\theta (Eq. (120)). Linewidth does not cap it but multiplies every point’s energy by 1/ηcoh1/\eta_{\mathrm{coh}} (Eq. (118)).
  • In practice, then, one coherent channel at 200 m delivers at most ≈375 kpts/s, and far fewer at realistic power, so a sensor that needs millions of points per second must run many channels in parallel (subsection 3).

3. The channel tax: channels, power and receivers

This subsection turns the dwell of subsection 2 into the number of parallel coherent channels a sensor needs, and into the power those channels draw. At 15 Mpts/s the answer is ≈190 channels, each with four receivers and drawing ≈385 mW of electrical power (receivers plus its share of the laser), against ≈20 mW per ToF channel. This matters because each coherent channel is four complete receivers fed by its own light, so the channel count drives both the power and the cost of an FMCW sensor.

Channels follow from average power. Each coherent channel measures one point per dwell, so a sensor that must deliver Ṅ\dot N points per second needs Nch=ṄTdwell=Ṅ(EptPch+2τ)=PoptPch+2τṄN_{\mathrm{ch}}=\dot N\,T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=\dot N\left(\frac{E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{P_{\mathrm{ch}}}+2\tau\right)=\frac{P_{\mathrm{opt}}}{P_{\mathrm{ch}}}+2\tau\dot N(122) simultaneous channels. Here TdwellT_{\mathrm{dwell}} is the dwell per point from Eq. (111), EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} the optical energy per point, PchP_{\mathrm{ch}} the CW optical power per channel, τ\tau the round-trip time (Eq. (109)) and Popt=EptṄP_{\mathrm{opt}}=E_{\mathrm{pt}}\dot N the sensor’s average optical power. Eq. (122) is Eq. (97) of §C7, rearranged.

  • The first term is the scene’s average optical power (subsection 1) divided by the power one channel can carry. The second is the round-trip occupancy.
  • Example: 15 Mpts/s at 0.30 µJ and 30 mW gives 4.5W/0.03W+2×1.33×10−6×15×106=150+40=1904.5\ {\mathrm{W}}/0.03\ {\mathrm{W}}+2\times1.33\times10^{-6}\times15\times10^{6}=150+40=190 channels. That equals 15×106×12.7×10−615\times10^{6}\times12.7\times10^{-6}.
  • The watts are fixed by the scene; the channel count is fixed by the channel. The scene needs only its average optical power, in any architecture. FMCW’s problem is that this power must be split into CW channels of ≤30 mW, each with its own LO-matched receiver.

The table applies Eq. (122) to four point rates at two dwells, both with the 2.67 µs of round trips at 200 m: the §C7a central dwell, 10 µs of integration (30 mW at 0.30 µJ), and a short one, 4 µs of integration.

2 Mpts/s (Aeries-class) 13 25
10 Mpts/s 67 127
15 Mpts/s (the parity point rate) 100 190
41 Mpts/s (RoboSense EM4, ToF) 273 519

How the table is computed [E]:

  • Nch=ṄTdwellN_{\mathrm{ch}}=\dot N\,T_{\mathrm{dwell}} (Eq. (122)), with Tdwell=Tint+2τT_{\mathrm{dwell}}=T_{\mathrm{int}}+2\tau (Eq. (111)); for example 41×106×6.67×10−6=27341\times10^{6}\times6.67\times10^{-6}=273 and 41×106×12.67×10−6=51941\times10^{6}\times12.67\times10^{-6}=519.
  • A 4 µs integration time is close to the lower practical end at 200 m. It means Tu=2T_u=2 µs per ramp and Tc=Tu+τ=3.33T_c=T_u+\tau=3.33 µs. The sampling rate is then fs≈1.9f_s\approx1.9 GS/s for a search to 200 m (subsection 2(c) table), or ≈2.7 GS/s for the 0–300 m search of the §C7a model (§C7a(d)), and each channel needs Pch=Ept/Tint=0.30μJ/4μs≈76P_{\mathrm{ch}}=E_{\mathrm{pt}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}=0.30\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/4\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}\approx76 mW (38 mW at 0.15 µJ).
  • “Aeries-class” refers to Aeva’s Aeries FMCW sensors. Aeva specifies 4 M raw points/s for Aeries II [P] (§C7a subsection 1), and its dataset paper reports ≈0.85 M delivered points/s [P] (Appendix 1), so 2 Mpts/s is a representative rate between the two [E]. The 41 Mpts/s row is RoboSense’s EM4, a ToF sensor (41.04 Mpts/s [P], §C3b), shown for scale.
  • In the §C7a design each channel carries four receivers, so the receiver count is four times these figures.

ToF also runs hundreds of receive channels. The difference is what each one costs.

  • ToF channel count. A SPAD macro-pixel is occupied for its listening time. In the §C6/§C7a model that is the 20.8 µs column time per point (≈10 shots), the time the scanned column of pixels spends on one direction. So 15 Mpts/s keeps 15×106×20.8×10−6=31215\times10^{6}\times20.8\times10^{-6}=312 macro-pixels listening at once, for example one 312-pixel column.
  • Power per ToF channel. At the §C7a central values (≈57 nJ of receive electronics and ≈0.36 µJ of laser electrical energy per ToF point):
    • receive: 15×106×57nJ=0.85515\times10^{6}\times57\ {\mathrm{nJ}}=0.855 W, i.e. 0.855W/312=2.70.855\ {\mathrm{W}}/312=2.7 mW per macro-pixel;
    • laser: 15×106×0.36μJ=5.415\times10^{6}\times0.36\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=5.4 W, i.e. ≈17 mW per macro-pixel.
    • Each macro-pixel is ≈30 µm of SPAD column plus a share of a time-to-digital converter (TDC, the timer that stamps each photon’s arrival) and of histogram memory (static random-access memory, SRAM): a few cents of silicon (§C7a(e)).
  • Power per FMCW channel. With 190 channels:
    • receive: 15×106×2.34μJ=35.115\times10^{6}\times2.34\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=35.1 W, i.e. ≈185 mW per channel, ≈46 mW for each of its four receivers (2.34 µJ is the §C7a receiver energy per point, ErxE_{\mathrm{rx}} below);
    • light: each channel transmits 30 mW continuously, round trips included, i.e. 0.030/0.15=2000.030/0.15=200 mW of electrical power at 15% wall-plug efficiency.
    • Each channel is four receivers, each an LO tap, a balanced photodiode pair, a TIA, a GS/s ADC and a pipelined FFT processor.
  • So the per-channel electrical power is ≈385 mW for FMCW (185 + 200 mW) against ≈20 mW for ToF (2.7 + 17 mW), ≈19× more. The FMCW channel is also far larger and costlier.

Optical and receiver power.

  • Optical power depends only on the energy per point, not on the dwell: Popt=EptṄ=4.5P_{\mathrm{opt}}=E_{\mathrm{pt}}\dot N=4.5 W at 0.30 µJ, or 2.25 W at 0.15 µJ. The power an ungated transmitter emits is larger by the dead-time factor Tdwell/TintT_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}, e.g. 190×30mW=5.7190\times30\ {\mathrm{mW}}=5.7 W in the §C7a central case.
  • Brighter channels do not save watts. They shorten the dwell and cut the channel count, which saves receiver chains, but they do not lower the watts per point. The round-trip waste even raises the transmitted energy (subsection 2 table).
  • Receiver power is Prx=ṄErxP_{\mathrm{rx}}=\dot N E_{\mathrm{rx}}, where ErxE_{\mathrm{rx}} is the receiver’s electrical energy per point.
    • The §C7a 2026 central value digitizes the 0–300 m search and keeps the analog front end on for the whole 12.67 µs dwell, round trips included (Eq. (104) with TdwellT_{\mathrm{dwell}} from Eq. (111)): Erx=4×(12,265×37.3pJ+10mW×12.67μs)=4×(0.457+0.127)≈2.34E_{\mathrm{rx}}=4\times(12{,}265\times37.3\ {\mathrm{pJ}}+10\ {\mathrm{mW}}\times12.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}})=4\times(0.457+0.127)\approx2.34 µJ per point, for four receivers. In each, the first term is the samples: 12,265 per point (the ≈12,300 of Eq. (113) at R=300R=300 m, taken in the two 5 µs useful windows) times ≈37.3 pJ each, the §C7a figure for an 8-ENOB ADC at 50 fJ per conversion step plus the FFT. The second term is the ≈10 mW per receiver that §C7a assumes for the TIA, bias and drivers, running for the whole dwell. A sensor that searched only to 200 m would digitize 8,900 samples per receiver (subsection 2(c)) and need 4×(8,900×37.3pJ+0.127μJ)=4×(0.332+0.127)≈1.844\times(8{,}900\times37.3\ {\mathrm{pJ}}+0.127\ \mu{\mathrm{J}})=4\times(0.332+0.127)\approx1.84 µJ.
    • At 15 Mpts/s that is 15×106×2.34×10−6=35.115\times10^{6}\times2.34\times10^{-6}=35.1 W of receiver electronics, about 4.3 times a whole 520-line ToF unit (35.1/8.2=4.335.1/8.2=4.3; ≈8.2 W at 12.5 Mpts/s in the §C7a model: 3W+12.5×106s−1×0.415μJ3\ {\mathrm{W}}+12.5\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times0.415\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}).

Published products (vendor figures [P], at different ranges). Electrical energy per point is the sensor’s electrical power PP divided by its point rate, Eel=P/ṄE_{\mathrm{el}}=P/\dot N [E, from the vendor figures]. The ranges and fields differ, so the comparison is of orders of magnitude, not like for like: the FMCW products spend 30–390 µJ per point against 2–9 µJ for the ToF products. Pointcloud works at 1,310 nm, where a photon carries 1,550/1,310=1.181{,}550/1{,}310=1.18 times the energy of a 1,550 nm photon, so in photons the gap is ≈3.7× [E].

3a. Sensor power at 10 Mpts/s and 300 m, and the 1,550 nm eye-safety ceiling

This subsection adds up a whole FMCW sensor’s electrical power from the dwell (subsection 2) and the channel count (Eq. (122)), and asks whether the 1,550 nm eye-safety allowance relaxes it.

(a) What limits a 10 Mpts/s sensor at 300 m: the light itself. Summing over all channels turns the dwell into power. With the ingredients of §C7a (laser wall-plug efficiency, per-receiver analog power, per-sample ADC and FFT energy, four receivers per channel), the sensor’s electrical power is

Pelec=ṄE′ηwp⏟usefullight+2τṄPchηwp⏟dead-timelight+NchNLPan⏟analog+ṄNLNADCes⏟ADCandFFT+Poh.P_{\mathrm{elec}}=\underbrace{\frac{\dot N E'}{\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}}}_{\mathrm{useful\ light}}+\underbrace{\frac{2\tau\,\dot N P_{\mathrm{ch}}}{\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}}}_{\mathrm{dead\text{-}time\ light}}+\underbrace{N_{\mathrm{ch}}N_LP_{\mathrm{an}}}_{\mathrm{analog}}+\underbrace{\dot N N_LN_{\mathrm{ADC}}e_s}_{\mathrm{ADC\ and\ FFT}}+P_{\mathrm{oh}} .(123)

Here Ṅ\dot N is the point rate; ηwp\eta_{\mathrm{wp}} the wall-plug efficiency of the CW laser with its amplifiers, the optical power out per electrical power in (≈0.15 in 2026, §C7a(b)); PanP_{\mathrm{an}} the analog power per receiver (TIA, bias and drivers, ≈10 mW); NL=4N_L=4 the receivers (looks) per channel; ese_s the energy per ADC sample including the FFT (≈37 pJ, Eq. (103)); PohP_{\mathrm{oh}} the fixed overhead (≈3 W); and Nch=Ṅ(E′/Pch+2τ)N_{\mathrm{ch}}=\dot N(E'/P_{\mathrm{ch}}+2\tau) the channel count (Eq. (122)). While photons set the window, Tu=E′/(2Pch)T_u=E'/(2P_{\mathrm{ch}}) and NADC=5R/ΔR+5fDTuN_{\mathrm{ADC}}=5R/\Delta R+5f_DT_u (Eq. (113)).

  • Only the channel terms depend on PchP_{\mathrm{ch}}. Substituting NchN_{\mathrm{ch}} and NADCN_{\mathrm{ADC}} splits PelecP_{\mathrm{elec}} into three parts:

Pelec=Ṅ[E′ηwp+5NLRΔRes+2τNLPan]+Poh⏟fixed+2τṄPchηwp⏟∝Pch+ṄE′NL(Pan+2.5fDes)Pch⏟∝1/Pch.\begin{aligned}P_{\mathrm{elec}}&=\underbrace{\dot N\left[\dfrac{E'}{\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}}+5N_L\,\dfrac{R}{\Delta R}\,e_s+2\tau N_LP_{\mathrm{an}}\right]+P_{\mathrm{oh}}}_{\text{fixed}}\\ &\quad+\underbrace{\dfrac{2\tau\,\dot NP_{\mathrm{ch}}}{\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}}}_{\propto\,P_{\mathrm{ch}}}+\underbrace{\dfrac{\dot NE'N_L\,(P_{\mathrm{an}}+2.5f_De_s)}{P_{\mathrm{ch}}}}_{\propto\,1/P_{\mathrm{ch}}} .\end{aligned}(124)

The first part is fixed by the point rate and the photons per point. The dead-time light grows with PchP_{\mathrm{ch}}, while the analog power and the Doppler share of the samples fall as 1/Pch1/P_{\mathrm{ch}}. Setting the derivative with respect to PchP_{\mathrm{ch}} to zero gives the optimum power per channel,

Pch*=ηwpE′NL(Pan+2.5fDes)2τ,P_{\mathrm{ch}}^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}\,E'\,N_L\,(P_{\mathrm{an}}+2.5f_De_s)}{2\tau}},(125)

  • Channels Nch=Ṅ(E′/Pch+2τ)N_{\mathrm{ch}}=\dot N(E'/P_{\mathrm{ch}}+2\tau): at 30 mW, 107×(15+4)μs=19010^{7}\times(15+4)\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=190.
