What moves the total [E], from Eq. (126):

  • Photons per point, E′E': it enters the dominant term linearly and the channel terms as a square root. Halving it (to the parity energy, subsection 5) saves 15+18.8×(1−1/2)=20.515+18.8\times(1-1/\sqrt2)=20.5 W.
  • Laser linewidth, through ηcoh\eta_{\mathrm{coh}}: at 300 m a laser of 10 kHz Lorentzian linewidth (E′=0.51E'=0.51 µJ, Eq. (118)) gives ≈73 W, one of 42 kHz (E′=0.76E'=0.76 µJ) ≈95 W and one of 100 kHz (E′=1.58E'=1.58 µJ) ≈160 W, against ≈68 W with no coherent loss. Worked (100 kHz): useful light 107×1.58μJ/0.15=10510^{7}\times1.58\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/0.15=105 W, channel terms 2×107×4×10−6×1.58×10−6×4×0.0183/0.15=35.22\times10^{7}\times\sqrt{4\times10^{-6}\times1.58\times10^{-6}\times4\times0.0183/0.15}=35.2 W, plus 14.8+1.6+314.8+1.6+3 W.
  • Wall-plug efficiency: doubling ηwp\eta_{\mathrm{wp}} to 0.30 saves the same ≈20 W as halving E′E', since both enter as E′/ηwpE'/\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}.
  • Channel electronics: halving PanP_{\mathrm{an}} and ese_s together saves ≈13.7 W: 7.4 W of range samples, 0.8 W of fixed analog power, and 18.8×(1−1/2)=5.518.8\times(1-1/\sqrt2)=5.5 W of channel terms.
  • A faster or wider-tuning laser: nothing, while photons set the window (subsection 2(g)).
  • More power per channel: nothing, or worse. The optimum is ≈30–40 mW; 100 mW per channel costs ≈11 W more, because 17 W more dead-time light outweighs the saving in receivers, unless the transmitter is gated (item (b)).

So is it just a matter of more optical power? Partly, in the sense that matters.

  • The useful light itself is large and expensive. FMCW needs ṄE′=107×0.45μJ=4.5\dot N E'=10^{7}\times0.45\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=4.5 W of useful CW light for 10 Mpts/s at 300 m even with a perfect laser, ≈5.9 W as emitted at the optimum, and each watt costs ≈7 W of electrical power at 15% wall-plug efficiency. That light and its heat are the largest problem; the four receivers per beam are the second (≈26 W).
  • More power per channel is not the lever. It only trades receivers against dead-time light, and past ≈35 mW it runs into the ADC floor (subsection 2(g)).
  • The levers are fewer photons per point, cheaper photons and cheaper receivers: a smaller E′E' (collection per look, coherence), a higher ηwp\eta_{\mathrm{wp}} and less power per receiver. Chirp speed, tuning range and beam steering are not the limits at these channel powers.
  • Against ToF, FMCW’s photon handicap shrinks with range (subsection 1(f)): at 10 Mpts/s and 300 m the same SPAD ToF model needs 0.16μJ×107s−1=1.60.16\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times10^{7}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=1.6 W of useful light with a fixed 25 mm lens, against FMCW’s 4.5 W, a ratio of 2.8 rather than the 4.2 of 200 m.

(b) What the 1,550 nm eye-safety allowance buys: range and brighter channels, not fewer watts per point. Class 1 eye safety caps how much light a lidar may emit, and at 1,550 nm the cap is far higher than at 905/940 nm (§C4c). The allowance does not lower the energy a point needs, which subsection 1 derives from collection and detection statistics; it raises the ceiling that energy must stay under.

  • The ceilings [E; §C4c, for the same 120° × 25° field scanned at 10 Hz and evaluated 100 mm from the sensor]:
    • 1,550 nm: the cornea limits the time-averaged irradiance to 1 kW m⁻², so a scanned CW beam may emit ≈9.1 W. What counts is the average power that reaches the eye over the exposure time. It is set by how often and how long the beam crosses the pupil, i.e. by the field and the scan, not by the chirp.
    • 905/940 nm: the retina limits each pulse to ≈80–230 nJ and the time average to ≈0.24–0.28 W for a small, collimated source. This is why SPAD ToF splits each point into ≈10 weak shots. Production units still emit watts, because a VCSEL (vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser) array behind a line-forming lens is an extended source, whose apparent size raises the limits by the IEC 60825-1 extended-source factor C6C_6 (§C4c; up to ≈67×).
  • How much of it the two designs use [E]:
    • A gated FMCW transmitter (dark during the last τ\tau of each ramp, item 2 below) emits ṄEpt\dot NE_{\mathrm{pt}}: 3.0 W at 10 Mpts/s and 200 m, a third of the 9.1 W, and 7.6 W at 25 Mpts/s, 83% of it. At 300 m it needs 4.5 and 11.3 W; the latter exceeds the allowance for this field. An ungated transmitter also emits during the round trips, 1.14–1.27 times as much at 16–30 mW per channel (Eq. (111)): 3.5–3.8 W at 10 Mpts/s and 8.6–9.6 W at 25 Mpts/s at 200 m, so at 25 Mpts/s it can exceed the allowance. The upper values, at 30 mW per channel, are the ungated §C7a central case [E].
    • SPAD ToF emits 0.72 W at 10 Mpts/s and 1.8 W at 25 Mpts/s, 7.2 nJ per shot and point. That is within the per-pulse limits but above the small-source average, so it relies on the extended-source relief that production units use.
    • At the 200 m operating point of this section neither design is limited by eye safety at 10 Mpts/s, so the per-watt comparison stands; at 25 Mpts/s the ungated §C7a central transmitter exceeds it (9.6 against 9.1 W).
  • What the headroom buys FMCW:
    1. Range at moderate point rates. At 10 Mpts/s the allowance covers 0.91 µJ per point, 3× the 200 m need. With an aperture matched to each range the energy grows only as RR (subsection 1(f)), so that is ≈600 m of eye-safe reach on a 10% target with a gated transmitter, or ≈470 m ungated at 30 mW per channel [E]. SPAD ToF, whose energy grows as R2R^2, would need 0.65 µJ per point at 600 m and 6.5 W at 10 Mpts/s, far beyond its small-source average limit of ≈0.24–0.28 W. At 25 Mpts/s the headroom shrinks to 0.36 µJ per point, i.e. ≈240 m gated or ≈190 m ungated.
    2. Brighter channels. The limit applies to the sensor’s total emission, not to each beam, so channels may carry 100 mW or more. Item (a) shows that this pays only if the transmitter is dark while its echo would be discarded: the dead-time light otherwise grows with PchP_{\mathrm{ch}}. A transmit SOA gated off during the last τ\tau of each ramp, whose echo would arrive in the next ramp’s discarded window, removes that term [E]. At 10 Mpts/s and 300 m the sensor then falls from ≈68 W to ≈59 W at the same 35 mW per channel, and to ≈53 W at 100 mW per channel (85 channels, 340 receivers, ≥2.5 GS/s converters). As Pch→∞P_{\mathrm{ch}}\to\infty it approaches ≈49 W: the useful light (30 W), the range samples (14.8 W), the analog power held during the round trips (1.6 W) and the overhead (3 W).
    3. One dwell per point. FMCW need not split a point into many weak shots, so it has no multi-shot accumulation to manage.
  • What it does not buy: fewer watts per point. At 300 m and 10 Mpts/s the gated floor of ≈49 W is still 49.4/11.7≈4.249.4/11.7\approx4.2 times the ≈11.7 W of the SPAD ToF sensor at the same range and rate. The allowance helps FMCW most where ToF meets its own eye-safety limits, at long range and high point rate, which is FMCW’s truck niche; it does not close the per-watt gap at 200 m.

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Use of the allowance: ṄEpt\dot NE_{\mathrm{pt}} with the §C7a energies, e.g. 2.5×107×0.303μJ=7.62.5\times10^{7}\times0.303\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=7.6 W; at 300 m, 2.5×107×0.45μJ=11.32.5\times10^{7}\times0.45\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=11.3 W against 9.1 W. An ungated transmitter emits more by the factor Tdwell/TintT_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}} of Eq. (111): 21.4/18.75=1.1421.4/18.75=1.14 at 16 mW and 12.7/10=1.2712.7/10=1.27 at 30 mW (subsection 2(b) table). At 10 Mpts/s that gives 3.03W×1.14=3.53.03\ {\mathrm{W}}\times1.14=3.5 W to 3.03W×1.27=3.83.03\ {\mathrm{W}}\times1.27=3.8 W, and at 25 Mpts/s 7.58W×1.14=8.67.58\ {\mathrm{W}}\times1.14=8.6 W to 7.58W×1.27=9.67.58\ {\mathrm{W}}\times1.27=9.6 W.
  • Reach: 9.1W/107s−1=0.919.1\ {\mathrm{W}}/10^{7}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=0.91 µJ per point, and 200m×0.91/0.30=600200\ {\mathrm{m}}\times0.91/0.30=600 m with Ept∝RE_{\mathrm{pt}}\propto R. Ungated at 30 mW, both terms of Eq. (111) grow as RR, so the factor 1.27 holds at every range and the reach is 600m/1.27≈470600\ {\mathrm{m}}/1.27\approx470 m. At 25 Mpts/s the allowance is 9.1W/(2.5×107s−1)=0.369.1\ {\mathrm{W}}/(2.5\times10^{7}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}})=0.36 µJ per point, so the reach is 200m×0.36/0.30≈240200\ {\mathrm{m}}\times0.36/0.30\approx240 m gated and 240m/1.27≈190240\ {\mathrm{m}}/1.27\approx190 m ungated. For ToF, 72nJ×(600/200)2=0.6572\ {\mathrm{nJ}}\times(600/200)^2=0.65 µJ, and 0.65μJ×107s−1=6.50.65\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times10^{7}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=6.5 W.
  • Gated transmitter: Eq. (123) without its dead-time term. At 100 mW, 107×0.45μJ/0.15=3010^{7}\times0.45\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/0.15=30 W of useful light, 85 channels × 4 receivers × 10 mW = 3.4 W of analog power, 107×4×(10,000+5×9×107×2.25×10−6)×37pJ=16.310^{7}\times4\times(10{,}000+5\times9\times10^{7}\times2.25\times10^{-6})\times37\ {\mathrm{pJ}}=16.3 W of ADC and FFT, and 3 W of overhead: 52.7 W. The floor is 30+14.8+1.6+3=49.430+14.8+1.6+3=49.4 W.
  • ToF at 300 m: the 3 W overhead, plus per point the laser’s electrical energy at the §C7a ToF wall-plug efficiency of 0.20, with the optical energy scaled by (300/200)2=2.25(300/200)^2=2.25, and ≈57 nJ of SPAD-SoC receive electronics (§C7a(c)): 3W+107s−1×(72nJ×2.25/0.20+57nJ)=3+8.7=11.73\ {\mathrm{W}}+10^{7}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times(72\ {\mathrm{nJ}}\times2.25/0.20+57\ {\mathrm{nJ}})=3+8.7=11.7 W.

4. What beam steering can and cannot do for FMCW

This subsection asks whether a better beam steerer (a mirror, polygon, MEMS device or optical phased array) could close FMCW’s gap. It cannot. Existing steerers already supply more beam positions per second than one coherent channel can use, faster scanning degrades coherent detection, and no steerer changes the photons each point needs. The subsection then tests one recent chip-scale scanner, the “photonic ski-jump”, against these criteria.

Steering is not the rate limiter.

  • What one channel can use. At 200 m, one channel can use at most 1/Tdwell1/T_{\mathrm{dwell}} beam positions per second, where TdwellT_{\mathrm{dwell}} is its dwell per point (Eq. (111)). That is 47–130 k at the realistic 16–30 mW, 176–240 k at 100 mW, and never more than 375 k (subsection 2).
  • What steerers supply. A steerer that sweeps a beam of angular width θb\theta_b at angular speed θ̇\dot\theta supplies θ̇/θb\dot\theta/\theta_b positions per second per beam:
    • a Falcon-class polygon (the rotating polygon mirror of Seyond’s Falcon lidar) at 45,600 °/s, the lower bound of §C4d [E], with a 0.05° beam gives 45,600/0.05=912,00045{,}600/0.05=912{,}000;
    • a resonant MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical system) mirror at 188,500 °/s peak gives 188,500/0.05=3.8×106188{,}500/0.05=3.8\times10^{6} (§C7 table);
    • the AT128’s mirror, by comparison, visits only 1,200×10=12,0001{,}200\times10=12{,}000 columns per second per channel (1,200 columns per frame at 10 frames per second).
  • So a faster steerer buys nothing in points per second per channel.

Faster scanning actively hurts above a threshold: about 10410^4 °/s for a 0.05° beam and 5 µs chirps, the scan rate at which one chirp lasts as long as the beam takes to cross its own width (Eq. (120), subsection 2(f)). Above this, two things happen (§C7):

  • scanner-induced Doppler spreads the beat over ≈Tcθ̇D/λ\approx T_c\,\dot\theta D/\lambda FFT bins, where DD is the aperture diameter and λ\lambda the wavelength;
  • receive walk-off costs signal: the receive mode has moved on by the time the echo returns.

Coherent designs therefore favour slow mechanical axes or step-and-stare (pointing the beam, holding it still for the measurement, then jumping to the next direction).

No steerer raises photons per point. The coherent collecting area is set by the beam footprint at the target (subsection 1(b)):

  • at most ≈65 mm² per look for any collimated beam at 200 m (Eq. (43)), ≈260 mm² for the four looks of the §C7a design;
  • 1.3 mm² if the beam is widened to fill a 0.05° cell. Equivalently, one mode’s étendue λ2\lambda^2 divided by the cell’s solid angle Ωcell=θcell2\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}=\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}^2, where θcell=8.7×10−4\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}=8.7\times10^{-4} rad is the cell’s angular pitch, gives λ2/Ωcell=(1.55×10−6)2/(8.7×10−4)2=3.2\lambda^2/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}=(1.55\times10^{-6})^2/(8.7\times10^{-4})^2=3.2 mm² before the mode and polarization factors.

A steerer changes where the footprint goes, not how large it must be. A larger steered aperture only narrows each mode’s angular acceptance, so the field then needs more samples or more channels. Only more modes per sample, i.e. more receivers, raises the collection per cell, and that returns to the channel tax.

What a steerer can buy (secondary, but real).

  1. Random access and foveation. Foveation, named after the eye’s sharp central fovea, means concentrating samples where they matter. FMCW can spend its scarce samples on tracked objects. Worked example [E]:
    • A 120° × 25° field is 3,000 deg². Put 80% of an Aeries-class 2 Mpts/s on the 5% of it (150 deg²) that holds tracked objects. The density there is 1.6×106/150=10,7001.6\times10^{6}/150=10{,}700 pts/deg²/s, about 2× a uniform 15 Mpts/s ToF (15×106/3,000=5,00015\times10^{6}/3{,}000=5{,}000), with velocity on every point.
    • The remaining 95% of the field (2,850 deg²) then gets 0.4×106/2,850=1400.4\times10^{6}/2{,}850=140 pts/deg²/s, 5,000/140≈36×5{,}000/140\approx36\times sparser than ToF. That is where an unexpected small obstacle must be found (§C10.6).
    • Foveation therefore helps tracking, not first detection.
  2. Step-and-stare without a moving mirror. This removes scanner Doppler and walk-off, which allows longer chirps. The trade is more photons per point for fewer points per second.
  3. Solid-state packaging and reliability. This matters less than it once seemed, because motor-driven one-axis mirrors have passed automotive qualification and shipped in millions (§C4d).

Case study: the “photonic ski-jump” [P: M. Saha, Y. H. Wen, A. S. Greenspon, M. Zimmermann et al. (MITRE, MIT, Sandia and others), “Nanophotonic waveguide chip-to-world beam scanning”, Nature 651, 356–362 (12 Mar 2026), open access, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-10038-6]. The paper is a useful test case because it claims a large gain in scanning speed per chip area, exactly the kind of steering advance that might be expected to help FMCW.

  • What it is: a 400 × 300 nm SiN (silicon nitride) waveguide on a ≈2 µm-thick AlN (aluminium nitride) piezoelectric cantilever, a tiny beam that bends when a voltage is applied. The cantilever curls ≈90° out of the chip plane, within <0.1 mm², so light leaves from its tip. It is made in a 200 mm CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) foundry.
    • It emits a mode ≈0.5–0.66 µm across (1/e² diameter; divergence half-angles 41° × 53°) and scans it resonantly at 1 kHz to >100 kHz.
    • Its mechanical quality factor (Q, 2π2\pi times the stored energy divided by the energy lost per oscillation cycle; high Q gives large motion for a small drive) is Q ≈ 10,000 in high vacuum against ≈5 at atmospheric pressure.
    • It is driven at 1–10 Vpp (volts peak to peak) in vacuum and holds a DC position with ≈10 nW.
  • Its figure of merit: 68.6 M spots s⁻¹ mm⁻², “>50-fold” that of state-of-the-art MEMS mirrors, “sufficient for one million pixels at 100 Hz from an approximately 1.5 mm diameter footprint”. (Check: 68.6×106×π(0.75mm)2=1.2×10868.6\times10^{6}\times\pi(0.75\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2=1.2\times10^{8} spots/s against 106×100=10810^{6}\times100=10^{8} needed.)
  • Demonstrations:
    • full-colour Lissajous image projection at 7–36 Hz (a Lissajous pattern is the path traced by two sinusoidal motions at different frequencies);
    • addressing of silicon-vacancy qubits (optically controlled quantum bits);
    • a 64-device array with <2% curvature spread;
    • a projected >1 gigaspot at kHz rates from <5 cm, given a further 10× in figure of merit.
  • Limitations the authors state: vacuum packaging, no true random access, a curved scan trajectory, and possible nonlinearity or thermal loading at higher optical power.
  • Tested against lidar needs [E]:
    • Dwell per spot. Consider a resonant raster at scan frequency ff with NlineN_{\mathrm{line}} resolvable spots per line and two lines per period (one each way). The time on each spot is tspot=1/(2fNline)t_{\mathrm{spot}}=1/(2fN_{\mathrm{line}}). A chirp of duration Tc=5T_c=5 µs per spot therefore allows at most Nline,max=1/(2fTc)N_{\mathrm{line,max}}=1/(2fT_c) spots per line.
      • At the lowest ≈1.3 kHz mode: 1/(2×1,300×5×10−6)=771/(2\times1{,}300\times5\times10^{-6})=77 spots per line.
      • At the ≈4.9 kHz lateral mode: 1/(2×4,900×5×10−6)=201/(2\times4{,}900\times5\times10^{-6})=20.
      • A 0.05°-class lidar needs ≈2,400 columns over 120°.
      • Off resonance the motion is small (≈29 µm of DC tip travel for ±50 V). Slowing the device to FMCW dwell times therefore sacrifices most of its range of motion.
    • Monostatic receive. A monostatic design receives through the same aperture it transmits from. In a focal-plane scanner, the echo images back onto the tip position at the moment of emission. Meanwhile the tip has moved Δx=vτ\Delta x=v\tau, where τ\tau is the round-trip time and v=2πfatipv=2\pi f\,a_{\mathrm{tip}} the tip’s peak speed for a sinusoidal oscillation of amplitude atipa_{\mathrm{tip}} at frequency ff.
      • With atip≈50a_{\mathrm{tip}}\approx50 µm and f≈5f\approx5 kHz: v=2π×5,000×50×10−6=1.6v=2\pi\times5{,}000\times50\times10^{-6}=1.6 m/s.
      • The fraction of the echo’s power that couples back into the tip’s mode is, for two identical Gaussian modes offset by Δx\Delta x, ηcpl=e−(Δx/wtip)2\eta_{\mathrm{cpl}}=e^{-(\Delta x/w_{\mathrm{tip}})^2}. Here wtip≈0.3w_{\mathrm{tip}}\approx0.3 µm is the 1/e² radius of the tip’s emitted mode.
      • At 20 m (τ=133\tau=133 ns): Δx=0.21\Delta x=0.21 µm and ηcpl=e−0.49\eta_{\mathrm{cpl}}=e^{-0.49}, i.e. −2.1 dB.
      • At 50 m: Δx=0.52\Delta x=0.52 µm and ηcpl=e−3.0\eta_{\mathrm{cpl}}=e^{-3.0}, i.e. −13 dB.
      • At 200 m: Δx=2.1\Delta x=2.1 µm and ηcpl=e−49\eta_{\mathrm{cpl}}=e^{-49}, i.e. nothing.
      • It therefore needs a separate or lag-offset receive path (compare Aeva’s lag-angle receive waveguides, §C3) or a much slower scan.
    • Wavelength and power. It is designed at 737 nm and shown broadband over 450–750 nm. Lidar-level CW power (15–30 mW or more per channel at 1,310/1,550 nm) was not tested; it is plausible on SiN [U] but undemonstrated.
    • Environment. Its Q needs high vacuum, and a PID loop (a proportional-integral-derivative feedback controller) tracks the resonance as it drifts. Its modes (1.3–7 kHz) sit near the automotive vibration band, which ISO 16750-3 (the automotive standard for mechanical loads) extends to ≈2 kHz (§C4d). Die-level vacuum packaging, −40 to +105 °C drift and vibration coupling are open questions.
    • Parallel beams. Arrays are natural: 64 were built, and >1,000 under one 12 mm lens are projected. Each beam, though, still needs its own coherent receiver chain and optical power. The device relocates the channel tax rather than removing it.
  • Assessment: a chip-to-free-space scanner, strongest for visible displays and qubit control, as the paper demonstrates. For automotive FMCW it is [R], and it attacks neither of FMCW’s binding costs: the photons per point and the cost per channel.
  • The same test applies to any steerer, including OPAs, LC (liquid-crystal) metasurfaces and switched FPAs (focal-plane arrays that select one of many on-chip emitters behind a lens). A steerer helps FMCW only where it enables step-and-stare, random access or cheap parallel beams, and parallel beams help only if the receiver chain per beam becomes cheap.

5. The parity arithmetic: all three conditions must land together

This subsection asks what FMCW must improve, and by how much, to match ToF’s point rate per watt. Three improvements must land together: a cheap, low-power multichannel coherent receiver, more efficient CW lasers and amplifiers, and a lower optical energy per point. With all three, a 15 Mpts/s sensor whose transmitter stays on through the round trips, as in the §C7a model, draws ≈14 W with 15 mW channels, just inside the 15 W target (below); with 30 mW channels it draws 16 W unless the transmitter is gated, which brings it to 12 W. Without the efficient laser, or without the lower energy per point, it stays near 23.5 W; without the low-power receiver it stays near 48 W. A receiver at 0.30 µJ per point, 8× better than today’s but 3× short of the goal, gives 17 W. Even at parity FMCW spends 1.8× the electrical energy per point of the 2026 SPAD ToF reference, which needs only 9.2 W at 15 Mpts/s.

The target. Parity, in this report, means ≥15 Mpts/s in ≤15 W at 200 m and 10% (§C7a subsection 5 summarizes the conditions derived here). The 2026 SPAD ToF reference of §C7a, at 0.415 µJ of electrical energy per point, meets it with room to spare: 3W+15×106s−1×0.415μJ=9.23\ {\mathrm{W}}+15\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times0.415\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}=9.2 W. Sensor power is overhead plus point rate times electrical energy per point: P=Poh+Ṅ(EptηwpTdwellTint+Erx),P=P_{\mathrm{oh}}+\dot N\left(\frac{E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}}\,\frac{T_{\mathrm{dwell}}}{T_{\mathrm{int}}}+E_{\mathrm{rx}}\right),(127) where PP is the sensor’s electrical power and PohP_{\mathrm{oh}} the fixed overhead that does not scale with point rate. Ṅ\dot N is the point rate, EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} the optical energy per point and ηwp\eta_{\mathrm{wp}} the laser and amplifier wall-plug efficiency (light out per electrical power in). Tdwell/Tint=1+2τPch/EptT_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\tau P_{\mathrm{ch}}/E_{\mathrm{pt}} (Eq. (111)) is the factor by which an ungated CW transmitter emits more than the useful energy: 12.67/10=1.2712.67/10=1.27 at the §C7a dwell, and 1 for a transmitter switched off during the last τ\tau of each ramp. The first term in the bracket is therefore the laser’s electrical energy per point. ErxE_{\mathrm{rx}} is the receiver’s electrical energy per point (samples, TIA and bias over the whole dwell; subsection 3). With Poh=3P_{\mathrm{oh}}=3 W, parity needs EptηwpTdwellTint+Erx≤15−3W15×106s−1=0.8μJ.\frac{E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}}\,\frac{T_{\mathrm{dwell}}}{T_{\mathrm{int}}}+E_{\mathrm{rx}}\le\frac{15-3\ {\mathrm{W}}}{15\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}}=0.8\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}.(128) In words: after the overhead, each point may cost at most 0.8 µJ of electricity, for its light and its receiver together, i.e. 0.8/0.415=1.90.8/0.415=1.9 times what the ToF reference spends per point. Eq. (127) is Eq. (123) of subsection 3a(a) with its useful and dead-time light combined in the factor Tdwell/TintT_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}, the per-channel receiver terms folded into ErxE_{\mathrm{rx}} (Eq. (104)) and no coherent loss (E′=EptE'=E_{\mathrm{pt}}), which holds to within 1 dB for a laser of ≲27 kHz at 200 m (≲55 kHz keeps the loss within 3 dB at 300 m; Eq. (119) and its table). Subsection 3a(a) evaluated Eq. (123) at 10 Mpts/s and 300 m, whereas this subsection evaluates Eq. (127) at 15 Mpts/s and 200 m, so the ≈68 W there and the ≈76.5 W below are different cases.

Reaching Ept≈0.15E_{\mathrm{pt}}\approx0.15 µJ means improving the terms of Eq. (101) without changing the geometry. The photoelectrons needed are fixed by detection statistics (120 for four looks, §C0 subsection 10.3), so the efficiency must carry most of it: raising η\eta from 0.25 to 0.40 gives 0.30×0.25/0.40=0.190.30\times0.25/0.40=0.19 µJ, the §C7a 2032 case, and η=0.50\eta=0.50 gives 0.15 µJ. The alternative is more looks per sample, each collecting its own AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}: eight looks ideally need ≈82 photoelectrons, ≈112 with the same margin, spread over twice the area, which gives 0.30×(112/120)×(4/8)=0.140.30\times(112/120)\times(4/8)=0.14 µJ at the price of eight receivers per beam. A better detector than the full FFT search helps less: a joint search over both ramps saves 12% (§C0 subsection 10.3).

The efficiency is also the least certain input. The FMCW value, 0.25, is a design value about 1.5× above the best coherent chain measured so far (subsection 1(c)). With the measured efficiencies, 0.112–0.168 for Waymo’s discrete fibre chain and 0.057 for Pointcloud’s integrated array, the optical energy per point grows by 0.25/η0.25/\eta, and the 2026 central case at 15 Mpts/s rises from ≈76.5 W to ≈95–124 W, or to ≈207 W. For example, at η=0.112\eta=0.112 the optical energy is 0.303μJ×0.25/0.112=0.680.303\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times0.25/0.112=0.68 µJ, or 0.86 µJ as emitted (×1.267\times1.267), and Eq. (127) gives 3+15×(0.86/0.15+2.34)=1243+15\times(0.86/0.15+2.34)=124 W. Parity’s η≈0.5\eta\approx0.5 is therefore 3–9× above the chains measured so far.

How the table is computed [E], row by row from Eq. (127) with Poh=3P_{\mathrm{oh}}=3 W and Ṅ=15×106\dot N=15\times10^{6} s⁻¹:

  • Worked row (“all three”): at 15 mW per channel the integration takes Tint=0.15μJ/0.015W=10T_{\mathrm{int}}=0.15\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/0.015\ {\mathrm{W}}=10 µs and the dwell Tdwell=10+2.67=12.67T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=10+2.67=12.67 µs, so the channel emits 0.150×12.67/10=0.1900.150\times12.67/10=0.190 µJ per point. Against §C7a’s 2032 ToF (0.280 µJ per point) its ratio is 1.738/0.280=6.21.738/0.280=6.2 rather than 4.2.

  • Ratio column: each total divided by the ToF reference’s 0.415 µJ, e.g. 0.733/0.415=1.80.733/0.415=1.8.

Brighter channels need a gated transmitter [E]. More power per channel at the same 0.15 µJ shortens the dwell and cuts the channel count, but an ungated transmitter then wastes a larger share of its light (Eq. (111)):

  • At 30 mW per channel: Tint=0.15μJ/0.03W=5T_{\mathrm{int}}=0.15\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/0.03\ {\mathrm{W}}=5 µs and Tdwell=7.67T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=7.67 µs, so 15 Mpts/s needs only 15×106×7.67×10−6=11515\times10^{6}\times7.67\times10^{-6}=115 channels.
    • Ungated, each point emits 0.15×7.67/5=0.2300.15\times7.67/5=0.230 µJ, and the total is 0.230/0.30+0.10=0.8670.230/0.30+0.10=0.867 µJ, i.e. 3+15×0.867=16.03+15\times0.867=16.0 W, above the target.
    • Switched off during the last τ\tau of each ramp (subsection 3a(b), item 2), the transmitter emits only EptE_{\mathrm{pt}}: 0.15/0.30+0.10=0.600.15/0.30+0.10=0.60 µJ, i.e. 3+15×0.60=12.03+15\times0.60=12.0 W, at any power per channel.
  • The ungated ceiling: Eq. (128) with ηwp=0.30\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}=0.30 and Erx=0.10E_{\mathrm{rx}}=0.10 µJ allows Tdwell/Tint≤(0.8−0.10)×0.30/0.15=1.40T_{\mathrm{dwell}}/T_{\mathrm{int}}\le(0.8-0.10)\times0.30/0.15=1.40, i.e. 2τPch/Ept≤0.402\tau P_{\mathrm{ch}}/E_{\mathrm{pt}}\le0.40, so Pch≤0.40×0.15μJ/2.67μs=22.5P_{\mathrm{ch}}\le0.40\times0.15\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/2.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=22.5 mW. Then Tint=0.15μJ/22.5mW=6.67T_{\mathrm{int}}=0.15\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/22.5\ {\mathrm{mW}}=6.67 µs, and 15 Mpts/s needs 15×106×(6.67+2.67)×10−6=14015\times10^{6}\times(6.67+2.67)\times10^{-6}=140 channels.
  • Parity therefore also forces a choice between many dim channels (140–190 at 15–22.5 mW, ungated) and fewer bright ones behind a transmitter switched off during the last τ\tau of each ramp (115 at 30 mW).

The three conditions reach parity, but narrowly [E].

  • Ungated, as in the §C7a model, the “all three” case draws 14.0 W at 15 Mpts/s, 1 W inside the target, and only while each channel carries ≤22.5 mW.
  • The receiver condition is the tightest: with the other two met, Eq. (128) leaves 0.8−0.633=0.170.8-0.633=0.17 µJ per point for the receiver, 14× below today’s 2.34 µJ.
  • Parity in this sense is not equality with ToF. The parity case still spends 0.733/0.415=1.80.733/0.415=1.8 times the electrical energy per point of the 2026 SPAD ToF reference, which delivers the same 15 Mpts/s in 9.2 W. Matching that reference point for point would need, even with a gated transmitter, ηwp=0.30\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}=0.30 and a 0.10 µJ receiver, an optical energy of (0.415−0.10)×0.30=0.095(0.415-0.10)\times0.30=0.095 µJ per point. By Eq. (101) that is a receive efficiency near 0.25×0.303/0.095=0.800.25\times0.303/0.095=0.80, far above the 0.5 that the parity case already assumes.

The per-channel budget at parity follows from these numbers:

  • 140–190 channels (560–760 receivers) at ≈15–22.5 mW of optical power each with an ungated transmitter, or 115 channels (460 receivers) at 30 mW with a gated one;
  • ≈8–13 mW of receive power per channel, i.e. ≈2–3 mW for each of its four receivers, including ≈1 GS/s ADCs and FFT. This comes from dividing the receiver power ErxṄ=0.10μJ×15×106s−1=1.5E_{\mathrm{rx}}\dot N=0.10\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times15\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=1.5 W by the channel count NchN_{\mathrm{ch}}: 7.9, 10.7 or 13.0 mW for 190, 140 or 115 channels, and 2.0, 2.7 or 3.3 mW per receiver. Today’s §C7a receiver draws ≈46 mW (2.337μJ/12.67μs/42.337\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/12.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}/4), 14–23× more.
  • The only merchant FMCW SoC today (a system-on-chip sold to any customer), indie Semiconductor’s Surya, offers four 1 GS/s ADC channels per chip, with power not published [P] (§C7a(d)).

6. What would have to change, ranked

This subsection ranks the changes that would move FMCW toward parity, the most important first, with the deployability status of each in brackets ([D] shipping, [NT] a plausible automotive path within about five years, [R] research-stage); the sixth, a hypothetical, carries the evidence tag [U]. Only the first three change the physics or the cost of a point; the fourth is about demand, the fifth is a different architecture, and the sixth is a hypothetical weakness in ToF.

  1. A coherent SPAD-SoC [NT/R].
    • What it is: a stacked or monolithic electronic-photonic IC (photonics and electronics on one chip, or on separate chips bonded on top of each other) with 115–190 channels of four LO-matched receivers each, 460–760 receivers in all (140–190 channels with an ungated transmitter, 115 with a gated one; subsection 5). Each receiver runs at ≈2–3 mW including ADC and FFT (subsection 5), for a few cents of silicon.
    • This is the single enabler that attacks the channel tax. Pointcloud’s own paper names the missing piece: an ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) to replace its RFSoC readout, a general-purpose radio-frequency system-on-chip [P].
    • Signpost: a published chip with ≥256 receivers (64 channels) at ≤5 mW each, a third to a half of the parity count (64/190=0.3464/190=0.34 to 64/115=0.5664/115=0.56) at about twice the parity power per receiver (5 mW against 2–3 mW). §C10.7’s signpost, ≥256 channels within ≈10 W (≈10 mW per receiver if each channel has four: 10W/1,02410\ {\mathrm{W}}/1{,}024), asks for more channels at a higher power per receiver.
  2. Efficient CW light at temperature [NT].
    • A wall-plug efficiency ηwp≥30%\eta_{\mathrm{wp}}\ge30\% (light out per electrical power in) at 105 °C for SOAs or lasers delivering ≈2.3–2.9 W of light across 115–190 channels on SiN or III-V: at the parity point, EptṄ=0.15μJ×15×106s−1=2.25E_{\mathrm{pt}}\dot N=0.15\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times15\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=2.25 W of useful light, and 190×15mW=2.85190\times15\ {\mathrm{mW}}=2.85 W as emitted by an ungated transmitter.
    • A comb or multi-wavelength source (one laser emitting many evenly spaced wavelengths) can feed many channels from one laser, but it does not reduce the receiver count.
  3. More modes per sample [R].
    • Diversity or multimode coherent reception beyond the four looks already assumed. Each further look collects its own AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}, so eight looks would roughly halve the optical energy per point (subsection 5), and many modes per sample would restore coverage, which subsection 1(b) caps at ≈2% of a 0.05° cell per collimated sample (§C10.3b, Result 2).
    • Each extra mode needs its own coherent receiver, so this costs receivers and presupposes item 1.
  4. A buyer for “fewer, richer points” [D] (trucks only).
    • Driverless trucks and highway L3, where 250–400 m detection and instantaneous velocity pay (§F6).
    • A safety-case credit for instantaneous Doppler would widen this market. (A safety case is the documented argument that a vehicle is acceptably safe; a credit would mean that argument counts directly measured velocity in the sensor’s favour.)
  5. Energy storage instead of CW [R].
    • The dwell–power link is specific to CW light. A pulsed coherent (pulse-compression) design fires chirped pulses from an energy-storing amplifier, so one channel delivers its energy in a short time. Pulsed coherent Doppler wind lidars do this with erbium-doped fibre amplifiers, whose excited-state lifetime is milliseconds [U].
    • This cuts the occupancy term Ept/PchE_{\mathrm{pt}}/P_{\mathrm{ch}} of Eq. (122), and so the channel count. It does not cut the photons per point, which subsection 1 shows are set by single-mode collection.
    • SOAs cannot store energy (their carrier lifetime is nanoseconds), and fibre amplifiers are bulky and costly. For automotive this is research-stage.
  6. A ToF failure mode (hypothetical, none documented) [U].
    • It would matter if mutual interference were documented at high penetration (§C9), i.e. when many lidar-equipped cars share the road, or if 905/940 nm ToF hit eye-safety and sunlight limits beyond 300 m.
    • Neither is documented today; ToF coding and randomization cope with interference.

What does not change the verdict:

  • faster or larger steering (subsection 4);
  • more OPA elements (8,192 are already demonstrated, §C7 and §C10.2b);
  • ultrafast chirps, which are bounded by detector and ADC bandwidth (subsection 2(c); §C7a(f));
  • the 1,550 nm eye-safety allowance on its own, since heat, not eye safety, is the ceiling (§C7a(b)).

7. Probabilities (my judgement; the §C7a table stands)

The table puts judgement-based probabilities on the outcomes discussed above. They complement the §C7a probability table and do not replace it. The low figures follow from subsections 4 and 5: steering alone cannot reach parity, and parity needs three advances at once.

The same class of chip in a qualified automotive product 2032 ≈8–12%

Signposts to watch:

  • channel count and per-channel power in the next coherent FPA (focal-plane array) or column chip, from Pointcloud, Voyant, Aeva or imec;
  • a published SOA wall-plug efficiency at 105 °C;
  • Aeva–Daimler 2027 volumes and the count of Aurora’s FirstLight (its in-house FMCW lidar) per truck;

C8. Chip-size and reticle limits across architectures

This section asks whether the size of a single chip limits any lidar architecture. A lithography scanner prints a chip one exposure field (the “reticle” field) at a time. A chip larger than that field must be stitched from several exposures or split across several dies, and both cost yield and money. The answer is that only architectures with one on-chip cell per look direction hit this limit at automotive resolution: staring arrays of single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) and switched focal-plane arrays for frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) lidar. For the others, photons, memory, pins or heat bind first. This is one reason scanned designs dominate today.

What sets the silicon area decides whether the reticle binds:

  • “One cell per look direction” architectures (staring 2D arrays, switched focal-plane arrays) grow with (FOV/θcell)2(\text{FOV}/\theta_{\mathrm{cell}})^2, so they meet the reticle first. Here FOV is the field of view and θcell\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} the angular pitch of one cell, so FOV/θcell\text{FOV}/\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} is the number of cells along one axis.
  • Scanned or phased architectures reuse a small array across many directions, so other limits usually bind before the reticle.

§C6(a) and §C7 treat SPAD columns and FMCW transmitters in detail. A single lithography exposure field is about 26×33 mm (858 mm²) [P, ASML], but it is an economic and engineering threshold, not a physical wall. Stitching, exposing adjacent fields so that their patterns join into one larger chip, can exceed it. CMOS (complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor, the standard silicon chip process) image sensors of 28.3×38.8 mm on 300 mm wafers, and a 203×179 mm, 1.8-gigapixel wafer-scale sensor, have been demonstrated [P, Zhu et al., ELEX 2016]. Wafer-scale stitched sensors are being qualified for particle physics (the ITS3 inner-tracker upgrade of CERN’s ALICE experiment, with its MOSS monolithic stitched-sensor prototype) [I].

C8.1 The comparison

At automotive resolution, only staring SPAD arrays and switched FMCW focal-plane arrays are clearly reticle-bound. The table compares what sets die area in each architecture and what usually binds first.

Abbreviations in the table:

  • a SiPM is a silicon photomultiplier;
  • a VCSEL is a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser, and an EEL an edge-emitting laser;
  • an OPA is an optical phased array, which steers a beam by setting the phase of many emitters;
  • a switched focal-plane array (FPA) selects one of many on-chip emitters behind a lens, one per direction;
  • TFLN is thin-film lithium niobate, an electro-optic material;
  • III-V, InP and GaAs are compound semiconductors, and GaN is used for fast laser drivers;
  • “e-scan” is electronic scanning, which addresses parts of the array in turn instead of moving a mirror;
  • LO is the local oscillator, the reference light each coherent pixel mixes with its echo;
  • a SPAD-SoC is a SPAD array stacked on its own timing and histogram logic as one system-on-chip (§C5);
  • an SOA is a semiconductor optical amplifier, and SiN is silicon nitride;
  • an ASIC is an application-specific integrated circuit;

Pointcloud: 352×53μm=18.7352\times53\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=18.7 mm by 176×53μm=9.3176\times53\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=9.3 mm. 0.1° over 120°×25° is 1,200 × 250 addresses: 1,200×53μm=63.61{,}200\times53\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=63.6 mm by 250×53μm=13.3250\times53\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=13.3 mm, or 30×6.2530\times6.25 mm at 25 µm pitch.
