At 1550 nm that is 1.55μm/(0.1×π/180)=0.891.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(0.1\times\pi/180)=0.89 mm for 0.1° and 1.78 mm for 0.05°. The optical aperture is therefore small; the die area goes into the phase shifters and routing that feed it.

C8.2 Four effects beyond the reticle itself

Die cost, optics, phase-shifter length and readout can each bind before the reticle does. Each item below explains one of these limits and when it bites.

1. Yield and cost grow faster than area. A die is lost if a single “killer” defect lands on it. With randomly scattered defects (a Poisson model), the yield, i.e. the fraction of dies that work, and the silicon cost per good die are Y=e−AD0,cost per good die∝AY=AeAD0,Y=e^{-AD_0},\qquad \text{cost per good die}\propto\frac{A}{Y}=A\,e^{AD_0},(129) where AA is the die area (cm²) and D0D_0 the density of killer defects (cm⁻²), here an illustrative D0=0.1D_0=0.1 cm⁻² [E]. The cost per good die grows faster than linearly with AA, because a larger die both uses more wafer and is more likely to be hit. The table evaluates Eq. (129) for four die areas, on one wafer and on two stacked wafers:

Die area 1 cm² 2.44 cm² (IMX479 die) 8.58 cm² (full field) 17.2 cm² (two stitched fields)
Single-wafer yield 90% 78% 42% 18%
Two stacked wafers × 95% bond yield (same area and D0D_0) 78% 58% 17% 3%
Relative cost per good die, single wafer reference ≈2.8× ≈18× ≈86×
Relative cost per good die, stacked reference ≈3.3× ≈39× ≈435×

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Single-wafer yield is Y=e−AD0Y=e^{-AD_0} (Eq. (129)) with D0=0.1D_0=0.1 cm⁻²: for the full field, e−8.58×0.1=e−0.858=0.42e^{-8.58\times0.1}=e^{-0.858}=0.42; for two fields (17.16 cm²), e−1.716=0.18e^{-1.716}=0.18.

  • Stacked yield multiplies two independent wafers of the same area and a 95% bond yield, 0.95e−2AD00.95\,e^{-2AD_0}, e.g. 0.95×0.422=0.170.95\times0.42^2=0.17 for the full field.

  • Relative cost is A/YA/Y divided by the 1 cm² value for the same process (single wafer or stacked). Single wafer, full field: (8.58/0.424)/(1/0.905)=20.2/1.105≈18(8.58/0.424)/(1/0.905)=20.2/1.105\approx18. Stacked, two fields: (17.16/0.0307)/(1/0.778)=559/1.286≈435(17.16/0.0307)/(1/0.778)=559/1.286\approx435.

  • Stacked SPAD-SoCs pay twice: wafer-level hybrid bonding (bonding a whole SPAD wafer to a whole logic wafer) cannot pre-select known-good dies.

  • Caveat: pixel arrays tolerate some defects (defective pixels can be mapped out), so real imager yields beat the Poisson logic-yield figure. Logic periphery, TDCs (time-to-digital converters) and memory are less tolerant.

  • Poisson is also pessimistic for large dies, because real defects cluster. A negative-binomial model allows for this: Y=(1+AD0α)−α,Y=\left(1+\frac{AD_0}{\alpha}\right)^{-\alpha},(130) where α\alpha is a clustering parameter: smaller α\alpha means stronger clustering, and α→∞\alpha\to\infty recovers Eq. (129). With α=2\alpha=2 it gives 49% and 29% yield for one and two fields ((1+0.429)−2=0.49(1+0.429)^{-2}=0.49 and (1+0.858)−2=0.29(1+0.858)^{-2}=0.29), against 42% and 18% for Poisson. The size of the penalty is therefore uncertain by about 1.2–1.6× (0.49/0.42=1.150.49/0.42=1.15 and 0.29/0.18=1.60.29/0.18=1.6).

  • The conclusion holds: cost per die rises steeply once area passes about a full field. That favours scanned column receivers and multi-die tiling over single giant staring arrays.

2. Optics scale with the die. For a fixed field of view and f-number (focal length divided by lens diameter), focal length and lens diameter scale with sensor size, and lens volume and mass roughly with its cube.

  • Example [E]: a focal-plane array at 53 µm pitch needs f≈30f\approx30 mm for 0.1° per cell. The focal length ff is the cell pitch pp divided by the angle per cell θcell\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} in radians: f=p/θcell=53μm/(1.745×10−3)=30.4f=p/\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}=53\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(1.745\times10^{-3})=30.4 mm. Covering 120° needs about 64 mm of image width even with an f-θ lens, a lens whose image position is proportional to field angle. The width is fΘf\Theta, with Θ\Theta the full field angle in radians: 30.4mm×2.09rad=63.630.4\ {\mathrm{mm}}\times2.09\ {\mathrm{rad}}=63.6 mm.
  • At 25 µm pitch: f≈14f\approx14 mm and about 30 mm width. At 10 µm: f≈6f\approx6 mm and about 12 mm. The same two relations, f=p/θcellf=p/\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} and width =fΘ=f\Theta, give f=14.3f=14.3 and 5.7 mm and widths of 30 and 12 mm.
  • Small cell pitch therefore matters as much for packaging (behind-glass modules are about 25–30 mm tall [U]) as for die area.
  • In a coherent FPA the aperture is not a free f-number choice [E]:
    • Each address is one spatial mode, so the useful aperture per address is about λ/θbeam\lambda/\theta_{\mathrm{beam}}, where θbeam\theta_{\mathrm{beam}} is the angular width of the beam: about 0.9 mm at 0.1° and 1550 nm (λ/θbeam\lambda/\theta_{\mathrm{beam}}, before the truncation and single-polarization factor t2/2t^2/2 of §C10.3b, which gives an equivalent diameter of ≈0.65 mm, 0.33 mm²; §C7).
    • Shrinking the pitch shortens ff (30 → 5.7 mm) without a photon penalty. In a SPAD staring array the same kind of shrink, from 10.08 to 4 µm SPAD pitch, cuts the f/1.2 entrance aperture from 28.5 to 11.5 mm, about six times less collecting area ((28.5/11.5)2=6.1(28.5/11.5)^2=6.1; §C6).
    • The difficulty moves to the antenna: contiguous sampling needs each cell’s mode to fill most of its pitch. Berkeley’s array shows the gap. Its lens has f=55μm/(0.6×π/180)=5.3f=55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(0.6\times\pi/180)=5.3 mm, so a 0.05° beam corresponds to a mode only fθbeam=5.3mm×8.7×10−4≈4.6μmf\,\theta_{\mathrm{beam}}=5.3\ {\mathrm{mm}}\times8.7\times10^{-4}\approx4.6\ \mu{\mathrm{m}} wide in the focal plane, a twelfth of the 55 µm pitch. The array therefore samples at 0.6° with 0.05° beams (0.6/0.05=55/4.6≈120.6/0.05=55/4.6\approx12; §C10.4).

3. Phase-shifter physics can make OPAs area-bound; this is the key TFLN trade. Low-power OPAs trade watts for millimetres. Each OPA element needs a phase shifter, and the two main kinds are either power-hungry or long.

  • Thermo-optic Si phase shifters (a heater changes the silicon’s refractive index) are short (about 60–200 µm) but draw about 0.1–25 mW per π\pi of phase shift each. Heaters with trenches or undercuts reach 0.14 mW/π but respond in 200–300 µs, while the thermal shifters of MIT’s 50-element array need 13 mW/π (§C10.2b). The upper end is a compact, fast heater without thermal isolation: a 61.6 µm doped-silicon heater in a standard oxide-clad CMOS process needs 24.77 mW/π at a 130 kHz modulation bandwidth [I, Harris et al., Opt. Express 22, 10487 (2014)]. With a mean phase of about π\pi, 1,000 elements need roughly 0.1–25 W of control power (1,000×0.141{,}000\times0.14 mW =0.14=0.14 W to 1,000×251{,}000\times25 mW =25=25 W) [E].
  • Electro-optic phase shifters (an applied field changes the refractive index directly) draw almost no static power, but they are long:
    • Their efficiency is quoted as VπLV_\pi L: the voltage VπV_\pi needed for a π\pi phase shift times the electrode length LL, so a smaller value means a shorter or lower-voltage device. The often-quoted TFLN VπL≈2V_\pi L\approx2–3 V·cm is a push-pull Mach–Zehnder figure, in which both arms of an interferometer are driven in opposite directions. A single OPA channel sees one arm’s phase, so its per-element VπLV_\pi L is about 4–6 V·cm.
    • A 2π2\pi swing then needs about 8–20 mm with bipolar ±3–5 V drive, or about 16–24 mm with unipolar 0–5 V (≈27–40 mm at 0–3 V) [E]. A 2π2\pi shift needs twice VπV_\pi, so the length needed is L2π=2VπLΔV,L_{2\pi}=\frac{2\,V_\pi L}{\Delta V},(131) where ΔV\Delta V is the total voltage swing the driver provides. With 4 V·cm and a 10 V swing (±5 V), L2π=8/10L_{2\pi}=8/10 cm = 8 mm; with 6 V·cm and a 6 V swing (±3 V), 12/6=212/6=2 cm = 20 mm; with 0–5 V, 8/5=1.68/5=1.6 cm to 12/5=2.412/5=2.4 cm; with 0–3 V, 8/3=2.78/3=2.7 cm to 12/3=4.012/3=4.0 cm.
    • Si depletion shifters have comparable VπLV_\pi L and much higher loss [U].
    • At 20–30 µm fan-in pitch (the spacing of the parallel phase-shifter waveguides before they converge on the emitters), 1,000 such elements occupy 20–30 mm of width. At 8–20 mm length that is about 20–70% of one exposure field, before fan-in tapers: 20×8=16020\times8=160 mm² is 19% of 858 mm², and 30×20=60030\times20=600 mm² is 70%.
    • Folded or high-confinement designs (about 1 V·cm push-pull has been demonstrated) and higher drive voltages trade area against loss and driver cost. Wrapping the phase modulo 2π2\pi still requires a full 2π2\pi range; going below it means accepting phase errors.
  • At 0–5 V (16–24 mm) the same 1,000 elements take 20×16=32020\times16=320 to 30×24=72030\times24=720 mm², 37–84% of one 858 mm² field; at 0–3 V (27–40 mm) they take 20×27=54020\times27=540 to 30×40=1,20030\times40=1{,}200 mm², 63–140%. Low-voltage electro-optic OPAs are therefore among the few transmitter designs that approach or exceed the reticle.

4. Readout and packaging often bind first. For coherent arrays the scaling cost is per simultaneously active channel, each needing LO power, a balanced detector and a digitizer for a 100–400 MHz beat, sampling at about 1 GS/s (10⁹ samples per second; §C7, §C7a); pixel count on the die is not the cost driver. This is the chip-level face of the channel tax of §C7b.

  • The Berkeley switched array bonded only 128×96 of its 128×128 cells because of package pins [P].
  • Pointcloud’s 352×176 coherent array reads up to 128 channels at once, and its authors say an ASIC would be needed for higher frame rates [P].
  • Pointcloud also notes that silicon’s nonlinear absorption limits optical power per waveguide (§C7a(b)), and proposes blended Si–SiN routing [P].

C8.3 Bottom line

  • Reticle is a real constraint mainly for “one cell per direction” designs at automotive resolution: staring SPAD arrays and switched FMCW focal-plane arrays.
  • For scanned SPAD columns, SiPMs, lasers and continuously steered OPAs, other limits usually bind first (photons, memory, pins, phase control, heat), and chip area matters mainly through yield and cost.
  • Stitching moves the wall at superlinear, yield-driven cost (∝AeAD0\propto A\,e^{AD_0}, Eq. (129), with AA the die area and D0D_0 the killer-defect density). Tiling known-good dies keeps silicon cost roughly linear in area, but adds packaging, alignment and optics cost.
  • The one-axis mechanical scan dominates today (§C4, item 6; §C4d) partly because it is effectively a silicon-area multiplier: it time-shares a small array across thousands of directions.
  • For FMCW, the most promising path to automotive resolution is hybrid: an on-chip array for one axis or a modest 2D sub-field, combined with a slow mirror, lens tiling or wavelength steering. A single wafer-scale coherent imager is not the likely route.

C9. Lidar-to-lidar interference as penetration rises

This section asks whether lidars on different cars will disturb one another as more cars carry them. Interference here means that my receiver picks up laser pulses fired by someone else’s lidar, which can create false points (“ghosts”, points where no object exists) or blind some pixels. In short, foreign pulses are common in dense traffic, and the receiver’s rejection logic decides whether they become false points. The residual risks are identical units firing in step, saturation when one lidar looks straight into another, and products without that logic; the judgement below gives the detail. This matters because interference immunity is often cited as a reason to prefer FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous-wave) lidar, whose coherent receiver rejects most foreign light.

Judgement. At today’s penetration, lidar-to-lidar interference is a manageable engineering requirement, not yet a decisive argument for FMCW (§F6). The raw collision rate is not small: percent-level of points in dense, fully overlapping traffic. The safeguard is therefore rejection logic, not rarity: coded or dithered firing, shot-to-shot consistency tests, filtering and a test standard. Any product without dither or coding is exposed.

  • Dithered firing shifts each shot’s firing time by a small pseudo-random amount, so foreign pulses do not line up from one shot to the next.
  • Coding gives a unit’s pulse train a distinctive pattern (in timing or pulse shape) that its own receiver can recognise and a foreign unit’s pulses do not match.
  • A shot-to-shot consistency test accepts a range peak only if it recurs at the same range on several shots of the same point.

Why it matters now. In China, lidar is in about 21–25% of newly sold new-energy vehicles (NEVs: battery-electric, plug-in hybrid and range-extended cars), and flagships carry up to six units (§B6, §F2).

  • Sales penetration is not fleet share. About 3.2–3.3 M lidar units were installed in 2025 (3.21 M in §B1; ≈3.32 M per NE Times in §B7.1). GGAI (高工智能汽车研究院), which counts cars as well as units, puts 2025 at 3.25 M units on 2.56 M new cars, i.e. 324.84/256.28≈1.27324.84/256.28\approx1.27 units per car, below the 1.3–1.6 assumed in §F2 [MR/E]. Earlier years add little: GGAI counts 0.11 M lidar cars in 2022 and 0.44 M in 2023 (0.13 M and 0.57 M units), about 4,000 in 2021 and 1.37 M in 2024 [MR/E], so about 0.004+0.112+0.440+1.374+2.563≈4.50.004+0.112+0.440+1.374+2.563\approx4.5 M lidar cars were on China’s roads at end-2025 [E]. Adding 2026 (985k units in Q1, §B1, and an assumed 4–5 M for the whole year) at 1.27 units per car gives 4.5+4/1.27≈7.64.5+4/1.27\approx7.6 M to 4.5+5/1.27≈8.44.5+5/1.27\approx8.4 M lidar cars by end-2026 [E]. That is about 2% (7.6/371≈2.0%7.6/371\approx2.0\% to 8.4/371≈2.3%8.4/371\approx2.3\%) of the 371 M automobiles registered in China at 30 June 2026, a count that includes trucks and buses [P, Ministry of Public Security], so lidar cars remain only a few percent of the fleet [E].
  • Units within 100 m of a car in dense traffic (100–200 vehicles in that radius) [E]: from about 3 to about 16 lidars today, depending on city and location, and dozens later as the fleet turns over; the estimate below takes 10–30 for that later case. The count is the number of vehicles in the radius, times the share of them that carry lidar, times the lidar units per car: 100×0.02×1.3≈3100\times0.02\times1.3\approx3 with the fleet-average share of 2%, and 200×0.05×1.6≈16200\times0.05\times1.6\approx16 where new cars are over-represented (the 5% local share is an assumption).
  • Most operate at 905 nm or 940 nm, so the interfering population is mainly the same-band fleet, which shares a passband. The two bands are about 35 nm apart, outside most receive filters (optical band-pass filters 10–40 nm wide in front of the detector). The exception is at temperature extremes, because a laser’s wavelength rises with temperature. A 905 nm edge-emitting laser (EEL), whose wavelength temperature coefficient is 0.27 nm/K, drifts to about 927 nm at +105 °C (905nm+0.27nmK−1×80K≈927905\ {\mathrm{nm}}+0.27\ {\mathrm{nm\,K^{-1}}}\times80\ {\mathrm{K}}\approx927 nm, taking 905 nm at 25 °C). That reaches a 940 nm receiver only through a filter wider than about 26 nm (2×(940−927)2\times(940-927) nm), at the wide end of the 10–40 nm range.

Two kinds of event matter.

  1. Indirect interference: another lidar’s pulse reflects off the scene into my pixel during my listening window (the time after each of my shots during which my receiver records returns) and produces a ghost point.
  2. Direct interference: I look straight into another lidar’s aperture, which can saturate pixels like a small sun or a retroreflector.
    • Order of magnitude [E]: let the foreign lidar emit power PP (W) into a beam of solid angle Ωb\Omega_b (sr). Looking straight into that beam from a distance RR (m), I receive an irradiance of P/(ΩbR2)P/(\Omega_bR^2) (W/m²). If the whole beam instead lands on a Lambertian (perfectly diffuse) surface of reflectance ρ\rho at the same distance RR from me, the scattered light gives me only about ρP/(πR2)\rho P/(\pi R^2). The direct path is therefore stronger by the ratio π/(ρΩb)\pi/(\rho\Omega_b), about 10710^7 for a 0.1° beam and ρ=0.1\rho=0.1: Ωb≈(1.745×10−3)2=3.0×10−6\Omega_b\approx(1.745\times10^{-3})^2=3.0\times10^{-6} sr, so π/(0.1×3.0×10−6)≈1.0×107\pi/(0.1\times3.0\times10^{-6})\approx1.0\times10^{7}. A glossy or retroreflective surface is not Lambertian and can return much more toward me than this.
    • Aligned hits, in which my active pixel looks at the foreign unit while its beam crosses my aperture, are rare [E]. Take two facing §C6-class units more than about 30 m apart, each scanning 2,400 columns of 20.8 µs per 50 ms frame. Each unit’s 0.05° column is then at least as wide as the other’s 25 mm aperture (8.73×10−4rad×30m=268.73\times10^{-4}\ {\mathrm{rad}}\times30\ {\mathrm{m}}=26 mm), so the foreign beam lights my aperture during one or two of its column periods per frame, and my pixel that images the foreign aperture listens during one or two of mine. With unsynchronized scans the two intervals overlap in 2/2,400=0.8×10−32/2{,}400=0.8\times10^{-3} to 4/2,400=1.7×10−34/2{,}400=1.7\times10^{-3} of frames, and each overlap saturates one to four points. Aligned hits therefore occur in about one frame in a thousand, a few points at a time.
    • Stray light is the larger risk. If lens flare or window scatter delivers even 10−510^{-5} of the directly received power to each of the other active pixels, each gets about 100 times the return of a 10% Lambertian target at the same range (10−5×107=10210^{-5}\times10^{7}=10^{2}). How many points each crossing of the foreign beam over my aperture costs then depends on how far that light spreads [E]:
      • In the localized case it spreads over about 2.5° around the foreign unit, the order of Popko’s direct-interference extent (§C9a item 5), and it reaches my active column only while my scan is within those 50 columns (2.5∘/0.05∘2.5^\circ/0.05^\circ), in (50+2)/2,400=2.2%(50+2)/2{,}400=2.2\% of frames. It then hits about 50 pixels in each of one or two columns: 50–100 points, or 4×10−54\times10^{-5} to 8×10−58\times10^{-5} of a 1.25 Mpt frame (50/(1.25×106)50/(1.25\times10^{6}) and 100/(1.25×106)100/(1.25\times10^{6})). Averaged over all frames, that is at most 0.022×100/(1.25×106)=1.7×10−60.022\times100/(1.25\times10^{6})=1.7\times10^{-6} of points.
      • In the column-wide case it reaches the whole active column at every crossing, and each frame loses 520×1=520520\times1=520 to 520×2=1,040520\times2=1{,}040 points, 4×10−44\times10^{-4} to 8×10−48\times10^{-4} of the frame. That is the order 10−310^{-3} of points per frame, and the upper end of this chain.

Order-of-magnitude estimate for indirect interference [E; illustrative worst case with fully overlapping scenes]

The estimate multiplies how often foreign shots land in my pixel’s footprint by how long my pixel listens per point. In symbols, let Ṅf\dot N_{\mathrm{f}} be the foreign lidar’s shot rate (shots/s), Ωf\Omega_{\mathrm{f}} the solid angle of its field (over which its shots are spread uniformly), Ωhit\Omega_{\mathrm{hit}} the solid angle within which one foreign shot’s spot overlaps my pixel’s footprint (the larger of the foreign spot and my pixel), TlistenT_{\mathrm{listen}} my total listening window per point, and nn the number of foreign lidars whose fields fully overlap mine. Then the rate of foreign shots landing in my pixel’s footprint is rf=ṄfΩhit/Ωfr_{\mathrm{f}}=\dot N_{\mathrm{f}}\Omega_{\mathrm{hit}}/\Omega_{\mathrm{f}}, the mean number of foreign shots per point from one foreign lidar is p1p_1, and the fraction of points with at least one foreign shot is P≥1P_{\ge1}:

p1=rfTlisten=ṄfΩhitΩfTlisten,P≥1=1−(1−p1)np_1=r_{\mathrm{f}}\,T_{\mathrm{listen}}=\dot N_{\mathrm{f}}\,\frac{\Omega_{\mathrm{hit}}}{\Omega_{\mathrm{f}}}\,T_{\mathrm{listen}},\qquad P_{\ge1}=1-(1-p_1)^{n}(132)

Because p1≪1p_1\ll1, it is also the probability that a given point collects a foreign shot from that lidar.

  • Assumptions:
    • A foreign lidar of the §C6 class measures 25 Mpts/s with 10 shots per point: Ṅf=2.5×108\dot N_{\mathrm{f}}=2.5\times10^8 illuminated 0.05°×0.05° spot-shots per second, spread over Ωf=\Omega_{\mathrm{f}}= 120°×26° (3,120 deg²).
    • My pixel is 0.05°×0.05°, the same size as the foreign spot, so Ωhit=0.0025\Omega_{\mathrm{hit}}=0.0025 deg².
    • The scenes fully overlap at similar range, so a foreign return is about as strong as my own per shot. The foreign unit is in my wavelength band, and only light scattered once by the scene is counted.
  • Chain:
    • About 200 foreign shots per second land in my pixel’s footprint: the foreign shots are spread over 3,120 deg² and my 0.05°×0.05° footprint is 0.0025 deg², so rf=2.5×108s−1×0.0025/3,120≈200r_{\mathrm{f}}=2.5\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times0.0025/3{,}120\approx200 s⁻¹. They arrive as one ten-shot column per 50 ms frame (10×20s−1=200s−110\times20\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=200\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}), which sets the ghost rate after rejection (§C9a item 3).
    • My pixel listens for the whole 20.8 µs column time per point, about 10 shots of ≈2 µs each (§C6), so Tlisten≈20.8T_{\mathrm{listen}}\approx20.8 µs.
    • A point therefore collects about 4×10−34\times10^{-3} foreign shots per fully overlapping foreign lidar (p1=200s−1×20.8μs=4.2×10−3p_1=200\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times20.8\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=4.2\times10^{-3}).
    • At 25 Mpts/s that is about 10510^5 single-shot ghost candidates per second per foreign lidar, before rejection (25×106×4.2×10−3=1.0×10525\times10^{6}\times4.2\times10^{-3}=1.0\times10^{5}).
  • Result: with today’s 3–16 such lidars within 100 m (above), if all of them overlapped fully, about 1.2–6.5% of points would carry at least one foreign shot in their histogram window (the set of time bins in which the receiver accumulates counts for one point), and the later 10–30 would give about 4–12%. From Eq. (132) with the unrounded p1=4.17×10−3p_1=4.17\times10^{-3} (200.3s−1×20.83μs200.3\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times20.83\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}), 1−(1−p1)n1-(1-p_1)^{n} is 1.2% for n=3n=3, 6.5% for n=16n=16, 4.1% for n=10n=10 and 11.8% for n=30n=30. §C9a item 2 scales these down for partial overlap and wavelength. A smaller foreign unit (2 Mpts/s, 0.1° pixel) gives about a third of this: at 10 shots per point it fires 2×1072\times10^{7} shots/s, each lighting 0.01 deg² (larger than my pixel, so Ωhit≈0.01\Omega_{\mathrm{hit}}\approx0.01 deg²), so 2×107×0.01/3,120≈642\times10^{7}\times0.01/3{,}120\approx64 shots/s land on my pixel, 64×20.8μs=1.3×10−364\times20.8\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=1.3\times10^{-3} per point, and 3–16 such units give 0.4–2.1% while 10–30 give 1.3–3.9%.

Why most of these never become ghosts. Dithered firing plus a shot-to-shot consistency test rejects them; a coincidence gate or a count threshold alone does not. The receiver assumed here is a SPAD (single-photon avalanche diode) array that fires several shots per point and accumulates the photon arrival times in a histogram of time bins; a peak in the histogram is reported as a point.

  • A foreign pulse is a time-correlated photon burst, not a stray background count.
    • In one shot it can add several counts to one bin, up to all nine SPADs of a 3×3 macro-pixel (a group of SPADs read out together as one pixel).
    • It passes an nthn_{\mathrm{th}}-of-NN coincidence gate as readily as a true return. Such a gate registers an event only if at least nthn_{\mathrm{th}} of the NN SPADs in a macro-pixel fire within a short coincidence window. Coincidence suppresses uncorrelated background (§C6(d′)), whose photons arrive independently, not pulses, whose photons arrive together.
  • Shot-to-shot inconsistency rejects it. With dithered firing times it falls in different bins on different shots, while a true return builds up in one bin over all shots.
    • With 5 cm bins (0.33 ns, 2×0.05m/c2\times0.05\ {\mathrm{m}}/c, where cc is the speed of light and the factor 2 accounts for the round trip), ±0.3 µs of dither spreads each foreign shot over about 1,800 bins (0.6μs/0.333ns0.6\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}/0.333\ {\mathrm{ns}}).
    • Even if about five foreign shots overlap one point, the chance that any two share a bin is about (52)/1800≈0.6%\binom{5}{2}/1800\approx0.6\%. Here (52)=10\binom{5}{2}=10 is the binomial coefficient, the number of distinct pairs among five shots, and each pair shares a bin with probability 1/1,800. Five is the mean number of shots that one foreign unit’s ten-shot column puts into my point when the two overlap; §C9a item 3 turns this into a ghost rate per point.
  • A count threshold alone is marginal for weak far targets. A 200 m, 10% return gives only about 21–33 counts per point (§C6(c)); a single saturating burst from a nearby bright surface, up to nine counts from the nine SPADs of a 3×3 macro-pixel, is 27–43% of that (9/339/33 to 9/219/21). Robust rejection therefore needs a consistency test (a peak present in at least mm of the NshotsN_{\mathrm{shots}} shots of a point), with m≥3m\ge3 if random ghosts are to be negligible in dense traffic (§C9a item 3), or code matching.
  • Synchronized, identical emitters carry the residual risk. Two units of the same model with identical shot periods put every overlapping shot at a fixed offset, which builds a ghost as strong as a real return. Coding and dither are required there, not optional.

Mitigations in use or in research:

  • Pseudo-random timing offsets and cross-PRF (pulse repetition frequency, the rate at which shots are fired) coding. A 2026 study adds ±0.3 µs pseudo-random offsets plus a dynamic receive window [I].
  • Multi-pulse codes, CDMA-like (code-division multiple access, in which each unit tags its pulses with its own code and the receiver correlates against that code) identity coding, and wavelength or channel diversity [I/P].
  • Temporal and spatial consistency filtering of point clouds.
  • Vendor anti-interference modes.
  • Standards: China’s national lidar standard GB/T 45500-2025 (performance requirements and test methods) includes anti-interference among its tested metrics (test conditions and limit in §C9a). The State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) listing gives publication and implementation both as 25 Apr 2025. It is recommended (GB/T), not mandatory; Hesai announced it in May 2025 as lead drafter [P].
  • FMCW: coherent receivers mix the return with a local oscillator (LO, a reference copy of the transmitted laser light) and respond only to light matched to the LO’s frequency and chirp (the linear frequency sweep). They are therefore largely immune, though FMCW-to-FMCW interference modes exist (§C7, §C9a).

What would change the judgement: public field data showing measurable ghost or blinding rates in dense Chinese traffic, or a documented incident attributed to interference. Such incidence data from real traffic is lacking, a genuine research and measurement gap. §C9a reviews the published measurements, models, mitigations and standards, and checks this estimate against them.

C9a. What the literature says, and how it checks the estimate above

This subsection compares the §C9 order-of-magnitude estimate with published measurements, models, mitigations and standards. The published work supports the §C9 estimate, but none of it quantifies interference from other vehicles’ lidars in real traffic. Mutual interference has been studied since at least 2015, mostly with 2-D industrial scanners or first-generation spinning units in controlled rooms.

Evidence tags are as elsewhere in the report (for example [P] primary document, [I] independent source, [E] my own estimate, [U] unverified); mitigation deployability is tagged [D] shipping, [NT] product path within about 5 years, and [R] research-stage. Key results were read from the papers’ tables and figures where the full text was open; otherwise they are marked abstract.

Measurements

The table lists published measurements of lidar-to-lidar interference: each study’s setup and what it found.

Study Setup Result
Kim, Eom, Park (Yeungnam/Daegu): IEEE IV 2015; SPIE 9504 (2015); IEMEK J. 12:43 (2017) [P] Two SICK LMS-511 (905 nm) in a small room, 24 h, ≈1.4×10⁹ points per arrangement Interfered-point fraction 6×10⁻⁶–1.7×10⁻⁴, depending on arrangement; bursts span up to 17 angles and 4 lines. Power analysis: a direct path saturates, a singly scattered foreign pulse looks like a normal return, and double scatter falls below threshold
Popko, Gaylord, Valenta (Georgia Tech): MS thesis 2019; Opt. Eng. 58:033103 (2019), 59:033104 and 59:053106 (2020) [P] SICK LMS531 pairs; two VLP-16 Total 0.022–1.04% of returns; scattered-only 0.022–0.031%. With a direct geometry, ≈1%, of which 91–96% is direct. Direct errors are <1 m; scattered errors spread to maximum range. A 905 nm filter passed a 903 nm VLP-16. Replicating Kim’s arrangements gave 1.4–2.4× Kim’s rate where only scattered light could interfere and up to ≈350× where direct view was possible (thesis Table 8), so geometry and method matter
Diehm et al. (Fraunhofer IOSB), SPIE 10796 (2018) [P] Two HDL-64E on one vehicle Worst frames 1.3–1.5% of points, recurring periodically because the rotation rates differed slightly; mostly via the vehicle’s own hardware ≈1 m away
Robinson et al. (WMG/NPL), RAAI 2022 [P] OS1-64 victim, five offenders at ≈2 m Authors report “no obvious effect”; their table lists ≈2–3×10³ extra outliers per 100 frames with an HDL-64E offender (≈5×10⁻⁴ of points [E], inferred from the stated frame format)
Robinson et al., IEEE IV 2025 [P] Two MEMS lidars (different makers) face to face at 1–3 m 98–652 interference points per cloud (baseline ≤15); ghosts hundreds of metres beyond the true range
Xu et al., ShanghaiTech mapping robot, arXiv 2406.16713 [I] Eight lidars on one robot Only the RoboSense Bpearls and Livox Avia were affected (temporal σ up to 2.5 m); Ruby, PandarQT and Neuvition M1 were unaffected
Dow et al., “SSCATeR”, arXiv 2512.08557 [I] Two drone-mounted DJI L1 Detector false positives in 1.0–2.2% of inference passes; no missed detections
Grollius et al., IEEE Sens. J. 22:12976 (2022) [P] SPAD flash lidars Direct illumination ≈10× indirect for a 60°×20° flash. Identical units at the same pulse rate are the critical case; unit-to-unit rate spread (σ ≈62 mHz at 10 kHz) smears an aggressor over ≈62 ns in 1,000 shots (as reported; the stated spread implies 1000×100μs×6.2×10−6≈6201000\times100\,\mu{\mathrm{s}}\times6.2\times10^{-6}\approx620 ns, so the two figures are inconsistent by a factor of 10 [E])
Sato et al., NDSS 2024 [P] Nine commercial lidars probed with a spoofer New-generation units have timing randomization or pulse fingerprinting (OS1-32, Livox Horizon, RoboSense Helios, Hesai XT32, Intel L515, Leddar Pixell), with randomization windows equivalent to 1.5–110 m of range (2×1.5m/c=102\times1.5\ {\mathrm{m}}/c=10 ns to 2×110m/c≈7302\times110\ {\mathrm{m}}/c\approx730 ns). A random 1 MHz attacker still injected 28–19,000 points, depending on model

In the table, σ denotes a standard deviation: of the measured range over time for Xu et al., and of the pulse repetition rate across units for Grollius et al. MEMS lidars steer their beam with a micro-electro-mechanical mirror, and flash lidars illuminate their whole field with each pulse instead of scanning it.

Models. Popko’s geometric model gives the fraction of time two coplanar scanners’ beams intersect as 0–½, typically ≈¼. It maps where scattered interference occurs: risk is highest for targets near and between the two scanners. Other analyses:

  • a probability model in Kim et al. 2015 [P, not verified];
  • CDMA pulse-code simulations: Liang et al. 2022 give 0.11% false alarms (points reported where there is no target) with 200 single-pulse interferers [P];
  • correlation ranging: Hwang & Lee, IEEE Access 2020, show false-alarm rates held at the preset 10−510^{-5} regardless of interferer power [P].

No traffic-level model of the form “number of lidars × field of view × shot rate × listening window” was found. The §C9 estimate, Eq. (132), appears to be new in that form.

Check of the §C9 numbers [E]:

  1. Pre-rejection collision rate: consistent.
    • Kim’s geometry [P, Kim et al. 2017, Table 1]. Each SICK LMS-511 fires 36 kHz pulses, one per 0.25° step at 25 rotations per second (36,000/25=1,44036{,}000/25=1{,}440 steps per 360°). Its beam diverges by 11 mrad (0.63°), it ranges to 80 m, and each point is one shot. SICK’s LMS511 datasheet gives a 0.2–80 m working range and, for its PRO variant, 11.9 mrad [P].
    • Prediction. The rate of foreign shots into one footprint of the victim scanner is the shot rate times the hit width over the field, rf=36,000s−1×θhit/360∘r_{\mathrm{f}}=36{,}000\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times\theta_{\mathrm{hit}}/360^\circ. The hit width θhit\theta_{\mathrm{hit}} lies between one beam width (0.63°, the larger-of-the-two rule of Eq. (132)) and two (1.26°, counting any partial overlap of two 0.63° spots), so rf=63r_{\mathrm{f}}=63–126 s⁻¹. The receiver listens for the round trip to its 80 m maximum range, Tlisten=2×80m/c=0.534T_{\mathrm{listen}}=2\times80\ {\mathrm{m}}/c=0.534 µs. Eq. (132) then gives p1=63s−1×0.534μs=3.4×10−5p_1=63\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times0.534\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=3.4\times10^{-5} to 126s−1×0.534μs=6.7×10−5126\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times0.534\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=6.7\times10^{-5} per point, with a central value of 5.0×10−55.0\times10^{-5}. This is the model’s prediction for Kim’s geometry, not a measurement.
    • Measurement. Kim measured 6×10−66\times10^{-6}–1.7×10−41.7\times10^{-4} over all four arrangements, as in the table above. Interfered points, summed over the burst lengths of the 2017 paper’s Table 4 and divided by the points scanned per arrangement in its Table 3, give 35,867/(1.38×109)=2.6×10−535{,}867/(1.38\times10^{9})=2.6\times10^{-5} face to face, 42,292/(1.38×109)=3.1×10−542{,}292/(1.38\times10^{9})=3.1\times10^{-5} and 230,916/(1.38×109)=1.7×10−4230{,}916/(1.38\times10^{9})=1.7\times10^{-4} side by side, and 4,691/(7.8×108)=6.0×10−64{,}691/(7.8\times10^{8})=6.0\times10^{-6} back to back. Back to back, the two fields do not overlap, so a foreign pulse must scatter more than once to arrive. The three arrangements with overlapping fields, the case Eq. (132) describes, give 2.6×10−52.6\times10^{-5}–1.7×10−41.7\times10^{-4}; the prediction lies inside that range, within a factor of 2.5 of either end. Popko measured 2–3×10⁻⁴ scattered-only, and his repeat of the Kim arrangement in which only scattered light could interfere gave 1.4–2.4× Kim’s rate.
    • Rescaling. Our flux × window, p1=4.17×10−3p_1=4.17\times10^{-3}, is 4.17×10−3/(5.0×10−5)≈834.17\times10^{-3}/(5.0\times10^{-5})\approx83 times the central prediction for Kim’s geometry. Multiplying the measured 2.6×10−52.6\times10^{-5} (Kim, face to face) to 3×10−43\times10^{-4} (Popko) by 83 gives 2.2×10−32.2\times10^{-3}–2.5×10−22.5\times10^{-2}, which brackets §C9’s 4.2×10−34.2\times10^{-3} per fully overlapping foreign lidar.
  2. The fully overlapping rates are worst cases, today’s 1.2–6.5% as much as the later 4–12%. In traffic, three factors reduce the rate of foreign shots into my footprints; each is an estimate [E]:
    • Scene overlap fovf_{\mathrm{ov}}, the share of a foreign unit’s shots that land inside my field: 0.25–0.6. The low end is Popko’s typical ≈¼ beam-intersection fraction for two coplanar scanners (Models, above); the high end is a car ahead facing the same way, most of whose 120° field lies inside mine.
    • In-band share fbandf_{\mathrm{band}}, the share of foreign units that my receive filter passes: 0.5–0.9. 9xx-nm units are ≈94–96% of Chinese installations (§C2), but this report does not quantify their 905/940 nm split, so the range assumes my band holds half to most of them.
    • Spot density fsd≈(R/Rf)2f_{\mathrm{sd}}\approx(R/R_{\mathrm{f}})^2, where RR and RfR_{\mathrm{f}} are my range and the foreign unit’s range to the surfaces I see: 0.5–1. It is 1 at equal range, as Eq. (132) assumes, and 0.5 when the foreign unit is 1.4 times farther (1/1.42=0.51/1.4^2=0.5), because the light of its spots on those surfaces falls as the square of its range. A unit closer to them than I am gives more than 1, so this factor is the least certain.
    • The product is F=fovfbandfsd=0.25×0.5×0.5=0.0625F=f_{\mathrm{ov}}f_{\mathrm{band}}f_{\mathrm{sd}}=0.25\times0.5\times0.5=0.0625 to 0.6×0.9×1=0.540.6\times0.9\times1=0.54, and Popko’s ≈¼ overlap alone sits inside that range. With Fp1F\,p_1 in place of p1p_1 in Eq. (132), 1−(1−Fp1)n1-(1-F\,p_1)^{n} gives about 0.08–3.5% of points carrying at least one foreign shot before rejection today (n=3n=3 with F=0.0625F=0.0625, n=16n=16 with F=0.54F=0.54) and 0.26–6.5% later (n=10n=10 and 30). Counting only single-scatter paths is right (Kim’s power analysis).
  3. Random ghosts: a 3-of-10 consistency test makes them negligible by day and night; 2-of-10 is marginal.

    • Ghosts are built from foreign shots, not counts. One foreign shot can fill a bin with up to nine counts (§C9), so a count threshold does not reject it; what rejects it is that it does not recur. The receiver is taken to apply an mm-of-10 shot-recurrence rule: a peak is accepted only if a significant per-shot event, for example a coincidence-gated one (§C6(d′)), recurs in the same bin on at least mm of the ten shots of a point, so a single foreign shot never passes. Background is treated in the sunlight bullet below.

    • The mean number of foreign shots per point is k‾=np1\bar k=n\,p_1 (Eq. (132)): 0.0125–0.0667 for today’s 3–16 units and 0.0417–0.125 for the later 10–30 (3×4.17×10−3=0.01253\times4.17\times10^{-3}=0.0125, 16×4.17×10−3=0.066716\times4.17\times10^{-3}=0.0667, 10×4.17×10−3=0.041710\times4.17\times10^{-3}=0.0417 and 30×4.17×10−3=0.12530\times4.17\times10^{-3}=0.125). The bins are Δtbin=0.333\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}=0.333 ns wide (the 5 cm bins of §C9), each shot’s histogram spans Tw=2T_{\mathrm{w}}=2 µs (the round trip to 300 m, Tw/Δtbin=6,000T_{\mathrm{w}}/\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}=6{,}000 bins), and dither spreads a foreign shot over Tdith=0.6T_{\mathrm{dith}}=0.6 µs (Tdith/Δtbin=1,800T_{\mathrm{dith}}/\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}=1{,}800 bins, §C9). Returns are taken to fall in one bin; a pulse spread over several bins widens the effective coincidence window, and the ghost rates below grow in proportion.

    • Shots from one foreign unit arrive together. A §C6-class unit fires one 20.8 µs column of ten shots at my footprint per 50 ms frame (a visit). A visit overlaps a given point with probability 2×20.8μs/50ms=8.3×10−42\times20.8\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}/50\ {\mathrm{ms}}=8.3\times10^{-4}, and its offset from my point’s window is then uniform, so it puts k=0k=0 to 10 of its shots into the point: over the 20 equally likely offsets of one shot period each, all 10 once, 1 to 9 twice each and none once. That is 5 shots on average, which reproduces p1=8.3×10−4×5=4.2×10−3p_1=8.3\times10^{-4}\times5=4.2\times10^{-3}, and the number of pairs (k2)\binom{k}{2} averages (2∑k=29(k2)+(102))/20=(240+45)/20=14.25(2\sum_{k=2}^{9}\binom{k}{2}+\binom{10}{2})/20=(240+45)/20=14.25, i.e. q2=14.25/5=2.85q_2=14.25/5=2.85 pairs per foreign shot. A unit with my shot period puts its shots at the same offset in each of my shots apart from the dither, so a pair shares a bin with probability Δtbin/Tdith=1/1,800\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}/T_{\mathrm{dith}}=1/1{,}800; a unit with another shot period spreads its shots further and coincides no more often.

    • Shots from two different units are independent. A point holds (n2)p12≈k‾2/2\binom{n}{2}p_1^2\approx\bar k^2/2 such pairs on average, and each shares a bin with probability Δtbin/Tw=1/6,000\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}/T_{\mathrm{w}}=1/6{,}000; this slightly overstates them, since the rule also needs the two on different shots. Under the 2-of-10 rule the ghost probability per point is therefore

      pghost≈q2k‾ΔtbinTdith+k‾22ΔtbinTwp_{\mathrm{ghost}}\approx q_2\,\bar k\,\frac{\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}}{T_{\mathrm{dith}}}+\frac{\bar k^{2}}{2}\,\frac{\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}}{T_{\mathrm{w}}}(133)

    • The first term dominates. Today it is 2.85×0.0125/1,800=2.0×10−52.85\times0.0125/1{,}800=2.0\times10^{-5} to 2.85×0.0667/1,800=1.06×10−42.85\times0.0667/1{,}800=1.06\times10^{-4}, against at most 0.06672/2/6,000=3.7×10−70.0667^2/2/6{,}000=3.7\times10^{-7} for the second; later it is 6.6×10−56.6\times10^{-5} to 2.85×0.125/1,800=2.0×10−42.85\times0.125/1{,}800=2.0\times10^{-4}, against at most 0.1252/2/6,000=1.3×10−60.125^2/2/6{,}000=1.3\times10^{-6}. A simulation of 10710^{7} dithered visits gives the same 14.25/1,800=0.79%14.25/1{,}800=0.79\% ghost chance per overlapping visit [E].

    • A 1.25 Mpt frame (2,400 × 520 points at 20 fps, §C6) therefore carries about 25–130 random ghosts today (2.0×10−5×1.25×106=252.0\times10^{-5}\times1.25\times10^{6}=25 to 1.06×10−4×1.25×106=1321.06\times10^{-4}\times1.25\times10^{6}=132) and about 80–250 later (6.6×10−5×1.25×106=836.6\times10^{-5}\times1.25\times10^{6}=83 to 2.0×10−4×1.25×106=2502.0\times10^{-4}\times1.25\times10^{6}=250), i.e. about 500–2,600 and 1,700–5,000 per second at 20 frames per second. At night that is up to a fifth of the 10−310^{-3} false points per point that the detection rule of §C0 subsection 10.3 allows (2.0×10−4/10−3=0.22.0\times10^{-4}/10^{-3}=0.2): tolerable, but not negligible. The traffic factor F=0.0625F=0.0625–0.54 of item 2 scales all of these down in proportion.

    • A 3-of-10 rule makes them negligible. Three shots of one visit must then share a bin, with probability (Δtbin/Tdith)2=1/1,8002(\Delta t_{\mathrm{bin}}/T_{\mathrm{dith}})^2=1/1{,}800^2 per triple, and the number of triples (k3)\binom{k}{3} averages (2∑k=39(k3)+(103))/20=(420+120)/20=27(2\sum_{k=3}^{9}\binom{k}{3}+\binom{10}{3})/20=(420+120)/20=27 per overlapping visit, i.e. q3=27/5=5.4q_3=27/5=5.4 per foreign shot. So p≈q3k‾/1,8002p\approx q_3\,\bar k/1{,}800^2, at most 5.4×0.125/(3.24×106)=2.1×10−75.4\times0.125/(3.24\times10^{6})=2.1\times10^{-7} per point: 0.26 ghosts per frame (2.1×10−7×1.25×1062.1\times10^{-7}\times1.25\times10^{6}), or about 5 per second. The rule costs a weak far return little, since a 200 m, 10% return gives 2.1–3.3 detected photons per shot (§C6(c)) and so registers on most of its ten shots.

    • These rates assume that background never supplies a recurrence, as at night. In bright sun it can: the rate and live fraction of §C0 subsection 10.3 put 1.83×108s−1×0.333ns×0.885=0.0541.83\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times0.333\ {\mathrm{ns}}\times0.885=0.054 background counts into a bin per shot, so a lone foreign burst would find a count in its bin on one of the other nine shots with probability 1−e−9×0.054=0.391-e^{-9\times0.054}=0.39. A per-shot event must then need two or more counts, which background supplies with probability 1−e−0.054(1+0.054)=1.4×10−31-e^{-0.054}(1+0.054)=1.4\times10^{-3} per shot. Under 3-of-10 that adds (92)(1.4×10−3)2k‾=7.1×10−5k‾\binom{9}{2}(1.4\times10^{-3})^2\,\bar k=7.1\times10^{-5}\,\bar k for lone bursts and 8×1.4×10−3=1.1%8\times1.4\times10^{-3}=1.1\% of the visit term for visit pairs, together 1.1×10−51.1\times10^{-5} per point at k‾=0.125\bar k=0.125 (14 per frame), while a 200 m, 10% return of 2.1–3.3 photons per shot (§C6(c)) still clears two counts on three or more of its ten shots in over 99% of points, if it falls in one bin. Under 2-of-10 the same test leaks 9×1.4×10−3k‾=1.6×10−39\times1.4\times10^{-3}\,\bar k=1.6\times10^{-3} per point at k‾=0.125\bar k=0.125, above the false-point budget, and a three-count test that avoids this loses up to 9% of those weak returns. In bright sun, then, the 3-of-10 rule is the one that works.

    • Without dither, every pair of a visit shares a bin. The 8.3×10−4×0.85=7.1×10−48.3\times10^{-4}\times0.85=7.1\times10^{-4} of points per foreign unit that receive two or more of its shots then all become ghosts, where 0.85 (17/2017/20) is the share of overlapping visits that put at least two shots into the point. That is n×7.1×10−4n\times7.1\times10^{-4}, i.e. 0.2–1.1% of points for today’s 3–16 units and 0.7–2.1% for the later 10–30, the identical-unit failure of §C9.

    • Published post-rejection false-alarm rates, from 10−510^{-5} (Hwang & Lee, a preset value) to 1.1×10−31.1\times10^{-3} (Liang et al., with 200 interferers), both from simulations of other receivers, span the 2-of-10 rate derived here and lie at or above the 3-of-10 rate (2×10−72\times10^{-7} at night, 1×10−51\times10^{-5} in bright sun). They are not a test of this model.

  4. Synchronized identical units remain the failure mode. Diehm’s periodic bursts and Grollius’s identical-rate case support §C9.
    • Dither suppresses them by 35–56 dB in demonstrations: 35–50 dB with a linear-feedback shift register (LFSR, a simple digital pseudo-random number generator) random delay (Carrara & Fiergolski, Fastree3D, Appl. Sci. 2019) [NT]; 56 dB (Tsai et al., Opt. Lett. 2020) [NT, abstract].
    • Those figures accumulate 10³–10⁵ shots. With ≈10 shots per point, protection comes from coincidence and consistency rules, not averaging.
    • An untested hypothesis worth measuring [U]: same-model sensors phase-locked to GPS pulse-per-second (PPS) or Precision Time Protocol (PTP) timing, a standard feature for rotation-phase synchronization (aligning spinning units’ rotation angle to a common clock), might fire in step on different vehicles unless the firing dither is independent of the lock.
  5. Direct view: the measurements fit the localized case of the §C9 chain.
    • Popko found direct interference 10–100× more frequent than scattered in coplanar 2-D scanners, but only at scan angles that view the other scanner or lie at most ≈2.5° beyond its angular extent; face to face, 90% of the direct events fell inside the other scanner’s angular extent. Popko attributes the spread to beam divergence and the receiver’s field of view [P, thesis §7.2]. That is the localized case of §C9, not stray light across the whole field.
    • Robinson 2025 found 98–652 interference points per cloud with two MEMS units face to face at 1–3 m. A §C6-class pair at that spacing would lose up to about 500–1,500 points per crossing in the localized case, the same order: the interferer’s column then takes 1+25mm/(8.73×10−4×3m)=10.51+25\ {\mathrm{mm}}/(8.73\times10^{-4}\times3\ {\mathrm{m}})=10.5 to 1+25mm/(8.73×10−4×1m)=29.61+25\ {\mathrm{mm}}/(8.73\times10^{-4}\times1\ {\mathrm{m}})=29.6 column periods to cross a 25 mm aperture, and 50×10.5=52550\times10.5=525, 50×29.6=1,48050\times29.6=1{,}480.
    • Neither measured a 3-D one-axis unit at road distance, where the chain gives at most 1.7×10−61.7\times10^{-6} of points per frame in the localized case and 4×10−44\times10^{-4} to 8×10−48\times10^{-4} if stray light reaches the whole active column.

Mitigations by deployability

The table sorts the published and shipping mitigations by how close each is to automotive use: [D] shipping, [NT] a plausible product path within about 5 years, [R] research-stage.

Tag Mitigation Result or status
[D] Randomized firing and pulse-pair fingerprints In shipping units (Sato et al.)
[D] Phase lock, azimuth masking and motor-speed offsets for sensors on the same vehicle Ouster, RoboSense; Hokuyo’s >300 rpm offset
[D] Incidental wavelength diversity (905 / 940 / 1,550 nm) Uncontrolled and leaky (903 nm passing a 905 nm filter)
[NT] LFSR random delays in SPAD flash 35–50 dB
[NT] Photon-triggered random timing 56 dB
[NT] Code-word switching 82.6–85.5% less interference in a driving simulation (Lee/Park/Kim 2023, abstract)
[NT] Dual-pulse discriminators >98% fewer false ranges (2026, abstract)
[NT] On-chip interference filters Samsung-affiliated 36-channel SPAD sensor reliable with 32 interfering lidars (JSSC 2021, abstract)
[NT] Spatio-temporal point-cloud filters Robinson 2025: 652 → ≈19 interference points per frame; not yet real-time; risk of deleting small far objects
[R] Carrier-hopping prime codes Kim/Eom/Park series, simulated
[R] Optical polar modulation ISSCC 2018, 18.6 dB
[R] Optical-chaos and random-modulation lidar +20 dB SNR at 100 m (2018); ≥15 dB tolerance (2024)
[R] Chaotic-microcomb ranging PKU, Nat. Photon. 2023: detection held to ≈30 dB interference-to-signal ratio against an FMCW jammer at ≈10 m. Lukashchuk et al., Nat. Photon. 2023: immunity argued from first principles
[R] Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) time sharing —

In the table, SNR is the signal-to-noise ratio. The dB figures are as reported by each study; they measure different things (interference suppression, SNR gain or tolerated interference-to-signal ratio) and are not directly comparable.

FMCW is not categorically immune: matched chirps can create ghosts. An FMCW receiver responds to any light that beats with its LO at a frequency inside its receiver band, so a foreign FMCW laser whose frequency sweep happens to coincide with mine in frequency and time can produce a false target.

  • Hwang, Yun & Lee (Optik 2020) distinguish transient interference, which lowers SNR, from in-band interference by matched chirps, which creates ghosts [P].

  • Esen, Gaylord & Valenta (SPIE 2025) require spatial, spectral and temporal alignment and show direct-path ghosts in simulation [P, abstract].

  • No traffic-level FMCW collision probability is published. A first-order extension of §C9 multiplies the spatial term of Eq. (132) by a spectral-overlap factor fspecf_{\mathrm{spec}}, the probability that a foreign laser’s frequency falls close enough to mine to produce a beat inside my receiver band [E]:

    fspec∼Bbeat+BrxΔνforeign≈10−2,Δνforeign=cΔλλ2f_{\mathrm{spec}}\sim\frac{B_{\mathrm{beat}}+B_{\mathrm{rx}}}{\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{foreign}}}\approx10^{-2},\qquad \Delta\nu_{\mathrm{foreign}}=\frac{c\,\Delta\lambda}{\lambda^2}(134)

    Here BbeatB_{\mathrm{beat}} is the frequency span over which a foreign laser can beat with my chirp, BrxB_{\mathrm{rx}} my receiver’s electrical bandwidth, Δνforeign\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{foreign}} the spread of the foreign lasers’ optical frequencies (assumed uniform), Δλ\Delta\lambda the same spread in wavelength, λ\lambda the wavelength and cc the speed of light. For example, assuming Bbeat+Brx≈1.5B_{\mathrm{beat}}+B_{\mathrm{rx}}\approx1.5 GHz (a 1 GHz chirp plus ≈0.5 GHz of receiver bandwidth) and foreign lasers spread over ≈1 nm, which is cΔλ/λ2≈125c\,\Delta\lambda/\lambda^2\approx125 GHz at 1,550 nm, the factor is 1.5/125≈1.2×10−21.5/125\approx1.2\times10^{-2}. That is roughly two orders below ToF (time-of-flight, pulsed direct detection) before rejection, not zero.

What the security literature adds. Randomization (random variation of each shot’s firing time or pulse pattern, as in the dither described in §C9) now ships, but consistency tests and saturation flagging are still needed.

  • Petit et al. (Black Hat EU 2015), Shin et al. (CHES 2017), Cao et al. (CCS 2019, USENIX 2023), Sun et al. (USENIX 2020) and Jin et al. (S&P 2023, abstract) show that first-generation lidars could be spoofed (fed fake points by an attacker’s laser) or blinded cheaply. Shin et al. recommended timing and waveform randomization, noting it “also can help mitigate inter-lidar interference”.
  • Sato et al. (NDSS 2024) showed that such randomization now blocks synchronized injection. It is sized for interference, not an adversary: random high-rate injection and removal attacks (which add false points or erase real ones) still work.
  • It removes correlated coincidences, not single uncorrelated counts or saturation.

Standards and tests.

  • GB/T 45500-2025 [P; read from the Jan 2024 draft for comment, so the final text may differ]:
    • Clause 5.1.8 requires an anti-interference false-point rate ≤0.1%.
    • Test 6.2.9 uses a lidar of the same model as interferer, windows facing at 0.5, 1 and 2 m, with at least one face-to-face exposure per frame. The room is ≥4×4×2 m with surfaces ≤10% reflectance, over ≥100 frames on and off; false points are those lying more than 6σ from the walls, where σ is the standard deviation of the measured wall points.
    • It is a direct-view test only: no scattered paths, multiple interferers or synchronized-unit case. For direct view, though, it is not a lenient bar [E]. At its 0.5–2 m spacing the interferer’s 0.05° column takes at least 1+25mm/(8.73×10−4×2m)=151+25\ {\mathrm{mm}}/(8.73\times10^{-4}\times2\ {\mathrm{m}})=15 to 1+25mm/(8.73×10−4×0.5m)=581+25\ {\mathrm{mm}}/(8.73\times10^{-4}\times0.5\ {\mathrm{m}})=58 column periods to cross a 25 mm aperture, against one or two at road distance (§C9). A §C6-class unit without dither or coding, whose foreign bursts then build consistent peaks, would put false points into 520×15/(1.25×106)=0.6%520\times15/(1.25\times10^{6})=0.6\% to 520×58/(1.25×106)=2.4%520\times58/(1.25\times10^{6})=2.4\% of its points in every frame if stray light reaches its whole active column, and fail the ≤0.1% limit. If the light stays within about 2.5° (50 pixels), at most 50×15/(1.25×106)=0.06%50\times15/(1.25\times10^{6})=0.06\% to 50×58/(1.25×106)=0.23%50\times58/(1.25\times10^{6})=0.23\% are hit, and only in frames where the two scans meet: near the limit, which such a unit can exceed at 1 m (50×29.6/(1.25×106)=0.12%50\times29.6/(1.25\times10^{6})=0.12\%) and 0.5 m. At road distance even the column-wide case stays below the limit, at 4×10−44\times10^{-4} to 8×10−48\times10^{-4} (§C9).
  • T/CAAMTB 180-2023 (flash lidar) adds facing, same-direction and infrared-lamp interference tests [P].
  • ISO/FDIS 13228 (FDIS: final draft international standard), Road vehicles — Test method for automotive LiDAR (ISO/TC 22/SC 32, Hesai-led), was at stage 50.00 in Aug 2026, with anti-interference and ghost points in scope [I].
  • IEC 61496-3:2018 (industrial safety scanners) has interference tests between identical 3-D devices [P].
  • DIN SAE SPEC 91571:2026-04 covers adverse conditions from a project whose scope included interference; clauses unverified [T/U].
  • No SAE J-standard or UNECE regulation on lidar interference was found.

Field incidents. None documented: no NHTSA (US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration) record, robotaxi report or Chinese-language report attributes a perception failure to another vehicle’s lidar. The only field-type data are same-vehicle crosstalk and multi-sensor robots. This confirms the measurement gap flagged in §C9.

Net effect on the §C9 judgement. Unchanged, and better anchored:

  • Pre-rejection collisions at the percent level are real.
  • Post-rejection random ghosts become negligible with dither plus a consistency test that needs a peak on three of the ten shots (at most 1.1×10−51.1\times10^{-5} of points in bright sun and dense, fully overlapping traffic); a two-of-ten test is marginal.
  • The residual risks are synchronized identical units (including the untested GPS/PTP-lock case), direct-view saturation, and products without randomization.
  • The Chinese national test checks only one of these, direct view by a same-model unit at 0.5–2 m, which column-wide stray light would fail.
