Sci. 9:2206 (2019) ; https://doi.org/10.1364/OL.384894 ; https://doi.org/10.1109/JSSC.2020.3048074 ; https://doi.org/10.1109/JSEN.2022.3228257 ; Hwang & Lee, IEEE Access 8:124123 (2020) ; Hwang, Yun & Lee, Optik 220:165109 (2020) ; https://doi.org/10.1117/12.3053799 ; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41566-023-01158-4 ; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41566-023-01246-5 ; https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-66787-4_22 ; https://doi.org/10.1109/ISSCC.2018.8310201 ; https://doi.org/10.3390/s26175462 ; https://openstd.samr.gov.cn/bzgk/gb/newGbInfo?hcno=025947B02F32ED0B39F97F04237FB509

C10. Can optical phased arrays compete at high resolution? FPAs, LC metasurfaces, and what “camera-like” resolution is worth

Solid-state beam steering, with no moving parts, has long been a goal for automotive lidar because it promises cheaper and more robust sensors. This section tests the leading chip-scale approach, the optical phased array, against the angular resolution that cars are now being offered, and compares it with focal-plane arrays and liquid-crystal metasurfaces. The short answer is that OPAs are unlikely to be the main long-range automotive lidar this decade, for physical, not only engineering, reasons. Very fine “camera-like” sampling is also cheaper to build with time-of-flight pixel arrays than with coherent receivers. For the market, this bears on which lidar architectures can keep up as resolution specifications rise.

This section asks four linked questions:

  1. Can an integrated optical phased array (OPA) become a real automotive contender, particularly at high angular resolution? An OPA is a photonic chip with many small optical emitters whose relative phases are set electronically, so that their combined beam points in a chosen direction without moving parts.
  2. Are focal-plane arrays (FPAs) a better solid-state route? An FPA is a chip of many switchable transmit/receive cells behind a lens; each point in a lens’s focal plane corresponds to one direction in the scene, so switching on one cell selects one look direction.
  3. How does Lumotive’s reflective liquid-crystal (LC) metasurface work, and where does it fit? It is a reflecting surface patterned with sub-wavelength structures whose optical phase is tuned by a liquid-crystal layer, so it steers the beam reflected from it.
  4. Does the push to “camera-like” lidar create value? Here camera-like means about 0.025–0.03°, an 8 MP camera’s pixel pitch over 120° (§C10.1); vendors’ “2,000+ line” claims go further, since 2,000 rows over a 25° vertical field is a 25∘/2,000=0.0125∘25^\circ/2{,}000=0.0125^\circ pitch.

Figures are published device parameters [P/I] or my own first-principles estimates [E], computed explicitly with stated assumptions so they can be checked or rerun. Coherent detection here means mixing the return with a local oscillator (LO), as in FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous-wave) lidar; ToF means pulsed time-of-flight with direct photon detection, typically on SPADs (single-photon avalanche diodes).

Summary of the verdicts [E]:

  • OPA as the primary long-range automotive lidar [R] (range ≥200 m on a 10%-reflectance target, horizontal field ≥100°, resolution ≤0.1°): unlikely by 2032. The obstacles are physical scaling laws, not only immaturity:
    • degrees of freedom: for a steerer built from element-level controls, the number of directions it can address efficiently is roughly its number of independent controls, while whole-aperture phase ramps (mirror tilt, wavelength sweep) escape this at a cost in dwell, bandwidth or loss (§C10.1);
    • the second steering axis: phase control on both axes needs about 10610^6 shifters at 0.05° over 120° × 25°, and wavelength steering over 25° needs ≈160 nm of tuning on Si (§C10.2, item 2);
    • optical loss, which counts twice in a monostatic design (one that transmits and receives through the same aperture);
    • single-mode receive étendue: a single-mode receiver’s collecting area times its accepted solid angle is only about λ2\lambda^2, the wavelength squared.
  • Where OPAs could matter: as a component (one on-chip axis in a hybrid), in short-range or robotic sensors, or as monostatic coherent sub-apertures.
  • FPAs are the more natural solid-state coherent architecture [NT, mid-range; §C7a]. A lens supplies a large physical aperture without per-element phase control.
    • But the cell count still bounds the mode-equivalent collecting area per look direction. The mode-equivalent collecting area AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} is the effective area with which a single-mode receiver collects light scattered by a diffuse target in one look direction; it is smaller than the lens area because only light matching one spatial mode is detected. For Pointcloud’s coherent FPA (Nature 2026, 1.31 µm), covering its whole field would leave an AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} equal to that of a lens under 1 mm across; the one beam its authors measured has a nominal footprint fraction (defined below) of only ≈1–2% at 11–22 m and gets ≈3.5–5 mm (§C10.3a, item 5).
    • The price is one cell per look direction. At automotive resolution FPAs become area- and readout-bound, so the realistic near-term form is a hybrid or tiled design.
  • LC metasurfaces (Lumotive) are the only non-mechanical beam steerer found in commercial production [D]. A large, free-space-fed aperture could address the solid-state receive problem, collecting many spatial modes from the steered direction (§C10.2, item 6), although no shipping product documents a receive-path metasurface yet (§C10.5). The limits are LC switching speed, one-dimensional steering, cold-temperature response and grating dispersion (the steering angle shifts with wavelength). Shipping products and reference designs reach ≈10–50 m, and one module shown at CES 2026 claims up to 100 m (§C10.5).
  • “Camera-like” resolution has real but narrow value.
    • The value is fine vertical sampling in a band a few degrees wide around the road horizon, for small debris at highway stopping distances, plus pixel-aligned RGB-D fusion (attaching a depth value to each colour-camera pixel). Uniform 2k-line sampling over the whole field adds mainly data volume, with little demonstrated perception benefit.
    • In hardware, the resolution race structurally favours ToF. For SPAD-column ToF (a column of SPAD pixels scanned across the field), finer vertical sampling is paid mainly in cheap parallel pixels and in photons per pixel, not in dwell time or per-channel coherent hardware. That is why the race happened there. For OPA or FMCW, every resolvable direction costs elements, cells or dwell time.
    • In photons, ToF’s advantage narrows. At fixed range and aperture, ToF’s required power scales as 1/Ωcell1/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}} (§C10.3), where Ωcell\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}} is the solid angle of one angular sample. The aperture cannot grow to compensate: at a fixed f-number (focal length divided by aperture diameter) and macro-pixel size a finer pixel angle needs a larger lens, and a behind-glass module holds only about 25–30 mm, so the pixels must shrink instead (§C10.3a, item 7). Ideal full-coverage coherent power does not grow as 1/Ωcell1/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}} (§C10.3; §C10.3a, item 4). The gap does not close at camera-like pitch, however: at the 0.0125° of “2,000+ line” claims, ideal full-coverage coherent detection still needs 4.2–13× ToF’s power (§C10.3).
    • Dense coverage is expensive for single-mode coherent receivers. At a fixed power and channel budget they trade wide field, long range and dense nominal footprint coverage. The nominal footprint fraction is the summed area of the beam spots in one frame divided by the area of the field. Illustrative designs have inferred nominal footprint fractions of about 0.5–4% as quoted (box or FWHM conventions, i.e. counting a spot as the rectangle of its quoted widths or as its full-width-at-half-maximum contour). Taking the quoted widths as FWHM, as the FS-4S datasheet states for its beam, the nominal 1/e² footprint fraction (§C10.3b convention: the spot is bounded where intensity falls to 1/e21/e^2 of its peak) is about 1.6–8%. These are not measured obstacle-detection rates (§C10.3).
  • Measured results (§C10.2b):
    • The best-documented OPA module, Analog Photonics’ FS-4S (2025 datasheet), is specified to reach 200 m at 10% only over 20° × 10°, at 35 W; this is a vendor claim [P].
    • Published actively steered OPA ranging reaches about 20 m to a little over 50 m, including 35 m at 10% for 8,192 elements. 100 m has been shown only on a 90% target, by Jilin University’s OPAs in 2021 and 2022 (§C10.2b; §D7), which is ≈33 m at 10% under R2R^2 scaling (100m×0.1/0.9=33100\ {\mathrm{m}}\times\sqrt{0.1/0.9}=33 m). The scaling holds because an extended diffuse target returns power proportional to ρ/R2\rho/R^2, with ρ\rho the reflectance and RR the range, so equal return needs R∝ρR\propto\sqrt{\rho}.

C10.1 What “high resolution” asks of any steerer

Camera-like resolution means millions of cells per frame, and each resolvable direction needs an independent control. This subsection first counts the cells (angular samples, one point each) that a given sampling pitch implies over a typical 120° × 25° automotive field, and then states the rule that ties the number of directions any steerer can address efficiently to its number of independent controls.

Angular sampling over 120°×25° Cells per axis Cells per frame Points per second at 10 Hz
0.1° 1,200 × 250 0.30 M 3 Mpts/s
0.05° 2,400 × 500 1.2 M 12 Mpts/s
0.025° (“camera-like”) 4,800 × 1,000 4.8 M 48 Mpts/s

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Cells per axis are the field divided by the sampling pitch, e.g. 120∘/0.05∘=2,400120^\circ/0.05^\circ=2{,}400 and 25∘/0.05∘=50025^\circ/0.05^\circ=500.
  • Cells per frame are the product of the two axes, e.g. 2,400×500=1.2×1062{,}400\times500=1.2\times10^{6}.
  • The point rate is cells per frame times the 10 Hz frame rate, e.g. 1.2×106×10s−1=1.2×1071.2\times10^{6}\times10\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=1.2\times10^{7} points per second, written 12 Mpts/s.

For comparison, an 8 MP camera over 120° has 3,840 pixels across, about 0.031° per pixel (120∘/3,840=0.03125∘120^\circ/3{,}840=0.03125^\circ). “Camera-like” lidar therefore means roughly 0.025–0.03°.

A degrees-of-freedom rule links every steerer built from independent element-level controls [E; standard antenna theory]:

  • A phased aperture with NN independently phased elements can efficiently form about NN resolvable directions at one wavelength. This is the space–bandwidth product: the number of independent spots is the angular range the aperture can steer over divided by its beamwidth, and both are set by the element layout.
    • Controls that impose a whole phase ramp can address many more states per control, at a cost in bandwidth, loss or dwell. Examples are mirror tilt, a wavelength sweep through a dispersive grating, and row–column addressing (§C10.3a, item 5, limit (b): the steering space–bandwidth product).
  • Filled periodic array. Let the elements sit at a regular pitch dd (centre-to-centre spacing), so that NN elements span an aperture NdNd, and let λ\lambda be the wavelength. Such an array forms grating lobes, unwanted copies of the main beam in other directions, once it is steered too far for its pitch. Steered over its full grating-lobe-free range, it resolves about as many spots as it has elements: the usable FOV (field of view) is ≈λ/d\approx\lambda/d in sine space (measured in sin⁡θ\sin\theta, where θ\theta is the steering angle), the beamwidth is ≈λ/(Nd)\approx\lambda/(Nd), and their ratio is NN.
  • Sparse array. Spreading N<NspotN<N_{\mathrm{spot}} elements over a larger aperture to get NspotN_{\mathrm{spot}} narrower spots leaves only a fraction of the power in the main lobe. The rest goes into sidelobes, the weaker secondary maxima of the far-field pattern outside the main beam:
    • Normalize the intensity radiated by one element to 1. The peak intensity is then N2N^2, because the fields of NN elements add in phase in the main-lobe direction, while the angle-averaged intensity is NN, because elsewhere their random phases add in power. Measured in units of the full steering range, the main lobe is 1/Nspot1/N_{\mathrm{spot}} wide, so it carries power N2/NspotN^2/N_{\mathrm{spot}} out of a total of NN, a main-lobe power fraction of N/NspotN/N_{\mathrm{spot}}. The mean sidelobe level is N/N2=1/NN/N^2=1/N of the peak: 10log⁡10(1/128)=−2110\log_{10}(1/128)=-21 dB for N=128N=128 and 10log⁡10(1/256)=−2410\log_{10}(1/256)=-24 dB for N=256N=256, as the Monte Carlo below finds.
    • A Monte Carlo check [E] placed NN isotropic elements independently and uniformly at random over an aperture L=Nspotλ/2L=N_{\mathrm{spot}}\lambda/2: 570λ=0.88570\lambda=0.88 mm for N=128N=128 and Nspot=1,140N_{\mathrm{spot}}=1{,}140, and 860λ=1.33860\lambda=1.33 mm for N=256N=256 and Nspot=1,720N_{\mathrm{spot}}=1{,}720, at 1.55 µm. It evaluated the far field over all of visible space, sin⁡θ\sin\theta from −1 to 1, which holds Nspot=2L/λN_{\mathrm{spot}}=2L/\lambda beamwidths, and counted the main lobe out to its first nulls, |sin⁡θ|<λ/L|\sin\theta|<\lambda/L. Over 200 trials it gave 9.2% main-lobe power for N=128N=128 (N/Nspot=11%N/N_{\mathrm{spot}}=11\%), with a peak sidelobe of −11.5 dB and a mean sidelobe of −21 dB, and 11.8% (N/Nspot=15%N/N_{\mathrm{spot}}=15\%), −13.0 dB and −24 dB for N=256N=256. Both fractions match the expectation 0.90N/(Nspot+N)0.90\,N/(N_{\mathrm{spot}}+N), 9.1% and 11.7%: 90% of the main lobe lies inside its first nulls, and the main lobe’s own power adds to the total.
    • The peak sidelobes are set mostly by the near-in −13.3 dB sidelobe of the aperture envelope (the first sidelobe of a uniformly illuminated aperture), not by the random floor. As expected, they improve only weakly with NN (1.5 dB, against 3 dB for the mean).
  • Consequence: sparse or aperiodic arrays cannot circumvent the element count at lidar dynamic ranges (the ratio between the brightest and faintest returns a lidar must handle, about 58 dB in §C10.2, item 4). The rule applies equally to OPAs (phase shifters), LC metasurfaces (drive electrodes, §C10.5) and FPAs (cells).

C10.2 OPA physics at high resolution: seven constraints

The phase-steered axis is no longer the barrier. The second axis, calibration, sidelobes, loss, receive étendue and point rate are. This subsection works through seven physical constraints that an OPA must meet at automotive resolution, each with an explicit estimate. Together they explain why OPAs remain far from a long-range automotive product even though chips with thousands of elements exist.

1. Element count per on-chip axis [E, λ=1550\lambda=1550 nm, uniform aperture FWHM 0.886λ/D0.886\lambda/D]. Along the phase-steered axis, three quantities fix the design: the largest element pitch dd that keeps grating lobes out of the field, the aperture length DD that gives the required beamwidth θB\theta_{\mathrm{B}} (full width at half maximum, FWHM, in radians), and the resulting element count NN:

d≤λ2sin⁡(FOV/2),D=0.886λθB,N=Ddd\le\frac{\lambda}{2\sin(\mathrm{FOV}/2)},\qquad D=\frac{0.886\,\lambda}{\theta_{\mathrm{B}}},\qquad N=\frac{D}{d}(135)

Here FOV is the full alias-free field of view along that axis, and 0.886 is the FWHM of the far-field pattern of a uniformly illuminated aperture in units of λ/D\lambda/D. The table evaluates Eq. (135) for three fields and three beamwidths θB\theta_{\mathrm{B}}.

Alias-free FOV (no grating lobe inside the FOV) Max pitch λ/(2sin⁡FOV2)\lambda/(2\sin\tfrac{\mathrm{FOV}}{2}) Beamwidth θB=0.1∘\theta_{\mathrm{B}}=0.1^\circ: aperture / elements θB=0.05∘\theta_{\mathrm{B}}=0.05^\circ θB=0.025∘\theta_{\mathrm{B}}=0.025^\circ
60° 1.55 µm 0.79 mm / 510 1.57 mm / 1,015 3.15 mm / 2,030
100° 1.01 µm 0.79 mm / 780 1.57 mm / 1,560 3.15 mm / 3,110
120° 0.89 µm 0.79 mm / 880 1.57 mm / 1,760 3.15 mm / 3,520

How the numbers are derived [E], term by term from Eq. (135):

  • Maximum pitch: when the beam is steered to one field edge, the first grating lobe sits at sin⁡θg=sin⁡FOV2−λ/d\sin\theta_g=\sin\tfrac{\mathrm{FOV}}{2}-\lambda/d, where θg\theta_g is the grating-lobe direction. Keeping it beyond the opposite edge needs sin⁡FOV2−λ/d≤−sin⁡FOV2\sin\tfrac{\mathrm{FOV}}{2}-\lambda/d\le-\sin\tfrac{\mathrm{FOV}}{2}, i.e. d≤λ/(2sin⁡FOV2)d\le\lambda/(2\sin\tfrac{\mathrm{FOV}}{2}). For 100°: 1.55μm/(2sin⁡50∘)=1.55/1.532=1.01μm1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(2\sin50^\circ)=1.55/1.532=1.01\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}.
  • Aperture: a uniform aperture of length DD has a FWHM beamwidth θB=0.886λ/D\theta_{\mathrm{B}}=0.886\lambda/D, so D=0.886λ/θBD=0.886\lambda/\theta_{\mathrm{B}}. For 0.1° (1.745×10−31.745\times10^{-3} rad): D=0.886×1.55μm/1.745×10−3=0.79D=0.886\times1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/1.745\times10^{-3}=0.79 mm. Halving the beamwidth doubles DD.
  • Elements: N=D/dN=D/d. For a 100° field at 0.1°: 0.787mm/1.012μm≈7800.787\ {\mathrm{mm}}/1.012\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}\approx780.

Two refinements [E]:

  • Stricter pitch. Excluding grating lobes from all visible space (every real angle from −90° to +90°), not just the FOV, needs d≤λ/(1+sin⁡FOV2)d\le\lambda/(1+\sin\tfrac{\mathrm{FOV}}{2}): 1.03, 0.88 and 0.83 µm for the three FOVs, i.e. 1.5×, 1.15× and 1.08× more elements. The element count scales as 1/d1/d, so the factor is (1+sin⁡FOV2)/(2sin⁡FOV2)(1+\sin\tfrac{\mathrm{FOV}}{2})/(2\sin\tfrac{\mathrm{FOV}}{2}); for 60° it is 1.5/1.0=1.51.5/1.0=1.5.
  • Field-edge beamwidth. The beamwidths above are at broadside (perpendicular to the array). A steered beam widens as 1/cos1/\cos of the steering angle, because the aperture looks shorter when seen obliquely, so holding the beamwidth at the field edge costs a further 1/cos⁡(FOV2)1/\cos(\tfrac{\mathrm{FOV}}{2}) in aperture and elements: 1/cos⁡30∘=1.151/\cos30^\circ=1.15, 1/cos⁡50∘=1.561/\cos50^\circ=1.56 and 1/cos⁡60∘=21/\cos60^\circ=2.

A 1D element count in the thousands is no longer the barrier: an 8,192-element, 1 µm-pitch OPA has been demonstrated (§C7) [P].

2. The second axis is the hard part.

  • 2D phase control for 2,400×500 spots (0.05° over 120° × 25°) would need about 2,400×500=1.2×1062{,}400\times500=1.2\times10^{6} phase shifters [E]. The largest integrated 2D phased arrays with a phase control per element found for this report are far smaller: 128 emitters in a waveguide-fed silicon chip (Fatemi et al., IEEE JSSC 2019) and 160 × 160 = 25,600 MEMS-actuated grating phase shifters in a free-space-fed chip with a 6.6° × 4.4° field (Wang et al., Optica 2019) [I], about 9,400 and 47 times fewer (1.2×106/1281.2\times10^{6}/128 and 1.2×106/25,6001.2\times10^{6}/25{,}600). Liquid-crystal-on-silicon modulators have millions of phase pixels but respond in milliseconds [I, as cited by Wang et al.].

  • The standard answer is wavelength steering with grating emitters. A grating emitter is a waveguide with a periodic corrugation of period Λ\Lambda that leaks light out at an angle θ\theta given by the grating equation sin⁡θ=neff−λ/Λ\sin\theta=n_{\mathrm{eff}}-\lambda/\Lambda, where λ\lambda is the wavelength and neffn_{\mathrm{eff}} the effective index of the guided mode (the refractive index the light “sees” in the waveguide). Tuning the laser therefore steers the beam along the second axis. Differentiating the grating equation with respect to λ\lambda, and writing ng=neff−λdneff/dλn_g=n_{\mathrm{eff}}-\lambda\,dn_{\mathrm{eff}}/d\lambda, gives the magnitude of the steering rate dθ/dλd\theta/d\lambda (radians of beam angle per nanometre of wavelength change):

    dθdλ=ng−sin⁡θλcos⁡θ≈ngλ(θ≈0)\frac{d\theta}{d\lambda}=\frac{n_g-\sin\theta}{\lambda\cos\theta}\approx\frac{n_g}{\lambda}\quad(\theta\approx0)(136)

    Here ngn_g, the group index of the waveguide, is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of a light pulse in the guide. Near normal emission Eq. (136) gives [E]:

    • Si waveguides (ng≈4.2n_g\approx4.2): ng/λ=4.2/1550nm=2.7×10−3n_g/\lambda=4.2/1550\ {\mathrm{nm}}=2.7\times10^{-3} rad/nm, about 0.155°/nm, so 25° needs about 25/0.155≈25/0.155\approx 160 nm of tuning and 10° about 10/0.155≈6410/0.155\approx64 nm;
    • SiN (ng≈2n_g\approx2): 2/1550nm=1.29×10−32/1550\ {\mathrm{nm}}=1.29\times10^{-3} rad/nm, about 0.074°/nm, so 25° needs about 25/0.074≈25/0.074\approx 340 nm and 10° about 135 nm.

  • The laser must therefore be widely tunable, linearly chirped, cheap and narrow in linewidth at once. Linewidth is the spectral width of the laser; it limits the coherence length and hence the range over which the return can still be mixed coherently with the LO. A 1–3 dB coherent loss at 300 m allows ≲18–55 kHz (§C7b subsection 2(e)); Waymo’s design value of ≲60–120 kHz at 250 m accepts a 2.7–5.5 dB loss (§C7a(f); §C10.3). Linearly chirped means that the laser frequency sweeps linearly in time, as FMCW requires. Such a laser is the least mature component in the architecture [E].

  • The FMCW chirp itself barely steers the beam. A chirp of bandwidth BB (the frequency range it sweeps) changes the wavelength by Δλ=λ2B/c\Delta\lambda=\lambda^2B/c, with cc the speed of light. A 1–5 GHz chirp is therefore 8–40 pm ((1.55μm)2×1GHz/c=8(1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}})^2\times1\ {\mathrm{GHz}}/c=8 pm for 1 GHz), which at 0.155°/nm moves a Si-grating beam only 0.155×0.008=0.001∘0.155\times0.008=0.001^\circ to 0.155×0.040=0.006∘0.155\times0.040=0.006^\circ.

  • Alternatives, each with a cost: slow-light or dispersion-engineered gratings (waveguides designed for a high group index, giving more °/nm, but with narrower bandwidth and higher loss); several lasers or bands; switched banks of gratings with different periods; or a slow mechanical second axis (the Voyant Carbon type of hybrid).

3. Phase control, calibration and temperature.

  • Power and area. Thermo-optic shifters (small heaters that change a waveguide’s refractive index, and hence its phase, by warming it) draw milliwatts each, so 2,000 elements means watts. Electro-optic thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) shifters, which change the index with an applied voltage, draw almost no power but are millimetres long, so they trade those watts for chip area (§C8.2).

  • Phase errors (Monte Carlo, N=256N=256–1,024 [E]):

    • The ideal uniform array puts 90% of its power in the main lobe (measured null to null, i.e. between the first zeros either side of the peak). The Strehl factor e−σ2e^{-\sigma^2} is the fraction of peak intensity kept when uncorrelated phase errors of rms σ\sigma (in radians) are present. For a residual random phase error of σ=0.3\sigma=0.3 rad it is e−0.09=0.914e^{-0.09}=0.914, which lowers the main-lobe share to 82% (0.90×0.914=0.820.90\times0.914=0.82), as the Monte Carlo finds.
    • The diffuse sidelobe floor (the power scattered by the errors into all other directions, relative to the main-lobe peak) scales as about σ2/N\sigma^2/N, roughly −40 dB at N=1,024N=1{,}024 (0.09/1,024=8.8×10−50.09/1{,}024=8.8\times10^{-5}, i.e. −40.6 dB).

  • Temperature drift of the grating emission angle is a separate, systematic effect [E]. The emission angle depends on the effective index neffn_{\mathrm{eff}} of the guided mode (item 2), and neffn_{\mathrm{eff}} changes with temperature at a rate dneff/dTdn_{\mathrm{eff}}/dT (the thermo-optic coefficient of the mode, per kelvin). At fixed wavelength the grating equation gives cos⁡θΔθ=Δneff\cos\theta\,\Delta\theta=\Delta n_{\mathrm{eff}}, hence the angle drift Δθ\Delta\theta for a temperature change ΔT\Delta T. Dividing it by the steering rate of Eq. (136) gives the wavelength change Δλcomp\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{comp}} needed per kelvin to hold the angle:

    Δθ≈Δneffcos⁡θ=(dneff/dT)ΔTcos⁡θ,ΔλcompΔT≈λ(dneff/dT)ng\Delta\theta\approx\frac{\Delta n_{\mathrm{eff}}}{\cos\theta}=\frac{(dn_{\mathrm{eff}}/dT)\,\Delta T}{\cos\theta},\qquad \frac{\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{comp}}}{\Delta T}\approx\frac{\lambda\,(dn_{\mathrm{eff}}/dT)}{n_g}(137)

    • Si: assuming dneff/dT≈1.6×10−4K−1dn_{\mathrm{eff}}/dT\approx1.6\times10^{-4}\ {\mathrm{K^{-1}}} near normal emission (cos⁡θ≈1\cos\theta\approx1), Δθ/ΔT≈1.6×10−4\Delta\theta/\Delta T\approx1.6\times10^{-4} rad/K, about 0.009°/K, i.e. about 0.0092×145K≈0.0092\times145\ {\mathrm{K}}\approx 1.3° over −40 to +105 °C, or about 26 cells at 0.05° (1.3∘/0.05∘=261.3^\circ/0.05^\circ=26);
    • SiN: assuming dneff/dT≈2.2×10−5K−1dn_{\mathrm{eff}}/dT\approx2.2\times10^{-5}\ {\mathrm{K^{-1}}}, about 0.0012°/K, i.e. about 0.00126×145≈0.18∘0.00126\times145\approx0.18^\circ.
    • Closed-loop wavelength and phase compensation is therefore mandatory, especially on Si.

  • Compensation uses up tuning range [E]. On Si, holding the angle needs, from the second relation in Eq. (137), Δλ≈λ(dneff/dT)/ng≈1550nm×1.6×10−4/4.2≈0.059\Delta\lambda\approx\lambda\,(dn_{\mathrm{eff}}/dT)/n_g\approx1550\ {\mathrm{nm}}\times1.6\times10^{-4}/4.2\approx0.059 nm/K, about 0.059×145≈8.60.059\times145\approx8.6 nm over −40 to +105 °C. That is 8.6/60=14%8.6/60=14\% of the 60 nm of RAY-H1 (Analog Photonics’ laser, §C10.2b), or 8.6/120=7%8.6/120=7\% of the 8,192-element array’s 120 nm. The whole C+L band (the conventional and long-wavelength telecom bands, ≈95 nm together) gives only ≈13–15° of steering on Si (95nm×0.1495\ {\mathrm{nm}}\times0.14 to 0.155∘/nm0.155^\circ/{\mathrm{nm}}) and ≈7° on SiN (95×0.07495\times0.074).

4. Sidelobes vs lidar dynamic range.

  • A uniformly weighted aperture has a first sidelobe at −13.3 dB. Amplitude tapering (driving the elements near the array edges more weakly than those at the centre) reaches about −25 to −30 dB at the cost of a wider beam.

  • Estimated dynamic range needed [E]: a retroreflective sign (RA≈500R_A\approx500 cd·lx⁻¹·m⁻²) at 30 m is about 58 dB brighter than a 10% Lambertian target at 200 m. RAR_A is the coefficient of retroreflection: the luminous intensity sent back toward the source per unit of illuminance on the sign and per unit sign area. In radiometric terms it is the returned intensity per watt of incident power, in sr⁻¹. Assume that both targets fill the beam, that the sign’s visible-band RAR_A holds at the lidar wavelength, and normal incidence. Then each return scales as the target’s radiant-intensity coefficient (returned intensity per incident watt) divided by the square of its range, so

    PsignPfar=RAρ/π(RfarRsign)2\frac{P_{\mathrm{sign}}}{P_{\mathrm{far}}}=\frac{R_A}{\rho/\pi}\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{far}}}{R_{\mathrm{sign}}}\right)^2(138)

    where PsignP_{\mathrm{sign}} and PfarP_{\mathrm{far}} are the received powers from the sign and the far target, ρ\rho is the far target’s reflectance, and Rsign=30R_{\mathrm{sign}}=30 m and Rfar=200R_{\mathrm{far}}=200 m are the ranges. A Lambertian (perfectly diffuse) surface at normal incidence has ρ/π=0.1/π=0.032sr−1\rho/\pi=0.1/\pi=0.032\ {\mathrm{sr^{-1}}} and the sign 500sr−1500\ {\mathrm{sr^{-1}}}, so the ratio is (500/0.032)×(200/30)2=1.6×104×44=7×105(500/0.032)\times(200/30)^2=1.6\times10^{4}\times44=7\times10^{5}, i.e. 58 dB. A ghost from a sidelobe landing on the sign must stay below the real far return.

  • The monostatic advantage [E]: a monostatic coherent OPA, transmitting and receiving through the same aperture, applies its sidelobe pattern twice, so about −29 dB one-way suffices (58/2=2958/2=29).

    • Measured devices fall well short. Measured one-way suppression of 10–19 dB (§C10.2b) gives only 20–38 dB two-way, which leaves the 58 dB retroreflector case 38 dB short (10 dB devices) to 20 dB short (19 dB devices).
    • Vernier Tx/Rx designs (Jilin) give less ghost rejection in the transmit grating-lobe directions. A Vernier design gives the transmit and receive arrays slightly different pitches, so that their grating lobes point in different directions and are suppressed in the combined pattern. The transmit lobe there is at 0 dB, so ghost rejection rests entirely on the receive sidelobe level of roughly −13 to −21 dB.
    • The 58 dB figure is a floor. Retroreflection RAR_A is specified at a 0.2° observation angle (the angle between the illumination and viewing directions); monostatic returns sit near 0°, where retroreflection is stronger.

  • The bistatic problem. An OPA transmitter paired with a separate ToF receiver (a bistatic design, with separate transmit and receive apertures) gets only one-way suppression, and −58 dB one-way is not realistic. Ghosts must then be removed in processing.

5. Loss and power handling. In a monostatic design every dB of OPA loss counts twice, because the light passes through the OPA once on the way out and once on the way back.

  • Link-budget example [E]. The number of detected signal photons NsN_s from one sample (one chirp or pulse) is the number of transmitted photons, times the fraction of them that a Lambertian target scatters into the receive mode, times the detection efficiency, times the OPA’s one-way transmission squared:

    Ns=EptEphρAmodeπR2ηηOPA2N_s=\frac{E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}\,\frac{\rho A_{\mathrm{mode}}}{\pi R^2}\,\eta\,\eta_{\mathrm{OPA}}^2(139)

    Here EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} is the optical energy transmitted toward one point, Eph=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda the photon energy (1.28×10−191.28\times10^{-19} J at 1550 nm), ρ\rho the target’s diffuse reflectance, RR the range, AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} the mode-equivalent collecting area (the effective area with which a single-mode receiver collects light scattered by a diffuse target, including its single-polarization and truncation factors), η\eta the end-to-end efficiency of the rest of the chain (optics × detector × mixing, without polarization or mode shape, which sit in AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}) and ηOPA\eta_{\mathrm{OPA}} the OPA’s one-way power transmission.

    • Assumptions: a cell-filling 0.05°×0.05° beam (the full-coverage case of §C10.3); a 10% Lambertian target at 200 m that fills the beam, at normal incidence, in clear air; that beam’s mode-equivalent collecting area Amode=t22λ2/Ωcell=0.419×(1.55μm)2/(8.73×10−4rad)2=0.419×3.15mm2=1.32A_{\mathrm{mode}}=\tfrac{t^2}{2}\lambda^2/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}=0.419\times(1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}})^2/(8.73\times10^{-4}\ {\mathrm{rad}})^2=0.419\times3.15\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}=1.32 mm², where Ωcell\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}} is the solid angle of one 0.05° cell (8.73×10−48.73\times10^{-4} rad on a side) and t2/2=0.419t^2/2=0.419 is the Gaussian model’s round-trip truncation factor t2=0.838t^2=0.838 times the single-polarization factor ½ (§C10.3b, Result 2), with tt the fraction of a Gaussian beam’s power that the finite aperture passes one way; 1 W for 5 µs; and η=0.8\eta=0.8, the detector’s quantum efficiency with ideal mixing: the OPA’s optical loss is counted separately in ηOPA\eta_{\mathrm{OPA}}, so the design value 0.25 of §C0 subsection 10.1, which already contains a free-space chain’s optics loss, would count it twice. The polarization factor ½ assumes a depolarizing target, which returns half its light in the polarization of the receive mode; a retroreflector largely preserves polarization, so the factor then differs.
    • The 5 µJ sample carries 5μJ/(1.28×10−19J)=3.9×10135\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}/(1.28\times10^{-19}\ {\mathrm{J}})=3.9\times10^{13} photons, and a Lambertian return delivers the fraction ρAmode/(πR2)=0.1×1.32mm2/(π×(200m)2)=1.05×10−12\rho A_{\mathrm{mode}}/(\pi R^2)=0.1\times1.32\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}/(\pi\times(200\ {\mathrm{m}})^2)=1.05\times10^{-12} of them to the mode. That gives about 41 photons in the mode before the efficiency and the OPA’s loss (3.9×1013×1.05×10−12=413.9\times10^{13}\times1.05\times10^{-12}=41), and 41×0.8=32.841\times0.8=32.8 after the efficiency.
    • After one-way OPA losses of 1, 3 and 7 dB, about 21, 8.2 and 1.3 photons are detected. The monostatic path applies each loss twice, so the factors ηOPA2\eta_{\mathrm{OPA}}^2 are 10−0.210^{-0.2}, 10−0.610^{-0.6} and 10−1.410^{-1.4}: 32.8×0.631=20.732.8\times0.631=20.7, 32.8×0.251=8.2332.8\times0.251=8.23 and 32.8×0.0398=1.3132.8\times0.0398=1.31.

  • Speckle raises the requirement. A rough target produces a speckle pattern, a random interference pattern of bright and dark spots. A single-mode receiver samples one speckle, whose power is exponentially distributed (Rayleigh-distributed amplitude), so the return sometimes fades deeply. For a detection probability PD=0.9P_D=0.9 at a per-bin false-alarm probability p=10−6p=10^{-6}, one look needs a mean of about 130 detected photons. This assumes shot-noise-limited coherent detection: the local oscillator’s shot noise dominates and thermal and dark-current noise are neglected, which at 105–125 °C holds only approximately (§C4c gives 82–94% of the shot-noise limit for Ge at 125 °C). With the detection threshold xthx_{\mathrm{th}} expressed in units of the mean noise power, and n‾\bar n the mean number of detected signal photons, p=e−xthp=e^{-x_{\mathrm{th}}} and PD=e−xth/(1+n‾)P_D=e^{-x_{\mathrm{th}}/(1+\bar n)}, the single-speckle detection law of Eq. (46) (§C0 subsection 10.3). Hence n‾=ln⁡p/ln⁡PD−1=13.8/0.105−1≈130\bar n=\ln p/\ln P_D-1=13.8/0.105-1\approx130, using −ln⁡10−6=13.8-\ln10^{-6}=13.8 and −ln⁡0.9=0.105-\ln0.9=0.105.

    • With polarization, wavelength or spatial diversity, the required total, summed over LL independent, incoherently added looks, is 61, 45 and 42 for L=2L=2, 4 and 8, or 30, 11 and 5.3 per look. These use the same threshold rule with the looks summed. The sum of LL independent exponential variables follows a gamma distribution with shape LL; the noise sum’s 10−610^{-6} tail sets the threshold, and the per-look mean n‾L\bar n_L is raised until a gamma sum with shape LL and scale 1+n‾L1+\bar n_L exceeds that threshold 90% of the time.
    • A non-fading return needs about 21. For a constant signal the detection probability is the Marcum Q-function Q1(a,b)Q_1(a,b): the probability that the envelope of a constant signal of normalized amplitude aa plus complex Gaussian noise exceeds a normalized threshold bb. With a=2n‾a=\sqrt{2\bar n}, b=2xthb=\sqrt{2x_{\mathrm{th}}} and xth=ln⁡106=13.8x_{\mathrm{th}}=\ln10^{6}=13.8, Q1=0.9Q_1=0.9 at n‾=20.8\bar n=20.8 [E].
    • These are single-bin figures at 10−610^{-6} per bin. The report’s per-point rule is stricter: at most 10−310^{-3} false points per point over a 0–300 m search, with the echo’s peak found in both chirp ramps (§C0 subsection 10.3). It raises the requirements to ≈259 detected photons for one look, 120 for two, 88.5 for four, 82 for eight and 39 for a non-fading return. The 120 for two looks is not the 120 of the §C7a model, which is the four-look requirement of 88.5 with a 1.36× margin. The power figures below use these per-point values.

  • A long-range OPA therefore needs:

    • about 11–31 W per beam at 5 µs of integration and 3 dB one-way loss [E], if the looks share one receive mode (wavelength or time diversity): ≈11 W for four-look and ≈31 W for single-look detection, or ≈1.0–2.9 kW for 92 beams at 12 Mpts/s. With polarization or spatial diversity each look adds a receive mode, which cuts the four-look figure about 4×, to ≈2.7 W per beam (≈250 W for 92 beams). At 3 dB one-way loss, 1 W for 5 µs yields 8.23 detected photons, so 88.5 photons need 88.5/8.23=10.888.5/8.23=10.8 W and 259 need 259/8.23=31.5259/8.23=31.5 W. Each beam emits that power for its whole dwell, the 5 µs of integration plus the two round trips, Tdwell=5μs+2.67μs=7.67T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=5\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}+2.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=7.67 µs at 200 m (§C7b, Eq. (111); item 7 below), so 12 Mpts/s needs 12×106s−1×7.67μs=9212\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times7.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=92 beams, hence 92×10.8≈99092\times10.8\approx990 W to 92×31.5≈2,90092\times31.5\approx2{,}900 W, and 92×10.8/4≈25092\times10.8/4\approx250 W with one receive mode per look;
    • a waveguide platform that carries ≈3–31 W per beam: Si trunks (the input waveguides that carry the full power before it is split among elements) are limited by two-photon absorption, a nonlinear loss that grows with intensity (§C8.2), whereas SiN handles watts (the Si–SiN chip of §C10.2b takes 20 W in, against the 11–31 W per beam of looks that share one receive mode);
    • no more than about 3 dB one-way loss;
    • on-chip diversity.

  • Current integrated OPAs do not combine these (open verification items in Appendix 1). In practical terms, full-field coverage by a long-range OPA would need about 1.0–2.9 kW of optical power at 3 dB one-way loss (≈0.25 kW if every look has its own receive mode), together with loss and diversity figures that no integrated chip has yet shown at once.

6. Receive étendue: an OPA collects only one spatial mode. A long-range direct-detection (ToF) receiver needs a large multimode aperture looking along the beam, and an OPA does not provide one.

  • A monostatic OPA is a single-mode antenna (ArxΩ≈λ2A_{\mathrm{rx}}\Omega\approx\lambda^2, §C7): its receive area ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} times the solid angle Ω\Omega it accepts, its étendue, is only about one wavelength squared.
  • A bistatic design (OPA transmitter plus a wide-field staring SPAD receiver, one that views the whole field at once) inherits exactly the staring-array étendue penalty of §C6.
  • A monostatic coherent design avoids the staring penalty because its receive mode tracks the beam. But it collects only one spatial mode per polarization per channel (§C10.3a, item 5, limit (a): receive modes per unit time).
  • Only a large-aperture free-space steerer on receive (§C10.5), or a scanned multimode receiver, keeps multimode collection.

7. Point rate. A single-beam FMCW OPA is limited to about 1/Tdwell1/T_{\mathrm{dwell}}, where the dwell Tdwell=Tint+2τT_{\mathrm{dwell}}=T_{\mathrm{int}}+2\tau is how long the beam stays on one point (§C7b, Eq. (111)): the integration time TintT_{\mathrm{int}}, the useful windows of an up- and a down-ramp, plus the round trip τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c that opens each ramp before the echo arrives, 2τ=2×2×200m/(3×108ms−1)=2.672\tau=2\times2\times200\ {\mathrm{m}}/(3\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}})=2.67 µs at 200 m. At 2–10 µs of integration that is 0.079–0.21 Mpts/s (1/(10+2.67)μs=1/12.67μs=0.0791/(10+2.67)\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=1/12.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=0.079 Mpts/s and 1/(2+2.67)μs=1/4.67μs=0.211/(2+2.67)\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=1/4.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=0.21 Mpts/s).

  • One sample per 0.05° cell over the full field (12 Mpts/s) would need 56–152 parallel coherent channels at 2–10 µs of integration. The number of channels is the required point rate Ṅ\dot N times the dwell: Nch=ṄTdwell=12×106s−1×4.67μs=56N_{\mathrm{ch}}=\dot N\,T_{\mathrm{dwell}}=12\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times4.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=56, and 12×106s−1×12.67μs=15212\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times12.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=152 at 10 µs of integration.

  • Each channel needs its own receiver and digitizer. For a single ramp, the beat at 300 m is 0.2 GHz at 10 µs and 1 GHz at 2 µs, which needs 0.4–2 GS/s (gigasamples per second) of real sampling, as derived next. In FMCW, the beat frequency fbf_b is the difference between the return and LO frequencies; for a linear chirp of bandwidth BB lasting TT (chirp rate κ=B/T\kappa=B/T, in Hz/s), a target at range RR and radial speed vv gives

    fb=2κRc=2BRcT,fD=2vλf_b=\frac{2\kappa R}{c}=\frac{2BR}{cT},\qquad f_D=\frac{2v}{\lambda}(140)

    where fDf_D is the Doppler shift, which moves the beat up or down with target motion, cc the speed of light and λ\lambda the wavelength. A shorter chirp raises the beat frequency: for B=1B=1 GHz, fb=2×109×300m/(3×108ms−1×10μs)=0.2f_b=2\times10^{9}\times300\ {\mathrm{m}}/(3\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}\times10\ \mu{\mathrm{s}})=0.2 GHz for a 10 µs chirp and about 1 GHz for a 2 µs chirp. Real sampling needs at least twice the beat frequency (the Nyquist criterion), hence 0.4–2 GS/s. If the integration time is split into an up-ramp and a down-ramp, as the dwell above assumes, each ramp’s useful window is half as long, so by Eq. (140) the beat frequency and the sampling rate double, to 0.4–2 GHz and 0.8–4 GS/s. Doppler adds about ±0.1 GHz: from the Doppler term of Eq. (140), ±0.1 GHz covers radial speeds up to 0.1GHz×0.775μm=780.1\ {\mathrm{GHz}}\times0.775\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=78 m/s, with λ/2=0.775\lambda/2=0.775 µm at 1550 nm.

  • One sample per cell is not full nominal coverage: a 20 mm aperture gives a nominal 1/e² footprint fraction of ≈2.1% at 200 m (§C10.3b). That is, the beam spots, bounded where intensity falls to 1/e21/e^2 of the peak, cover only about 2% of the field in each frame.

  • Multi-beam OPAs are possible, for example with wavelength-multiplexed rows, but they do not remove the per-channel cost.

C10.2b What has been built: measured OPA state of the art

This subsection compares devices that have actually been built and measured with the degrees-of-freedom rule of §C10.1 and the constraints of §C10.2; seven findings follow the table. Measured devices bear out §C10.2: the phase axis scales, but loss, sidelobes, the wavelength axis and ranging distance fall far short of automotive needs. The table lists record or representative devices with their measured figures. [S] marks a value taken from a peer-reviewed review table (mainly the 2025 npj Nanophotonics OPA review and the Pointcloud Nature 2026 comparison table) rather than from the original paper.

How to read the table: sidelobe suppression is the ratio, in dB, of the main-lobe peak to the strongest sidelobe (larger is better); main-lobe power is the fraction of emitted power that goes into the main beam; loss is counted, where the source defines it, from the optical input to the power in the main lobe. EO and PN shifters are electro-optic phase shifters (PN: a silicon p–n junction), CW is continuous-wave input, and TX/RX denote the transmit and receive arrays.

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Analog Photonics 512: the phase-axis aperture is 512×1.65μm=0.84512\times1.65\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}=0.84 mm, and a uniform aperture’s FWHM is 0.886λ/D=0.886×1.55μm/0.84mm=1.6×10−30.886\lambda/D=0.886\times1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/0.84\ {\mathrm{mm}}=1.6\times10^{-3} rad =0.093∘=0.093^\circ, which is why the <0.04° figure is attributed to the grating axis.
  • Losses in decibels are 10log⁡10(Pin/Pout)10\log_{10}(P_{\mathrm{in}}/P_{\mathrm{out}}): ZJU 10log⁡10(20/1.5)=11.210\log_{10}(20/1.5)=11.2 dB; imec 10log⁡10(60/3.7)=12.110\log_{10}(60/3.7)=12.1 dB; Jilin 25−11=1425-11=14 dB.
  • ZJU driver power: about 1 mW per element times 4,096 elements is 4.1 W.
  • Analog Photonics 9,216: by Eq. (135) a 50° alias-free field allows a pitch of at most 1.55μm/(2sin⁡25∘)=1.831.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(2\sin25^\circ)=1.83 µm. All 9,216 elements on one phase axis would then span 7.1–16.9 mm (pitch λ/2=0.775\lambda/2=0.775 µm to 1.83 µm), with a FWHM of 0.886λ/D=0.011∘0.886\lambda/D=0.011^\circ to 0.886×1.55μm/16.9mm=8.1×10−50.886\times1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/16.9\ {\mathrm{mm}}=8.1\times10^{-5} rad =0.005∘=0.005^\circ. The listed 0.05° is about 5–11 times wider, so it cannot be the phase-axis beamwidth of a single 9,216-element row; which axis it describes is not stated.

Seven concrete findings [E unless tagged]:

  1. The phase axis is no longer the barrier. Element counts of 10³–10⁴ at λ/2–1 µm pitch exist. The 8,192-element array resolves about 8,100 spots over its 100° phase axis: its 8.19 mm aperture spans 8.19mm×2sin⁡50∘/1.55μm≈8,1008.19\ {\mathrm{mm}}\times2\sin50^\circ/1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}\approx8{,}100 beamwidths in sine space, close to its element count, as the rule of §C10.1 predicts (dividing by the broadside beamwidth instead, 100∘/0.01∘100^\circ/0.01^\circ, gives 10410^{4}). Multi-reticle stitching of more than 49,152 elements (24 OPAs combined coherently over four reticles) has been reported in a conference abstract [I], without ranging.
  2. Published data bear out the sparse-array arithmetic of §C10.1. DTU’s 120-element array is one aperiodic row of 120 grating emitters at a mean pitch of about 50 µm across 6 mm, each grating 5 mm long and steered by wavelength along the other axis, so it is sparse along one axis only [P]. Its simulated main-lobe fraction of 0.8% comes from the array factor alone, with a flat element pattern over the ±90° field, and it is what §C10.1 predicts: counting spots in angle as the paper does, Nspot=πD/λ=π×6mm/1.55μm≈12,200N_{\mathrm{spot}}=\pi D/\lambda=\pi\times6\ {\mathrm{mm}}/1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}\approx12{,}200 (the paper’s ≈12,000 simulated resolvable points), so N/Nspot=120/12,200=1.0%N/N_{\mathrm{spot}}=120/12{,}200=1.0\%, and random 120-element layouts give 0.9% [E]. Its measured floor, only 3–6 dB below the peak, is set mostly by the camera’s 0.13° resolution, about 9 main-lobe widths (λ/D=1.55μm/6mm=2.6×10−4\lambda/D=1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/6\ {\mathrm{mm}}=2.6\times10^{-4} rad =0.015∘=0.015^\circ, with D=6D=6 mm the aperture). The camera spreads the main lobe over those 9 widths and reads its peak about 9.5 dB low (10log⁡10910\log_{10}9), while it averages the floor to its mean, 1/N=1/1201/N=1/120 of the true peak (−21 dB). The observed peak therefore stands only about 11 dB above the mean floor, and the floor’s highest points lie about 5–6 dB above that mean, so only about 4–6.5 dB below the observed peak, close to the measured 3–6 dB [E: 20 layouts of 120 random emitters over 6 mm with exact amplitudes, seen through a 0.13° Gaussian response, give 11 dB from the observed peak to the mean floor and 4–6.5 dB to the floor’s highest point]. The paper itself attributes the gap from its simulated 12.8 dB to amplitude variation in its cascaded directional couplers [P]. The npj review tabulates aperiodic arrays at 4.6–28 dB beam-forming loss and 4–14 dB sidelobe suppression.
  3. Measured peak sidelobes (−10 to −19 dB) sit near the −13.3 dB first sidelobe of an untapered aperture, far above the calibrated random-phase floor.
    • That floor has a mean of about σ2/N≈−40\sigma^2/N\approx-40 dB for an rms phase error σ=0.3\sigma=0.3 rad and N=1,024N=1{,}024 elements; its peak is about 8 dB higher. The largest of KK independent, exponentially distributed sidelobe samples is about ln⁡K\ln K times their mean, and taking K≈NK\approx N gives 10log⁡10(ln⁡1,024)=8.410\log_{10}(\ln1{,}024)=8.4 dB [E].
    • Reaching −29 dB one-way therefore needs amplitude tapering plus control of deterministic effects: crosstalk, amplitude errors, and phase errors inside long grating apertures, which input-side shifters cannot correct.
    • Waveguide-width errors, correlated along each guide, accumulate a phase (2π/λ)(∂neff/∂w)(2\pi/\lambda)(\partial n_{\mathrm{eff}}/\partial w) per unit width error and length: about 12 rad per nm of width error per mm for a 400 nm wide Si strip (∂neff/∂w=3×10−3nm−1\partial n_{\mathrm{eff}}/\partial w=3\times10^{-3}\ {\mathrm{nm^{-1}}} at 1,550 nm, Rizzo et al., Opt. Lett. 2023) and about 6.5 rad for the common 500 nm strip (1.6×10−3nm−11.6\times10^{-3}\ {\mathrm{nm^{-1}}}, Yang et al., Opt. Express 2015) [I; (2π/1.55μm)×3×10−3nm−1×1mm=12(2\pi/1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}})\times3\times10^{-3}\ {\mathrm{nm^{-1}}}\times1\ {\mathrm{mm}}=12 rad]. After a few millimetres the uncalibrated phases are therefore effectively random. Yang et al. measured the phase-coherence length of 220 nm SOI waveguides, the length LcohL_{\mathrm{coh}} at which the random phase reaches an rms of 2\sqrt2 rad (its rms is 2L/Lcoh\sqrt{2L/L_{\mathrm{coh}}} for a length LL, so ⟨eiΔϕ⟩=e−1\langle e^{i\Delta\phi}\rangle=e^{-1} at LcohL_{\mathrm{coh}}), at 4.2 mm for strip and 1.6 mm for rib waveguides, from 800 Mach–Zehnder interferometers across one 6-inch foundry wafer [I].
  4. Loss is still about 10–14 dB one-way in the devices that report it (DTU, ZJU, imec), i.e. about 20–28 dB round trip in a monostatic design. The npj review’s itemized state of the art sums to about 4–10 dB, and Analog Photonics specifies its FSOC-B1 steerer at ≤7.5 dB from fibre to beam (products table below; vendor claim [P]). Every dB counts twice (§C10.2, item 5).
  5. The wavelength axis is where the budget breaks. Demonstrated tuning is about 38–120 nm, which gives 3°–17° and at most a few hundred spots. The 8,192-element array’s 17° used 1515–1635 nm at 0.14°/nm (120nm×0.14∘/nm=16.8∘120\ {\mathrm{nm}}\times0.14^\circ/{\mathrm{nm}}=16.8^\circ), which at its 0.039° grating-axis beamwidth is 17/0.039≈44017/0.039\approx440 spots. The ZJU chip is limited to 5.2° by its laser.
  6. No paper found reports the temperature stability of calibration. Each group found calibrates once against a far-field camera (look-up table, genetic algorithm, gradient search). The ZJU paper runs on a thermoelectric cooler (TEC) and warns that thermal gradients would force recalibration.
  7. Actively steered OPA ranging records are short.
    • 35 m at 10% (8,192 elements) [S]; more than 50 m for the 9,216-element array, reflectance not stated [I, abstract]; 22 m for Jilin’s Vernier array, to an indoor wall whose reflectance the paper does not state (10% in the npj review [S]); and 20 m for imec, on a retroreflective traffic-sign-type target [P]. 100 m has been shown only on 90% targets over mirror-folded paths: by Jilin University’s 128-channel OPA (Li et al., Photon. Res. 2021), with a fibre collimator on the other side of the link [P], and, at 109 m, by the 64-channel OPA of Jilin University and the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics (CIOMP), with a bulk lens in front of the chip (36 m without it; Zhang et al., Opt. Express 2022, §D7) [P]. 100 m on a 90% target is ≈33 m at 10% under R2R^2 scaling.
    • Optical energy per point for OPA lidars is 1,360–1,700 nJ in Pointcloud’s comparison table [S]. The 1,360 nJ is that of Jilin University’s 128-channel OPA (Li et al., Photon. Res. 2021) at 100 m on a 90% target, and the 1,700 nJ that of the 8,192-element array at 35 m on a 10% target. The table counts energy per pulse or per up-and-down chirp pair, and Li et al.’s 26 dBm input, less its 17.7 dB system insertion loss, over 2×1002\times100 µs of chirp gives the same figure [E: 398mW×10−1.77=6.8398\ {\mathrm{mW}}\times10^{-1.77}=6.8 mW and 6.8mW×200μs=1.35μJ6.8\ {\mathrm{mW}}\times200\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=1.35\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}]. Pointcloud’s FPA uses 46 nJ (at 65 m and 30%), and the 512-pixel coherent receiver array of Rogers et al. (Nature 2021, §C10.4) 212 nJ, from the same table [S].
    • Scaling each measured energy per point to 200 m at 10% as R2/ρR^2/\rho (the return from an extended diffuse target is proportional to ρ/R2\rho/R^2, with ρ\rho the reflectance) gives ≈49–56 µJ per point [E: 1.36μJ×(200/100)2×(0.9/0.1)=1.36μJ×36=49μJ1.36\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times(200/100)^2\times(0.9/0.1)=1.36\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times36=49\ \mu{\mathrm{J}} and 1.7μJ×(200/35)2=1.7μJ×32.7=56μJ1.7\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times(200/35)^2=1.7\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times32.7=56\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}]. That sits at or just below the low end of the cell-filling link budget of §C10.2, item 5, Eq. (139): 54–157 µJ for 88.5–259 photons at 3 dB one-way loss (5 µJ yields 8.23 detected photons there, so 5μJ×88.5/8.23=54μJ5\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times88.5/8.23=54\ \mu{\mathrm{J}} and 5μJ×259/8.23=157μJ5\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times259/8.23=157\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}). The 8,192-element array’s 0.01° × 0.039° beam is much narrower than a 0.05° cell, so each of its samples collects more photons than a cell-filling one would, at the price of sparse coverage (§C10.3a, item 4).
    • At 12 Mpts/s this is about 590–670 W of optical power (49μJ×12×106s−1=59049\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times12\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=590 W, 56μJ×12×106s−1=67056\ \mu{\mathrm{J}}\times12\times10^{6}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}=670 W). That is 17–19 times the 35 W that the whole FS-4S module draws and 74–84 times the 8 W of the Hesai ATX (table below): a gap of one to two orders of magnitude.

Analog Photonics as the reference case [P, company datasheets Rev A, June–July 2025; figures are vendor claims]

In my reading, Analog Photonics is the strongest evidence that an OPA can be engineered into a product-like module, and its own datasheets quantify the limits.

Who they are. Analog Photonics (Boston) was founded about 2012 by Michael Watts of MIT, who remains CEO [P/S]. Federal records show subawards from Nov 2013 and SBIR (US Small Business Innovation Research) awards from 2015 [I]; the company’s own timeline starts with a 2016 award under the MOABB (Modular Optical Aperture Building Blocks) programme of DARPA, the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (§C3a). Its platform is MOABB-funded 300 mm silicon photonics with flip-chip CMOS drivers (electronic driver chips bonded face-down onto the photonic chip). Company milestones [P]: a joint development agreement with a Tier 1 (a supplier selling directly to carmakers) in 2018, on-car tests in 2019, a second Tier 1 agreement in 2020 and a narrow-linewidth FMCW laser in 2021. Funding, size and the departure of the lead author of its OPA papers are covered in §C3a.

Its 2023 company-authored IEEE Spectrum article anticipated “large numbers of samples” for automotive in 2025 [P]. No production award or sample shipment was found in public sources. Funding is mostly from US government contracts and grants: $45.2 M of federal prime obligations (money committed under contracts and grants the company holds itself) and $34.2 M of subawards (money passed on by other prime holders) [I], ≈$79 M over 2013–2026 [E] (§C3a); no venture round was found. A 2025 talk by the CEO emphasized drone and counter-drone (counter-UAS, where UAS means unmanned aircraft system) lidar and drone-to-drone optical links [P].

C10.3 The photon arithmetic that decides it: coherent vs ToF as resolution rises

The “photon arithmetic” of this subsection is a count of photons. For each receiver type it asks how many detected photons one angular sample yields for a given transmitted energy, and hence how much average laser power is needed to sample a whole automotive field at a given range, resolution and frame rate. The two receivers compared are a direct-detection time-of-flight (ToF) receiver, which counts every photon that its lens collects, and a single-mode coherent receiver, which detects only the light in one spatial mode matched to its local oscillator. The comparison matters because it decides which architecture can afford the fine angular sampling that “camera-like” lidar promises.

For a 10% target at 200 m and 10 Hz, gap-free single-mode coherent coverage of 120° × 25° needs 58.5–175.5 W at a non-fading threshold of 10–30 detected photons, and about 518–1,515 W once speckle fading is counted under the report’s per-point rule, or ≈130 W if each of four looks has its own receive mode (caveat 4; §C10.2, item 5); ToF needs 0.215–13.8 W at 0.1° to 0.0125° sampling. Coherent designs therefore sample sparsely with narrow beams. The gap closes only as ToF cells approach the diffraction limit: at the 0.0125° pitch of “2,000+ line” claims, coherent coverage still needs 4.2–13× ToF’s power.

Name the receiver, not the laser. The usual comparison is direct detection (pulsed ToF/SPAD) versus coherent detection, which mixes the return with a local oscillator (LO), often in FMCW. A direct-detection lidar can also transmit a highly coherent laser. What matters is the receiver: a direct-detection pixel can sum many received spatial modes, whereas one coherent mixer measures one selected spatial and polarization mode. Parallel coherent channels can recover more modes Piggott et al., 2025, §2.

Assumptions of the photon arithmetic [E]. The estimates below hold under these conditions; each can fail in the way stated.

  • Lambertian target. The target is perfectly diffuse, with radiance ρ/π\rho/\pi times the irradiance on it, large enough to fill the illuminated patch, and seen at normal incidence. Glossy paint and retroreflectors are not Lambertian: depending on angle they return far more or far less toward the sensor.
  • One polarization. A coherent receiver detects one polarization. A depolarizing target returns about half its light in that polarization; a retroreflector largely preserves polarization, so the factor then differs. That factor ½ is not part of η\eta: with the round-trip truncation t2=0.838t^2=0.838 it forms the factor t2/2=0.419t^2/2=0.419 of the mode-equivalent area (Eq. (142) below), as in §C0 subsection 10.1 and §C10.3b.
  • Speckle. The coherent thresholds nreq=10n_{\mathrm{req}}=10–30 bracket the single-bin non-fading requirement (≈21 detected photons) and lie below the per-point one (≈39). A single speckle has exponentially distributed intensity, and a fading return needs more photons (caveat 4 below and §C10.2, item 5).
  • Shot-noise-limited coherent receiver. The local oscillator’s shot noise dominates, and thermal and dark-current noise are neglected. At 105–125 °C this holds only approximately; §C4c gives 82–94% of the shot-noise limit for Ge at 125 °C.
  • Ideal modes. Beams are ideal TEM00 Gaussians (the fundamental transverse mode, with beam-quality factor M2=1M^2=1; this MM is not an APD gain) with perfect mode matching and alignment, and there is no atmospheric turbulence.
  • Clear air. Atmospheric transmission is taken as 1.
  • Sunlight. For ToF, nreq=21.7n_{\mathrm{req}}=21.7 already corresponds to bright sun: an ideal counter needs 15.0 counts there (§C0 subsection 10.3), and the §C7a model applies its ×1.45 implementation margin, 1.45×15.0≈21.71.45\times15.0\approx21.7. The dead time that sunlight causes is in η\eta, through the SPAD live fraction 0.885. At night ≈5 counts suffice.

One photon budget, two receiving rules [E]. Both receivers share one transmitted energy per sample, but they differ in how much of the return they can use. The symbols are:

  • ΩFOV\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}, the solid angle of the field of view, and Ωcell\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}, the solid angle of one angular sample (resolution cell), both in steradians;
  • Nsamp≃ΩFOV/ΩcellN_{\mathrm{samp}}\simeq\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}, the number of uniformly spaced samples per frame;
  • Ept=P/(fframeNsamp)E_{\mathrm{pt}}=P/(f_{\mathrm{frame}}N_{\mathrm{samp}}), the optical energy transmitted toward one sample, with PP the average optical power and fframef_{\mathrm{frame}} the frame rate;
  • Eph=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda, the photon energy at wavelength λ\lambda;
  • η\eta, the end-to-end efficiency from photons arriving at the aperture to signal photoelectrons: optics × detector, and for the coherent receiver also × mixing (§C0 subsection 10.1). It excludes the coherent receiver’s polarization and mode-shape factors, which sit in AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}, and for SPAD ToF it includes the live fraction that sunlight-induced dead time leaves;
  • ρ\rho, the target’s reflectance; RR, the range; and ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}}, the receive-aperture area.

For a large Lambertian target that fills the illuminated patch, the number of photons a direct-detection receiver detects is approximately

ndirect=ηρEptEphArxπR2∝ArxΩcell.n_{\mathrm{direct}}=\frac{\eta\rho E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}\frac{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}{\pi R^2}\ \propto\ A_{\mathrm{rx}}\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}.(141)

The factor Arx/(πR2)A_{\mathrm{rx}}/(\pi R^2) is the fraction of the light scattered by a Lambertian target at normal incidence that enters an aperture of area ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} at range RR.

  • Direct detection carries one factor of Ωcell\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}, because finer sampling divides fixed frame energy among more points (Ept∝1/Nsamp∝ΩcellE_{\mathrm{pt}}\propto1/N_{\mathrm{samp}}\propto\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}). The receiver’s étendue adds no second factor: the lens collects light from the whole illuminated cell, whatever its size.

  • A matched single-mode coherent receiver uses the mode-equivalent collecting area AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} of §C10.2, item 5, instead of the hard area. Only light matching its one spatial mode counts, so its area and accepted solid angle together are limited to about λ2\lambda^2. The coherent count is Eq. (141) with AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} in place of ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}}, which is also Eq. (139) with ηOPA=1\eta_{\mathrm{OPA}}=1:

    ncoh=ηρEptEphAmodeπR2,Amode≃t22λ2Ωcelln_{\mathrm{coh}}=\frac{\eta\rho E_{\mathrm{pt}}}{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}\frac{A_{\mathrm{mode}}}{\pi R^2},\qquad A_{\mathrm{mode}}\simeq\frac{t^2}{2}\,\frac{\lambda^2}{\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}}(142)

    If the received mode is widened until its Gaussian 1/e² spot fills one angular cell, the Gaussian model gives the second relation (Eq. (148) of §C10.3a, item 4, with a footprint fraction of one), where t2/2=0.419t^2/2=0.419 is the round-trip truncation t2=0.838t^2=0.838 times the single-polarization factor ½; at 0.05° it is 1.32 mm². The two cell-angle factors (in EptE_{\mathrm{pt}} and in AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}) then cancel. That is the ideal full-coverage scaling used below, subject to beam shape and receive-mode overlap at the cell corners.

  • A practical coherent system can instead keep a larger aperture and a narrow beam, collecting more photons in each sampled direction but leaving gaps between beam footprints (§§C10.3a–b).

Required average optical power to cover 120°×25° at 10 Hz and reach 200 m on a 10% target. Setting the detected count of Eq. (141) or Eq. (142) equal to the required count nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} and solving for P=fframeNsampEptP=f_{\mathrm{frame}}N_{\mathrm{samp}}E_{\mathrm{pt}} gives

Pcoh=nreqEphπR2fframeΩFOVρt22λ2η,PToF=nreqEphπR2fframeΩFOVρArxΩcellη\begin{aligned}P_{\mathrm{coh}}&=\dfrac{n_{\mathrm{req}}E_{\mathrm{ph}}\pi R^2f_{\mathrm{frame}}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}}{\rho\,\tfrac{t^2}{2}\lambda^2\,\eta},\\ P_{\mathrm{ToF}}&=\dfrac{n_{\mathrm{req}}E_{\mathrm{ph}}\pi R^2f_{\mathrm{frame}}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}}{\rho\,A_{\mathrm{rx}}\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}\,\eta}\end{aligned}(143)

nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} is the number of detected photons (photoelectrons) required per sample, as in §C0 subsection 10.1. The ToF inputs are those of the 940 nm SPAD model of §C0 subsection 10.3 and §C7a: a 25 mm aperture, nreq=21.7n_{\mathrm{req}}=21.7 [E: the bright-sun requirement with the model’s ×1.45 margin] and η=0.5×0.37×0.885=0.164\eta=0.5\times0.37\times0.885=0.164 [E: optics × PDE × the bright-sun live fraction]. They belong to the model’s 0.05° × 0.05° macro-pixel and are held fixed across the grids below, although a coarser pixel collects more sunlight and a finer one less. Single-mode coherent: 1550 nm, nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} 10–30 and η=0.25\eta=0.25, the design value of §C0 subsection 10.1, needing 58.5–175.5 W on every grid, because Ωcell\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}} does not appear in PcohP_{\mathrm{coh}}; Waymo’s measured chain efficiency of 0.112 (§C0 subsection 10.1) would raise this 2.23-fold. Both powers grow as R2ΩFOVR^2\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}, which is why §C10.2b and the product comparison below rank by R2ΩR^2\Omega.

What the table means [E]:

  1. In this fixed-threshold example, gap-free single-mode coverage of a full automotive field to 200 m needs 58.5–175.5 W, even before speckle fading (caveat 4). A coherent design must allocate range by elevation: 200 m within a ±1.5° horizon band and 50 m elsewhere cuts the required power about 5.7×. Required power scales as R2R^2 times solid angle (Eq. (143)), so the mix costs [3∘×1+22∘×(50/200)2]/25∘=0.175[3^\circ\times1+22^\circ\times(50/200)^2]/25^\circ=0.175 of the uniform 200 m case, and 1/0.175=5.71/0.175=5.7. It must also narrow its field, lower its point rate or accept sparse footprints. Some FMCW products are long-range, narrower-field truck sensors (§C7, §F6), while the scanned 120°-wide ones sample sparsely (the R2ΩR^2\Omega table below).
  2. The resolution race narrows the gap only as fast as Ωcell\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}} shrinks. Power parity arrives only near 0.0035–0.006°, where a 25 mm ToF receiver itself approaches the diffraction limit (ArxΩcell→λ2A_{\mathrm{rx}}\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}\to\lambda^2): its étendue per cell then shrinks to a single mode, the same as a coherent receiver’s. Because the ratio scales as θcell2\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}^2, with θcell\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} the cell width, parity needs θcell=0.1∘/272=0.0061∘\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}=0.1^\circ/\sqrt{272}=0.0061^\circ to 0.1∘/816=0.0035∘0.1^\circ/\sqrt{816}=0.0035^\circ; the diffraction limit itself is at θcell=λ/Arx=0.940μm/22.2mm=4.2×10−5\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}=\lambda/\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}=0.940\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/22.2\ {\mathrm{mm}}=4.2\times10^{-5} rad =0.0024∘=0.0024^\circ. That is beyond even “camera-like” resolution, and finer than the 0.0125° of “2,000+ line” claims, at which full-coverage coherent detection still needs 4.2–13× ToF’s power.
  3. Optical phased array (OPA) random access is worth less than it seems. Range requirements depend mostly on elevation, which is static geometry. A static, non-uniform allocation (more power, dwell or channels near the horizon) therefore captures most of the benefit of foveation, which means concentrating resolution or power where it is needed, as the eye’s fovea does. Scanned ToF units already do this with denser central lines and region of interest (ROI) modes.
  4. Caveats.
    • Sunlight is already included in the ToF inputs: nreq=21.7n_{\mathrm{req}}=21.7 is the bright-sun requirement, and η=0.164\eta=0.164 contains the bright-sun live fraction 0.885. A fully sunlit scene of reflectance 0.9 doubles the background to 3.66×1083.66\times10^{8} counts/s per macro-pixel, which lowers the live fraction to e−0.244=0.784e^{-0.244}=0.784 (each of the nine SPADs has rτd=3.66×108/9×6ns=0.244r\tau_d=3.66\times10^{8}/9\times6\ {\mathrm{ns}}=0.244) and raises the ideal requirement only to 17.3 counts (b=3.66×108s−1×1ns×10×0.784=2.87b=3.66\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times1\ {\mathrm{ns}}\times10\times0.784=2.87 background counts per bin, threshold 15; §C0 subsection 10.3; background model in §C6(d)). PToFP_{\mathrm{ToF}} then rises by (17.3/15.0)×(0.885/0.784)=1.30(17.3/15.0)\times(0.885/0.784)=1.30.
    • FMCW buys velocity and interference immunity, which this photon count does not value.
    • The choices of nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} and η\eta move the numbers but do not change the scaling with Ωcell\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}. The measured chain efficiency of 0.112 in place of the design value 0.25 raises the coherent powers 2.23×, and speckle raises the coherent nreqn_{\mathrm{req}} to 88.5–259, 3–26× the 10–30 of the table (next bullet).
    • Speckle. nreq=10n_{\mathrm{req}}=10–30 is at or below the non-fading requirement: ≈21 detected photons for PD=0.9P_D=0.9 at p=10−6p=10^{-6} in one bin, and ≈39 under the report’s per-point rule, which searches 0–300 m and needs the peak in both chirp ramps (§C0 subsection 10.3). If the looks share one mode’s collection (wavelength or time diversity), that raises the coherent requirement to about 518–1,515 W: at fixed η\eta, Eq. Looks that each add a mode (polarization or spatial diversity, as in §C7a) collect four times as much, which brings the four-look case back to ≈130 W (518/4518/4).

Relaxing the cell-filling assumption: coherent designs trade coverage for photons [E, checked against the full text of Piggott et al. (Waymo), arXiv 2502.09736, 2025]

The table assumes that the coherent beam fills its resolution cell. A monostatic coherent system need not do so:

  • Collected mode power depends on beam overlap, not on the sampling grid alone. For a matched monostatic Gaussian beam on a diffuse target, Piggott et al. give the speckle-averaged received power (their Eq. 15) as ⟨PRX⟩=λ2ηρPTX/(2πAbeam)\langle P_{\mathrm{RX}}\rangle=\lambda^2\eta\rho P_{\mathrm{TX}}/(2\pi A_{\mathrm{beam}}), the link loss of Eq. (41) (§C0 subsection 10.2) with Abeam=πw(R)2A_{\mathrm{beam}}=\pi w(R)^2 and no truncation (t=1t=1), where ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle denotes the average over speckle, PTXP_{\mathrm{TX}} the transmitted power, η\eta the detection efficiency, ρ\rho the target reflectance, λ\lambda the wavelength, and Abeam=πw(R)2A_{\mathrm{beam}}=\pi w(R)^2 the effective beam area on the target (w(R)w(R) is the 1/e² beam radius at range RR), not the receive-aperture area Piggott et al., Eq. 15. The 2 in the denominator matches the single-polarization factor ½ of §C10.3b’s t2/2t^2/2. Only in the far field, for a well-matched beam, does this recover the familiar PRX∝ρPTXArx/R2P_{\mathrm{RX}}\propto\rho P_{\mathrm{TX}}A_{\mathrm{rx}}/R^2 scaling, with ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} the receive-aperture area; in the near field the spot size and range dependence differ.

  • A larger useful aperture can buy photons at the cost of coverage: the sampling pitch is unchanged, but narrow footprints leave gaps between samples. The system can use an aperture much larger than λ2/Ωcell\lambda^2/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}} and sample the scene with narrow Gaussian footprints. The single-mode space–angle product (area times accepted solid angle) remains of order λ2\lambda^2 per polarization. The resulting coverage fraction counts nominal beam footprints, so its value depends on the chosen intensity contour and detection threshold.

  • Waymo’s automotive worked example makes this choice. For 250 m, 120° × 25°, 0.05° sampling, a 5% target, a detection probability PD=0.9P_D=0.9 and a false-alarm probability p=10−6p=10^{-6} per bin:

The design choice. At automotive fields and ranges, a single-mode coherent receiver trades aggregate optical power, parallel channels, field size and nominal footprint coverage against one another. The ideal full-coverage example (58.5–175.5 W) and Waymo’s sparse example (6.2 W) are different points in that design space; neither is a universal limit. Direct-detection ToF can tile the field with multimode pixels, provided its illumination and detector fields also tile it. For the “camera-like” question, dense angular coverage is costly specifically for a single-mode coherent receiver, whereas higher sample counts, dwell time and channel count cost both architectures (§C10.3a).

The one physics argument that favours non-mechanical steering for coherent long range. The scanner keeps moving during the round trip, so the transmit and receive modes walk off by the angle the scanner turns while the light travels to the target and back:

Δθ≈2Rθ̇c\Delta\theta\approx\frac{2R\,\dot\theta}{c}(144)

where RR is the range, θ̇\dot\theta the angular scan rate of the beam (rad/s), 2R/c2R/c the round-trip time and cc the speed of light. A single-mode receiver loses signal once this walk-off becomes comparable with the beam’s own divergence, because the returning light no longer overlaps the receive mode.

  • For a 360° spin at 10 Hz and 250 m, the walk-off is about 0.006°, larger than the beam’s 0.0036° angular radius at that range. [E: θ̇=3,600∘/s=62.8\dot\theta=3{,}600^\circ/{\mathrm{s}}=62.8 rad/s, so from Eq.   • Waymo concludes that fast mechanical scanning is impractical much beyond about 100 m for coherent collection. It prefers step-and-stare steering (the beam jumps to a direction and holds still while the return arrives) by an OPA, a focal-plane array (FPA) or another non-mechanical steerer.
  • Aeva’s patent addresses the same issue with “satellite” receive waveguides at lag angles (offset to catch the walked-off return), alongside a galvo-mirror scanner (a mirror tilted by a galvanometer motor) [P, US 11,372,105 B1].
  • This is a genuine point in favour of solid-state steering for FMCW. On its own, it cannot overcome the loss, second-axis and channel-count problems above.
