C10.3a Physical background: one spatial mode versus an integrating pixel

This subsection explains the physics behind the photon arithmetic of §C10.3. It asks two questions. Why do a coherent lidar and a direct-detection time-of-flight (ToF) lidar with similar apertures end up using very different numbers of photons? And why must the coherent one leave gaps between its samples? A coherent lidar mixes the return with a local oscillator (LO), usually in frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) ranging; a ToF lidar times a pulse with a photodetector that simply counts the light it receives. The short answer is that a multimode direct-detection pixel sums every speckle it collects, whereas a single-mode coherent receiver keeps only about one. At fixed laser power a coherent design must therefore trade photons per sample against nominal footprint coverage (the share of the field that the nominal beam spots cover, defined in items 3–4), the number of parallel channels and dwell time. That is the trade behind §C10.3, and it decides whether coherent lidar can follow ToF into “camera-like” resolution.

The target is diffuse and extended. The estimates below are mostly far-field; the Gaussian model of §C10.3b also covers the near field. Optical throughput, detector efficiency, mode coupling and polarization are each accounted for separately rather than lumped together. Numbers are calculated estimates [E] unless tagged. Photon counts per sample in §§C10.3a–b are detected photons, i.e. photoelectrons, unless stated otherwise.

Assumptions used throughout §§C10.3a–b. Each is repeated where it matters; when one fails, the photon counts below change.

  • Lambertian target. The surface is perfectly diffuse: its bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) is ρ/π\rho/\pi, i.e. it sends radiance ρ/π\rho/\pi times the incident irradiance into every direction, where ρ\rho is its diffuse reflectance. Retroreflectors (signs, licence plates) and glossy or wet paint are not Lambertian. Depending on angle they return far more or far less toward the sensor, and the counts below then do not apply.
  • Fully developed speckle. A single coherent speckle has exponentially distributed intensity (a Rayleigh-distributed amplitude), so a single look can fade deeply. Summing NspN_{\mathrm{sp}} independent speckles narrows the distribution.
  • Shot-noise-limited coherent receiver. The LO is strong enough that its shot noise dominates; thermal and dark-current noise are neglected. At 105–125 °C this holds only approximately: §C4c gives 82–94% of the shot-noise limit for Ge at 125 °C.
  • Ideal beams. The transmitted beam and the LO are TEM00 beams, i.e. ideal Gaussian beams in the fundamental transverse mode (beam-quality factor M2=1M^2=1; this M2M^2 is unrelated to the multiplication gain MM of an avalanche photodiode, or APD), perfectly mode-matched and aligned. There is no atmospheric turbulence, the air is clear, and incidence is normal.
  • Depolarizing target. A rough target scrambles polarization, so a single-polarization coherent receiver keeps half of the light: the factor ½ used below. A retroreflector largely preserves polarization, and the factor then differs.

1. Start with the photons that reach the aperture.

Both receivers start from the same aperture-limited count. A Lambertian target re-radiates into a hemisphere, so the power reaching a collecting aperture of area ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} at range RR is about ρPArx/(πR2)\rho P A_{\mathrm{rx}}/(\pi R^2) for a transmitted power PP, whatever the detector does. Per sample, the number of photoelectrons this yields after the efficiency η\eta (defined below) is

naperture=ηρEph⋅PfframeNsamp⋅ArxπR2n_{\mathrm{aperture}}=\frac{\eta\,\rho}{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}\cdot\frac{P}{f_{\mathrm{frame}}\,N_{\mathrm{samp}}}\cdot\frac{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}{\pi R^2}(145)

where:

  • PP is the average transmitted optical power (W), fframef_{\mathrm{frame}} the frame rate (Hz) and NsampN_{\mathrm{samp}} the number of samples per frame, so that Ept=P/(fframeNsamp)E_{\mathrm{pt}}=P/(f_{\mathrm{frame}}N_{\mathrm{samp}}) is the transmitted energy per sample;
  • Eph=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda is the photon energy at wavelength λ\lambda (hh is Planck’s constant and cc the speed of light);
  • ρ\rho is the target’s diffuse reflectance, RR the range and ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} the receive-aperture area;
  • η\eta is the end-to-end efficiency of §C10.3 and §C0 subsection 10.1, from photons at the aperture to photoelectrons: optics × detector, and for the coherent receiver also × mixing. It excludes coherent mode selection and polarization loss, which are counted separately below, in AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}.

Eq. (145) assumes that the object fills the illuminated spot, that the return fits within the direct detector’s field, and that ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} is the receive aperture of whichever receiver is evaluated (20 mm for the coherent receiver and 25 mm for ToF below).

Example: 1 W, 1.2 M samples per frame, 10 Hz, 200 m, 10% reflectivity and an illustrative η=0.1\eta=0.1 for both receivers, so that only the apertures and wavelengths differ (§C10.3 uses the model values, 0.25 for coherent and 0.164 for ToF). Each sample carries Ept=P/(fframeNsamp)=1W/(10s−1×1.2×106)=83E_{\mathrm{pt}}=P/(f_{\mathrm{frame}}N_{\mathrm{samp}})=1\ {\mathrm{W}}/(10\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times1.2\times10^{6})=83 nJ, and πR2=1.26×105\pi R^2=1.26\times10^{5} m².

  • A 20 mm coherent-system aperture at 1550 nm collects about 16 photoelectron equivalents (photons at the aperture times η\eta), before projection into its selected mode [E: 83nJ/1.28×10−19J=6.5×101183\ {\mathrm{nJ}}/1.28\times10^{-19}\ {\mathrm{J}}=6.5\times10^{11} photons, times ηρ=0.01\eta\rho=0.01, times 314mm2/1.26×105m2=2.5×10−9314\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}/1.26\times10^{5}\ {\mathrm{m^2}}=2.5\times10^{-9}].
  • A 25 mm direct-detection ToF aperture at 940 nm has about 15 [E: 83nJ/2.11×10−19J=3.9×101183\ {\mathrm{nJ}}/2.11\times10^{-19}\ {\mathrm{J}}=3.9\times10^{11} photons, times 0.01, times 491mm2/1.26×105m2=3.9×10−9491\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}/1.26\times10^{5}\ {\mathrm{m^2}}=3.9\times10^{-9}]; a well-matched multimode pixel can use nearly all of these after the common losses.

The totals are similar because the smaller aperture area ((20/25)2=0.64(20/25)^2=0.64) is roughly offset by more photons per joule at 1550 nm (1550/940=1.651550/940=1.65). They are not the detected coherent photon count. A coherent receiver does not collect over its hard aperture area but over its mode-equivalent collecting area AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}. This is the area of an ideal direct-detection lens that would collect, from the same Lambertian target, the same signal as the coherent receiver collects in its single LO mode and polarization; §C0 subsection 10.2 derives it and §C10.3b evaluates it. At 200 m, the 20 mm Gaussian model of §C10.3b has Amode=64mm2A_{\mathrm{mode}}=64\,{\mathrm{mm}}^2 against a 314mm2314\,{\mathrm{mm}}^2 hard aperture. It therefore yields about 3.3 usable signal photoelectrons (16×64/31416\times64/314), not 16, under this example’s common η=0.1\eta=0.1. The mode-equivalent collecting area already includes the model’s single-polarization factor; do not apply that factor again. In practical terms, the photons arriving at the two apertures are similar, but the coherent receiver can use only a fraction of its share.

2. What a single-mode receiver can use: speckle and modes.

A rough surface returns a speckle pattern: a random pattern of bright and dark grains, produced by interference among the light scattered from different parts of the lit spot. One coherent mixer uses only about one speckle’s worth of it, because it responds only to the single spatial mode of its LO. The van Cittert–Zernike theorem states that light from a spatially incoherent source (here the rough, lit spot) acquires a coherence width of about λR\lambda R divided by the source size after travelling a distance RR. The speckle size at the aperture is therefore about λR/(spot size on target)\lambda R/(\text{spot size on target}). The number of speckles across the aperture equals the number of spatial modes it accepts:

Nspk∼ArxΩspotλ2N_{\mathrm{spk}}\sim\frac{A_{\mathrm{rx}}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{spot}}}{\lambda^2}(146)

where ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} is the receive-aperture area, Ωspot\Omega_{\mathrm{spot}} the solid angle of the illuminated spot seen from the sensor (spot area divided by R2R^2) and λ\lambda the wavelength. Eq. (146) is the antenna theorem in counting form. That theorem says that one spatial mode occupies an étendue (collecting area times acceptance solid angle) of about λ2\lambda^2 per polarization, AΩ≈λ2A\Omega\approx\lambda^2. A receiver whose area–solid-angle product is ArxΩspotA_{\mathrm{rx}}\Omega_{\mathrm{spot}} therefore sees about that many λ2\lambda^2-sized modes; §C0 subsection 10.2 states the theorem with its source (Siegman 1966). NspkN_{\mathrm{spk}} counts spatial speckles per polarization, to order of magnitude; polarization accounting is separate.

  • If power is spread roughly uniformly over NspkN_{\mathrm{spk}} independent modes, one coherent mixer uses of order 1/Nspk1/N_{\mathrm{spk}} of the aperture power. The exact coupling depends on illumination and pupil shape. A single-mode receiver still fades like one look, however many speckles fall across its aperture.
  • A sufficiently large direct-detection pixel sums the intensities of all the modes.

The table below compares three receivers at 250 m: a monostatic coherent receiver, a ToF pixel and a coherent receiver with a cell-filling spot. For each it gives the spot on the target, the speckle size and speckle count at the aperture, and the share of the collected light that the detector can use. Monostatic means that transmit and receive share one aperture and one optical mode. The confocal optimum is the aperture whose collimated Gaussian beam is smallest at the target range, Dopt=λR/π/0.45D_{\mathrm{opt}}=\sqrt{\lambda R/\pi}/0.45 (§C0 Eq. (43); item 3).

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Spot on target: a cell-filling spot is one 0.05° cell at 250 m, 250m×8.73×10−4=22250\ {\mathrm{m}}\times8.73\times10^{-4}=22 cm (0.05° is 8.73×10−48.73\times10^{-4} rad); the monostatic spot is the 3.3 cm 1/e² diameter of the 20 mm Gaussian model at 250 m (§C10.3b, Result 2). The 1/e² diameter is the width at which the beam intensity falls to 1/e21/e^2 of its peak.
  • Speckle size at the aperture: λR/Lspot\lambda R/L_{\mathrm{spot}}, where LspotL_{\mathrm{spot}} is the spot diameter on the target, e.g. 1.55μm×250m/3.3cm=121.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}\times250\ {\mathrm{m}}/3.3\ {\mathrm{cm}}=12 mm (monostatic), 0.940μm×250m/22cm=1.10.940\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}\times250\ {\mathrm{m}}/22\ {\mathrm{cm}}=1.1 mm (ToF) and 1.55μm×250m/22cm=1.81.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}\times250\ {\mathrm{m}}/22\ {\mathrm{cm}}=1.8 mm (cell-filling coherent).
  • Speckles across the aperture: Nspk≈ArxΩspot/λ2N_{\mathrm{spk}}\approx A_{\mathrm{rx}}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{spot}}/\lambda^2 (Eq. (146)). ToF: 491mm2×(8.73×10−4)2/(0.940μm)2=423≈420491\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}\times(8.73\times10^{-4})^2/(0.940\ \mu{\mathrm{m}})^2=423\approx420, against 451 from Goodman’s formula. Monostatic: (aperture diameter ÷ speckle size)², (20/12)2≈3(20/12)^2\approx3, consistent with the Goodman counts of §C10.3b, Result 1 (3.3 at 200 m and 6.2 at 100 m; no 250 m value is computed there). Cell-filling coherent: 314mm2×(8.73×10−4)2/(1.55μm)2=100314\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}\times(8.73\times10^{-4})^2/(1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}})^2=100, against 106 from Goodman’s formula.
  • Fraction used: one coherent mode out of NspkN_{\mathrm{spk}}, ≈1/100\approx1/100 for the cell-filling spot, counting spatial modes only. With polarization and truncation included, that spot’s mode-equivalent collecting area is 1.32 mm² of the 314 mm² hard area, i.e. 1/238≈1/2401/238\approx1/240 (§C10.3b, Result 2). For the monostatic case, the hard area is 4.2× AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} at 250 m (§C10.3b, Result 2).

A well-aligned monostatic system can match the transmitted beam and the back-propagated receive mode (the LO mode traced backwards through the optics to the target) on the target, which keeps NspkN_{\mathrm{spk}} relatively small. The remaining mode and polarization penalties still matter, and the matched angular footprint can be much smaller than the sampling pitch.

In the numerical model of §C10.3b, the monostatic receiver keeps about 1/4–1/11 of the power landing on a 20 mm hard aperture at 100–300 m (the hard area is 3.8× AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} at 300 m and 10.9× at 100 m, §C10.3b, Result 2). The loss has three parts:

  • polarization costs 2×;
  • the Gaussian mode shape and truncation cost 1.47× (derived below);
  • the rest is near-field loss, because a 20 mm aperture is larger than the confocal optimum at short range (≈16 mm at 100 m).

How the numbers are derived [E]: D=20D=20 mm is the aperture diameter and w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D the Gaussian beam’s waist, its 1/e² intensity radius at the aperture (0.45 is the model’s waist-to-aperture ratio, as in §C0 subsection 10.2). The factor t=0.915t=0.915 is the one-way power transmission of that Gaussian through the aperture, so t2=0.84t^2=0.84 covers transmit and receive. In the far field Amode→t2πw02/2A_{\mathrm{mode}}\to t^2\pi w_0^2/2, so the hard area π(D/2)2\pi(D/2)^2 exceeds AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} by 2(D/2)2/(t2w02)=2×1/(4×0.452×0.84)=2×1.47=2.92(D/2)^2/(t^2w_0^2)=2\times1/(4\times0.45^2\times0.84)=2\times1.47=2.9: polarization (2) times mode shape and truncation (1.47).

These losses are one reason a coherent receiver’s photon budget is tighter than ToF’s, even when it is perfectly aligned.

3. The angular response: a narrow Gaussian versus an integrating pixel.

A coherent sample weights a narrow Gaussian spot; a ToF pixel integrates everything inside its cell. The difference matters because it decides whether a small object lying between two sample directions is seen at all.

  • Coherent: a narrow response. In the far field a single coherent mode has an angular acceptance (solid angle) of order λ2/Arx\lambda^2/A_{\mathrm{rx}}: the antenna theorem again, since the mode’s collecting area times its acceptance solid angle is about λ2\lambda^2. At a fixed range, enlarging the aperture helps only up to a point. A collimated Gaussian beam with waist w0w_0 (its 1/e² intensity radius at the aperture) has, at range RR, a 1/e² radius given by w(R)2=w02+(λR/πw0)2w(R)^2=w_0^2+(\lambda R/\pi w_0)^2. The first term is the aperture-sized beam and the second the diffraction spread. The spot is smallest at w0=λR/πw_0=\sqrt{\lambda R/\pi}, where the Rayleigh range zR=πw02/λz_R=\pi w_0^2/\lambda (the distance over which the beam stays roughly collimated) equals the target range: the confocal condition. This is the best spot at one range; a range-agnostic lidar may choose a different waist.

    The table gives, for 50–500 m, the confocal waist, the aperture that launches it, the spot on the target and the share of a 0.05° sampling-grid cell that this spot covers. Its last column, the nominal footprint fraction, is the share of each grid cell covered by the beam’s 1/e² spot.

    Range Optimal w0w_0 (beam diameter 2w02w_0) Matching aperture Dopt=w0/0.45D_{\mathrm{opt}}=w_0/0.45 Spot radius at target 1/e² spot half-angle 0.05° grid spacing Nominal 1/e² footprint fraction on that grid

    • Matching aperture: Dopt=w0/0.45=7.0mm/0.45=15.6D_{\mathrm{opt}}=w_0/0.45=7.0\ {\mathrm{mm}}/0.45=15.6 mm (§C0 Eq. (43), with the waist-to-aperture ratio 0.45 of item 2); the bracketed 2w02w_0 is the beam’s diameter, not the aperture’s.

    • Grid spacing: Rθcell=100m×8.73×10−4=8.7R\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}=100\ {\mathrm{m}}\times8.73\times10^{-4}=8.7 cm, where θcell\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} is the grid pitch in radians (0.05° =8.73×10−4=8.73\times10^{-4} rad).
    • Footprint fraction: spot area over cell area, πw(R)2/(Rθcell)2=2λ/(Rθcell2)\pi w(R)^2/(R\theta_{\mathrm{cell}})^2=2\lambda/(R\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}^2) (using w(R)2=2λR/πw(R)^2=2\lambda R/\pi at the confocal condition) =2×1.55μm/(100m×7.62×10−7)=4.1%=2\times1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(100\ {\mathrm{m}}\times7.62\times10^{-7})=4.1\%, with θcell2=7.62×10−7\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}^2=7.62\times10^{-7}.

    This single-range optimum helps explain Waymo’s w0≈10w_0\approx10 mm choice for 250 m. In this model, a long-range coherent sample has a nominal spot a few centimetres across, while a 0.05° grid pitch spans tens of centimetres. Nominal footprint and overlap fractions, here and in the rest of §§C10.3a–b, are geometric bookkeeping: they depend on the chosen contour, ignore Gaussian tails, speckle, reflectance and the detector threshold, and are not detection probabilities.

  • ToF: an integrating pixel. Its receive field of view is set mainly by pixel size divided by focal length, and can be chosen largely independently of the receive aperture. With gap-free detector fields and matching illumination, pixels tile the field and integrate the intensity falling within each response. Real pixels have optical point-spread functions, imperfect fill factor and thresholds; the literal box used below is only a simple model.

The analog-to-digital converter (ADC) analogy.

  • A coherent sample resembles an ADC with a narrow sampling aperture. It weights a small region strongly, has nonzero Gaussian tails, and can alias small features on a coarse grid, i.e. miss them or misplace them.
  • A direct-detection pixel resembles an integrating ADC. Its wider spatial response averages a cell, which reduces aliasing but mixes objects and backgrounds within that cell.
  • At equal aperture-incident photons the spatial transfer functions differ; so do usable photons and detection thresholds.

What each response costs in practice. The next table takes three small objects and asks, for a uniformly random grid alignment, how often a coherent spot overlaps the object, under the two binary rules of §C10.3b, Result 4, and how much of one ToF pixel the object fills at best.

Object Angular size Coherent: geometric overlap fraction for one random grid offset (0.05° pitch; centre-in-object to 1/e²-touch rule) Coherent: overlap over 5 independent offsets (same two rules) ToF: maximum one-pixel fill fraction
20 × 15 cm at 200 m 0.057° × 0.043° 0.86–1.00 ≈1.0 0.86
15 × 10 cm at 150 m 0.057° × 0.038° 0.76–0.95 ≈1.0 0.76
10 × 10 cm at 250 m 0.023° × 0.023° 0.21–0.37 0.69–0.90 0.21

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Angular size: object size over range, e.g. 0.10m/250m=4×10−40.10\ {\mathrm{m}}/250\ {\mathrm{m}}=4\times10^{-4} rad =0.023∘=0.023^\circ.
  • ToF maximum one-pixel fill: min⁡(1,W/p)min⁡(1,H/p)\min(1,W/p)\min(1,H/p), where WW and HH are the object’s width and height and p=Rθcellp=R\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} is the grid pitch at the target; at 250 m, p=21.8p=21.8 cm and (10/21.8)2=0.21(10/21.8)^2=0.21.
  • Coherent, one random offset: the two binary rules of §C10.3b, Result 4, applied to the 20 mm collimated beam, whose 1/e² radius ww is 1.22, 1.42 and 1.64 cm at 150, 200 and 250 m. The lower value counts an overlap when the beam centre lands inside the object, min⁡(1,W/p)min⁡(1,H/p)\min(1,W/p)\min(1,H/p). The upper value counts one when the 1/e² circle touches the object, i.e. when the centre lands inside the object grown by ww on every side, of area WH+2w(W+H)+πw2WH+2w(W+H)+\pi w^2, with a grown side that exceeds the pitch capped at one pitch. For 10 × 10 cm at 250 m, (10/21.8)2=0.21(10/21.8)^2=0.21 and (100+65.6+8.5)cm2/476cm2=0.37(100+65.6+8.5)\ {\mathrm{cm^2}}/476\ {\mathrm{cm^2}}=0.37. For 15 × 10 cm at 150 m the grown width, 17.4 cm, exceeds the 13.1 cm pitch, so the upper value is (10+2.4)/13.1=0.95(10+2.4)/13.1=0.95.
  • Five independent offsets: the chance that at least one of five frames overlaps, 1−(1−P1)51-(1-P_1)^5, where P1P_1 is the one-offset fraction, e.g. 1−0.795=0.691-0.79^5=0.69 and 1−0.635=0.901-0.63^5=0.90.

These are nominal overlap fractions in the sense defined above, not detection probabilities. They assume uniformly random grid alignment, and the five-offset (five-frame) values need independent dithers (small, uncorrelated shifts of the grid between frames). Neither rule includes received-energy variation at the edge, speckle, reflectance, obscuration or the detector threshold.

  • An object wider than the grid pitch in both dimensions contains at least one grid centre for any grid offset. That guarantees only geometric centre overlap, not detection or a full pixel return. Sub-grid objects sharpen the sampling distinction:
    • Coherent: a narrow beam can miss a small object between samples. Partial overlaps give graded returns, and speckle adds fading.
    • ToF: a gap-free tiled pixel array always has some geometric overlap with the object, but the pixel fill fraction dilutes the object’s return, which may fall below threshold. Edge pixels can mix ranges and do not resolve the object’s position within a cell.
  • Consequence: for coherent lidar, grid spacing (and hence samples per second) sets small-object capability, so the resolution race becomes a race in samples and channels.

4. The budget: photons × coverage per mode is fixed.

This item shows that, for a single-mode receiver at fixed laser power, photons per sample and coverage of the field can only be traded against each other, not raised together.

Define ffpf_{\mathrm{fp}} as the nominal footprint fraction, ffp=NsampΩfootprint/ΩFOVf_{\mathrm{fp}}=N_{\mathrm{samp}}\Omega_{\mathrm{footprint}}/\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}, capped at one. Here NsampN_{\mathrm{samp}} is the number of samples per frame, Ωfootprint\Omega_{\mathrm{footprint}} the solid angle of one sample’s nominal beam footprint seen from the sensor, and ΩFOV\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}} the solid angle of the whole field of view. It is a nominal fraction in the sense of item 3. Let nmoden_{\mathrm{mode}} be the mean number of signal photoelectrons per sample collected in the one selected coherent mode. With a consistently defined ideal single-mode footprint and mode area, the photon–footprint scaling is

nmode×ffp=K=t22ηρPλ2πR2fframeΩFOVEphn_{\mathrm{mode}}\times f_{\mathrm{fp}} \;=\; K \;=\; \frac{t^2}{2}\,\frac{\eta\,\rho\,P\,\lambda^2}{\pi R^2\,f_{\mathrm{frame}}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}\,E_{\mathrm{ph}}}(147)

where:

  • KK is the budget constant: photoelectrons per selected mode times footprint fraction;
  • η\eta is the end-to-end efficiency of Eq. (145), which excludes truncation and polarization; these enter through t2/2=0.419t^2/2=0.419, the round-trip truncation t2=0.838t^2=0.838 times the single-polarization factor ½ of the Gaussian model (§C10.3b);
  • ρ\rho, PP, λ\lambda, RR, fframef_{\mathrm{frame}} and EphE_{\mathrm{ph}} are as in Eq. (145).

The mode-area–footprint identity. Multiplying the mode-equivalent area of Eq. (41) (§C0 subsection 10.2), Amode=t2λ2R2/(2πw2)A_{\mathrm{mode}}=t^2\lambda^2R^2/(2\pi w^2), by one sample’s nominal footprint fraction ffp=πw2/(Rθcell)2f_{\mathrm{fp}}=\pi w^2/(R\theta_{\mathrm{cell}})^2, where θcell\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} is the mesh pitch (rad), cancels both the beam radius ww and the range RR:

Amodeffp=t22(λθcell)2A_{\mathrm{mode}}\,f_{\mathrm{fp}}=\frac{t^2}{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}}\right)^2(148)

with t2=0.84t^2=0.84 the round-trip truncation factor, ½ the single-polarization factor and λ\lambda the wavelength. This is the antenna theorem in the form the Gaussian model gives it, AmodeΩfootprint=t22λ2A_{\mathrm{mode}}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{footprint}}=\tfrac{t^2}{2}\lambda^2, since one sample’s footprint fraction is Ωfootprint/Ωcell\Omega_{\mathrm{footprint}}/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}; an ideal single mode without truncation or polarization loss would have λ2\lambda^2. A design can therefore buy collecting area (photons per sample) only by giving up footprint fraction (coverage), and vice versa; only the mesh pitch and the wavelength move the product (§C10.3b, Result 2, evaluates it).

Eq. (147) follows from Eq. (145) with the hard area ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} replaced by the mode-equivalent area AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} and combined with Eq. (148). Multiplying nmoden_{\mathrm{mode}} by ffpf_{\mathrm{fp}} then cancels NsampN_{\mathrm{samp}} and the collecting area.

Aperture and sample count drop out of this ideal scaling:

  • Spreading fixed energy over the field gives more nominal footprint coverage and fewer signal photons per selected mode. Concentrating it into narrow beams does the reverse.
  • A wide transmit beam paired with a much narrower receive mode wastes the light outside the receive mode’s target overlap.
  • Exact numerical coefficients depend on beam profile, polarization and the chosen footprint contour.

For 200 m, 10% reflectivity, a 120° × 25° field (ΩFOV=0.914\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}=0.914 sr), 10 Hz, the coherent design efficiency η=0.25\eta=0.25 of §C10.3 and t2/2=0.419t^2/2=0.419 at 1550 nm (λ2=2.40×10−12\lambda^2=2.40\times10^{-12} m²), the per-watt budget constant K/PK/P is about 0.17 photoelectrons per watt [E: K/P=0.419×0.25×0.1×2.40×10−12m2/(1.26×105m2×10s−1×0.914sr×1.28×10−19J)=0.171W−1K/P=0.419\times0.25\times0.1\times2.40\times10^{-12}\ {\mathrm{m^2}}/(1.26\times10^{5}\ {\mathrm{m^2}}\times10\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}\times0.914\ {\mathrm{sr}}\times1.28\times10^{-19}\ {\mathrm{J}})=0.171\ {\mathrm{W^{-1}}}]. The table turns this into the largest nominal footprint fraction that each laser power allows at 30 and at 259 photoelectrons per mode:

For 20 W, 0.171×20/30=11%0.171\times20/30=11\% at 30 photoelectrons and 0.171×20/259=1.3%0.171\times20/259=1.3\% at 259. Full coverage at 30 photoelectrons needs P=30/0.171=175P=30/0.171=175 W, the ≈175 W row, where 259 photoelectrons give 0.171×175/259=12%0.171\times175/259=12\%. The 175 W is the PcohP_{\mathrm{coh}} of Eq. (143) for nreq=30n_{\mathrm{req}}=30, as it must be, since both rest on the same cell-filling mode.

  • The 259-photoelectron column is the ideal single-look requirement, without design margin, for 90% detection under the report’s per-point rule: at most 10−310^{-3} false points per point over a 0–300 m search, with the echo’s peak found in both chirp ramps (§C0 subsection 10.3; §C10.2, item 5). A look is one independent speckle realization; with several looks the receiver sums returns whose speckle is uncorrelated, which reduces fading. The 30-photoelectron column is the §C7a four-look design value: 30 per look, a 1.36× margin over the ideal 22 per look (88.5 in total).
  • The table already contains the Gaussian model’s single-polarization and truncation factor t2/2=0.419t^2/2=0.419 (the round-trip truncation factor t2=0.838t^2=0.838 times the single-polarization factor ½) and uses the design efficiency η=0.25\eta=0.25. With the measured chain efficiency of 0.112 (§C0 subsection 10.1), K/PK/P falls to 0.077 photoelectrons per watt (0.171×0.112/0.250.171\times0.112/0.25), and 100 W then yields about 26% nominal footprint fraction at 30 photoelectrons (0.077×100/300.077\times100/30), not 57%.
  • A quoted efficiency that already includes polarization or truncation must not be reduced again.

In engineering terms: at 1–20 W, even the ideal bound lets a single-mode coherent lidar with this field and range cover only 0.6–11% of the scene with its nominal footprints at 30 photoelectrons per mode. Covering more needs more receive modes per sample (below), more power or a smaller field.

More modes per sample scale the budget. Receiving NmN_{\mathrm{m}} spatial modes per sample, each with its own coherent channel and summed incoherently (in intensity), gives

nΣ×ffp∼NmKn_\Sigma\times f_{\mathrm{fp}}\sim N_{\mathrm{m}}\,K(149)

where nΣ=Nmnmoden_\Sigma=N_{\mathrm{m}}\,n_{\mathrm{mode}} is the photoelectron count summed over the NmN_{\mathrm{m}} selected modes and KK is the single-mode budget constant of Eq. (147). Four modes at 30 photoelectrons each, as in the §C7a four-look design, therefore have the coverage bound of one mode at 30 (the 30-photoelectron column of the table above).

  • A ToF macro-pixel (a group of SPAD cells read out together as one pixel; SPAD is a single-photon avalanche diode) in this 0.05° example at 940 nm sums of order 420 spatial speckles per polarization in one intensity detector, i.e. Nm∼Nspk≈420N_{\mathrm{m}}\sim N_{\mathrm{spk}}\approx420, subject to its optical acceptance.
  • A coherent receiver needs extra optical modes, with matching mixing and digitization capacity, to capture that light in parallel. Multiplexed implementations can share hardware at a cost in time or bandwidth. NmN_{\mathrm{m}} independent modes can also supply speckle diversity if their returns are genuinely decorrelated.
  • Wavelength. Because K∝λ2/Eph∝λ3K\propto\lambda^2/E_{\mathrm{ph}}\propto\lambda^3 at fixed power in this ideal model (Eph=hc/λE_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda falls as 1/λ1/\lambda), 1550 nm gains a nominal 5.0× over 905 nm and 1.66× over 1310 nm ((1550/905)3=5.0(1550/905)^3=5.0, (1550/1310)3=1.66(1550/1310)^3=1.66). These ratios are not measured product advantages: material reflectance, detector efficiency, beam divergence, atmospheric transmission and permitted emission must be compared separately.

5. The mode–time budget: where the étendue limit bites.

Étendue is the product of a system’s collecting area and the solid angle over which it accepts light. Passive optics cannot shrink it without losing light, and one spatial mode occupies about λ2\lambda^2 of it. A mode–time slot is one spatial mode observed for one dwell (the time the receiver spends on one direction). Accepting a nominal fraction ffpf_{\mathrm{fp}} of a field ΩFOV\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}} through an aperture of area ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} within one frame involves of order ArxΩFOVffp/λ2A_{\mathrm{rx}}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}\,f_{\mathrm{fp}}/\lambda^2 spatial mode–time slots. This counts optical degrees of freedom accepted, not independently digitized image samples: a direct detector sums many accepted modes into one measurement, while a single-mode coherent channel selects one. The table compares, for each system, the mode–time slots needed for full nominal coverage of 120° × 25° at 10 Hz with the optical mode–time slots its channels and dwells supply per frame (optical modes × scan slots):

Coherent, scanned monostatic: 20 mm aperture, 128 channels × (0.1 s ÷ 12.67 µs dwell for 10 µs of integration) 1.2×10⁸ 1.0×10⁶ ≈0.8%
Same with 2 µs of integration (4.67 µs dwell) 1.2×10⁸ 2.7×10⁶ ≈2.3%

Closing the coherent gap costs either channels or photons:

  • Covering the whole field with the native 1/e² spots of a 20 mm aperture (a nominal footprint fraction of one, not the widened “area-matched” spot of §C10.3b) would need about 5,600–15,200 parallel channels by this mode count (1.2×1081.2\times10^{8} slots divided by 2.14×1042.14\times10^{4} or 7,8907{,}890 dwells per channel per frame, for 4.67 µs or 12.67 µs dwells, i.e. 2 µs or 10 µs of integration). The footprint count of §C10.3b gives about half that, ≈2,700–7,300: the 1.2×1061.2\times10^{6} cells, divided by the 2.1% footprint fraction of one sample at 200 m (§C10.3b, Result 2; 2.08% unrounded), need 1.2×106/0.0208=5.77×1071.2\times10^{6}/0.0208=5.77\times10^{7} samples per frame, and 5.77×107/2.14×104=2,7005.77\times10^{7}/2.14\times10^{4}=2{,}700 and 5.77×107/7,890=7,3005.77\times10^{7}/7{,}890=7{,}300 channels. The factor of two arises because one nominal footprint spans ≈2 hard-aperture modes at 200 m. It is also why the table’s ≈0.8% is half the 1.75% that §C10.3b’s per-sample footprint gives for the same 1.01×1061.01\times10^{6} samples per frame (2.08%×1.01×106/1.2×106=1.75%2.08\%\times1.01\times10^{6}/1.2\times10^{6}=1.75\%).
  • Alternatively, with 128 channels, a ≈2 mm aperture gives an area-matched spot at 200 m, but about 60× fewer usable photons per sample than the 20 mm collimated Gaussian case in §C10.3b. [E: 128 channels at a 12.67 µs dwell (10 µs of integration) give 1.01×1061.01\times10^{6} samples per frame, a 0.054° mesh (0.914sr/1.01×106=9.5×10−4\sqrt{0.914\ {\mathrm{sr}}/1.01\times10^{6}}=9.5\times10^{-4} rad, 19 cm at 200 m). With aperture diameter D=2D=2 mm, waist w0=0.9w_0=0.9 mm and Rayleigh range zR=πw02/λ=1.6z_R=\pi w_0^2/\lambda=1.6 m, the 1/e² radius at 200 m is w=11w=11 cm, slightly overfilling such a cell, whose area-matched radius is 19cm/π=10.719\ {\mathrm{cm}}/\sqrt{\pi}=10.7 cm. Then Eq. (41) of §C0 gives Amode=t2λ2R2/(2πw2)=1.07A_{\mathrm{mode}}=t^2\lambda^2R^2/(2\pi w^2)=1.07 mm², against 63.7 mm² for 20 mm, a ratio of 60.]
  • Neither area matching nor this channel count by itself guarantees an object-detection threshold at grid corners.

The étendue limit therefore acts in three places, called “bites” (a)–(c) below:

  • (a) Receive modes per unit time: single-mode coherent systems. A finite channel and dwell budget shows up as sparse nominal footprints (large aperture), fewer photons per mode (small aperture) or a narrower field. Adding simultaneous modes, power or time enlarges the budget, at a cost in hardware or latency.
  • (b) Steering space–bandwidth product: a challenge for wide-field non-mechanical systems. The space–bandwidth product is the number of distinct beam directions an aperture can resolve. The order ArxΩFOV/λ2A_{\mathrm{rx}}\,\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}/\lambda^2 counts these resolvable angular states at one wavelength and aperture. It is not a requirement for the same number of electrical controls: wavelength tuning, row–column addressing and time multiplexing can address states with fewer controls, each with its own bandwidth, loss and dwell costs (§C10.1).
    • A 20 mm mirror can address many angular states sequentially with one actuator; it does not observe them simultaneously.
    • Analog Photonics’ 8,192-element optical phased array (OPA; 8 × 5 mm aperture, 100° × 17°) must support about 8.6×10⁶ modes. It supplies about 3.6×10⁶ (8,192 phase controls × ≈440 wavelength-steered spots), the same order. [E: ArxΩFOV/λ2=40mm2×(100∘×17∘)(π/180)2/(1.55μm)2=4×10−5×0.518/2.40×10−12=8.6×106A_{\mathrm{rx}}\Omega_{\mathrm{FOV}}/\lambda^2=40\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}\times(100^\circ\times17^\circ)(\pi/180)^2/(1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}})^2=4\times10^{-5}\times0.518/2.40\times10^{-12}=8.6\times10^{6}, with ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} the OPA’s shared transmit–receive aperture; the ≈440 is the 17° wavelength-steered axis divided by the 0.039° grating-axis beamwidth, 17∘/0.039∘17^\circ/0.039^\circ (§C10.2b).]
    • Pointcloud’s 61,952-pixel focal-plane array (FPA, §C10.4) could fill its field only with a mode-equivalent collecting diameter of ≈0.9 mm behind its 50 mm lens. The one beam its authors measured, behind a 25 mm test lens focused at 11.1 m [P, Settembrini et al. 2026, Methods and Extended Data Fig. 2c], has a nominal 1/e² footprint fraction of ≈1% at that focus and ≈2% at 22 m on that lens’s 0.12° address grid, and hence a mode-equivalent collecting diameter of ≈5 mm and ≈3.5 mm. [E: the full-coverage bound is the identity Eq. (148), derived in item 4, with ffp≤1f_{\mathrm{fp}}\le1. For the 0.061° address pitch of the 50 mm lens, θcell=53μm/50mm=1.06×10−3\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}=53\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/50\ {\mathrm{mm}}=1.06\times10^{-3} rad, it gives Amode≲t22(λ/θcell)2=0.42×(1.31μm/1.06×10−3)2=0.64A_{\mathrm{mode}}\lesssim\tfrac{t^2}{2}(\lambda/\theta_{\mathrm{cell}})^2=0.42\times(1.31\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/1.06\times10^{-3})^2=0.64 mm², an equivalent diameter 2Amode/π=0.92\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{mode}}/\pi}=0.9 mm. On the 25 mm lens’s pitch, θcell=53μm/25mm=2.12×10−3\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}=53\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/25\ {\mathrm{mm}}=2.12\times10^{-3} rad, its footprint fraction ffp=πw2/(Rθcell)2f_{\mathrm{fp}}=\pi w^2/(R\theta_{\mathrm{cell}})^2 is 5.39mm2/(23.5mm)2=1.0%5.39\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}/(23.5\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2=1.0\% at 11.1 m and, with w=3.72w=3.72 mm, 43.5mm2/(46.6mm)2=2.0%43.5\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}/(46.6\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2=2.0\% at 22 m. (148) requires.]
    • These examples show why aperture, address density, field and loss must be evaluated together. They do not establish a universal aperture limit for all OPAs or FPAs.
  • (c) ToF detector étendue: staring arrays. A staring array (a 2D detector that views the whole field at once, without scanning) has a fixed étendue, about πAdetNA2\pi A_{\mathrm{det}}{\mathrm{NA}}^2 for detector area AdetA_{\mathrm{det}} and receive numerical aperture NA, which a wide field spreads over many directions. §C6 (“The physics behind it: receive étendue and silicon area”) quantifies the cost: IMX479’s 15.8 mm array at f/1.2 gets a ≈28.5 mm aperture as a 26° scanned column but only ≈3.8 mm staring over 120°, 1.8% of the collecting area and about 7.5× less range. A one-axis scanner avoids this by sharing a small detector across many time slots without adding controls; §C6 judges it the cheapest proven way to do so at current automotive volumes.

6. Specifics of scanned monostatic coherent systems.

Most coherent products scan mechanically, so this item asks what a moving mirror adds and what it costs.

  • Mechanical scanning supplies time slots, not modes. It removes bite (b), the steering space–bandwidth limit of item 5, and lets the aperture approach the confocal optimum. Each channel still receives one mode per dwell, so bite (a) remains.

  • Smear does not automatically improve reliable coverage. With a column of channels swept once per frame (an optical scan rate θ̇=120∘×10\dot\theta=120^\circ\times10 Hz, about 1,200°/s), a 12.67 µs dwell (10 µs of integration plus 2τ=2.672\tau=2.67 µs at 200 m, §C7b, Eq. (111)) moves the beam about 1,200∘/s×12.67μs=0.015∘1{,}200^\circ/{\mathrm{s}}\times12.67\ \mu{\mathrm{s}}=0.015^\circ: roughly four 1/e² beam radii of the 250 m confocal spot (0.015∘/0.0036∘=4.20.015^\circ/0.0036^\circ=4.2), or 2.1 full 1/e² widths (0.015∘/0.0072∘0.015^\circ/0.0072^\circ). The swept geometric footprint is larger, but coherent integration and speckle decorrelation depend on the chirp and processing, and only the 10 µs of useful windows is integrated. The enlarged trail cannot be counted at unchanged signal strength.

  • Scanner-induced Doppler. The same motion broadens the beat spectrum (the spectrum of the FMCW beat signal, whose peak gives the range) by Δfscan≈θ̇D/λ\Delta f_{\mathrm{scan}}\approx\dot\theta D/\lambda per pass (Eq. (94), §C7), where θ̇\dot\theta is the optical scan rate in rad/s (a scanning mirror itself turns at θ̇m=θ̇/2\dot\theta_{\mathrm{m}}=\dot\theta/2) and DD the beam diameter on the scanner. At 1,200°/s and a 20 mm beam this is 0.27 MHz (20.9rads−1×20mm/1.55μm20.9\ {\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}}\times20\ {\mathrm{mm}}/1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}), or ≈3 bins of a 10 µs chirp. The fast-Fourier-transform (FFT) bin width of a chirp of duration TcT_c is 1/Tc=1001/T_c=100 kHz for Tc=10T_c=10 µs. Spreading over ≈3 bins lowers the beat peak by roughly that factor (§C7).

  • Lag angle. During the round-trip delay τ=2R/c\tau=2R/c (with cc the speed of light) the scanner keeps turning, so the receive mode points away from the returning light by the walk-off of Eq. (144), Δθ≈2Rθ̇/c\Delta\theta\approx2R\dot\theta/c, where θ̇\dot\theta is the optical scan rate in rad/s and RR the range. The table shows how it grows with scan rate:

    Scan Rate θ̇\dot\theta Lag at 250 m Compared with the 0.0036° 1/e² half-angle
    Column sweep 1,200°/s ≈0.002° About half the half-angle; noticeable loss
    360° spin at 10 Hz 3,600°/s ≈0.006° 1.7× the half-angle; most of the signal lost

    How the numbers are derived [E]: Δθ=2Rθ̇/c\Delta\theta=2R\dot\theta/c with θ̇\dot\theta in rad/s. For the column sweep, θ̇=1,200∘/s=20.9\dot\theta=1{,}200^\circ/{\mathrm{s}}=20.9 rad/s and Δθ=2×250m×20.9s−1/(3×108ms−1)=3.5×10−5\Delta\theta=2\times250\ {\mathrm{m}}\times20.9\ {\mathrm{s^{-1}}}/(3\times10^{8}\ {\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}})=3.5\times10^{-5} rad =0.0020∘=0.0020^\circ, about 0.56 of the 0.0036° 1/e² half-angle of the 250 m confocal spot (item 3). The 360° spin is three times faster, 0.006°, or 1.7 half-angles. §C10.3 compares the same lag with the 0.0028° far-field half-angle of a w0=10w_0=10 mm beam instead.

    ToF’s 0.05° pixel field of view is about 25× the walk-off (0.05∘/0.002∘0.05^\circ/0.002^\circ), so ToF is insensitive to it. For coherent designs, lag caps the scan speed at long range; the extra lag-angle receive waveguides in Aeva’s patent are, in effect, extra modes and channels.

7. Effective aperture in practice.

The efficiency-weighted aperture is the collecting area (the hard area for direct detection, AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} for a coherent receiver) multiplied by the efficiency η\eta of §C10.3 (optics × detector, × mixing for a coherent receiver, and for SPAD ToF also the bright-sun live fraction). It is the area of a lossless, perfectly efficient detector that would yield the same signal photoelectrons. On the report’s efficiencies, 0.164 for ToF and 0.25 for coherent, a 25 mm scanned ToF receiver keeps about 4–11× the efficiency-weighted aperture of one mirror-scanned FMCW receiver at 100–300 m. The four receivers per point of §C7a narrow the gap to about 1.3× at 200 m.

In the table, PDE is the SPAD’s photon detection efficiency, f/1.0–1.4 are lens f-numbers (focal length over aperture diameter), and “flash” ToF lights and images the whole field at once.

Long-range scanned ToF ≈15–30 mm Module height (25–30 mm behind glass), f/1.0–1.4 lens ≈80 mm² for 25 mm (η=0.5×0.37×0.885=0.164\eta=0.5\times0.37\times0.885=0.164: optics × PDE × bright-sun live fraction)
Mirror-scanned monostatic FMCW ≈10–25 mm Confocal optimum (Dopt=λR/π/0.45D_{\mathrm{opt}}=\sqrt{\lambda R/\pi}/0.45, §C0 Eq. (43): ≈16 mm at 100 m, ≈25 mm at 250 m) ≈7–21 mm² per receiver for 20 mm at 100–300 m: §C10.3b’s mode-equivalent areas, which include its near-field, polarization and mode-shape losses, times η=0.25\eta=0.25; a far-field-only estimate of ≈27 mm² is optimistic
OPA or FPA coherent chip ≈1–8 mm Element or pixel count (bite b) ≈4 mm² (8 mm) down to ≈0.07 mm² (1 mm) before on-chip loss, and 4–100× less after 3–10 dB of it each way
Solid-state flash ToF ≈3–5 mm Staring étendue (bite c) ≈1–3 mm²

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Long-range ToF: π(12.5mm)2×0.164=491×0.164=80\pi(12.5\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2\times0.164=491\times0.164=80 mm². In a fully sunlit scene the live fraction falls to 0.784, and the area to 491×0.5×0.37×0.784=71491\times0.5\times0.37\times0.784=71 mm².
  • Mirror-scanned FMCW, per receiver: the mode-equivalent areas of §C10.3b, Result 2 (28.8, 63.7 and 82.0 mm² at 100, 200 and 300 m), times η=0.25\eta=0.25 (optics × detector × mixing; polarization and mode shape are already in AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}}): 28.8×0.25=7.228.8\times0.25=7.2 mm² at 100 m, 15.9 mm² at 200 m and 20.5 mm² at 300 m. ToF’s 80 mm² is 80/20.5=3.980/20.5=3.9 to 80/7.2=1180/7.2=11 times larger; the four receivers per point of §C7a collect 4×15.9≈644\times15.9\approx64 mm² at 200 m, 80/64≈1.380/64\approx1.3 times less than ToF. The far-field-only figure takes the far-field limit of item 2, Amode→t2πw02/2=0.838×π(9mm)2/2=107A_{\mathrm{mode}}\to t^2\pi w_0^2/2=0.838\times\pi(9\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2/2=107 mm² (the hard area divided by 2.9), times the same η\eta: 107×0.25=27107\times0.25=27 mm².
  • OPA or FPA chip: the far-field AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} of the hard aperture (its area divided by 2.9, item 2) times η=0.25\eta=0.25, before on-chip loss: π(8mm)2/4/2.9×0.25=4.3\pi(8\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2/4/2.9\times0.25=4.3 mm² for 8 mm and 0.785mm2/2.9×0.25=0.070.785\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}/2.9\times0.25=0.07 mm² for 1 mm. An on-chip loss of 3–10 dB each way multiplies these by 10−0.6=0.2510^{-0.6}=0.25 to 10−2=0.0110^{-2}=0.01.

IMX479 staring over 120° gets a ≈3.8 mm aperture, 1.8% of the 28.5 mm scanned column’s area (item 5, bite (c)), i.e. π(1.9mm)2×0.164=1.9\pi(1.9\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2\times0.164=1.9 mm².

Caveats that move the comparison:

  • Speckle and polarization favour ToF. Single-mode detection fades (exponential single-speckle statistics). Under the report’s detection rule it needs ≈88 photoelectrons with four looks and ≈259 with one for reliable detection, against ≈5 counts for SPAD ToF at night and ≈15 in bright sun (§C0 subsection 10.3). Piggott et al. (Waymo) put coherent detection about 6 dB behind ToF at long range: 3 dB for the single polarization and ≈3 dB because their 30 mm ToF lens, sized not to clip the coherent beam’s Gaussian wings (w0=10w_0=10 mm), has (15/10)2=2.25(15/10)^2=2.25 times the coherent mode’s far-field collecting area πw02\pi w_0^2 before polarization [P, §2.5, Fig. 5(a)]. The far-field factor of item 2 in this model is 2.9×, or 4.7 dB, because its Gaussian fills the hard aperture more fully (w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D, an aperture radius of 1.11w01.11w_0 against 1.5w01.5w_0) and pays 1.47× (1.7 dB) for mode shape and truncation instead of 2.25× (3.5 dB); the polarization factor is the same [E].

  • Sunlight can favour coherent detection. For SPAD ToF, bright sun costs mainly dead time and pile-up rather than per-bin signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) (§C6(d)): after each detection a SPAD is blind for a dead time, so background light both hides returns and biases the timing. In a fully sunlit scene of reflectance 0.9 this cuts the effective PDE by about a sixth at 940 nm behind a 10 nm filter, and by about a half to three-quarters at 905 nm behind 20–40 nm filters (§C6(d): at PDE 0.3 and the 0.05° × 0.05° macro-pixel, Eq. (90) with rτd=2.97×108/9×6ns=0.20r\tau_d=2.97\times10^{8}/9\times6\ {\mathrm{ns}}=0.20 gives a dead fraction of 16.5–18% at 940 nm, and 42–77% at 905 nm; §C7a’s central case uses a live fraction of 0.885), and a larger aperture collects proportionally more background. Only for a purely background-limited detector, with fixed angular acceptance and integration time, does SNR scale as Arx\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{rx}}}. A narrowband LO receiver strongly rejects broadband sunlight (about 10310^3 photons/s in one mode, §C6(d′)), though it is not literally background-free; its aperture scaling still depends on beam propagation, mode overlap and noise regime.

  • Finer resolution needs a larger ToF aperture than a module can hold. At fixed f-number F#F_\#, D=ppx/(θcellF#)D=p_{\mathrm{px}}/(\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}F_\#), where DD is the aperture diameter, ppxp_{\mathrm{px}} the macro-pixel size and θcell\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} the pixel angle (the focal length is f=ppx/θcellf=p_{\mathrm{px}}/\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} and D=f/F#D=f/F_\#). With 30 µm macro-pixels at f/1.2, for example, 0.05° (8.73×10−48.73\times10^{-4} rad) gives D=30μm/(8.73×10−4×1.2)=29D=30\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}/(8.73\times10^{-4}\times1.2)=29 mm:

    Pixel angle Usable aperture
    0.1° ≈14 mm
    0.05° ≈29 mm
    0.025° ≈57 mm, which does not fit a behind-glass module

    Smaller pixels or smaller apertures follow (§C6). This is how the resolution race quietly erodes ToF’s photon advantage.

  • Non-Lambertian targets break the picture. Retroreflectors return strongly regardless of aperture, and largely preserve polarization; wet or glossy surfaces at grazing angles return little; targets smaller than the spot produce fewer, larger speckles.

8. Summary.

  • Every lidar has an étendue budget: modes observed per unit time.
  • Direct-detection pixels can sum many spatial modes. One coherent mixer selects one mode per polarization; arrays or multiplexing can add more.
  • Scanning supplies successive time slots but is limited by dwell, motion and scan lag. A non-mechanical steerer has a finite optical space–bandwidth product, but its electrical control count need not equal its number of resolvable angular states.
  • At a specified optical power, detection threshold and channel budget, wide field, long range and dense nominal footprint coverage compete in the single-mode architecture.
  • The footprint fractions in this subsection (0.8–8% for item 3’s confocal spots, 0.6–11% for item 4’s bounds at 1–20 W and ≈0.8–2.3% for item 5’s channel budgets), and the box or FWHM values of 0.5–4% for the designs in §C10.3 (1.6–8% at 1/e²), are inferred nominal footprint fractions for particular design examples (item 3), not measured coverage or detection probabilities.
  • For dense “camera-like” coverage, the lever is not better steering but cheap, dense coherent receive channels: a coherent counterpart of the SPAD-SoC (a SPAD array and its timing and processing electronics on one system-on-chip), with per-pixel mixing and low-power digitization. Pointcloud-type coherent pixel arrays point in that direction.

C10.3b Numerical check: mode counts, usable aperture and the sampling mesh at the target

This subsection gives the explicit numerical model [E] whose results §C10.3a quotes, and checks the order-of-magnitude scalings there. It pins down two numbers: a matched 20 mm monostatic aperture still sees 3–6 speckles at 100–200 m, and an area-matched coherent sample at 0.05° keeps only 1.3 mm² of mode-equivalent collecting area. These two numbers fix how many photons a coherent lidar gets per sample, and therefore how sparsely it must sample at a given power. The model uses the assumptions listed at the start of §C10.3a: a Lambertian, depolarizing target; fully developed speckle; ideal, perfectly matched TEM00 beams; no turbulence.

What was computed.

  • Code and outputs. The code is build/figures/coherent_mode_coverage.py, stored with the report; its printed tables are in coherent_mode_coverage_tables.txt.
  • Coherent model: a monostatic (shared transmit–receive aperture), single-mode, single-polarization Gaussian beam at 1550 nm.
    • The waist (1/e² intensity radius at the aperture) is w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D inside a hard aperture of diameter DD; the ratio 0.45 is the far-field optimum derived in §C0 subsection 10.2. The truncation efficiency is t=0.915t=0.915 each way: tt is the one-way power transmission of a Gaussian with w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D through the aperture.
    • The beam is collimated (waist at the aperture, not focused on any one range), so the design is range-agnostic.
    • Full Gaussian propagation, including the near field, gives the spot at the target: the 1/e² radius is w(R)=w01+(R/zR)2w(R)=w_0\sqrt{1+(R/z_R)^2} (§C0 Eq. (42)), with Rayleigh range zR=πw02/λz_R=\pi w_0^2/\lambda.
    • Received power follows Piggott et al.’s monostatic link equation, written as a mode-equivalent collecting area AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} (Eq. (41) of §C0, quoted below). It differs from Piggott et al.’s Abeam=πw(R)2A_{\mathrm{beam}}=\pi w(R)^2, which is an effective beam area at the target. The code calls AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} a_coh.
  • ToF model: a hard 25 mm aperture at 940 nm, the wavelength of the SPAD model of §C0 subsection 10 and §C7a, with a polarization-insensitive multimode pixel whose field of view equals one mesh cell.
  • Mode counts: Goodman’s integrated-speckle formula for the degrees of freedom of speckle integrated over a uniformly weighted aperture [I, J. W. Goodman, Speckle Phenomena in Optics, 2007, §4.6.1], Nspk=Arx2/∫Kap(Δ)|μ(Δ)|2d2ΔN_{\mathrm{spk}}=A_{\mathrm{rx}}^2\big/\!\int K_{\mathrm{ap}}(\Delta)\,|\mu(\Delta)|^2\,d^2\Delta, where ArxA_{\mathrm{rx}} is the aperture area and Δ\Delta a separation vector between two points in the aperture plane.
    • Kap(Δ)K_{\mathrm{ap}}(\Delta) is the aperture autocorrelation: the overlap area between the aperture and a copy of itself shifted by Δ\Delta.
    • μ(Δ)\mu(\Delta) is the complex coherence factor of the returned light between two points separated by Δ\Delta. |μ|2|\mu|^2 comes from the van Cittert–Zernike theorem: Gaussian for a Gaussian spot, sinc2×sinc2\mathrm{sinc}^2\times\mathrm{sinc}^2 for a uniformly lit square cell, with sincx=sin⁡(πx)/(πx)\mathrm{sinc}\,x=\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x).
  • Target: diffuse, depolarizing and extended; powers are speckle-averaged.

The mode-equivalent collecting area. AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} is the area of an ideal direct-detection lens that would collect, from the same Lambertian target, the same signal power as the coherent receiver collects in its single LO mode. In this model it is Eq. (41) of §C0 subsection 10.2, Amode(R)=t2λ2R2/[2πw(R)2]A_{\mathrm{mode}}(R)=t^2\lambda^2R^2/[2\pi\,w(R)^2], where tt is the one-way truncation efficiency (t2t^2 for transmit and receive), λ\lambda the wavelength, RR the range and w(R)w(R) the beam’s 1/e² radius at the target. The factor ½ (the 2 in the denominator) is the selected polarization of a depolarizing target. Physically, a single-mode receiver collects the target’s radiance times λ2\lambda^2 (the antenna theorem, stated with its source in §C0 subsection 10.2, Siegman 1966). A smaller spot at the target means higher radiance, so AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} grows as w(R)w(R) shrinks. AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} is not a physical area: it depends on range and beam, and is usually much smaller than the lens.

How the numbers are derived [E]: the simple column is ArxΩ/λ2A_{\mathrm{rx}}\Omega/\lambda^2. For a ToF pixel or a widened coherent spot, Ω=θcell2\Omega=\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}^2 is the solid angle of one cell, with θcell\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} the cell angle in radians, e.g. 491mm2×(8.73×10−4)2/(0.940μm)2=423491\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}\times(8.73\times10^{-4})^2/(0.940\ \mu{\mathrm{m}})^2=423 at 0.05° and 314mm2×(8.73×10−4)2/(1.55μm)2=100314\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}\times(8.73\times10^{-4})^2/(1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}})^2=100 for the 20 mm coherent aperture. For the matched spot, Ω=πw2/R2\Omega=\pi w^2/R^2 is the solid angle of its 1/e² area, e.g. 314mm2×π(14.2mm)2/(1.55μm×200m)2=2.1314\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}\times\pi(14.2\ {\mathrm{mm}})^2/(1.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}\times200\ {\mathrm{m}})^2=2.1 at 200 m. The numerical column evaluates Goodman’s integral over the aperture autocorrelation in coherent_mode_coverage.py; it has no closed form. It is never below the simple count and tends to one, not zero, when the aperture spans less than one coherence area, which is why the matched-spot counts exceed the simple ones most.

  • A ToF pixel integrates hundreds of speckles, but the count falls as the square of the pixel angle. The resolution race cuts ToF’s mode count from about 1,750 to about 120, still far above one.
  • A coherent receiver facing a cell-filling spot sees about 100 speckles and can use only one.
  • Even the matched monostatic case sees a few speckles across a 20 mm hard aperture at 100–200 m. At 100 m the 20 mm aperture is larger than the confocal optimum (≈16 mm), so the target sits in the beam’s near field. At 200 m it is close to the optimum (≈22 mm), yet the hard aperture still spans about two coherence areas of the speckle, Arxπw2/(λR)2=314mm2/152mm2≈2.1A_{\mathrm{rx}}\pi w^2/(\lambda R)^2=314\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}/152\ {\mathrm{mm^2}}\approx2.1, because the Gaussian launched with w0=0.45Dw_0=0.45D does not fill it. The simple expectation Nspk≈1N_{\mathrm{spk}}\approx1 is therefore too optimistic even at the optimum.

For comparison, the modelled 25 mm ToF aperture has 491 mm² hard area, and its pixels’ response fields tile the grid, before optical and PDE losses.

Reading Result 2 [E]:

  • Each coherent sample is a nominal 1/e² spot 2–4 cm across on a 4–26 cm grid (2.8 cm spots on a 17.5 cm pitch at 200 m), a nominal 1/e² footprint fraction of about 1.6–15% (nominal in the sense of §C10.3a, item 3).

  • The monostatic receiver keeps about 1/4 to 1/11 of what lands on the 20 mm lens at 100–300 m. §C10.3a, item 2, breaks down the loss; in the far field it falls to about 3×.

    • For an ideal collimated Gaussian optimized separately for one specified range, the mode-equivalent-area ceiling is λR/4\lambda R/4: 39, 78 and 116 mm² at 100, 200 and 300 m before truncation (i.e. without the factor t2t^2). At the confocal waist w(R)2=2λR/πw(R)^2=2\lambda R/\pi, so λ2R2/(2πw2)=λR/4\lambda^2R^2/(2\pi w^2)=\lambda R/4, e.g. 1.55μm×200m/4=781.55\ \mu{\mathrm{m}}\times200\ {\mathrm{m}}/4=78 mm².
    • Enlarging the lens alone cannot beat that collimated-Gaussian result at the selected range. Focusing or other beam designs change the assumptions and may trade performance at other ranges.

  • Matching the nominal Gaussian 1/e² spot area to one square grid cell shrinks the mode-equivalent collecting area to an equivalent diameter of about 1.3 mm, whatever the physical lens. That is 238× (23.8 dB) below the 20 mm hard-aperture area (314/1.32=238314/1.32=238 and 10log⁡10238=23.810\log_{10}238=23.8 dB), and in this model it is range-independent. Equal spot and cell areas do not guarantee gap-free 1/e²-contour coverage: at a square cell corner the Gaussian intensity is only e−π≃4.3%e^{-\pi}\simeq4.3\% of its peak. A stricter corner-intensity or detection requirement costs more power or more samples.

  • Photons and coverage trade one for one. By the identity of Eq. (148) (§C10.3a, item 4), Amodeffp=t22(λ/θcell)2A_{\mathrm{mode}}f_{\mathrm{fp}}=\tfrac{t^2}{2}(\lambda/\theta_{\mathrm{cell}})^2, a design can buy collecting area only by giving up footprint fraction; only the mesh pitch (and the wavelength) moves the product:

    Mesh pitch AmodeffpA_{\mathrm{mode}}\,f_{\mathrm{fp}}
    0.1° 0.33 mm²
    0.05° 1.3 mm²
    0.025° 5.3 mm²

How the numbers are derived [E]:

  • Centre in object: with the grid offset uniform over one pitch p=Rθcellp=R\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} in each axis (pp is the mesh pitch at the target, WW and HH the object’s width and height), the probability is min⁡(1,W/p)min⁡(1,H/p)\min(1,W/p)\min(1,H/p); for 10 × 10 cm at 200 m, (10/17.45)2=0.33(10/17.45)^2=0.33.

  • 1/e² circle touches the object: the centre must land inside the object dilated (grown on all sides) by the spot’s 1/e² radius ww, of area WH+2w(W+H)+πw2WH+2w(W+H)+\pi w^2 when no dilated side exceeds the pitch. For 10 × 10 cm at 200 m (w=1.42w=1.42 cm): (100+56.7+6.3)cm2/305cm2=0.54(100+56.7+6.3)\ {\mathrm{cm^2}}/305\ {\mathrm{cm^2}}=0.54. Where a dilated side exceeds the pitch (20 × 15 cm at 250 m), the code caps it at one pitch.

  • The two coherent columns are binary geometry tests: whether a beam centre lands inside the object, and whether the drawn 1/e² circle touches it. Actual Gaussian overlap, coherent speckle, object reflectance and detection threshold give graded received signals, so these fractions are not detection probabilities.

  • A gap-free ToF pixel grid always overlaps the object somewhere. The tabulated value is the maximum fill fraction of a single pixel under the simplified square-response model; it does not predict that pixel’s range detection or SNR.

  • For a sub-pitch rectangular object, the centre-in-object fraction equals the object’s area divided by the cell area. If the object fits wholly within one cell, that also equals its maximum one-pixel fill fraction. The numerical equality illustrates sampling versus integration; it does not equate detection performance.

What the numerical model shows.

  • A mirror-scanned coherent receiver’s efficiency-weighted aperture is about 7–21 mm² at 100–300 m (Result 2’s AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} times η=0.25\eta=0.25), not the ≈27 mm² of the far-field formula alone (both are worked in §C10.3a, item 7). A 25 mm ToF unit’s ≈80 mm² is about 4–11× larger (80/20.5=3.980/20.5=3.9 to 80/7.2=1180/7.2=11), and the four receivers per point of §C7a narrow this to 1.3× at 200 m. ToF’s η=0.164\eta=0.164 already contains the bright-sun live fraction (≈71 mm² in a fully sunlit scene); sunlight’s other cost, a higher detection threshold, sits in the photon requirement (§C10.3a, item 7, caveats).
  • With truncation and single polarization included, the area-matched coherent mode-equivalent collecting area at 0.05° is 1.3 mm². It is 1.6 mm² without the truncation factor t2=0.84t^2=0.84, and 3.2 mm² without the single-polarization factor ½ as well; that last value is the ideal λ2/Ωcell\lambda^2/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}, where Ωcell=θcell2\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}=\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}^2 is the solid angle of one mesh cell. The cell-filling estimates of §C10.2, item 5 and §C10.3 use the 1.3 mm². Gap-free detection at a stated threshold needs a separate target-overlap and noise calculation.

C10.4 Focal-plane arrays: switched and coherent

A focal-plane array (FPA) steers a lidar beam by switching between antennas placed in the focal plane of a lens, instead of phasing many emitters as an optical phased array (OPA) does. This subsection asks whether that makes it a better route to high-resolution solid-state coherent lidar. The answer is partly yes: an FPA avoids OPA phase calibration and takes its aperture from passive glass. It keeps the single-mode photon budget of §C10.3a, however, and needs one cell per look direction, so chip area and channel count become its main costs.

Principle. An FPA places a grid of on-chip antennas in the focal plane of a lens, and the lens supplies the aperture. Selecting a pixel selects a look direction ϕ=x/f\phi=x/f, where xx is the pixel’s distance from the lens axis and ff the focal length.

  • Address spacing and beam width are set separately:
    • the address spacing (the address pitch) is θcell=p/f\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}=p/f, the angle between neighbouring pixels at pixel pitch pp;
    • the beam width is θB∼λ/D\theta_{\mathrm{B}}\sim\lambda/D, where λ\lambda is the wavelength, D≈2NAefD\approx2NA_ef the filled lens aperture and NAeNA_e the emitter numerical aperture (the sine of the half-angle of each on-chip antenna’s emission cone).
    • Both are decoupled from element count per beam, and there are no phase shifters to calibrate. The two can differ greatly: Berkeley’s 0.05° beams sit on a 0.6° address grid.
  • Each single-mode pixel obeys the same mode-area–footprint identity as an OPA, Eq. (148) of §C10.3a: Amodeffp≃t22(λ/θcell)2A_{\mathrm{mode}}f_{\mathrm{fp}}\simeq\tfrac{t^2}{2}(\lambda/\theta_{\mathrm{cell}})^2. Here AmodeA_{\mathrm{mode}} is the mode-equivalent collecting area (the area of an ideal direct-detection lens that would collect the same signal as the pixel’s single mode), ffpf_{\mathrm{fp}} the nominal footprint fraction (the share of each address cell covered by the beam’s 1/e² spot), t=0.915t=0.915 the Gaussian truncation factor and θcell\theta_{\mathrm{cell}} the address pitch. For a cell-filling footprint (ffp=1f_{\mathrm{fp}}=1) this gives Amode=t22λ2/ΩcellA_{\mathrm{mode}}=\tfrac{t^2}{2}\lambda^2/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}, where Ωcell=θcell2\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}}=\theta_{\mathrm{cell}}^2 is the solid angle of one address cell; the ideal λ2/Ωcell\lambda^2/\Omega_{\mathrm{cell}} omits truncation and polarization. The difference from an OPA is that the glass supplies the aperture passively.

Published designs. The table lists the published coherent FPA designs with their pixel count and pitch, addressing scheme, beam width against address spacing, demonstrated result and main limit. In the table, FPSA is Berkeley’s focal-plane switch array; MEMS means microelectromechanical switches; row–column addressing selects a pixel by driving one row line and one column line; FWHM is the full width at half maximum; DFB is a distributed-feedback laser; GF 45SPCLO is GlobalFoundries’ monolithic silicon-photonics process; and an ASIC is an application-specific integrated circuit.
